en: The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree during the Great Tang Dynasty.
The initial summary verse says:
Permission to use various medicines, Ointments and oils for treating scabies,
Eye salves and [remedies for] wind-epilepsy, And the case of Pilindavatsa, etc.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣus fell ill during the autumn; their bodies were jaundiced, emaciated, haggard, and they were afflicted by suffering and lacked strength.
Having seen this, the Blessed One, knowing the reason, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"For what reason are the bodies of these bhikṣus so pale and yellowish, emaciated, and lacking strength?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
Since the autumn season has set in, the bhikṣus have become afflicted by various illnesses; their bodies are withered and pale, emaciated and lacking strength."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Because of this suffering from illness, I now permit the bhikṣus to consume various medicinal compounds.

Thus, once the World-Honored One had permitted the consumption of medicine, the bhikṣus consequently took it only at the proper time and not at improper times; their bodies remained frail, emaciated, and lacking strength.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the reason] yet asking deliberately, said to Ānanda:
"I have already permitted the bhikṣus to consume various medicines; yet why is this bhikṣu still so emaciated?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, although you have permitted the bhikṣus to consume various medicines, these bhikṣus all take them only at the proper time and do not take them at improper times; for this reason, their bodies are withered and yellow, emaciated and lacking strength.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"I now authorize four kinds of medicine for the bhikṣus:
first, medicine for the proper time (kālabhaiṣajya);..."
2. Medicines for a day and night;
3. Medicines for seven days;
4. Medicines for as long as life lasts.
Regarding "timely medicines":
first, parched grain flour;
second, cakes.
3. Wheat and bean cakes; 4. Meat; 5. Rice.
These are all medicines to be consumed during the proper time; therefore, they are called "timely medicines" (*kālabhaiṣajya*).
As for what are called "subsequent medicines," they refer to the eight kinds of syrups. What are the eight?
1. *Zhao* (招) juice: A fruit from a tree in the Western Regions, also called *diàntǔlí*.

Its pods resemble those of the *zàojiè* (soapberry), and its flavor is like that of the plum. The pods are about one or two fingers wide and three or four inches long; people of the time ate them regularly. 2. *Mao* (毛) juice:
This is the fruit of the plantain (*bājiāo*). Place a small amount of ground black pepper on top of the fruit and rub it vigorously with the hands until it all turns into water.
Third, the kola-juice has the appearance of sour jujube; its flavor is of a single kind, for these jujubes alone are without sweetness.
Fourth, the aśvattha fruit;
fifth, the udumbara, whose fruit is as large as a plum.
Sixth, the *pārūṣaka* fruit resembles the *yǐwù* (blackberry) in shape and its flavor is similar;
seventh, the *mṛdvīkā* juice is the grape fruit;
eighth, the *kharjūra* juice is shaped like a small jujube, sweet yet astringent; its trees mostly grow independently, resembling the form of a *tāla* palm.
"All these various syrups must have the hands washed clean and be filtered thoroughly before they are fit for drinking.
A summary verse within states:
Coconut, plantain, and jujube, Aśvattha fruit, and udumbara.
Raisin, grape, and *kṣudraka*—these are known as the eight kinds of syrups that should be recognized.
"Seven-day medicines" are:
ghee, oil, molasses, honey, and rock sugar.
“Medicines for the duration of one’s life consist of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of resinous medicines, five kinds of ash medicines, five kinds of salt medicines, and five kinds of astringent medicines.”
"What are root medicines?
They are nut-grass, sweet flag, turmeric, fresh ginger, and white aconite.
If there are other substances of this same category that are fit to serve as medicine, they may be used as one sees fit."
"Regarding stem-medicines: sandalwood incense, *kālānusāri*, *devadāru*, *amaravalli*, and *śiṃśapā*; or other substances of a similar category, should be used according to the preceding principle."
"Regarding leaf medicines, there are three types of leaves:

namely, *aśvakarṇa* (which does not exist in this region), *piṇḍītaka* (the *nimbū* tree, which is the *karañja* tree), and *khaśārkī* (which does not exist in this region), as well as other similar varieties; these should be used according to the preceding rules."

"Flower medicines refer to *vāsaka* flowers, *nimba* flowers, *tagara* flowers, *nāgapuṣpa* flowers, and lotus flowers; there are other such varieties as well, which should be used according to their specific requirements."

"Regarding fruits used as medicine: these refer to harītakī fruit, āmalaka fruit, vibhītaka fruit, black pepper, and long pepper; if there are other similar types, they should be used according to the preceding rules."
"The five kinds of adhesive medicines are as follows: asafoetida, lac, red resin, yellow wax, and guggulu.
As for the medicine asafoetida, it refers to the resin that exudes from the *hiṅgu* tree."
"Black resin" refers to the exudate produced by the *sāla* tree.
"Lac" refers to the sap that exudes from the branches of trees.
"Yellow wax" refers to the residue remaining after honey has been extracted.
"Anusitaka incense is tree resin.
'The five kinds of ash' refers to the ash of *kangu* grain, the ash of sesame, the ash of *kangu* flour, the ash of *goji* grass, and the ash of *vatsa* tree leaves."
"The five kinds of salt are: black salt, red salt, white rock salt, *bījaja* salt, and sea salt.
What are the five kinds of astringent medicines?"
These are the *amra* tree, the *tinduka* tree, the *jambū* tree, the *śirīṣa* tree, and the *kovidāra* tree.
"Among these, 'timely medicine' (*kālabhojana*) refers to that which is consumed during the [proper] time."

If medicinal substances for further use, seven-day medicines, or lifetime medicines are mixed with medicines for the proper time (*kālabhojana*), they should be consumed during the proper time and must not be consumed outside of the proper time.

If *yāmika* (time-limited) medicine, *saptāhika* (seven-day) medicine, or *yāvajjīvika* (lifetime) medicine are mixed with *yāmika* medicine, they may be consumed until the end of the first watch of the night; beyond this, they should not be consumed.
If a seven-day medicine is mixed with a lifetime medicine, it should be consumed for seven days;
if the seven days have passed, it should not be consumed.
If it is a lifetime medicine, it should be kept and consumed for as long as one lives.
However, these four medicines may be mixed together and taken according to whichever is most potent.
If one is not ill or if the illness has been cured, one should not take them; otherwise, they should be given to fellow practitioners of the holy life.
One should maintain it in this manner:
first, having washed one's hands and received the medicine, one should squat before a single bhikṣu, hold the medicine, and speak these words:
"Venerable one, please attend to me!"
"I, the bhikṣu [name], having this occasion of illness, now formally accept for my own use this medicine for life, for the purpose of consumption.
This should be recited three times, including for fellow practitioners of the holy life.
"If it concerns seven-day medicines or medicinal tonics, they should be formally accepted in accordance with this.
The occasion was at Śrāvastī.
A certain bhikṣu suffered from a wind-disorder (vāta-roga) and went to a physician, asking:
“O Wise One! I am afflicted by a wind-disorder; please prescribe a remedy for me.
Then that physician replied:
"Noble one!
You should consume the fat of a sentient being, and your illness will surely be cured.
The bhikṣu replied:
“O noble one! How could it be appropriate for me to eat this fat now?
The physician replied:
“There is only this medicine; nothing else can cure it.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One. The Buddha said:
“If a bhikṣu is ill and a physician says that only this is the medicine and nothing else can cure him, he should consume fat.”
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know what kind of fat to consume, so they questioned the physician again.
The physician replied, "Since your teacher is an omniscient one, you should go and consult him; he will surely know."
Then the bhikṣus went at once to question the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"There are five kinds of fat:
first, fish fat; second, river otter fat; third, shark fat; fourth, bear fat; and fifth, pig fat."
These five kinds of fats, if boiled at an improper time, strained at an improper time, received at an improper time, or kept in reserve at an improper time, should not be consumed.
If boiled at the proper time, but strained at an improper time, received at an improper time, or kept in reserve at an improper time, they should not be consumed.
If it was boiled at the proper time and filtered at the proper time, but received at an improper time and kept until an improper time, it should not be consumed.
If it was boiled at the proper time and filtered at the proper time, and received at the proper time, but kept until an improper time, it should not be consumed.
It should be consumed when boiled, when strained, when received, and when formally maintained.
Following the method for consuming oil, it should be taken for seven days; after the seventh day, it should not be consumed.
That sick bhikṣu, having taken the fat because of this, was subsequently cured of his illness.
Once he had recovered, he discarded the remaining medicine altogether.
At that time, there was another bhikṣu who also suffered from a wind-disorder (vāta-roga); he went to a physician and asked:
“O virtuous one!
I am afflicted by a wind-disorder; please prescribe a remedy for me.
The physician replied:
"You should take medicated fat.
There is already a bhikṣu who recovered by taking fat; you should go and seek him out.
Thereupon, that bhikṣu went to where the bhikṣu who had taken the medicine was and asked:
“Venerable one!
You previously took this fat and were cured of your wind ailment; the physician instructed me to take this same fat as well.
You have some remaining fat; please bestow it upon me.”
The bhikṣu said,
"I have already discarded all the remaining fat.
He replied:
"You have acted improperly; this was not what you should have done.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"One who has used medicinal fat should not discard it entirely, but must collect and store it.
I shall now explain the method for its collection and storage:
if a bhikṣu has used some medicinal fat and another bhikṣu comes to request it, he should give it to that person immediately."
If there is no one who requests it, one should send it to an infirmary, where they will store it well.
If anyone requires it, they may take it from that place, maintain it according to the rules, and consume it.
"One who does not follow this instruction shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The setting and circumstances are as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu suffering from a skin disease of scabies; he went to a physician and asked:
“O worthy one! I am afflicted with a scabies rash; please prescribe a remedy for me.
The physician replied:
“Noble one!
You should take astringent medicine, and your illness will surely be cured.
The bhikṣu replied:
“O noble one! Am I truly a person addicted to sensual desires?
The physician replied:
"This astringent medicine can cure scabies and sores; other medicines will not effect a cure.
The bhikṣu asked, "What kind of astringent medicine should I take?"
The physician replied, “Noble one!
Your teacher is omniscient; he fully knows this matter.”
The bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One, and the Buddha said:
"There are five kinds of astringent medicines:
first, āmra; second, nimba; third, jambu; fourth, nyagrodha; and fifth, kuśāmra."
"O Bhikṣus, you should know that these various medicinal substances—whether bark or leaves—should all be pounded and boiled in water to be applied to the body.
After they had applied it, sores broke out on their bodies again. The Buddha told the Bhikṣus:
"You should prepare them as medicinal powders."
The bhikṣus pounded them while wet and formed them into a single mass rather than grinding them into powder. The Buddha said:
"One should not pound them while wet; they should be dried by exposing them to the sun."
The bhikṣus dried their medicines in the intense heat of the sun, which caused them to lose their potency.
The Buddha said, "One should not expose medicines to the scorching sun.
When the bhikṣus dried them in the shade, mildew grew upon the medicines. The Buddha said:
"It may be dried in the morning sun.
When the bhikṣus applied the astringent medicine to their bodies and immediately bathed, the medicine fell off and its efficacy was lost. The Buddha said:
"Wait until it is dry, then rub it into the skin; only after bathing again once it has been applied, and bathing again after that application, will the disease of the sores be cured."
After that sick bhikṣu’s wound had healed, he discarded all his remaining medicine.
Another bhikṣu, who was suffering from a skin eruption, went to a physician and said,
"O worthy one!..."
"I suffer from such painful ailments; please prescribe a remedy for me.
The physician returned and instructed him to apply an astringent ointment, further reporting:
"A certain monk previously suffered from scabies; he was made to apply this same medicine, so you should go to him and seek it."
The bhikṣu went immediately and asked, "Venerable one!
You previously used astringent medicine; I have been sent by a physician to use astringent medicine."
"If you have any leftover medicine, please bestow it upon me.
He replied,
"As for all the leftover medicine, I have already discarded it."
The bhikṣu replied,
"One should not discard things in this manner without first putting them away.
Then that bhikṣu reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One who uses astringent medicine should know the rules of conduct: the remains of the medicine used should not be discarded.
If there are other sick bhikṣus who request it, one should give it to them;
if no one requests it, it may be sent to the infirmary, stored in the treasury according to the regulations, and provided to those who are ill."
"One who does not act accordingly incurs an offense against the Dharma.
The setting was the city of Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a bhikṣu suffering from an eye ailment; he went to a physician and asked, "O worthy one!"
"I am now suffering from an eye ailment;
please prescribe a treatment for me. The physician replied, "Noble One!"
"You should use the medicine *āñjana*, and you will surely recover.
The bhikṣu replied,
"How could I be a person of lustful desire?"
The physician replied, "Venerable One!
This is an excellent eye medicine; apart from this, no other medicine can cure it."
For this reason, the bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One.
The Buddha said:
"If a physician says:..."
"If it is said, 'This is for treating eye ailments;
nothing else can cure them,' then one should use *añjana*.
However, that bhikṣu did not know which kind of *añjana* to use.
He then questioned the physician, who replied, "Noble One!
Your teacher possesses all-encompassing wisdom; you should go and ask him."
For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One. The Buddha said: "There are five kinds of añjana: [1] añjana from the Himavat mountains; [2] añjana from the Sindhu river;
[3] añjana from the ocean; [4] añjana from the earth; and [5] añjana produced by insects."
First, flower-añjana; second, liquid-añjana; third, powder-añjana; fourth, pill-añjana; fifth, *sāpila-śilā-añjana*.
These five types are all capable of treating eye ailments.
Therefore, monks, if you suffer from eye disease, you should apply *añjana* (collyrium) to achieve a cure.
Once his illness had been cured, he discarded all the remaining *añjana*.
There was another bhikṣu who also suffered from eye disease and, as before, consulted a physician.
The physician instructed him to use *añjana* medicine again, saying:
"A certain bhikṣu previously suffered from eye disease; he was previously taught to use *añjana* medicine, so you should go to him and seek it."
The sick bhikṣu went to inquire according to those instructions:
"Venerable one!
I am currently suffering from an eye ailment; do you have any leftover *añjana*?"
However, that bhikṣu could not find the leftover medicine and said,
"Venerable friend!
I cannot find my leftover medicine now."
On account of this matter, they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣus!"
If there is any leftover *añjana*, one should not discard it immediately without first collecting and storing it.
Regarding the ritual for the practice of *añjana*, I shall now explain the method for its proper placement.

As for the *añjana*, it should be placed in a secure location: the flower *añjana* is placed in a copper vessel, the liquid medicinal *añjana* is placed in a small casket, and the powdered medicinal *añjana* is placed inside a bamboo tube.
Thereafter, each [item] should be placed inside a bag, wrapped in cloth, or tied to a peg driven into a wall.
The *ānanda*-bearing bhikṣu should act according to the prescribed ritual; one who does not follow it incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).
The setting was as before.

At that time, there was a venerable bhikṣu named Kheṭaka who suffered from a wind-induced madness and wandered about everywhere. When brahmins and householders saw him, they asked one another, "Whose son is this?"
Someone who recognized him beforehand told the crowd,
"This is the son of such-and-such a lay devotee.
The crowd said:
"Because of this solitude, he has been made to go forth as a renunciant within the teaching of the Śākya-sons.
Had he not gone forth, his relatives would surely have treated his wind-disorder."
On account of this matter, the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One.
The Buddha said,
"Bhikṣus, you should inquire of that physician on behalf of the bhikṣu Sīghraga, for the purpose of treating his wind-disorder."
Then the bhikṣus went to the physician and asked, "O worthy sir!
There is a bhikṣu suffering from such-and-such an illness; please provide a prescription for him."
The physician said, "You should consume raw meat; you will surely recover.
The bhikṣu replied:
“O Noble One! Could that bhikṣu possibly be a meat-eater?
The physician replied:
"Noble one! This is the medicine for treating wind disorders.
Apart from this medicine, nothing else can cure it."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If a physician declares that this is the only medicine and nothing else can cure it, one should give him raw meat."
At that time, the bhikṣus gave him raw meat, but the man saw it with his own eyes and refused to eat it.
The Buddha said:
"One should cover his eyes with an object, and only then give him food."
At that time, because the robe was being given to him, the monk removed the binding cloth immediately; however, seeing blood on his hand, the sick monk vomited. The Buddha said:
"One should not remove the binding cloth immediately."
Once he had finished eating and had washed his hands clean, [the physician] set aside fragrant and delicious food and only then removed the bandages and bindings, saying to him:
"You should eat this fine food; then your illness may be cured."
"Once he had recovered, he constantly remembered that medicine.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
'If one has recovered from illness, one should follow the usual practice; whoever deviates from it shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.'"
The setting was in Rājagṛha.
At that time, as soon as the venerable Pilindavatsa had gone forth, he became afflicted with many illnesses.
Then, all the bhikṣus came to inquire after him and speak with him.
"Venerable one!
How are your four limbs?
He replied:
"It is extremely unstable; it is constantly afflicted by various diseases.
The bhikṣu replied, "Venerable friend!"
"What medicine have you been taking since long ago?
He replied, "In the past,
I kept a pouch of various medicines and would take them as needed."
The bhikṣus asked,
"Why do you not take it now?
He replied:
"The World-Honored One has not yet permitted it.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to carry medicinal bags.
Consequently, the bhikṣus accumulated many medicines, but their bags were too small to hold them.
The Buddha said:
“They tied the medicine into a bundle and fastened it to a wooden peg driven into an elephant tusk.
The medicine then became rotten and spoiled. The Buddha said:
“Dry it in the sun at the appropriate time.”
He exposed the medicine to the intense heat of the midday sun, which caused it to lose its potency. The Buddha said:
"One should not expose medicine to the direct rays of the sun; rather, one should dry it in the shade."
The medicine became rotten and spoiled.
The Buddha said, "It should be placed in a shaded, dry place.
Again, when wind and rain arrived, the bhikṣus did not dare to collect it. The Buddha said:
"If there are no laypeople or novices [to do so], you should collect and put them away yourself.
Remove those that have been touched by others and use the remainder; do not harbor any doubts regarding this."
"It was permitted because of difficulty; it is not permitted when there is no difficulty.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was the Venerable Kṣemaka, who at all times took no pleasure in seeking or searching, such that those who saw him were often suspicious.
At that time, the bhikṣus collectively named him Kṣemadatta because of his fewness of desires.
Later, during the morning, the one of few desires put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
As he went on his alms-round in due order, he heard the sound of sugarcane being crushed; he immediately went to see and found they were making sugar lumps by mixing them with rice flour.
The bhikṣu said to them, "Do not add flour when kneading the balls."
The man asked,
"Is there anything else besides this that can be used to form candied sugar?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I truly do not know what else there might be;
however, we have no choice but to eat sugar at this improper time, which is why it is not appropriate to add flour.
He replied:
"Noble one!
Whether it is the proper time or not, whether you eat or do not eat, this ball of food contains flour and nothing else; it is not suitable for anything else.
The bhikṣu then departed.
Later, on one occasion during a non-appropriate time, sugar lumps were being distributed among the assembly.
However, that bhikṣu, out of doubt, did not dare to eat them.
His disciple asked:
“Upādhyāya! The entire community is eating the sugar-candy; why do you not eat it?
He replied:
“Venerable ones!
Because there is sometimes food mixed [with impurities] here,” those disciples also did not eat.
At that time, the bhikṣus asked,
"Venerable one!
While the community is eating granulated sugar, why do you not eat it?"
He replied, "My upādhyāya said:
'It is because the food is mixed at certain times.'"
"Those who hear it shall likewise not eat.
Consequently, many people became unwilling to eat.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is not because of this that defilement arises; such is the nature of the Dharma.
Since its source is pure, it should be eaten; do not harbor any doubt."
At that time, the Venerable Kṣemavatī, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl, entered the city to beg for alms.
Proceeding by stages, he came before a shop selling perfumes and saw a man with flour smeared on his hands, who was then rolling balls of granulated sugar.
Having taken the sugar, he then smeared flour on his hands.
When the bhikṣu saw this, he said to him,
"O worthy one!"
"Since your hands are already smeared with flour, do not take the sugar;
I must eat this sugar at an improper time. That person replied, "Noble One!"
"Who, moreover, would repeatedly wash their hands with water before being permitted to touch [the food]?
Subsequently, that bhikṣu, out of doubt, did not dare to eat; his disciples and followers likewise all refrained from eating, and the circumstances were identical to those previously described.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If it was originally tainted, it is unfit for consumption.
Since its original substance is pure, there is no offense in eating it."
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
The Venerable Śāriputra was afflicted with a wind-related illness. Seeing that he was ill, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"I have frequently attended to Śāriputra’s medical needs in the past without consulting a physician; this time, I ought to consult one."
He immediately went to the physician and asked, "O worthy one!
The Venerable Śāriputra is suffering from such-and-such an illness; please provide a prescription for him."
The physician replied, "Venerable One!
Observing the symptoms of your ailment, you should take salt and vinegar; thus you shall be cured."
Having obtained the vinegar, he wished further to obtain salt. The Venerable Pilindavatsa replied, "I previously had salt which I stored in a horn;
I have maintained it for as long as I live."
"If the Blessed One permits its consumption, I shall provide it to you.
When the Venerable Śāriputra heard these words, he replied to Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"I have a doubt: if a medicine for life-long use is mixed with a medicine for a specific time, it should not be consumed at an improper time."
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Maudgalyāyana!

If *yāmika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for a watch of the day), *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for seven days), or *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for life) are mixed with *kālābhyavahāra-bhaiṣajya* (medicines to be taken at the proper time), they should be consumed as *kālābhyavahāra-bhaiṣajya*; they must not be consumed outside of the proper time.”

If *yāmika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for a watch of the night) is mixed with *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for life-long use), it should be consumed only up to the limit of that watch; beyond this limit, it should not be consumed.
If *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya* is mixed with *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for seven days), it should be consumed for seven days; beyond seven days, it should not be consumed.
"If [a medicine] is mixed with a life-long medicine, it should be consumed for the duration of one's life.
Should one not act accordingly, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the country of Śālīya, traveling through the human realm until he arrived at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Seers near Vārāṇasī.
Within that city, there was an elder named Mahāsena, who was wealthy, affluent, and possessed of many enjoyments.
That man had a wife named Mahāsenā, who was devoted to the Triple Gem, virtuous, upright, and pure in intention.

Having heard that the Blessed One was wandering through the country of Śroṇāparāntaka and had arrived at Vārāṇasī, staying at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages (Ṛṣipatana), he thought to himself:

"This must be my Great Teacher, the Blessed One. Although I have frequently made offerings to him, they have not been complete; now I shall take all the wealth currently in my possession and present it to the Unsurpassed Compassionate One, briefly extending my service."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to where the Buddha was. Upon arrival, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the householder Mahāsena in accordance with his needs, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him. Having expounded the sublime Dharma through various skillful means, the Buddha remained silent.

At that time, having heard the Dharma, the householder Mahāsena was filled with great joy. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in homage to the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray only that the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus will accept my invitation for the three-month summer retreat; I shall provide offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Seeing that the Buddha had granted his permission, the elder was filled with great joy; he prostrated before the Buddha and departed.
Thereafter, for three months of the rainy season retreat, the elder provided the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus with various offerings, ensuring they lacked for nothing.
Every morning at dawn, the elder prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and then proceeded to inspect the sick bhikṣus.
Among them was one bhikṣu who was afflicted with a grave illness.
He went to consult a physician, who instructed him to eat meat soup.
Having finished his inquiry, the householder returned home and said to his wife,
"O virtuous lady!..."
There is a sick bhikṣu for whom a physician has prescribed that he must eat meat soup to be able to cure his illness.
You should prepare it and deliver it quickly to the place where the sick bhikṣu resides.
At that time, the elder immediately ordered a young maidservant to take the money and goods to the various slaughterhouses with the intent to buy meat.
On that very day, however, the king gave birth to a son, whereupon the slaughter of animals was suspended;
anyone who violated this decree would be punished with a heavy penalty.
"Even if one were to purchase it at a high price, it still could not be obtained.
Then that young maidservant reported all the aforementioned matters to her mistress.
At that time, the householder’s wife reflected thus:
"For three months, I have made offerings to the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus, ensuring that none of my household possessions were lacking.
If I do not obtain this medicine now, I fear that the bhikṣus may pass away because of it; that would be my own fault."

Having thought thus, he immediately took a sharp blade, entered his own room, and cut flesh from his thigh. He gave it to a young maidservant, instructing her to mince it finely, boil it into a delicious soup, and deliver it urgently for that sick bhikṣu to eat.
At that time, the young maidservant immediately prepared and sent it to him; having received it, the sick bhikṣu ate it, and his illness was subsequently cured.
That sick bhikṣu did not know that the wife of the householder had cut flesh from her own body, and he thought to himself:

"Since I have accepted this offering, it is not right for me to remain idle; I should now cause those who have not attained to attain, those who have not realized to realize, and those who have not understood to understand."

Exerting diligent effort, he severed all defilements and attained the fruit of arhatship. Possessing the three knowledges and the six superknowledges, and endowed with the eight liberations, he attained knowledge in accordance with reality:
"Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence."

The mind is free from obstruction, like a hand waving through space; whether cut by a blade or smeared with incense, neither love nor hatred arises. One views gold and earth as equal and without distinction, renouncing all fame and profit without exception, such that even Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas all pay him reverence.
At that time, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One took up his robe and bowl and, accompanied by the great assembly, proceeded to the house of Mahāsena.
Having arrived there, he sat down before the assembly and addressed the elder, saying:
"Where is your young wife now?"
He replied,
“Inside the room.
Through the inconceivable power of the World-Honored One’s protection, all the flesh at the site of the incision was restored to its original state, its color and appearance no different from before.
At that time, the householder’s wife conceived a heart of joy toward the World-Honored One.
Having emerged from her chamber, she approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
The Buddha said to the woman,
"What is your cause that enables you to resolve upon the bodhisattva practice within the perilous path of birth and death?
The woman then joined her palms and spoke in verse:
“Within the cycle of birth and death, this body is easily obtained;
yet throughout hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, a sublime and exalted state is difficult to encounter.

At that time, having seen that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the great assembly were all seated at ease, the elder immediately provided offerings of various pure, superior, and delicious foods to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, satisfying them all.
Having set aside his eating vessels and finished chewing the tooth-stick, he washed his hands clean.
Then the householder took another small seat and sat to one side in order to listen to the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the sake of the elder, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. Having expounded the Dharma through countless skillful means, he rose from his seat and returned to his original dwelling.
Having assembled the bhikṣus, he sat upon his seat in the midst of the great assembly and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The eating of human flesh is detested by all; among all types of meat, human flesh is the most foul, putrid, and loathsome. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should not eat it again."
If one eats human flesh, they incur the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
I now establish the rules of conduct for the senior monks (*sthavira*) among the assembly.
Whenever the community is eating, if a person brings meat intending to serve it, the senior monk should first ask:
"What kind of meat is this?
If the senior elder is aged and infirm, or lacks discernment, or cannot remember, the second senior elder should ask.
"If the Elder does not inquire, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣus had doubts they could not resolve and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"The wife of the householder Mahāsena cut flesh from her own body to offer to the bhikṣu, and consequently caused his illness to be cured."
Due to these causes and conditions, he felt profound shame and remorse; through unremitting diligence, he attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Yet, having eaten human flesh, he was censured and disparaged by the multitude, which was contrary to the Dharma and deserved rebuke.
By what cause and condition, then, did he attain the exhaustion of outflows?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That bhikṣu has not only received the offerings of this woman in this life; throughout immeasurable kalpas in past lives, she has constantly offered her own flesh to this bhikṣu."
For this reason, I now offer flesh as an offering once again.

However, because of this woman, that bhikṣu attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) in a past life, and in this present life he has perfected the six supernormal powers and realized the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
I shall explain the causal conditions for you in detail.

In the distant past, there was a householder in the city of Vārāṇasī who was immensely wealthy and possessed great riches; he was benevolent, righteous, faithful, and compliant, and his wife was likewise so.
There was a brahmin, intelligent and widely learned, surrounded by disciples numbering five hundred, who taught them the *Vidyā-sthāna* (the sciences).

A very wealthy householder conceived deep faith in that brahmin and invited the entire assembly of brahmins to his home, providing them with every possession as an offering until the end of his life, his mind never wearying.
At that time, the great wealthy householder was by nature compassionate; every morning he would survey his entire assembly to ascertain whether they were at ease.
One of the brahmin’s disciples was afflicted with illness and went to consult a physician, who replied:
"You should eat meat broth."
At that time, the elder went to the place of the Māṇavaka, offered his greetings, and said to him:
"Your body is suffering from illness; what medicine did the physician prescribe for you to take?"
He replied, "Let him eat meat soup. Then,
having finished his inquiries, the elder returned home and informed his wife:
"There is the son of a brahmin who is suffering from illness and requires meat soup.
You should have a young maidservant take money to the market to buy meat and prepare the soup, then send it to him so that he may eat."
On that day, the king’s consort gave birth to a son, whereupon he issued an edict to prohibit slaughter;
anyone who violated it would certainly be punished with severe penalties.
Consequently, even if they possessed money or goods, there was no way to obtain meat.
When the maidservant returned, she related these events in full.
Upon hearing this, the householder’s wife reflected to herself:
"I have already invited a company of Brahmins to my home for offerings; since this sick young Māṇavaka has not obtained medicine, he will surely die without a doubt, and this is my fault."
Having formed this thought, he entered his own room, took a sharp knife in hand, and immediately cut the flesh from his thigh, instructing a maidservant to prepare a soup and send it to the sick man.
Once he had finished eating the soup, his illness was immediately cured.
The patient reflected:
"Since meat has been forbidden, there would have been no way for me to obtain it; this must surely be the wife of this elder who cut her own flesh to give to me."
Having formed this thought, he felt deep shame and remorse, and further reflected:

"I must cause that which I have not yet realized to be realized, and that which I have not yet attained to be attained; regarding that which I have not yet manifested, I shall now apply myself with unremitting diligence."
"Through such diligent application, he attained the five supernormal powers.
O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thought:
who else could that wife of the great wealthy householder be who gave the meat in the past?"
This lady of the householder Mahāsena is she.
The sick man of that time is the present sick bhikṣu.
In a past life, by virtue of the cause of this woman’s gift of meat, he attained the five supernormal powers; now, he has fully realized the fruit of arhatship.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If one performs purely black karma, one will obtain a purely black retribution;
if one performs purely white karma, one will obtain a purely white retribution."
"If one performs mixed karma, one will receive mixed retribution.
Therefore, O Bhikṣus, you should abandon black karma and mixed karma, and cultivate purely white karma.
This was spoken with Śrāvastī as the setting.
At that time, King Prasenajit, the lord of Kośala, had a premier elephant that suddenly died of an epidemic.
As it was a year of famine, the brahmins, householders, and all the people of the country were eating elephant meat.
At mealtime, the six bhikṣus dressed themselves, took up their bowls, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food in sequence, arriving at the house of a householder.
At that time, elephant meat was being cooked in the house, and steam was rising from the cauldron.
Entering the house to beg for alms, the elder’s wife said,
"I have no food at present.
The bhikṣu asked:
"From within the cauldron, vapor is emerging; what thing is this?
His wife said, "O Noble One!..."
"This is elephant meat.
How could you, sirs, possibly eat elephant meat?
They replied:
"We rely solely upon our donors for our livelihood; if you eat elephant meat, we shall eat it as well—please give us some.
The wife then took the meat and handed it to the bhikṣu; having received it, he filled his bowl-bag with it and departed.
Another bhikṣu, seeing this, asked:
"Venerable sir, what is that in your alms-bowl bag?
It is filled to overflowing."
He replied,
"Elephant meat.
[The other asked,] "How could you, sirs, eat elephant meat?"
He replied, "Venerable sir!
It is a time of famine, and no food can be found; how could I endure hunger and die?"
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "You bhikṣus!"
Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, kings, and ministers all show reverence toward the bhikṣus; how then could you eat the flesh of a royal elephant?
When the King hears of this, he will surely say:
"Because the bhikṣus ate the elephant's flesh, my premier elephant has perished on this account.
Thus, he will give rise to censure and shame.
Therefore, bhikṣus should not eat elephant meat.
If one eats it, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
As it is with elephant meat, so it is with horse meat.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Kākaṇḍa-pāda monastery on the bank of Lake Gaggara in the city of Campā.

In that lake there was a nāga king named Cāpāla, who was faithful and virtuous; every month on the eighth and fourteenth days, he would emerge from his palace, transform himself into human form, and go to the bhikṣus to receive the eight precepts.
Having received it, he returned to his original form in a public place, and he did not cause harm or distress to other sentient beings.

At that time, as there was a famine, emaciated people—including those who tended cattle and sheep, woodcutters, wanderers, those who made their living by the right path, and those who made their living by wrong paths—all came together to gouge and cut [the flesh], taking it back to eat.
At that time, the six bhikṣus, having donned their robes and taken up their bowls, entered the city to beg for food and arrived at the house of a lay elder.
At that house, dragon meat was currently being cooked; as steam rose from the cauldron, they immediately entered the residence to beg for alms.
The householder’s wife said,
“I have no food now.
The bhikṣu asked:
“Venerable One, what is this substance that emits vapor from within the cauldron?
He replied, “Noble One!”
"This is dragon meat.
How could you, sirs, possibly eat dragon meat?
They replied:
"We live solely by depending on the almsgivers.
If you eat, we shall also eat; please give us some.
The wife then took the meat and gave it to the bhikṣu.
Because of this, those people took even more meat.
At that time, the nāga wife thought to herself:
"Since the bhikṣus eat nāga flesh, everyone else eats it as well; when will my husband ever be spared from such suffering?"
"Based on these circumstances, it is fitting that I go to question the Buddha.
Having passed the first watch of the night, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and sat down to one side.
The radiance from the dragon girl’s body shone everywhere, illuminating the entire vicinity of the Ganges pool with complete clarity.
Then the dragon girl joined her palms in reverence and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“O Virtuous One!”
"My husband is faithful and virtuous; every month on the eighth and fourteenth days, he emerges from the dragon palace, assumes human form, and goes to the bhikṣus to receive the eightfold precepts."
In a public place, she resumed her dragon form, yet she did not harm or distress any other sentient beings.

At that time, it was a year of famine, and there were hungry people who together cut off her flesh; because of this, the bhikṣus all took it to satisfy their hunger. [The woman thought: "When will my husband be freed from his suffering?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will look upon us with compassion and pity, and decree that the bhikṣus shall not eat the flesh of nāgas.
When the World-Honored One heard these words, he remained silent.
At that time, the dragon girl, knowing that the Buddha had silently granted his consent, took her leave and withdrew.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, the World-Honored One prepared a seat before the great assembly and sat down. He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Last night, after the first watch had passed, a Nāga girl from Campā arrived at my dwelling, her radiance blazing brilliantly. Having paid her respects, she sat to one side."
The majestic radiance of his body shone forth everywhere, illuminating the entire side of Lake Gaiya, as he spoke these words:
"Venerable Sir!
My husband is faithful and virtuous; every month on the eighth and fourteenth days, he emerges from the dragon palace, transforms himself into human form, and observes the eightfold precepts."
In a public place, he resumed his dragon form, yet he did not harm or afflict other sentient beings.

At that time, during a year of famine, there were hungry people who cut off their own flesh to eat; because of this, the bhikṣu also ate the dragon’s flesh, thinking, "When will my husband be released from this suffering?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will prohibit the bhikṣus from eating the flesh of nāgas, out of compassion for living beings.
Having heard these words, I remained silent.
At that time, seeing that I remained silent, the nāga girl paid her respects, took her leave, and departed.
For this reason, bhikṣus, you should not eat the flesh of nāgas.
Those who eat nāga flesh are despised by all the devas and nāgas; they destroy wholesome dharmas and are not true sons of the Śākya.
"Therefore, O bhikṣus, you should not eat the flesh of nāgas; whoever eats it shall incur a *vinayātikrama* offense.
*Vinaya-vastu-bhaiṣajyavastu*, Fascicle One. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*.
Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The Buddha was in the kingdom of Magadha, traveling through the human realm until he reached the city of Rājagṛha, where he stayed in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, King Bimbisāra heard that the Buddha was traveling through his realm and had arrived at its borders. Having heard this, he reflected:
"Although I have frequently made offerings to the Buddha in the past, I have never yet invited him for a three-month summer retreat, using all my household wealth as an offering."

Having formed this thought, he offered all that he possessed to invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a three-month *varṣā* retreat, providing them with offerings; furthermore, he dispatched Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, to supply whatever medicines were required for those who were ill or emaciated.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, having formed this thought, was surrounded by his ministers and attendants as he departed from the palace and proceeded to where the Buddha was.
Upon arrival, he prostrated himself in salutation and withdrew to sit at one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the king, preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma through various skillful means, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him, before remaining silent.
Then the Great King rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my invitation for the three-month summer retreat within my palace. I shall provide all necessary provisions and personal requisites for your offerings, and I shall also dispatch Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, to treat all ailments and suffering."
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.
Having earnestly entreated the World-Honored One, the king paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
Returning to the palace, he prepared various offerings and provided them for the three months of the summer retreat.

At that time, King Prasenajit of the Kingdom of Kośala heard that King Bimbisāra had invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a three-month summer retreat, providing various offerings as well as the great physician Jīvaka to supply medicinal decoctions.
Having heard this, he reflected:
"That man is a great king who was able to provide offerings with his household wealth and Jīvaka and others.
I too am now the sovereign of a great kingdom; if the World-Honored One comes to this country, I shall likewise provide offerings with all my household wealth and the physician Ātreya."

Thus, the Blessed One remained in Rājagṛha for the three-month rains retreat. Having completed his robes, he took up his bowl and outer robe and, surrounded by a great assembly, set out for Śrāvastī. Traveling by stages, he eventually arrived at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in that country.
At that time, King Prasenajit heard that the Buddha had arrived and was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.
Having heard this, he went to visit him; upon reaching the Anāthapiṇḍada Park and seeing the World-Honored One, he prostrated himself in salutation and withdrew to sit at one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the king, expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma through various skillful means; having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him, he remained silent.
Then King Prasenajit rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with both knees upon the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One:

"I pray only that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will accept my invitation for the three-month rains retreat, and that I may provide offerings of all necessary requisites as well as the physician Ātreya."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
When King Prasenajit, the Lord of Kośala, saw that the Buddha had granted his permission, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and departed.
Returning to the palace, he prepared various offerings and dispatched physicians to provide all necessary supplies for three months, making offerings to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.

At that time, King Prasenajit was by nature compassionate and merciful; every morning he would go to the vihāra, personally prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, inquire after his well-being, and survey the entire assembly to ascertain whether they were at peace.
He saw a bhikṣu whose body was afflicted with hemorrhoids, emaciated and lacking strength; having seen him, the king then asked:
"Noble one, why are you so emaciated and lacking strength?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"Great King,
I have become emaciated because I am afflicted with hemorrhoids."
Then the king returned and commanded the physician Ātreya to treat his illness.
The physician followed the command and went there; however, as this physician did not have faith in the Triple Gem, he was unwilling to provide medical treatment for the patient.
At a later time, the king saw the patient again and, wondering at this, asked:
"Venerable one!
Did the physician not treat you?"
"My body is still weak and emaciated.
The patient replied,
"Although Your Majesty dispatched physicians, they ultimately did not come to provide me with medical treatment."
When the king heard this, he immediately rebuked him in anger and dispatched a messenger to pursue and seize him.
The king said, "I previously commanded you to attend to the sick bhikṣu; why have you failed to provide medical treatment until now?"
"If you do not treat him, I shall strip you of your official rank.
However, this physician had never possessed a sense of faith; having been rebuked by the king, his anger and resentment intensified, and he reviled him with harsh words:
"Would I lose my office for the sake of people like you?"
They seized the sick bhikṣu and, having gone outside the monastery gate, bound his hands and feet and proceeded to excise his hemorrhoids.
At that time, as the bhikṣu was subjected to such oppression, his mind was wracked with agonizing pain; he cried out loudly and thought to himself:
"I am beset by extreme suffering; will the World-Honored One, in His great compassion, not take pity on me?"
It is the constant nature of the Tathāgata that at all times there is nothing he does not know or see; thus, alerted by the power of his great compassion, he went to where the bhikṣu was.
When the physician saw the Buddha approaching from afar, his anger still unabated, he spoke these words: "Come here!
“O maidservant’s son!
Behold how your disciple’s lower parts are!

When the World-Honored One heard these words, he departed in silence. Returning to his original place, he spread out his seat and sat down. With a serene and joyful smile, five-colored light issued from his mouth; at times it shone downward, and at other times it ascended upward.
The light that descended reached as far as the Avīci Hell; those dwelling in the scorching heat all obtained coolness, while those in the freezing ice found warmth.
Those sentient beings each attained peace and happiness, and they all thought:
"Have you and I died from this hell to be born in another place?"
At that time, in order to inspire faith in those sentient beings, the World-Honored One manifested further signs.
Upon seeing these signs, they all thought:
"We have not died here to be reborn elsewhere."
"However, it must be due to the majestic power of the Unsurpassed Great Sage that my body and mind now experience peace and happiness.

Having thus conceived reverence and faith, one is able to extinguish all sufferings, receive a superior and wondrous body within the realms of humans and devas, become a vessel for the Dharma, and perceive the principle of the True Truths.

Those who ascended rose into the light at the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*), where they proclaimed the teachings of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and further recited two verses:
"Seek liberation; Diligently practice the Buddha's teaching.
Subdue the army of birth and death, As an elephant destroys a house of straw."
"In this Dharma and Vinaya, those who diligently seek with heedfulness can exhaust the ocean of afflictions and shall reach the ultimate end of suffering.
At that time, the light shone throughout the trichiliocosm and returned to the presence of the Buddha.
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, speaks of past events, the light enters through his back;
if he speaks of future events, the light enters through his chest;
if he speaks of matters concerning the hells, the light enters through the soles of his feet.
If he speaks of matters concerning animals, the light enters through his heels;
if he speaks of matters concerning hungry ghosts, the light enters through his toes;
if he speaks of matters concerning humans, the light enters through his knees.
If he speaks of the affairs of a Cakravartin King of Power, the light enters through the palm of his left hand;
if he speaks of the affairs of a Cakravartin Universal Monarch, the light enters through the palm of his right hand;
if he speaks of celestial matters, the light enters through his navel.
If he speaks of the matters concerning śrāvakas, the light enters through his mouth;
if he speaks of the matters concerning pratyekabuddhas, the light enters through his shoulders;
if he speaks of the matters concerning anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the light enters through the crown of his head.
At that time, the light circled the Buddha three times and entered through his mouth.
Then the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha smiles with a joyful countenance; it is not without cause or condition.
He then spoke these verses to request the Buddha's teaching:
"From his mouth issue various wondrous rays of light, Filling the great trichiliocosm in manifold forms."
Pervading all lands throughout the ten directions, like the sun’s light illuminating the entirety of space;
the Buddha is the most supreme cause for sentient beings, able to remove arrogance as well as grief and sorrow.
Without a specific cause, he does not open his golden mouth; when he smiles, he will surely proclaim something extraordinary.
The serene and discerning Honored One of the Munis, who delights in speaking for those who wish to hear, utters a sublime roar like the lion king; we pray that you resolve our doubts.
Like the King of Wondrous Mountains within the great ocean, Which does not shake unless there is a cause or condition;
So you, with sovereign compassion, manifest a smile, To explain the causes and conditions for those who look up in longing.
At that time, the Blessed One said to Ānanda: "It is so, Ānanda;
it is not without cause or condition that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, suddenly manifests a smile."
Ānanda! The physician-king Ātreya has brought about his own ruin by uttering evil insults against the Buddha, calling him a "son of a slave woman."
I recall that from the time of King Mahāsammata until my own present body, there has never been anyone who reviled me as a person of low birth.
Yet this Āḍiya has used foul language to insult me; by virtue of this evil karma, in seven days he shall surely vomit blood and meet his end, falling into hell to suffer for a long time.
Therefore, monks, you should not send a monk to attend to the sick, like the untrustworthy physician Atiya.
There are two methods for treating hemorrhoids:
first, by means of incantations; second, by means of medicine.
If a bhikṣu is ill, he should not send those of unfaithful character, such as Ātiyas, to provide medical treatment.
If he causes them to treat him, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, because the bhikṣu suffering from hemorrhoids had sent Āḍiya to treat him, the latter employed a means that ultimately caused the bhikṣu’s death.
Then a high minister reported the matter to the King, saying:
"Āḍiya reviled the World-Honored One, calling him the son of a lowly slave-girl, and intentionally caused the death of the bhikṣu suffering from hemorrhoids whom he was treating."
At that time, the king became greatly incensed and dispatched a high minister to behead the wicked man.
The minister replied,
"Great King!..."
Āḍiya was already a dead man; why should he be killed again?
The World-Honored One has already prophesied:
"Seven days from now, he shall vomit hot blood and his life will immediately end."
"After his life ends, he shall fall into hell.
The king said, "If it is so,
then drive him out of my kingdom."
At that time, the minister immediately followed the command and drove him out of the kingdom to the city of Sāketa.
Once he arrived at that city, a benevolent deity rebuked him; having scolded him most bitterly, the deity drove him out of the boundaries once more and said:
"O foolish man!"
"You have already insulted the Great Honored One of the Three Realms by calling him the lowly son of a slave-girl; how can you remain here?
Having said this, he departed from there and went to the city of Vārāṇasī, but was driven out from there as well by benevolent deities;
from there he went to the city of Vaiśālī, yet was again driven out.
He went again to Rājagṛha, where he was likewise driven out;
he went again to Campā, where he was driven out once more.
Arriving at the foot of a tree to rest for a short while, the tree deity drove him away.
From this point until the location of the flowing springs and ponds, they were all driven out and not permitted to rest.
Having been thus expelled, they reflected:
"Even creatures such as jackals are still able to find a place to stay within Jambudvīpa."
"I am a human being, yet even under this tree there is no room for me.
Having thought this, his inner heart was consumed with anguish; he spat blood and died, and after death, he fell into the Avīci Great Hell.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person is born into this world, And utters evil words from their mouth,
It is as if they were constantly using a sharp blade or axe To cut and sever their own body."
To praise the wicked and to disparage the virtuous;
for such faults born of the mouth, one shall never reap a pleasant fruit.
Though one may lose at gambling, that transgression is still relatively light.
To disparage and insult the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is a transgression of extreme gravity.
If a person speaks with an evil mind to revile the noble ones,
they shall dwell within the Arbuda hell for hundreds of thousands of years.
"Furthermore, because of these evil insults and the slander of the noble ones,
he fell into the Blue Blister Hell and remained there for forty-two thousand years.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the country of Śāleyya, traveling through the human realm and arriving at a certain village.
There was an old dwelling place where no boundary had previously been established; he stayed overnight there.
At that time, due to these circumstances, the World-Honored One’s wind-disorder (vāta-roga) was provoked.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda thought to himself:
"I have always made offerings to the World-Honored One, yet I have never consulted a physician.
Now that I am afflicted by a wind-disorder (vāta-roga), I shall go to consult a physician.
Having arrived, he asked:
“O worthy one!
The Blessed One now suffers from a wind-disorder; please prescribe a remedy for me.
The physician replied:
“Venerable One!
It would be well to prepare a decoction by boiling three types of astringent medicines with clarified butter; upon consuming it, you will be cured.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda prepared the medicine by boiling the ingredients together and went to present it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, knowing this, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"What is this? Ānanda replied:
I thought to myself:
"This person constantly makes offerings to the World-Honored One, yet he does not consult a physician. It would be appropriate for me now to go and consult a physician.
Having asked him, the physician replied:
"It would be appropriate to fry three types of astringent medicines in ghee; thus they shall be cured.
Therefore, we have prepared this to offer to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! Where did you cook it? He replied:
“Within the boundary.
The Buddha asked,
“Who cooked it?”
Ānanda said, "I cooked it myself.
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! If it is cooked within the boundary and stored overnight within the boundary, it should not be consumed.
If it is cooked within the boundary and stored overnight outside the boundary, it should not be consumed.”
"If it is cooked outside the boundary and kept overnight inside the boundary, it should not be consumed.
If it is cooked outside the boundary and kept overnight outside the boundary, it should not be consumed.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Ānanda! A bhikṣu must not, under any circumstances, take any medicinal substances that he has handled himself or cooked himself.
If a bhikṣu handles any medicinal substances himself or cooks them himself, he must not consume them.”
"If a *śrāmaṇera* or a layperson cooks [food] outside the boundary, a bhikṣu may consume it.
This account took place in Śrāvastī.
A certain householder went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the elder, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; having spoken the Dharma through various skillful means, he remained silent.
Then that householder rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, bowed his head with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One and assembly of bhikṣus, please accept my humble invitation for tomorrow at my home."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
Then, at dawn the following day, the householder prepared seats within his home, placed large jars filled with pure water in the courtyard, and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"Now that the time has come and the offerings are prepared, may the Holy One know it is time."

At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the community of bhikṣus donned their robes, took up their bowls, and went to the house of the elder, where they sat down in order and accepted food as was appropriate; only the Buddha did not go.
The Buddha has five reasons for not attending an invitation and instead sending someone to request food.
What are these five? First, to attend to the sick;
second, to inspect bedding and furniture; third, to enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); fourth, to preach the Dharma to the devas; and fifth, to establish the precepts (*śīla*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to establish a precept, did not accept the invitation; instead, he sent someone to request food.
It is the constant practice of the Tathāgata that if he does not attend an invitation himself, he commands Ānanda to request the meal.
At that time, the householder returned home, prepared a sumptuous meal, and offered it to the bhikṣus.
The rice was somewhat undercooked; having received the food, the Venerable Ānanda thought:
"This rice is somewhat undercooked; how can it be fit for consumption?"
"The World-Honored One has previously suffered from wind-disorders; if he were to eat this rice, I fear it would cause them to flare up further.
He then thought again:
"If I do not accept it, the World-Honored One will not have permitted it. I should now rather receive it all in its entirety."
Having returned to his own place, he boiled the rice again until it was thoroughly cooked and offered it to the World-Honored One, thinking:
"The World-Honored One will surely establish a precept on account of this.
He then returned to his own place, boiled the rice until it was cooked, placed it in his bowl, and brought it to offer to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, knowing yet asking intentionally, said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Is there any difference between this rice and that which is given to the bhikṣus for them to eat?"
"Are they not different?
Ānanda replied, "They are different."
"The rice consumed by those bhikṣus is somewhat raw.
The Buddha asked again,
"Where did you obtain this rice?"
Then Ānanda reported the matter in full to the Buddha, who said:
“Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!”
"Although I have not yet spoken of this, you well know the proper time.
From now on, I permit the bhikṣus: if they receive raw rice, they should cook it until it is thoroughly done before eating."
At that time, on account of this matter, the group of six bhikṣus personally begged for raw rice, and having received it, they boiled and ate it.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If among the grains of rice, two parts are cooked and one part remains raw, you are permitted to cook them yourself and eat.
As for vegetables, flowers, fruits, fish, or meat, first boil them until their color changes."
Once it has been accepted, one is permitted to cook it oneself before eating.
If it is a liquid substance such as milk, it should be boiled three times; having thus prepared it, one may accept it, cook it oneself, and eat it, and in all such cases there is no offense.

If one cooks and eats rice, raw vegetables, flowers, fruits, fish, meat, and so forth before their color has changed, or milk and other such items before they have been boiled three times, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (vayadharmika-āpatti).
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī.

At that time, in the city of Śūrpāraka, there was an elder named Īśvara, who belonged to a noble and wealthy clan; he possessed abundant treasures and goods, was well-supplied with wealth, had many kinsmen, and maintained a large retinue, like the divine king Vaiśravaṇa.
In that city, there was another wealthy householder of a similar clan who had an only daughter, who was upright and beautiful.
The Householder Svayambhū then took her as his wife, and they lived together in joy.
Not long thereafter, the wife became pregnant.
Consequently, a sentient being came to dwell within her womb, and when nine months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a son.
Once the son was born, they enjoyed themselves and partook in pleasures for twenty-one days.
After twenty-one days had passed, he gathered his kinsmen to bestow a name upon his son.
At that time, the elder asked the kinsmen:
"What name should be given to this son?"
Then his kinsmen said to the elder,
"Since he is the son of Svayambhū, he should be named Ananda (Peaceful Joy). Later,
while the elder was enjoying himself with his wife within his home, another son was born, whom they named Rakṣita (Guardian).
Later, another son was born, whom they named Ānanda.
Eventually, when the householder Īśvara fell ill and lay upon his bed, he became violent and impulsive due to the suffering of his illness, and he reviled his relatives with harsh abuse.
Therefore, he abandoned both his wife and children and departed, ultimately providing them with nothing.
At that time, the elder had previously kept a maidservant who was deeply compassionate and thought to herself:
"This elder is my master; he has always sustained me with his wealth and provisions."
"Now that my illness is so grave, how could I not attend to it?
Although my wife and children do not provide for me, I shall serve him with my very life.
Having formed this thought, he went to the physician and asked him:
“O noble one! Do you know that householder Īśvara?
The physician replied:
"I was previously acquainted with him; why must you ask?
The maidservant replied, "He is currently suffering from a grave illness, and his wife and children have abandoned him; I pray that you will provide a prescription for him."
The physician replied,
"Woman! Since you have already abandoned your wife and children, who will attend to you?"
The maidservant replied,
"O worthy one! I am looking after it alone."
"Since he has no relatives and his resources are meager, please seek out for him medicines that are easy to obtain.
At that time, the physician immediately prepared a prescription.
He secretly took a small amount of goods from the man's wife and children, and further reduced his own provisions, using these to purchase medicine and provide care for him.
Not long thereafter, his illness was cured.
Once the householder had recovered, he thought to himself:
"My wife and children abandoned me and did not look after me; it was only this servant who preserved my life, and now I have been restored to health."
"I must repay this kindness.
Having thought thus, he said to the maidservant:
"My wife and children have all abandoned me and gone; you alone have looked after me."
"By your kindness, my life has been saved.
What wish do you now desire to have fulfilled?
At that time, the maidservant said:
"O all of you, please know this!
I have no other desire; if you would grant me your permission, I pray that you will accept me as your wife.
The elder replied:
"What is the use of having you as a wife?
I shall now give you five hundred million pieces of gold, grant you my family name, and let you depart.
The maidservant replied:
“Noble son!
Even if you were to give me wealth, grant me your surname, and depart for another place, I would still not escape the name of ‘slave girl’ elsewhere;
but if I become your wife, this ignoble title will cease.”
At that time, the elder, knowing the maidservant’s firm resolve, granted her request and further told her:
"When your menses are about to end, you should bathe yourself and come to see me."
When the maidservant knew that her time had come, she bathed and went [to the householder].
Upon seeing her, the householder took pleasure with her, and she immediately became pregnant.
Once she had conceived, all his storehouses became completely filled. When the months were full, she gave birth to a son whose appearance was upright and handsome, and whose faculties were complete.
As soon as he was born, all his wealth and possessions increased spontaneously. He gathered his kinsmen together to confer upon him a name.
The relatives deliberated and agreed that he should be named Pūrṇa.
He dispatched eight nurses to attend to him:
two to carry him, two to feed him milk, two to wash him, and two to play with him.
These eight nurses attended to him day and night, providing him with milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, and even the finest cream as his food.
His requisites for adorning the body—food, drink, and medicinal decoctions—were each day twice as excellent as before.
Due to these causes and conditions, he grew up rapidly, like a lotus flower blooming in a pure pond.

Once he had grown up, he was instructed to study writing, arithmetic, and the methods of sealing, as well as the recording of documents, the classification of goods, the appraisal of clothing and precious jewels for their quality, and furthermore, the discernment of the excellence or defect of wood, the superiority or inferiority of elephants and horses, and the noble or humble characteristics of boys and girls.
These eight types [of texts] were all to be recited and practiced until they were mastered.
Having attained full comprehension, he was further able to teach them to others.
At that time, the elder had three sons who had all taken wives; they indulged together in play and became deeply attached to sensual pleasures, causing all their family affairs to fall into ruin.
At that time, the elder supported his cheek with his hand and remained there in a state of sorrowful reflection.
When his three sons saw this, they asked their father,
"For what reason do you remain here supporting your cheek with such grief?"
The elder said to him:
"Do you know now?
In the past, it was only when I had a full hundred thousand pieces of gold that I took a wife; yet even until this day, I have sustained myself by my own efforts."
"You have each now taken wives and become addicted to sensual pleasures; all your family estates have been dissipated and ruined.
After my death, by what means shall you survive?"
"Such a matter as this has never been considered.

Then the eldest son of that elder, who previously wore a precious gem as an earring upon his ear, immediately removed it; he then took a piece of wood and fashioned it into an earring, making this vow:
"If I am unable to manage my affairs and obtain a profit of one hundred thousand pieces of gold, I shall never wear this precious gem earring again."
The second son likewise removed his jeweled earrings and instead took earrings adorned with red copper.
The third son, in turn, removed his earrings and took earrings adorned with lead and tin.
Thus, after the three sons had discarded their earrings, the first son, who was originally named Ananda, became known in the world as "Wooden Earring" (*Dāruka*) due to these circumstances;
the second son, originally named Rakṣita, became known as "Copper Earring" (*Tāmra-piṇḍaka*);
and the third son, originally named Nandika, became known as "Lead Earring" (*Sīsa-piṇḍaka*).
Each took their goods and traveled by sea for trade.
At that time, the fourth son of the elder, named Pūrṇa, addressed his father, saying:
"I too now wish to cross the sea for trade."
The elder said, "You are still young and not yet fit to cross the sea; you should instead attend exclusively to managing the shop.
At that time, the younger son followed his father's command and remained at the stall.
Later, the sons returned from the sea, having acquired much wealth and treasure, arriving safely and soundly.
Once they had rested from their fatigue, they said to their father:
"We pray that you, Father, will examine our riches."
At that time, the father took the goods obtained by his three sons; each was worth one hundred thousand pieces of gold.
The youngest son came to where his father was, prostrated at his father’s feet, and said to him:
"This is the wealth I obtained from the marketplace."
"I also wish for you to examine it.
The father said to his son, "You have not traveled far nor sought extensively; what is there to examine in the things you have obtained?"
The son spoke again, saying:
"Although I am nearby, I pray that my father will take pity on me and grant me an inspection.

The father followed his son’s wish and proceeded to examine the wealth and goods possessed by the youngest son; finding that in all his business dealings he had never practiced deception, he calculated the principal and interest, which were found to be double those of the other sons.
When the householder Vaiśravaṇa saw this, he was filled with great joy; it accorded perfectly with his own wishes, and overcome with celebration, he thought to himself:
"My young son possesses great merit and fortune; though he has not traveled far, he has been able to acquire such vast wealth."
Later, at another time, the householder Īśvara suddenly fell ill. On account of this, he thought to himself:
"After my death, my sons will surely divide [the estate]. I should now anticipate this and devise a skillful means."
He said to his sons,
"Brothers, you may bring some firewood.
Hearing their father's command, the sons each took hold of wood, until a great pile was formed.
The father then said,
"We may burn it together.
Once the fire had become fierce, the father told his son:
"You all should divide these firebrands among yourselves so that they are all separated from one another.
Those sons then followed their father's command and vied with one another to divide the firewood; consequently, the fire, having been divided, was extinguished.
The father said to his sons,
"Do you see this? They all replied:
“I have seen it.
Thereupon, the householder spoke these verses:
“Various fires, through mutual dependence, produce a blazing flame; if they are dispersed, the light is extinguished.”
"Brothers living together should also act like this; if you should suddenly divide the estate, it shall surely lead to destruction.
Having spoken these verses, the elder further addressed his sons:
"You should know that after my passing, you must not heed the words of your wives and children."
He spoke a verse, saying:
"If one follows the words of a wife, the family is destroyed; When a sober man hears the wailing, his heart must surely break.
The ruin of a kingdom is always due to wicked ministers; It is because of excessive greed that affection and love are severed."
At that time, having spoken these words, the elder sent his other three sons out of the gate while leaving the crown prince behind, and addressed him, saying:
"After my death, you and my youngest son must always dwell together; do not let us be separated."
All material wealth may be abandoned;
however, this young child must not be forsaken.
