The reason for this is that this young child is a person of great merit and virtue.
Having spoken these words, he uttered this verse:
"All accumulations come to an end; All that is lofty must fall.
All meetings end in separation; All who have life return to death."
Having spoken these verses, he passed away.

The elder’s sons prepared the funeral equipment with great care, adorning the bier with interlaced five-colored silks and making offerings of various fragrant flowers as they escorted him to the charnel ground.
Having reached the forest, he set it on fire.
Returning home, he cultivated filial conduct and said to his family members:
"During my father's lifetime, all our food and clothing were obtained through his strength; it was by his power that we were able to survive."
"Our father has now passed away; we ought to exert our efforts together to seek wealth and property, and invest the family assets for profit.
His younger brother said, "If you go abroad to seek fortune, I must go as well."
The eldest brother said:
"Since you wish to travel, there is no need to go far; you may stay and conduct trade right here, while we others shall engage in commerce in distant lands."
Having spoken these words, they dispersed and departed, each taking their wealth and goods to engage in trade in distant lands.
The youngest brother remained at home, becoming fully acquainted with all the family’s business affairs.
Once the elder brother had departed on his journey and both his wife and children were at home, he sent a maidservant to the younger brother’s place to seek the necessary utensils for food and drink.
At that time, many merchant travelers were surrounding the younger brother’s residence and staying there, so she was unable to enter;
only after the crowd dispersed was she finally able to see him.
Because of this long delay, his sister-in-law became greatly suspicious and rebuked her maidservant.
The maidservant replied, "A great many merchants surrounded my brother as he stayed there; for this reason, the time was delayed and she could not see him sooner."
At that time, the eldest sister-in-law became angry with her brother-in-law and said:
"This slave girl has taken over as the mistress of the house; how can any of us expect to remain in peace?"
He told the maidservant,
"After you have watched for the departure of the merchants, go back to them and demand the goods.
The maidservant immediately went and, at the appointed time, went there to demand the goods.
She soon found it quickly and came to his place, whereupon she felt great joy.
The other maidservants also went to seek their goods, but they encountered a large gathering and did not obtain their items immediately; for this reason, they arrived late.
Everyone reproached these maidservants and asked the first one,
"When you went to fetch goods, why did you return so quickly?
Why has my fetching of goods caused such a long delay?"
The maidservant replied,
"I always take my things at the proper time, which is why I have come early.
As for you, you always arrive there after the proper time, which is why you are late."
Those maidservants then went together with the former maid to fetch the goods, obtaining them immediately upon arrival.
The two sisters-in-law asked the maid:
"Previously, when you fetched goods, it always took an extremely long time; why have you come so quickly this time?"
Her sister-in-law replied, "Now I wish for my elder sister-in-law long life and freedom from illness; by following your wife there to fetch the goods, we shall obtain them immediately."
When his two sisters-in-law heard these words, they again gave rise to resentment and thought to themselves:
"Now that this servant girl knows the affairs of the household, how could things possibly go well?"
Later, at another time, the three brothers all returned home together; having traveled far across various kingdoms and returning from the sea, they had acquired much wealth and treasure.
Once they had arrived home, the eldest brother asked his wife:
"Did my younger brother manage the household affairs after me, and were all the necessary provisions provided to his satisfaction?"
His wife replied,
"My younger brother-in-law treats me with the utmost care, just like a biological elder brother or his own son.
Then each of his second and third brothers asked their wives:
"How shall my younger brother provide for you?
Each wife replied to her husband,
"How could one find happiness while being governed by a lowly servant-woman?"
The husband then thought to himself:
"All women are prone to strife and discord; they can cause brothers who love one another to be separated.
Later, on another occasion, his younger brother opened the storehouse of Kāśī silk.
Once the storehouse was opened, the eldest brother’s son arrived at the location; his uncle then took out a superior garment and gave it to him.
When the second and third sisters-in-law saw this and learned that he had obtained the object, they each sent their own sons to go and demand it back.
When he arrived later, that storehouse was already closed; they instead brought out coarse garments from another storehouse.
Seeing his son arrive, the uncle immediately gave these garments to him.
Each of these sons put on their respective garments and departed, returning to their own rooms.
When their mother saw this, she said to her husband:
"Did you see that just now?"
"The elder brother's son has obtained fine garments, while my son, upon requesting them, received only coarse clothing.
At that time, her husband thought to himself:
"The elder brother's son must surely have access to the storehouse of Kāśi cloth."
"My sons and others should also have access to the other storehouses.
Later, on another occasion, his younger brother opened the honey storehouse.
When his eldest nephew came to the location of the storehouse, his uncle saw him and gave him a bundle of honey.
When his two or three sisters-in-law saw this, they immediately sent their son to fetch the rock honey.
When the son arrived, the storehouse was already closed; due to the power of karma, he was unable to eat it.
Upon encountering an open storehouse of granulated sugar, his uncle saw it and took some with him before departing.
When the sisters-in-law witnessed this event, they said to their husband,
"Do you see this now?"
"The other son has obtained rock honey, while my beloved son has instead received granulated sugar.
Thus his wife slandered and provoked him again and again without ceasing. His second and third brothers were then on the verge of separating from him; they deliberated together, and one said:
"If we do not divide the property immediately, all our wealth will surely be lost; we should divide it at once."
Another said again: "This will not do;
we should call for our eldest brother. Yet another spoke:
"This matter cannot yet be divided; we should deliberate upon it together.

If it must be divided, let the household goods and the external fields and estates constitute one portion, the items in the storehouse and the assets for trade constitute another portion, and Pūrṇa shall constitute the third portion."
"If our elder brother takes the estates and household goods, we shall take the treasury and the trade goods; this will suffice for our livelihood.
If our brother takes the treasury and the trade goods, we shall take the estates and the household goods; likewise, we shall be able to support our wives and children."
"Once we have divided that one person who is complete among us, we shall each punish ourselves for our own suffering.
Having deliberated thus, they went to their elder brother and said to him:
"If we do not divide [the inheritance] now, none of us will survive."
The elder brother replied to him, saying, "The ruin of our family estate is entirely due to your wife; you should now reflect upon this most carefully.
His younger brother answered:
"We two have already investigated thoroughly and understood in detail; we know full well that they ought to be separated.
His elder brother replied to them, "If it is so, you should assemble those who are skilled in adjudicating legal cases."
His younger brother replied:
"I have already deliberated and the proportions are settled; why is it necessary to summon a judge?
Divide what we possess into three parts: [one for myself, one for my mother, and one for you]."
Household goods and cultivated fields constitute one portion; the contents of the storehouses along with trade goods constitute the second portion; and the cattle constitute the third portion.
His elder brother replied, "Why have you divided it into only three parts? Does our younger brother, Pūrṇa, have no share?
The two younger brothers answered:
“Since Pūrṇa is the son of a slave woman, how could he have a share?
Nevertheless, I have already set aside one portion from the total of our household assets.
If you desire it, brother, take it as your portion.”
At that time, the elder brother thought to himself:
"When my father was approaching his death, he spoke these words:
'You must protect and guard him; do not abandon him.'"
“Even material wealth and possessions may yet be abandoned;
however, this younger brother of yours, you ought to take him in.
Having thought thus, he immediately replied:
"As you have said, I shall now take full possession.
Once the property had been divided, the one who received the house took up residence therein and drove his sister-in-law out, saying:
"Leave my house at once; do not enter it again."
His sister-in-law asked,
"For what reason is this so?
His brother replied:
"I have now received my share.
Then the treasurer and the merchant quickly went to the storehouse and spoke these words:
"Pūrṇa, come out; do not return again."
Pūrṇa asked, "Why is it so?
His elder brother replied:
"I have already received my share.
Then his elder sister-in-law departed with Pūrṇa and went to the home of their relatives.
At that time, the sons were crying from hunger, so the sister-in-law said to Pūrṇa:
"The child is crying from hunger; you may give him some food.
Pūrṇa replied, "Give me money instead."
His sister-in-law said, "You conduct trade with hundreds of millions of gold coins according to the seasons; how could you possibly allow your son to lack even the money for his daily meals?
Pūrṇa replied:
"How could I have known beforehand that I would encounter such dispersal and the ruin of my household affairs?
Had I foreseen this, I would have taken my immeasurable billions of gold and stored them elsewhere."
It is the nature of women to often tie up bad coins in the corners of their garments.
At that time, the elder sister-in-law immediately untied the bad coins from within her garment and gave them to her brother-in-law, instructing him to buy food and drink.
Having obtained the money, the uncle immediately went through the streets and alleys to seek food and drink; there he encountered a man carrying firewood to sell.
The firewood he was selling was actually floating wood from the sea—ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*).
At that time, the wood-seller was struck by the bitter cold and stood there shivering from hunger.
Seeing him, Pūrṇa asked,
"For what reason are you trembling like this now?"
The man replied, "I do not know why this is so;
I am merely shivering from the cold while carrying this firewood.
Pūrṇa, being well-acquainted with various woods, immediately inspected it and saw that within the bundle was gośīrṣa sandalwood. He then asked:
"How much money do you require for these logs that you are now selling?
The man replied,
"I require five hundred."
Pūrṇa replied, "I shall give you five hundred coins. Having said this,
he took the sandalwood from the bundle of firewood, went to the marketplace, and cut it into four pieces.
Having sold the ends of the wood he had cut for a thousand coins, he took five hundred of them and gave them to the wood-seller.
He instructed him to deliver the firewood to his sister-in-law's place, sending word ahead to say:
"Pūrṇa has sent this to be delivered."
The man took the firewood to his sister-in-law’s place and told her,
“Pūrṇa sent me to deliver this firewood.
Upon seeing him, his sister-in-law immediately beat her breast and spoke these words:
"How bewildering is his ruin! His wealth has been dissipated, yet why is his wisdom likewise absent?
He sends for cooked food, but only raw wood is delivered; there is nothing even to cook."
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Fascicle II;
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya,
Fascicle III.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
At that time, the King of Śūrpāraka was afflicted with a fever so severe that he became delirious and fainting.
A physician prescribed a remedy, stating that the king’s body should be anointed with powdered gośīrṣa-candana.
The Emperor commanded his great ministers, "Seek out and procure ox-head sandalwood (gośīrṣa-candana) with all speed.
Those ministers arrived at the place of Pūrṇa and asked him, "We now require ox-head sandalwood; do you have any?"
Pūrṇa replied, "I have but a little now. He asked:
"How much money is required?
He replied,
"One thousand coins are needed."

Then, having given the money, that minister obtained a small amount of sandalwood powder; he brought it to the king, ground it, and applied it to the king’s body, whereupon the ailment was immediately cured.
At that time, the king had this thought:
"If a king's treasury does not contain gośīrṣa sandalwood, how can he truly be a king?
He then asked his ministers:
"From where did you obtain this sandalwood that you have brought?
The minister replied,
"I obtained it from the place of Perfection."
The king then immediately dispatched a messenger to summon Pūrṇa.
The messenger went to him and said,
"The king summons you now."
Pūrṇa thought to himself: "Why am I being called?
Is it not because of this sandalwood tree that they are calling for me?"
He then took three pieces of sandalwood, wrapped one in his robe and tucked it into his bosom, while holding another in his hand as he departed.
Once the King had seen him, he asked: "Pūrṇa!"
"Do you have this sandalwood now?
Pūrṇa immediately showed him the wood, and the king asked,
"How much is this wood worth?"
He replied,
"The value of this wood is one hundred million taels of gold.
The king asked again:
"Do you have anything more? Pūrṇa replied,
"I do indeed have more."
He then took three pieces and presented them to the king.
The king immediately said to his ministers,
"Give Pūrṇa four hundred million taels of gold."
Pūrṇa said to the king:
"As for the three pieces, take their value;
as for one piece, I shall present it to Your Majesty."
The king immediately gave him three hundred million taels of gold and said to him,
"I am now greatly pleased with you.
What boon do you wish to seek from me?"
"I shall grant you everything.
Pūrṇa replied, "If Your Majesty,
being pleased, would grant me this wish, I pray that I may dwell in the kingdom without being deceived or oppressed."
Then the king immediately said to his ministers:
"From this day forward, it would be better to restrain the princes than to restrain this Pūrṇa."

After Pūrṇa had taken his leave of the king and departed, there were merchants in that city who heard that five hundred merchant travelers were coming from the sea and arriving at the city of Śūrpāraka.
The merchants gathered together and deliberated, saying:
"Now that these merchant travelers have arrived, we must all engage in trade collectively; none among us shall purchase goods individually."
The merchants among them replied,
"Pūrṇa must also be summoned for consultation. Others also said:
"Pūrṇa is currently destitute and has nothing; why should he be summoned?
At that time, Pūrṇa went out from the city on his rounds and heard that five hundred merchants had returned safely from the sea.
Having heard this, he immediately went to the merchants and asked,
"What goods have you brought here now?
The merchants replied:
"I have brought such and such items as these, all of which are here now. Pūrṇa replied,
"What is the price of these various items?"
The merchant replied:
"O caravan leader!
Why must you now ask again about this price?"
"You should know this for yourself.
Pūrṇa replied, "Although I know this to be so, I am now buying it myself; I should not set its own price."
"Set whatever price you wish and I shall purchase it.
The merchants set the value of their entire cargo at eighteen billion gold pieces, to which Pūrṇa replied,
"Take three billion gold pieces now, and the goods shall all be mine."
"As for the remaining gold, I shall pay it once my goods have been sold.
The merchant agreed and immediately paid him the three hundred million taels of gold he had obtained from the king.
He immediately sealed all his goods and departed, leaving them behind.
At that time, the merchants in the city sent men to inquire:
"What merchandise do you have?"
The merchant said,
"I now possess such and such goods.
The messenger replied:
“Such goods as these are already fully provided for in our own storehouses.
The merchant replied,
“Regardless of the quantity of goods in your storehouses, this item has already been sold by me.”
The messenger asked,
"To whom did you sell it first?
The merchant replied:
"Sell it to Pūrṇa.
The messenger replied,
"If you give it to Pūrṇa, you shall receive a great price."
The merchant replied,
"The goods that Pūrṇa set as his fixed price are now in my possession.
Even if I were now to sell them all to you at that fixed price, I observe that you would not be able to pay for them."
The messenger asked,
"What did you first receive from Pūrṇa?
The merchant replied:
"I obtained three hundred million taels of gold.
The messenger replied,
"Pūrṇa has stolen the property of his own brothers to the utmost degree."
Having spoken these words, he returned to the city and informed the merchant leader, saying,
"Those goods have already been sold.
The merchant leader asked:
"To whom did he sell it?
The messenger replied,
"He sold it to Pūrṇa."
The merchant leader replied, "He gave it to Pūrṇa; he should receive much wealth.
That messenger answered:
"Even if you were permitted to sell all the items set aside by Pūrṇa as a single lot, you still would not be able to complete the purchase.
The merchant leader asked,
"What kind of items did Pūrṇa set aside?"
The messenger replied,
"Three hundred million gold pieces must be left behind.
The merchant leader responded:
"He ought to steal his brother's property entirely.
Then the merchant leaders sent a messenger to summon him; once Pūrṇa had arrived, they said to him:
"We previously established an agreement that no one was to go alone to purchase goods; rather, we must collectively determine the price and then divide it among us."
"For what reason have you now arbitrarily contravened the collective regulation and purchased it alone?
Pūrṇa replied, "You established the regulation together; why then did you not inform my brothers?"
"You all should firmly uphold this regulation; it is not my business.
At that time, the merchant leader, failing to examine the reasoning, rebuked them and fined them, demanding sixty *kārsāpaṇas* from each.
At that time, Pūrṇa had not yet paid the money, so they left him exposed in the scorching heat of the sun.
Then, the king sent someone to investigate, who happened upon Pūrṇa being scorched by the midday sun and reported it to the king.
The king commanded his messenger to summon the merchant leader and Pūrṇa, and upon their arrival, he questioned them, saying:
"For what reason have you now exposed Pūrṇa to the midday sun?"
The merchant leader said, "Your Majesty, you should know that the merchant guild has established a regulation:
one must engage in trade collectively; it is not permitted to purchase goods individually."
"Now, because Pūrṇa has violated the communal regulations,
he is therefore punished. Pūrṇa replied,
"Great King!"
"Did the caravan leader inform me on the day he established the regulations?
And did he summon his elder brother?
The caravan leader replied:
"No," the King replied to the people,
"Pūrṇa has spoken well."
He then released them and they departed.
Later, when King Śubhavyūha required various goods, he summoned the merchant leaders and said to them:
"I now require such and such items; give them to me."
The merchant leader said,
"Whatever Your Majesty requires is available at Pūrṇa.
The king said:
“Pūrṇa has fulfilled my previous command and bestowed peace and happiness upon them;
for this reason, I do not seek it from him now.
You all should now go to Pūrṇa’s place and purchase it there.”
Then that merchant leader sent a messenger to summon Pūrṇa, who replied,
"I cannot go. After the messenger returned with this report,
the merchant leaders gathered at Pūrṇa’s location and arrived outside his door.
Then the gatekeeper informed Pūrṇa, saying,
"The various merchant leaders have all gathered outside the gate and wish to see you for a moment.
Pūrṇa was arrogant and only went out after several days had passed.
Having seen this, the merchant leader said to him:
"Great merchant leader!
I now wish to obtain such and such items; please provide them to me at their original price."
Pūrṇa replied, "I am a merchant leader,
and my primary purpose is to seek profit.
If I were to accept the original price, how could I truly be considered a merchant leader?"
That person replied, “Great caravan leader!
I shall now give you a double profit; please give it to me.”
Pūrṇa thought to himself:
"These merchants have all come here; they should be treated with respect. Since they have already received double the price, I ought to give it to them."
Having formed this thought, he immediately gave it to him.
From among the goods, he sold only those worth fifteen billion *niṣkas* of gold to repay the remaining debt, while the rest of the items were left in the warehouse.
He thought to himself:
"Like the morning dew, how could it ever fill a jar?
I must enter the great ocean to seek precious treasures."
At that time, the merchant leader Pūrṇa immediately dispatched a messenger to the city of Śūrpāraka to beat the drum and assemble the crowd, proclaiming these words:
"You merchants of this city, you should know now that the merchant leader Pūrṇa intends to go to the great ocean in order to seek precious jewels."
"Whoever wishes to go, let them depart together with Pūrṇa.
At whatever place they must travel, there is no need to purchase the path.
At whatever ferry-crossing they reach, they shall cross the great ocean without having to pay the fare."
"All those who wish to go [to sea], bring whatever goods are fit for the ocean here.
Having thus proclaimed, the five hundred merchants brought all the goods suitable for entering the sea and arrived.

Then the merchant leader Pūrṇa, together with the other merchants, having made auspicious vows, entered the great ocean surrounded by five hundred merchants; they acquired vast wealth and returned in safety.
Thus, these six [merchants] entered the sea and all returned safely and soundly, their fame spreading far and wide.
Eventually, there were merchants in Śrāvastī who took many goods and came to enter the city of Tāmraliptī.
Having come to rest, they went to Pūrṇa and said to him:
"Caravan leader!
We, too, wish to enter the great ocean."
He replied, "Have you ever heard of those who entered the sea by means of the six perfections and returned in safety? Would it be possible for you to enter as well?
The people reported back, saying:
"We have come from afar,
relying entirely upon you, O Benevolent One, to ensure our safe entry into the sea.
If you do not go, how could we dare to proceed!"
When Pūrṇa heard these words, he thought to himself:
"Although I do not seek wealth for myself now, for the sake of benefiting him, I ought to go to sea."
Having formed this thought, he immediately entered the great ocean together with the merchants.

Those merchants constantly recited throughout the day and night the Udāna verses, the verses of the Elders (Theragāthā), the Sela verses, the verses of the Muni, the Saṃyuttanikāya, and so forth, reciting them with wondrous voices that were clear and resonant.
Having heard this, Pūrṇa asked,
"You are truly skilled at singing.
The merchants replied:
“Caravan leader!
This is not singing. Pūrṇa asked:
"What words are these?
the merchant replied,
"These are the words spoken by the Buddha."
Pūrṇa had never before heard the name of the Buddha-Dharma; hearing it today, the hairs on his body stood on end and he conceived deep faith.
He then asked the merchants, "Who is the Buddha?"
He replied:

"There is a śramaṇa Gautama, born of the Śākya clan, who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robe, and out of right faith has gone forth from home. Having abandoned his kingdom and city, he dwells in the mountain forests and has attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; he is called the Buddha."
He asked him again,
"Where does the Buddha reside at this time?
He replied:
"He is currently at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī.
Having heard this, Pūrṇa took these words to heart and returned safely with the merchants.
At that time, his elder brother Ananda thought to himself:
"My younger brother Pūrṇa has endured great hardship crossing the ocean; I should find him a wife.
Having had this thought, he said to him:
“Whose daughter among the families of wealthy elders or merchant lords do you now desire? I shall now take her as your bride for you.
Pūrṇa replied, “I have no desire to take a wife now; I pray that my elder brother will permit me to go forth into the religious life.”
His elder brother replied, "In the past,
when I was destitute, why did I not leave the household life?
Now that I possess abundant wealth and treasures, how could I wish to renounce the world!"
Pūrṇa replied,
“One cannot go forth into homelessness when one is destitute;
now that I possess wealth, I ought to go forth.”
Knowing that his brother’s resolve was firm, the elder brother granted him permission, saying,
"I certainly allow you to go forth.
He then replied to his brother:

"Those who enter the great ocean encounter many perils and sufferings; those who enter are extremely numerous, while those who return are extremely few. One must certainly not enter the great ocean again."
"The many treasures and riches I have obtained are all due to the power of my merit and are not deceptive.
As for the wealth obtained by my second and third elder brothers, it is entirely impure."
"If after my passing, you should live together with your elder brother and your two younger brothers, you must certainly not consent to this.
Having spoken thus, he took a single attendant and immediately departed for Śrāvastī.
Having arrived at a grove, he stayed there and sent a messenger to inform the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"The caravan leader Pūrṇa is now in the grove and wishes to see you."
Having heard this, the elder reflected:
"The caravan leader Pūrṇa has undergone great toil and fatigue crossing the sea; now he has come here by land.
He then asked the messenger:
“Pūrṇa, how many things have you brought with you now?
The messenger replied, “I am merely your attendant; I have brought nothing.”
At that time, the householder again had this thought:
"This is a person of great merit; he should not enter the city in such a manner. I ought to go out to meet him with elephants, horses, and attendants."
Having had this thought, he immediately escorted the elephant and horse to his home, bathed them with scented water, and prepared various foods and drinks.
When the meal was finished, the elder asked:
"O Merchant Lord!..."
"For what reason have you come now?
Pūrṇa replied, "O Householder!"
"I now wish, within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata, to go forth, receive the precepts, and become a bhikṣu.
At that time, the elder straightened his body, extended his hands, and exclaimed:
"How extraordinary! How rare!"
The appearance of the Triple Gem—the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha—in this world is rare; that you, O benevolent one, have been able to renounce the household life is likewise rare.
To possess abundant wealth and a vast circle of kinsmen, yet to relinquish them all and go forth as a renunciant, is even more rare.
Then that householder, together with the caravan leader, went in person to where the Buddha was.

At that time, the World-Honored One was teaching the Dharma to an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus; he saw the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and the caravan leader Pūrṇa approaching the place where the Buddha was.
Having seen this, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This householder Anāthapiṇḍada has offered me a priceless jewel; among those who deliver sentient beings within the Buddha-dharma, none surpasses him."
After Anāthapiṇḍada the Elder and the caravan leader Pūrṇa had prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, they withdrew to sit on one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This is the caravan leader Pūrṇa; he desires to go forth in this well-spoken Dharma, to receive full ordination, and to attain the status of a bhikṣu."
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will allow him to go forth and receive the precepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently granted his consent.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the merchant leader Pūrṇa:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!
You should practice the holy life.

As soon as the Blessed One had spoken these words, Pūrṇa’s hair and beard fell away instantly, just like those who have been shaved for seven days; the saṃghāṭī robe naturally appeared upon his body, and he held his water flask and bowl, endowed with perfect deportment, no different from a bhikṣu of a hundred years' standing.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The World-Honored One commanded, 'Come! Hair fell away and robes and bowl were complete;
All faculties became tranquil and settled, And as he thought, all was accomplished."
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇa prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I pray only that the World-Honored One will skillfully expound for me the essential points of the Dharma, so that having heard those essential points from the Buddha, I may dwell alone in a secluded place without further negligence, and by practicing with single-minded diligence, attain dwelling in peace and security.”

Therefore, I have now renounced my home and family, left the household life out of right faith, shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and practiced the holy life, so as to realize and attain supernormal knowledge and wisdom within this very life.
"My births are exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.
After he had spoken these words, the World-Honored One said to him:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
As you have requested, you shall hear the essentials of the Dharma, leading even to the state of no further existence. Therefore, Pūrṇa!
Listen attentively and reflect well upon it!
I shall explain it for you.
When there is visual consciousness, one perceives forms that possess lovely radiance; these are pleasing things associated with desire, which cause people to become attached.
When a bhikṣu perceives these various desires, he gives rise to a longing for them, praises and becomes attached to them; from this, a heart of fondness and delight arises.
Once there is fondness and delight, greed immediately arises;
because of this greedy mind, he becomes united with desire.
Because it is associated with joy and craving, it is far removed from nirvāṇa.
Paripūrṇa! Since there is auditory consciousness, one cognizes sounds;

The nose-consciousness cognizes odors; the tongue-consciousness cognizes tastes; the body-consciousness cognizes tangibles; and the mind-consciousness cognizes mental phenomena (*dharma*). These are lovely and radiant, as explained in detail above, up to and including the seclusion of *nirvāṇa*.
“Pūrṇa! When one possesses the eye and perceives forms— those that are lovely, radiant, pleasing, and so forth—
as previously described, if one is able to remain free from attachment, one draws near to Nirvāṇa.”
"I have explained this essential, abbreviated teaching for you.
Now, in what state do you wish to abide? Pūrṇa replied:
"I have now heard the essential meaning of the Dharma from the Buddha and wish to dwell in that country of Sūrpāraka.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"The people dwelling in that country are for the most part violent and evil, fierce, coarse, and cruel; they are prone to anger and malicious abuse."
If those people were to revile you with harsh words, treat you with anger and brutality, and humiliate and slander you in the midst of the assembly—regarding such matters, what would you think?
Pūrṇa replied: "If they revile me, or even slander me, I shall form this thought:
'These people are indeed virtuous and good, for they do not strike me with sticks, wood, tiles, stones, fists, feet, or the like.'"
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"The people of that country are exceedingly violent and evil, fierce, coarse, and cruel, harboring malice and anger.
If they were to strike you with wood, stones, or the like, what would you think?"
Pūrṇa replied:
“World-Honored One!
If the people of that country were to come and strike me with wood, stones, their hands, or other means, I would think to myself:”
"The people of that country are exceedingly virtuous and good; they did not harm me with swords or blades.
The Buddha again addressed Pūrṇa, saying:
"The people of that country harbor extreme malice; they are fierce, violent, and cruel."
"If someone were to harm you with swords, blades, wood, or stones, what would you think?
Pūrṇa replied: "I would think thus:"
"Those people were exceedingly virtuous; although they harmed me with swords and blades, they did not take my life.
The Buddha again addressed Pūrṇa, saying, "The people of that country harbored extreme malice and were fierce, coarse, and cruel."
"If your life were to end right now,
what would you think? Pūrṇa replied,
"If that person were to take my life, I would think thus:"

"There are disciples of the Buddha who, weary even of their karmic bodies and the various sufferings they endure, harbor a sense of shame and take their own lives by means of weapons, poison, or other expedients."
"The people of that country who are able to take my life are most virtuous and good; they enable me to leave this defiled body without having to undergo personal hardship.
At that time, the Buddha said to Pūrṇa:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
That you are now able to accomplish an intention that is gentle, pliant, patient, and compliant, and thus gain entry into that land—this is right.
You should go there; you shall transcend suffering, and you should also lead others across.
"You shall swiftly attain liberation and should likewise liberate others;
you shall attain peace and security and should likewise bring peace and security to others;
you shall attain nirvana and should cause others to attain nirvana."
When the Venerable Pūrṇa had heard what the Buddha said, he was filled with great joy, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇa stayed overnight at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park; then, in the early morning, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city to beg for alms.
Having finished his meal, he gathered his bedding and left it behind, then took up his robes and bowl and traveled toward the country of Suṇāparantaka.
Wandering through the human world, he arrived at the outskirts of a city and stayed there for the night; at dawn, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
He encountered a hunter holding a bow and arrows who was about to leave the city to roam and hunt.
Upon seeing Pūrṇa, he spoke these words:
"I am now about to go hunting; to see a shaven-headed śramaṇa is most inauspicious."
He immediately drew his bow and, heading toward Pūrṇa, ran swiftly with the intent to shoot.
Seeing this, Pūrṇa immediately lifted his robe, exposing his belly, and said to him:
"O noble one!"
"You may shoot at its belly.
He then spoke a verse, saying:
"Wild birds in the sky and deer in the forest, For the sake of seeking food and drink, are caught in nets and snares."
Those who engage in battle, grasping swords and blades, Mutually slaughter one another until they meet their destruction.
Tormented by the suffering of hunger and thirst, hungry ghosts Seek food in the form of iron balls and molten copper;
Because of this belly of mine from time immemorial, I have been permitted to undergo all manner of sufferings within saṃsāra.
At that time, the hunter thought to himself:
"This renunciant has cultivated patience and has now perfected it; how could I ever harm such a person?"
He immediately conceived faith.
Then, the Venerable Pūrṇa preached the sublime Dharma to him, leading him to take refuge in the Triple Gem and receive the five precepts.

At that time, there were separately five hundred men who became upāsakas and five hundred women who became upāsikās; they constructed five hundred monasteries (vihāras) within that city and provided them with countless rope beds, wooden beds, and bedding of various sizes.
Having completed [the preparations], he remained there for the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*).

When the three months were fulfilled, within this very body he severed all afflictions and realized the fruit of Arhatship. Possessing the three knowledges (*trividyā*) and the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and endowed with the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), he attained knowledge in accordance with reality:
"Birth has been exhausted; the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence."

The mind is without obstruction, like a hand waving through space; whether cut by a blade or smeared with incense, love and hatred are equal; viewing gold and earth as identical and without distinction; there is nothing among fame or profit that is not relinquished; and Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas pay him complete reverence.
Later, at another time, the elder brother, the brahmin Karṇila, had two younger brothers whose wealth and resources had both been entirely squandered.
Then those two younger brothers went to their elder brother and said,
"That man without marks is truly destitute and impoverished."
"Now he has already departed from our home.
We, his brothers, ought to live together again and dwell in harmony.
Then, Mudrāpāṇi asked her younger brother:
"Who is the one without marks?
The two younger brothers replied,
"That Pūrṇa is."
The elder brother replied again:
"This is Śrīgupta; how could he be without auspicious marks?
Yet, in our family, it is one with superior marks who is born, not one who is destitute and lacks auspicious marks."
At that time, the two younger brothers spoke again to their elder brother, saying:
"Since Paripūrṇa, who possesses both marks and lack of marks, has now departed, we shall simply remain together in harmony, dwelling in one place."
The elder brother replied again:
"The wealth you have acquired is entirely unlawful;
the wealth I have acquired is all lawful. Therefore, I shall not live together with you."
The two younger brothers said again:
"Because that servant girl entered the great ocean and traveled back and forth seeking wealth, she has obtained treasures which she intends to give all to her elder brother."
"Having obtained another's wealth, our elder brother has begun to praise it and disparage us.
What power does he have that enables him to enter the great ocean to seek out precious treasures?"
Upon hearing his younger brother’s words, the elder brother was filled with resentment and pride, and he thought to himself:
"I shall go forth once more into the great ocean.

He immediately boarded a large ship and set out for the place of treasures. Suddenly, a violent storm arose, driving the vessel until it reached an island where the mountains were entirely composed of ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*).
Then the merchants said to one another, "In the past we have heard of ox-head sandalwood, but only now have we seen it; it is guarded by the Great Sovereign Yakṣa, who possesses wondrous crystal."
"At that time, the yakṣa was not present; you may fasten your resolve and cut it down immediately.
Thereupon, they used five hundred axes to hew it down all at once.
At that moment, there was a yakṣa named Kāraka who saw the merchants using their various axes to fell the forest.
Having seen this, he immediately went to the abode of the yakṣa Maheśvara and reported:
"O Lord of Spirits!
Within the sandalwood grove, five hundred men are cutting down the trees."
"You may know this, O Benevolent One.

At that time, having finished his business, the Great Yakṣa conceived a sense of indignation; by means of his supernatural power, he unleashed a great and violent wind, and his body followed it as it traveled to that continent.
At that time, the helmsman, seeing the wind arrive, addressed the crewmen, saying:
"Gentlemen, you should know that what was formerly heard of as 'black winds' is this very wind; it is truly difficult to encounter. You must reflect deeply and skillfully employ expedient means."
Upon hearing this, those merchants were struck with terror; their hair stood on end, and each called to mind the deity they traditionally worshipped, speaking in verse:
"Lord of Water, Wind, and Devas, Śakra, and the celestial sages;
The Nāga kings, the hosts of Yakṣas, and the deities of the Asuras."
Now that I have encountered this calamity, I pray only to those Honored Ones;
overcome with extreme terror, save me from this perilous distress.
Whether seeking Śakra elsewhere, or prostrating before Mahābrahmā—
"O tree deity of the stage of mastery, you who are able to provide protection—
now that I have encountered this 'demon-wind,' I pray only that you will grant me protection.
At that time, the wooden peg remained silent, paying no heed to the celestial deity.
Then the merchant leaders and others asked him, saying:
"We are beset by extreme calamity and suffering is pressing upon us; why do you remain silent?
He replied:
"My younger brother once said:
'Those who enter the great ocean all undergo extreme toil and hardship, and there are many perils and afflictions.
Because they are intoxicated by greed, those who enter the sea are many, but those who return are few; you must certainly not enter the sea.'"
"I disregarded my brother's words and entered the great ocean; now that I have encountered this calamity, what should I do?
The merchants asked, "Who was this brother of yours?"
He replied, "It is Pūrṇa.
The merchant said:
"He is the noble one Paripūrṇa, a person of great merit; you all should take refuge in him.
Then the merchants, with single-mindedness and in unison, cried out:
"Namo to the noble Paripūrṇa!"
"Homage to the Noble One Pūrṇa!

At that time, there was a goddess who had previously conceived faith and reverence toward the Venerable Pūrṇa. Seeing that the merchant had dedicated his merit through the intention of making an offering, she went to Pūrṇa’s location; having arrived, she addressed him, saying, "Noble One!..."
"Your elder brother, O Benevolent One, is undergoing extreme suffering; you ought to bring him to mind.
Having heard these words, Pūrṇa gave rise to mindfulness and entered such a meditative concentration.
By means of his power of concentration, he vanished from the human realm of Sūrpāraka and immediately went to the ocean, where he sat atop the mast of his elder brother’s ship.
At that moment, the black wind immediately turned back, as if obstructed by Mount Sumeru.
Then the yakṣa Maheśvara thought to himself:
"In the past, all ships have been driven astray by this black wind, destroyed and submerged."
"Why has this black wind now turned back, as if obstructed by Mount Sumeru, unable to cause any harm?
At that time, the yakṣa looked about in every direction and saw the Venerable Pūrṇa sitting cross-legged atop the mast of the ship.
Upon seeing this, the yakṣa immediately said:
"Noble Maṇḍanapūrṇa! Why do you trouble me?"
Pūrṇa replied, "O Leader!
How could I have troubled you?"
"If I do not obtain these merits, I shall surely cause my elder brother to perish,
leaving his name in vain. Mahādeva Yakṣa said,
"Noble One!"
"This grove of ox-head sandalwood is protected by me as a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin King)," Pūrṇa replied.
"O Leader! [he continued].
"What do you think: between the Buddha and a wheel-turning monarch, which is more noble?
The yakṣa asked, "Noble one!"
"World-Honored One, has he now appeared in the world?
Pūrṇa replied, "He has indeed appeared in the world."
The yakṣa replied, "If it is so, while the ship is not yet full, you should take on a heavy load.
At that time, those merchants had previously been seized by terror and their lives were nearly at an end; hearing these words now, they suddenly revived.
Once those merchants had attained safety, they conceived a sense of reverence for the noble Pūrṇa.
They then took a ship filled with gośīrṣa sandalwood and departed, arriving at the city of Śroṇāparāntaka.
Having arrived, Paripūrṇa said to his elder brother,
"If one encounters shipwreck at sea and, by reciting that person's name, returns safely through the power of their mindfulness, whatever goods they obtain shall belong entirely to them."
"Brother, you may now take these various precious objects and give them to the merchants.
As for me, I shall now use this ox-head sandalwood to construct a sandalwood vihāra for the Buddha."
The elder brother immediately took those precious objects and distributed them among the merchants.
As for the *gośīrṣa-candana*, Pūrṇa wished to establish a vihāra for the Buddha; he therefore summoned skilled artisans to deliberate upon its value:
"O craftsmen, would you prefer to take five hundred coins per day, or one handful of *gośīrṣa-candana* powder per day?"
The master craftsmen replied, "We wish to take one handful daily of powdered gośīrṣa sandalwood.
Once this agreement was reached, they immediately began construction; before many days had passed, the vihāra was completed.
Having entrusted the work to the craftsmen, he took the remaining wood shavings and fine dust, mixed them together, ground them, and used the paste to coat the vihāra.
The brothers Pūrṇa and his sibling, who had previously harbored mutual resentment, were all made to reconcile; he then spoke these words:
"Now you should invite the Tathāgata and his disciples."
The elder brothers asked,
"Venerable Pūrṇa! Where is the Tathāgata,
the World-Honored One, now residing?"
The Noble One replied, “In Śrāvastī.
He asked again:
"Is this city near or far? Pūrṇa replied,
"It is about a hundred li or so."
The elder brothers replied, "We wish first to seek an audience with the King of our own country; will he grant us permission?
The Noble One replied:
"Consult as you wish.
Then his elder brothers went to the king's presence and said,
"Great King!"
"We now wish to invite the Buddha and the Sangha to offer them a供养 (dāna). We pray that Your Majesty will grant us permission and assist us in its preparation.
The King said, "Do as you please;
I shall assist you in providing the offerings."

At that time, Pūrṇa ascended to the upper story of the high pavilion; kneeling with both knees upon the ground, he gazed afar toward the Jeta Grove, burning incense and scattering flowers, purifying the site with water from a golden pitcher, and extending his invitation from a distance by speaking these verses:
"O you of pure precepts and wondrous wisdom, Who can know those who take refuge;
You who skillfully discern those without protection— I pray that you accept my humble request."

Having spoken these verses, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, the flowers he had scattered merged into a single canopy, which traveled directly to the Jeta Grove and remained suspended in mid-air above the Buddha’s head.
The incense that was burned, through the Buddha’s supernormal power, formed a mass of clouds in the void.
The water poured from the golden vases, through the Buddha’s supernormal power, appeared like pillars of vaidūrya.
The Venerable Ānanda, seeing these auspicious signs, joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"These auspicious signs must surely indicate that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus are being invited."
"I do not know from where I have come now.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
"I have come from the city of Śūrpāraka.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How far is that city from here?"
The Buddha said, "It is some one hundred li away. Go there and take the voting sticks, and announce to the bhikṣus:
'If you are able to accept the invitation of Pūrṇa from the city of Śrughna tomorrow, you should take this stick.'"
Ānanda replied, “So be it, World-Honored One.
He then took up the tally and stood before the Buddha; he passed it on in succession, and the Buddha himself took the tally, as did the elder bhikṣus who received them in turn.
At that time, the Venerable Elder Pūrṇa Māṇava was also among them, wishing to take a voting tally.
Then Ānanda spoke a verse for the sake of Pūrṇa:
"Venerable one, you should know: Now he is no longer the Lord of the Sārās."
Nor was it at the home of Sudatta, nor did Lady Gopikā provide the food and drink.
To the city of Śrāvastī shall those who have attained supernormal powers go.
"You should remain silent.
At that time, the Elder Pūrṇa possessed great wisdom but had not cultivated supernatural powers (abhijñā). He thought to himself:
"Although I have severed all afflictions (kleśa), because I have not cultivated supernatural powers, my state is no different from the supernatural powers possessed by the non-Buddhists (tīrthika)."
Having formed this thought, he immediately exerted great diligence and attained supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

At that time, as Ānanda was distributing the voting sticks (*śalākā*), when it reached the third elder and before the stick had been received, the monk Pūrṇa, who was using his head as a pillow, reached out his hand with his supernatural power to take the stick and spoke this verse:

"One does not attain supernatural powers through physical appearance, Nor through extensive learning or eloquence in speech; [One attains them] by abandoning all defilements And by cultivating the path of the noble ones."
"Yet by the power of tranquility, ethical discipline, and wisdom, one may realize [the goal] even if the body is old and diseased.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This Pūrṇa Māṇava is the foremost among my assembly of bhikṣu śrāvakas; none can surpass him in receiving the voting tally through supernormal powers (ṛddhi). He should be given it first."
"It is said that the Elder’s bowl and pillow were perfected, and by means of drawing lots, he immediately realized the six supernormal powers.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"You should inform the bhikṣus:"
"I have previously taught you, O bhikṣus: whatever wholesome deeds you have performed, they should be kept concealed;
whatever unwholesome deeds you have performed, they should be confessed."
"Now, there are many followers of various non-Buddhist paths within that city; therefore, you should manifest your supernatural powers, go to that city, and receive the perfect meal."
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
Having received these instructions, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The Blessed One has given this instruction: 'I have previously commanded that all good deeds of the bhikṣus should be concealed, and all evil deeds should be confessed.'"
"Now, within that city, there are many non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas). Therefore, you all should go into that city and manifest supernatural powers (ṛddhi).

At that time, the king of that country cleared away the filth and refuse within the city, sprinkled the ground with sandalwood-scented water, burned various exquisite incenses in precious censers, hung up banners and canopies, and scattered flowers of various colors, adorning and embellishing the city on all sides.
Within that city there were eighteen gates, and the king had seventeen sons; outside each gate they arrayed various offerings.
The king and his ministers stood at the main gate, arranging their mounted attendants to await the World-Honored One.
His seventeen sons were at another small gate waiting for the World-Honored One.

At that time, Pūrṇa, Dāruka, and Trapuṣa were also outside the gate; eventually, the Buddha appointed five officials to perform the duties, who arrived at the house first by means of their supernormal powers.
What are these five?
First, knowing the matter of vegetables; second, knowing the utensils; third, knowing the fodder for eating; fourth, knowing pure water; and fifth, knowing cooked food.
When the king saw the five men arriving through the air, he asked Pūrṇa,
"Is this the World-Honored One? Pūrṇa replied:
"These are the five officials who have come here to conduct an inspection;
that is to say, those who oversee everything from the vegetables up to the cooked food.
Before the World-Honored One arrives, they first manifest various and immeasurable supernatural powers."
"The elders have also not yet arrived.
The King asked again:
"Venerable Pūrṇa!"
“World-Honored One, why have you come so late?
He replied, “I first sent the overseer to come; the World-Honored One arrived afterwards.”
At that time, another upāsaka spoke in verse:
"Lions, tigers, elephants, and dragons, and oxen, Adorned their seats with various precious objects;
Some had jeweled canopies and jeweled mountains, With exquisite jeweled trees and chariots all interlaced."
Some ride upon clouds in the midst of space, manifesting great radiance as an adornment;
by the power of their supernormal faculties, they dwell in the void and come joyfully to this city.
Some emerge from the earth, while others enter the earth from the sky;
some surge up into the air and sit in silence—behold these inconceivable miraculous transformations.

At that time, the World-Honored One washed his two feet outside the door, returned to his original chamber, arranged his bedding and seat, and sat cross-legged with body upright and mindfulness established, pressing the ground with his raised foot.

At that time, the great earth shook in six ways: namely, it moved, shook everywhere, and shook equally everywhere; it even quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; it surged in the east and subsided in the west, surged in the west and subsided in the east, surged in the south and subsided in the north, surged in the north and subsided in the south, surged in the center and subsided at the edges, and surged at the edges and subsided in the center.
Then the king asked Pūrṇa:
"Noble One! What kind of omen is this?"
Pūrṇa replied, "This is because the World-Honored One pressed the earth with his foot within his own chamber, whereby the great earth shook in six ways.
At that time, the Tathāgata emitted golden light; by this radiance, the entire earth was illuminated as if it were molten gold.
The king, seeing this rare and wondrous sign, felt joy arise in his heart and asked Pūrṇa:
"Noble One! What is the cause of this?"
Pūrṇa replied, "This is the Tathāgata emitting golden light, by which this great earth has all become golden.
At that time, the World-Honored One was himself tamed and surrounded by those who were tamed.
"Being himself serene, surrounded by those who are serene," and so forth, as explained at length.
He went with five hundred arhats to the city of Śūrpāraka.
At that time, in the Jeta Grove, a goddess held a branch of a bhallātaka tree and followed behind the World-Honored One, shading him from above.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the latent tendencies, faculties, and inclinations of that goddess, taught her the Dharma of the Noble Truths according to her aspirations. Having heard the Dharma, the goddess used the vajra-pestle of wisdom to shatter the twenty peaks of the mountain of afflictions—the views of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi)—and immediately realized the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti).

Later, at another time, five hundred upāsikās from a different location saw the World-Honored One from afar. His body was adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, his majestic radiance blindingly brilliant; he was like the simultaneous light of a thousand suns shining forth, upright and exquisite, like a mountain of jewels.
When that upāsikā saw the World-Honored One, she was filled with immense joy, just as a person who has diligently practiced meditative concentration for twelve years feels in their heart;
yet the joy felt by one destined for deliverance upon seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is many times greater than that.
It is like a person who has no son obtaining a son, a poor man obtaining treasure, or an ordinary person becoming a king—their body and mind are filled with joy;
when those who delight in roots of goodness first see the Buddha, the joy that arises in their hearts is even greater than that.
At that time, the Blessed One, knowing that the time had come to discipline that female lay devotee (upāsikā), sat down upon a seat prepared within the assembly of bhikṣus.
Then the upāsikā approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having understood her latent tendencies, faculties, nature, and inclinations, taught her the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. Having heard the Dharma, that upāsikā used the vajra-pestle of wisdom to shatter the twenty peaks of the mountain of afflictions consisting of the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and she immediately realized the fruit of stream-entry, perceiving the principles of the Four Truths.
When the upāsikās had attained the fruit, they all spoke these words:
"All of this is through the power of our World-Honored One, which has enabled us to attain the fruit of the unsurpassed path and perceive the principles of the Noble Truths."
This causal condition could not have been produced by my parents, nor by my kinsmen, kings, ministers, humans, devas, śramaṇas, or brahmins.

Furthermore, it can cause me to dry up the ocean of blood, destroy the mountain of bones, close off the evil realms, open the gates to the good realms and the door to nirvāṇa, establish me among gods and humans, and enable me to transcend birth and death.
"We now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and receive the five precepts to become upāsikās.
Having spoken these words, they rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"World-Honored One!"
"What practice or deed should we now perform as an act of worship?
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal power, bestowed the Buddha’s hair and nails upon the upāsikā. Having received the hair and nails, she immediately erected a stūpa.
Then the deva of that Jetavana Grove took a hundred-ribbed parasol and planted it within the stūpa, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I shall constantly make offerings to this stūpa."
Having spoken these words, he then resided by the stūpa.
At that time, the people there called it the "Household Deity Stūpa," or alternatively, the "Central Pillar of the Bakula Tree."
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Three;
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya,
Volume Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree:
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually traveled on again until he reached the dwelling place of five hundred rishis.

At that time, the flowers and fruits in that dwelling were flourishing and abundant, and food and drink were more than sufficient; yet those rishis took no heed of them, allowing all people who came to eat as they pleased.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the time had come to subdue that rishi, went to the rishi’s dwelling.

Upon arrival, by means of his supernormal power, he caused all the flowers and fruits belonging to that rishi to fall away; the clear springs and beautiful streams likewise dried up; the famous flowers and soft grasses turned withered and black; and the earthen couch where he resided spontaneously collapsed.
When the assembly of sages saw this, they rested their palms against their cheeks and remained silent, lost in sorrowful reflection.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the sages, saying:
"For what reason do you remain here lost in sorrowful reflection?"
The sages replied,
“O Noble One! Because you,
a supreme field of merit among two-legged beings, have come, our dwelling place has been transformed in such a way that we behold such suffering as this.”
The World-Honored One said:
"O assembly of sages!
For what reason have the trees, flowers, and fruits in the grove where you dwell now withered and perished?"
"Do you now wish for these flowers and fruits to be restored to their former state?
The rishi replied,
"I wish for them to be as they were before."
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal power, causing those flowers and fruits to flourish once more.
The sages were filled with extreme wonder, and they conceived faith and devotion toward the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the inclinations and latent tendencies of those hosts of sages, preached the Dharma according to their capacities.

Having heard the Dharma, the five hundred sages realized the fruit of non-returning and also attained supernormal powers. With palms joined in reverence before the World-Honored One, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We all wish to go forth within the well-expounded discipline and Dharma of the Tathāgata, receive full ordination, become bhikṣus, and practice the holy life."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words:
"Welcome, bhikṣu!
You may practice the holy life."

Having spoken these words, the hair and beards of those five hundred seers fell away of their own accord; they were clothed in saffron robes and held alms bowls and water jars. Their deportment was perfectly composed, appearing just like bhikṣus of a hundred years’ standing.
Then they spoke this verse: “The World-Honored One has proclaimed, ‘Welcome! Hair falls away and robes and bowl appear;
All faculties are tranquil and settled, Everything is accomplished as soon as it is thought of.”

At that time, those rishi-monks, through their diligent application of effort, attained the fruit of arhatship; they became weary of and detached from the three periods of time, viewing gold and earth as equal and without distinction. With their eyes, they beheld the dharma-realm as clearly as seeing the palm of their hand, remaining indifferent whether cut by a blade or anointed with fragrance.

With the sword of wisdom, he shattered the shell of birth and death; possessing the three insights and six supernormal powers, he was endowed with the eight liberations. His eloquence was unimpeded, and he completely renounced all worldly wealth, gain, craving, and offerings; thus Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas all came to make offerings to him.
Then those seers’ original preceptor addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By assuming the appearance of seers, I have deluded and misled the people of the world, causing them to fall into the three evil realms.”
“Only after I have first disciplined them will I then go forth into homelessness.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the assembly of five hundred sages who had gone forth and the bhikṣus, all traveling through the air by means of their supernormal powers in the shape of a crescent moon, gradually reached Mount Musala and settled at the dwelling place of the sage Bakula.

At that time, the seer saw from afar the World-Honored One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor excellencies; his halo extended a fathom, brilliant as a thousand suns, like a mountain of jewels, majestic and complete in every direction.
As soon as the rishi saw him, he conceived a heart of faith and devotion toward the Buddha and thought to himself:
"I shall quickly descend the mountain, wishing to see the World-Honored One so that I may draw near to him."
"However, I fear that once the Tathāgata has finished taming both himself and others, he will immediately pass away;
it would be better for me now to hurl myself down from this mountain to reach the presence of the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, that rishi threw himself down.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas never to forget their mindfulness; seeing that seer cast himself down, the World-Honored One immediately received the seer with his supernormal powers.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the seer’s inclinations and latent tendencies, preached the Dharma according to his capacity.
Having heard the Dharma, he realized the fruit of non-returning and attained supernormal powers.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Listen to me as I enter the homeless life within this well-expounded Dharma, become a bhikṣu, and constantly practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of the Tathāgata.
Then the World-Honored One said,
"Welcome, bhikṣu!"
"You should practice the holy life.

When the Buddha had finished speaking, the hair and beard of that seer fell away of their own accord, the saṃghāṭī robe was donned upon his body, and he took up the water flask and alms bowl. His deportment became perfectly composed, as described in detail previously. Then he spoke in verse:
"The World-Honored One proclaimed, 'Welcome! Hair fell away and robes and bowl were complete;
"All faculties are utterly tranquil and settled; whatever is brought to mind is fully accomplished.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Among my assembly, this bhikṣu is the most preeminent; among the śrāvakas and among those of faithful understanding, he is likewise the most preeminent—this is the bhikṣu who wears garments of tree bark."
At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by a thousand bhikṣus, performed various supernatural transformations as he proceeded toward the city of Supratiṣṭhita.
Then the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"If I enter through the gates, I fear that the gatekeepers will harbor improper thoughts."
"I should enter through the air by means of my supernormal power.
Having formed this thought, he immediately descended from the sky through his supernormal power and entered the city of Supāra.

At that time, the king of that country, along with the Venerable Pūrṇa, the one with the earring of black wood, the one with the copper earring, and the one with the tin earring, together with those seventeen princes, each accompanied by their own retinues and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people, all proceeded to where the Buddha was.

At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the great assembly before and behind him, proceeded to the palace of Candanamālā; having arrived, he spread out his seat and sat before the great assembly.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had entered the sandalwood hall, the great assembly, not seeing the Tathāgata, intended to destroy the sandalwood hall.
Then the World-Honored One reflected on this matter:
"If this hall is destroyed, it will cause the merit of these donors to vanish in darkness; I should now use my power of supernatural transformation to change it into crystal."

At that time, the interior and exterior of this hall were brilliantly illuminated, and everyone beheld the Tathāgata, who, knowing the inclinations, latent tendencies, and temperaments of those in the assembly, preached the Dharma according to their capacities.

Having heard this, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings realized great and sublime attainments: some produced the roots of goodness conducive to liberation, some entered the path of wisdom, and some realized the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship. Some gave rise to the mind of a śrāvaka-bodhi, some gave rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha-bodhi, and some gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. All those sentient beings, with single-minded reverence toward the Tathāgata, delighted in hearing the True Dharma; with the community of bhikṣus as their leaders, they remained there in silence.
At that time, the three brothers, including Mu’er-dang and his companions, made various preparations and having solemnly arranged the seats, sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
“The hour has now arrived; the meal is ready.”
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will know the time and come early.
At that time, there were two dragon kings in the great ocean:
the first was named Kāla Dragon King, and the second was named Kautumba Dragon King; they then had this thought:
"The World-Honored One is now expounding the sublime Dharma in the city of Supāra; I shall go there quickly to hear the Buddha preach the Dharma.

At that time, each of the dragon kings, together with five hundred attendants, manifested five hundred flowing rivers through their dragonic power and proceeded toward the location of the city of Supāra.
At that time, the Tathāgata thought to himself:
"If these two dragon kings reach the city of Supratiṣṭhita, they will cause this entire kingdom to be submerged and destroyed."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Maudgalyāyana: "Eat first.
For what reason?
Maudgalyāyana, you should know that there are five urgent circumstances for which one should take food first.

What are these five? First, those who have come from afar; second, those about to travel to a distant place; third, those who are ill; fourth, those who are nursing the sick; and fifth, those who are assigned administrative duties.
"For this reason, I shall have you eat first.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had first given food to Maudgalyāyana, he went quickly to the place of the Dragon King.
Having arrived, he addressed the Dragon King, saying:
“You should cherish the city of Supāra and not allow it to be destroyed.
The Naga King replied, “We have come with virtuous intentions;
we do not intend to harm even creatures as small as ants, much less wish to injure the city of Supāra or its sentient inhabitants.”
At that time, the Nāga King came to where the Buddha was. The World-Honored One said to the Nāga King:
"It should be spoken thus.
Having heard the Dharma, he took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and received the five precepts.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had bestowed the precepts of refuge, he proceeded to the place where the meal was being served.
Then the Dragon Kings and others came to observe the Buddha’s meal, each thinking to themselves:
"May the World-Honored One first accept my food; may the World-Honored One first accept my water."
The World-Honored One thought to himself:
"If I accept water from one dragon, there will be no end to those from the others; I must employ a skillful means.
He then summoned Maudgalyāyana and addressed him, saying:
"Now these five hundred dragon kings have each offered me water; it would be impossible for me to receive them individually. You should take a bowl and fetch one bowlful from the water."
Maudgalyāyana accepted the command and immediately went to fetch water, bringing it back to offer to the Buddha.
The Buddha accepted it and drank from it.
Then, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
“The World-Honored One previously said:
‘Parents perform what is difficult for their children; they nourish and raise them with milk, and teach them the various affairs of Jambudvīpa.’”
Suppose there were a person who carried their father on one shoulder and their mother on the other for a full hundred years; even so, they could not repay the kindness of their parents.
Furthermore, even if they offered all the rare treasures and ornaments of the great earth to their parents, they still could not repay them, for such acts would not constitute profound reverence.
If one's parents do not have faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, to gradually teach and lead them to believe in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha is to repay their kindness.
If one's parents previously lacked virtuous conduct, to be able to gradually teach them so that they uphold the precepts;
if one's parents are stingy and greedy, to be able to cause them to practice renunciation and giving; [this is to repay their kindness.]
"If one lacks wisdom, to cause them to possess wisdom—
such a matter as this is what is called repaying kindness.
At that time, after Maudgalyāyana had formed this thought, he further reflected:
"As the Buddha has previously taught, I have never committed such an act.
He then entered meditative concentration to observe: "In what realm has my deceased mother been reborn?
Using his divine eye, he saw that his deceased mother had been reborn in the world of Mālīcī. Having seen this, he reflected:
"Who is able to go there and transform them through the Dharma?
He further reflected to himself:
"Only the Buddha can do this; no one else is capable."
Having had this thought, he went to where the World-Honored One was and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
Parents perform for their children what is difficult to do."

"My compassionate mother has been reborn in the world of Mārīcī; as no one else is capable of going to that realm to teach and transform her, I pray only that the World-Honored One will provide instruction."
The World-Honored One replied,
"By whose supernatural power will you go to that realm?
Maudgalyāyana answered:
“I only pray that the Great Compassionate One will bestow his grace upon me; by means of my supernatural power, may I go to that world together with the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

Thereupon, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, by means of his own supernatural power, together with the Buddha, the World-Honored One, moved a single footstep such that it traversed one world-system and one Mount Sumeru.
By means of such supernatural power, he reached that realm after seven days.
When his mother saw Maudgalyāyana approaching from afar, she said, "It has been so long since we last saw you;
how have you managed to come here?"
When the people of the world of Mārīcī heard these words, they said to one another, "This girl is young; how can her son be so old?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"This woman raised me; she is my biological mother.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the inclinations, latent tendencies, and spiritual disposition of Maudgalyāyana’s mother, immediately preached the principle of the Four Noble Truths for her, enabling her to attain realization and understanding.

Having heard this, she attained the Dharma and saw the Dharma, realizing the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*). With the vajra-pestle of wisdom, she shattered the twenty mountains of the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); having destroyed the view of a self-body through the realization of the principles of the Truths, she then spoke of three causes and conditions:
"The Blessed One has benefited me. This benefit was not something that could be accomplished by my parents, the king, the devas, my kinsmen, nor by śramaṇas or brahmins."

This is the work of the Buddha: he is able to exhaust the ocean of blood, destroy the mountain of bones, close the gates to the evil realms, reveal the path to nirvana, and establish the karma of humans and devas.
He then spoke in verse:
"By the power of the World-Honored One, The paths to the evil realms are closed;
Though the evil paths abound with obstacles, He reveals the gate to Nirvāṇa."
The World-Honored One eliminates faults and can cause the eye of wisdom to arise;
having reached the source of purity, he has crossed the shore of this sea of suffering.
The World-Honored One, Teacher of Gods and Humans, skillfully removes old age, sickness, and death.
"Difficult to encounter in hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, I have now encountered it and realized this fruit.
Having spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and become an upāsikā; for as long as life shall last, I shall constantly take refuge. I now wish to make offerings to the Buddha and Maudgalyāyana.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted [the offering] in silence.

Then that woman presented food to the Buddha; the Buddha dispatched Maudgalyāyana to receive the various foods and drinks from the woman. Having finished eating, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, and sat with his body upright.
At that time, the woman took a small seat and sat down before the Buddha in order to hear the Dharma.

Then the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for her. Afterward, the Buddha instructed Maudgalyāyana to take the bowl and wash it. Once the bowl had been washed, the Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana, "You should now return to your native land."
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha,
"By whose supernormal power shall we return to our own land?
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"By my supernatural power.
Having said this, he immediately arrived at the Jeta Grove.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now that we have arrived at the Jeta Grove, it is truly marvelous. World-Honored One, what is the name of this supernatural power you have just displayed?
The Buddha replied, "It is called the supernatural power of swift recollection."
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:

“I did not previously understand the profound realm of the Buddhas. Had I known beforehand such a profound realm as this, I would have taught and transformed every single sesame seed, causing them all to attain the knowledge of the Unsurpassed, Perfectly Complete Enlightenment.”
"I have now already attained the fruit of Arhatship and burned away my afflictions; I am unable to achieve this great practice for Bodhi.
At that time, the assembly of bhikṣus in the Jeta Grove all became doubtful and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What karma did the bhikṣu Paripūrṇa plant in the past to so swiftly realize the fruit of Arhatship?"
What karma did he plant to be born into a noble family?
By what karmic conditions was he conceived in the womb of a maidservant?
What karmic retribution did he plant to sever all afflictions and realize the fruit of non-arising?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"The bhikṣu Pūrṇa, having accumulated karmic actions and gathered the provisions for the Path, with his mind thus universally directed toward such objects, abided amidst the drifting [of saṃsāra] and attained definitive awakening."
The Bhikṣu Pūrṇa has accumulated his own karma and reaps its fruit himself.

He does not cause the earth element to experience the results of his actions, nor do the elements of fire, water, or wind experience them; rather, he alone experiences the fruits within his own body, and these are not experienced by the aggregates, the elements, or the six sense bases.
Regarding the maturation of karma, as it is said in a verse:
"Even if a hundred eons should pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
