when the causes and conditions meet, its fruit and retribution are experienced by oneself."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, at that very time, the Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world—perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a charioteer of men, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One—and he resided in the city of Vārāṇasī."
At that time, Pūrṇa went forth as a renunciant within that teaching; having mastered the Tripitaka, he served as the monk appointed by rotation to oversee the monastery's affairs.
Subsequently, it was the turn of an arhat who was in charge of sweeping; he then began to sweep.
Having finished sweeping, the ground was repeatedly covered with dust and filth blown there by the wind.
At that time, the Arhat thought to himself:
"I shall wait for the wind to subside first, and then sweep again.
When the Tripitaka Master Pūrṇa saw that the ground was covered in dust and dirt, he assumed they had not been swept; filled with anger, he reviled him with harsh words.
"Who is this servant girl currently sweeping the ground?
When the arhat heard these words, he thought to himself: "She is currently angry with me;
it is not yet appropriate for her to see me. I should remain silent for now and report this matter later."
Once his anger had subsided, that arhat went to Pūrṇa, the Master of the Tripiṭaka, and said to him:
"Do you now know what kind of person I am?"
Pūrṇa replied, "I know that you have gone forth in the teaching of Kāśyapa Buddha; I too shall go forth.
The Arhat said:
"Although we have both left the household life, as for the work of renunciation, I have already completed it; I have attained liberation from bonds, while you remain bound.
Your verbal karma was unwholesome; you should quickly repent so that your transgression may be extinguished."

Upon hearing this, Pūrṇa confessed his remorse. Due to his previous transgression, he was destined to fall into hell; however, because he confessed his regret, he extinguished that karmic retribution for hell and instead obtained a human body, born from the womb of a maidservant. For five hundred lifetimes, he constantly resided within the wombs of maidservants, and this present life is his final birth from such a womb.

For this reason, through the influence of past conditions and habitual karma, he was born into a noble and wealthy family; he was diligent in attending to monastic affairs, possessed wisdom in recitation and study, and was skillful regarding the aggregates, elements, sense bases, causes and conditions, and what is possible and impossible.
"By virtue of this karma, he has gone forth within my teaching, severed all afflictions, and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Those whose actions are purely black receive purely black retribution."
Those whose karma is purely white obtain a purely white retribution;
those whose karma is both black and white obtain a retribution that is both black and white.
Therefore, bhikṣus!
"Those actions that are purely black or mixed with black should be abandoned;
those actions that are purely white should be diligently cultivated.
When the Blessed One had spoken these words, the bhikṣus received them with faith and practiced accordingly.
The setting was in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there were two nāga kings who constantly resided within the city of Rājagṛha.
Those two nāga kings were:
The first is named Mountain and the second is named Wondrous.

By the majestic power of these two dragon kings, there are always five hundred deep pools and five hundred gushing springs; all the ponds and lakes never dry up, and rain falls in season, harmonious and abundant, so that seeds and crops do not fail to flourish.
At that time, the Blessed One tamed the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda.
These two nāga kings would regularly descend from the slopes of Mount Sumeru to make offerings to the Blessed One.
At that time, the two nāga kings Śaila and Sunetra had this thought:
"Now these two nāga kings Nanda and Upananda constantly descend from Mount Sumeru to make offerings to the World-Honored One."
"How is it that we have remained here until now without ever expressing our sympathetic joy?
This was unwholesome; we too should perform various offerings before the Blessed One."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The World-Honored One then instructed these two nāgas according to the Dharma.
Having heard this, the two nāgas took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and then received the pure precepts.
Once they had received the precepts, their bodies and all their possessions spontaneously increased and flourished.
Those two nāga kings later went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Having taken refuge in and observed the precepts under the World-Honored One, our bodies and all our resources have increased and flourished of their own accord.”
"We pray that you grant us permission to move to the great ocean.
The World-Honored One replied, "You have always resided in dependence upon the royal cities and towns; if you now wish to depart, you must first consult the king before you may go."
Having heard this, the two nāgas deliberated thus:
"If the World-Honored One permits us to enter the great ocean, he should not require us to question that king."
Having deliberated thus, they remained there and did not depart.
Since the two dragon kings remained and did not leave, they constantly engaged in this practice:
if they came to the World-Honored One during the day, they assumed the form of householders.
When he came at night, he would transform himself into a celestial body and, taking his palaces with him, travel to pay homage to and make offerings to the Buddha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, being of the Kṣatriya caste and possessed of haughtiness and pride, would always act in this manner:
whenever he wished to go to the Buddha’s dwelling, he would first have his attendants and ministers go ahead to the Buddha’s presence and command them to inform all people [of his arrival].
"If you see the King approaching, rise and pay him due respect.
The attendant official then went to where the Buddha was and delivered the King's command, only to find that the two householders were sitting upright as before.
Having seen them, the messenger thought to himself:
"These two householders live in dependence upon the king.
If they see the king coming, how could they fail to rise in respectful greeting?"
The messenger returned and reported to the king, saying: "Great King!
There are two householders residing within your majesty's realm who are now seated before the Buddha."
The king thought to himself:
"Could it be that he saw me fail to rise in respectful greeting?
I shall go to him now."
The king immediately proceeded to where the Buddha was.
At that time, those two nāgas saw the king approaching from afar and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"That king is now coming; should we pay him respect, or should we respect the Dharma?
The World-Honored One told them:
"Dragon King!..."
"One should revere the Dharma; all Buddhas revere the Dharma, and all those worthy of offerings revere the Dharma.
And he spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgatas of the past, And those of the future;"
The Buddhas of the present, who are able to eliminate manifold afflictions,
who now move through the midst of space and shall likewise traverse the void—
those Perfectly Enlightened Ones all revere the Dharma with the utmost respect.
"Those who wish to benefit others, as well as those who delight in sublime virtue,
should all give rise to respect and constantly keep the Buddha’s teaching in mind.
When the two nāgas heard these words, they remained seated and did not rise.
At that time, Bimbisāra immediately gave rise to resentment and said to the Buddha,
"I pray that you will show me the True Dharma.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"When there is hatred, there is no purity; if anger dwells within the mind, one cannot understand the Dharma taught by all the Buddhas.
Sever the heart of hatred and eliminate impure aspirations."
"If there is no malice, one is capable of knowing the True Dharma.
At that time, having heard these verses from the Buddha, King Bimbisāra thought to himself:
"It is because of these two householders that the World-Honored One has not preached the Dharma for me."
Having formed this thought, he prostrated before the Buddha and returned.
Once outside the gate, he addressed his attendant ministers, saying:

"When these two householders have finished taking their leave of the Buddha, you may say to them: [The King says: 'I am now old and advanced in years; my life is near its end. I wish to entrust my kingdom to one of you. May you accept it.'"
"You need not remain within the borders of my kingdom.
At that time, the two lay devotees prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took their leave of him, and went to see the king and his ministers, where they fully explained the king's intention.
The lay devotees replied,
"Now, in accordance with the king's command, we shall not remain within the king's realm.
At that time, the two lay devotees thought to themselves:
"We have always wished to enter the great ocean; now that we have received the King's word, it perfectly accords with our desire.
Then, by the power of the dragon, the householder created a torrential flood that overflowed small pools, as well as large and small rivers, and thereby entered the great ocean.
Once those two dragon kings had reached the great ocean, their bodies grew vast and they were accompanied by many retinues.

Later, at another time, because the dragon kings had entered the sea, the five hundred green ponds, flowing springs, gushing fountains, marshes, lakes, and pools within the city of Rājagṛha gradually became parched and dried up.

The clouds and rain that fell no longer followed the proper seasons; the hundred grains and sprouting crops all failed to flourish, and famine was seen daily, making it difficult for the bhikṣus to obtain almsfood through begging.
When King Bimbisāra saw this, he thought to himself:
"In this city of Rājagṛha, there were formerly two nāga kings dwelling within its borders."
"By virtue of his majestic power, springs, ponds, marshes, and lakes were all overflowing; wind and rain came in their proper seasons, and the hundred grains ripened in abundance.

Now, why is it that these springs, ponds, and other bodies of water have suddenly and gradually dried up? Why do the clouds, winds, rain, and moisture no longer follow the seasonal cycles? Why have the five grains failed to flourish, leading to famine within the kingdom, such that it is difficult for the bhikṣus to obtain alms?"
May these two nāgas not be devoured by garuḍas, nor die of their own accord, nor be seized and carried off by long-beaked birds, nor, out of fear, flee to another place.
"I should now go to question the World-Honored One.

Having formed this thought, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, related these matters in detail.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Bimbisāra, saying:

"Your Majesty, you should now know that those two dragon kings are still alive; they have not been devoured by a garuḍa, nor have they been seized and carried away by a long-beaked bird, nor have they fled elsewhere out of fear, for it was due to your Majesty’s relocation [of them]."
The King said:
“World-Honored One!
I do not recall ever having seen this dragon king, much less having moved him.”
The Buddha said:
"O King, I now cause you to recollect, so that you may attain awakening.
Great King!..."
"Do you remember now?
Previously, when the two householders were in my assembly where I was preaching the Dharma, you once drove them away and expelled them from your kingdom.
The King said:
"I have understood this matter," [the bhikkhu] said.
The Blessed One told him:
"These are the two great nāga kings, Sela and Sāmā."
The King said:
"World-Honored One!
Where are these two dragon kings now?"
The Buddha said,
"He is now in the midst of the ocean.
The king said:
“World-Honored One!
I and the people of this country will surely suffer decline.
The Buddha said:
“Great King! You should repent of your transgression, so that neither you nor the people of the kingdom shall suffer decline hereafter.
The king said:
"How can he offer an apology while remaining in the great ocean?
The Buddha said,
"Those two dragon kings regularly assume the form of lay devotees on the eighth day of every month and come to pay their respects to me."
"When he comes, I shall manifest a sign so that you will recognize him yourself;
you must then offer an apology. The King asked, "Should I prostrate at his feet, or should I not?"
The Buddha said:
"Simply extend your hand and say:
'Nāga King, you must endure.'"
When the king heard the Buddha say,
"I am waiting specifically for this day,
hoping that the Dragon Kings will come," the two Dragon Kings subsequently assumed the forms of laymen and went to where the Buddha was; the king followed shortly after.
At that time, the Tathāgata manifested a sign through his skillful means, whereupon King Bimbisāra immediately reached out his hand and said to the two nāgas:
"I pray that you will restrain your anger and return to dwell here."
The two nāgas replied,
"Great King, you should know that since we took refuge in and received the precepts from the World-Honored One, our bodies as well as our resources have increased greatly."
"If we were to return now to this city of Magadha, there would be no place for us to stay.
Although the population of the country has somewhat diminished at present, it shall later become peaceful and secure.
The King said:
"How can we ensure that there will be no further decline?
The two nāgas replied,
"Your Majesty should construct two palaces for us, and at the completion of every six months, you should constantly provide offerings with various kinds of requisites."
"I shall leave my retinue to dwell here and constantly provide protection.
On the day of the offering, I myself will come.
When King Bimbisāra heard these words, he built a palace for the two nāgas; thereupon, the two nāga kings left their retinues to dwell within it at all times.
When the time for the offering arrived, those two dragon kings would always come to receive it.
Later, at another time, the dragon kings' retinue became arrogant; an evil dragon took advantage of this opportunity and sent down rain and hail.

At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a brahmin who was most proficient in the incantations for rain and hail; whenever he perceived a hail cloud about to arise, he would immediately dispel it.
He distributed all the taxes and profits obtained from the people of Rājagṛha among them.
At that time, there was another brahmin in the kingdom of South India who was also the most eminent in the incantations for rain and hail.

Upon hearing that in the city of Pāṭaligāma in the kingdom of Northern India there was a king named Atirāja who ruled the country with righteous transformation, and that within that city lay the palace of the Nāga King Sūndara, whose power and prowess were matchless, [the dragon] thought:
"I shall go there and subdue him."

Then the sorcerer proceeded by stages until he reached the residence of a sorcerer in Rājagṛha. There he saw clouds rising in the sky as if hail were about to fall; the resident sorcerers were unable to stop it and could only pace back and forth in agitation.
A visiting sorcerer asked the wife of the resident sorcerer,
"Virtuous lady!
For what reason does your husband, the sorcerer, come and go in such a state of agitation?"
The woman replied, "Good man!
The hail clouds are so intense that they cannot be stopped."
The visiting sorcerer replied,
"If your husband, the teacher, does not stop it, I shall stop it.
His wife reported this, saying:
"Excellent!
The visiting mantra-reciter then took a small amount of water, consecrated it with mantras, and sprinkled it into the air; the clouds immediately dispersed.

When the brahmins, householders, and others in the city of Rājagṛha witnessed this event, they were filled with great wonder. They all presented the mantra-reciter with wealth and goods as rewards and said to him:
"The people residing in the city of Rājagṛha have developed the utmost faith; you should accept all the wealth they offer.
The former exorcist said, "For what reason do you wish to bestow these goods upon me?"
The crowd replied,
"Because the hail clouds have dispersed, we have come to offer our reward.
The former incantation-master said:
"I cannot extinguish it; only a guest mantra-master can disperse these evil clouds.
Thereupon, that multitude of people took their wealth and went to the guest mantra-master, addressing him together, saying:
"You should remain here; we shall all share our tax-revenues and provide for you."
The visiting incantation-master said,
"I shall now comply with your wish," and stayed there without departing.
Then the visiting incantation-master immediately established a ritual of spells to restrain the malevolent clouds so that they would no longer arise, and the rain and hail were consequently cut off.
The brahmins and householders of Rājagṛha all thought to themselves:
"It is by the power of our own merit that the wind, thunder, hail, and rain shall not fall again."
"What is the use of us dividing our tax-revenues with that mantra-practitioner?
they said, and so they did not give him any.
At that time, the visiting mantra-practitioner harbored resentment, withdrew his mantra-rites, and departed on his way; subsequently, rain and hail began to fall.
The people of the city went to ask the former incantation master, saying,
"Where is that visiting incantation master now?
The former incantation master replied:
"Because you did not give him his due share, he has now departed! Everyone said,
"If he should come again, please inform us."
The mantra-practitioner replied, "So be it.
As the guest mantra-practitioner gradually proceeded forward, he reached the borders of the city of Jayasena.
Having arrived at that city and seen King Jayasena, he approached the king with reverence and said,
"May the King live long.
Having spoken thus, he addressed the king:
"Great King, you should know that within your realm there is a nāga king named Sundara.
Now, within his nāga palace there is a most excellent medicine; whoever consumes it will quickly obtain its power."
"I pray that Your Majesty will visit my dragon palace;
if I obtain the medicine, I shall share it with you.
The king said:
“Brahmin! That nāga is extremely fierce; do not provoke him, for he will surely harm you.
The mantra-master said:
"Great King, you should know!
I possess the power of mantras; even if the entire Jambudvīpa were filled with Sūndara nāgas, I could still subdue them all. They cannot destroy my name, much less a single Sūndara nāga!"
"Great King!
Within your kingdom, are there any who have committed crimes such that they deserve death?
The King replied:
"Yes," the mantra-master said,
"you may send this man to that dragon palace to look for my dragon's location."
Then King Jayasena immediately summoned the criminal and ordered him to follow the mantra-master to that nāga palace to inspect the dragon’s dwelling.
At that time, the criminal obeyed the king’s command and, together with the mantra-master, arrived at the palace of the venomous dragon;
looking from afar toward the dragon’s location, he said, “In that secluded and tranquil grove of trees, the dragon dwells.”
Having seen this, the mantra-practitioner went before the palace, took the dragon-medicine, and returned with it all his strength; he arrived at the place of King Jayasena and gave a portion to him.
Taking his leave of the king, he returned to his own country and arrived at the city of Rājagṛha.
When the former incantation-master saw that the visiting incantation-master had arrived, he immediately informed the people within the city.
Once the populace learned of this, they each brought offerings and came to present them as gifts, saying to the incantation-master:
“Virtuous one, you may stay here; we shall provide for all your needs.
The mantra-master replied, “You have deceived me; I will not stay now.”
At that time, the multitude earnestly entreated him to remain; seeing their sincere persistence, he stayed there. The people of the city then provided him with a stipend for his maintenance.

It is the nature of people in that age to abandon decline when prosperity is at its height and to become arrogant and dissolute when dwelling in wealth; thus, he took a woman from his own clan as his wife. Before long, a son was born whom they named Little Mountain (Kṣudraparvata), and later a daughter was born whom they named Lightning Flash (Vidyutprabhā).
The brahmins collectively bestowed a name upon the incantation-master, calling him Sunda; his wife was named Vajra, and the bride was named Vijayacakra.
Once their names were established, they were filled with joy. At that time, the incantation-master thought to himself:
"If I must repeatedly stop these hailstorms for them, it will be an exhausting labor. It would be better to perform a rite to permanently prohibit thunder and hail, so that they never arise again."
Having formed this thought, he then employed a magical incantation to suppress the hail and rain, ensuring they would never arise again.
At that time, the people of Rājagṛha deliberated among themselves, saying:
"It is by the power of our own merit that the thunder and hail have not fallen; why then should we divide our tax-revenues with that foreign sorcerer?"
Having deliberated thus, they immediately ceased providing him with supplies.
That visiting mantra-practitioner was stingy regarding his secret mantras and did not teach them even to his own son;
he was addicted to games and amusements and did not apply himself to practice himself. He never dried or aired any of the medicinal herbs he possessed, so that they all became rotten and spoiled.
Later, at another time, he wished to practice that art, but he had already forgotten it.
The incantation master, who harbored long-standing resentment toward the people of Rājagṛha, sought an opportunity to find fault with him and went to various teachers of heterodox schools, asking:
"What skillful means are there by which one may obtain a method that accords with one's desires?"
At that time, those other teachers said:
"One attains it by entering fire," or they said:
"Consume poison," or it is said:
"Throw yourself from a high cliff."
Others said, "Tie a rope around his neck and suspend him from a tree branch.
All the teachings he propounded were intended to cause one to lose their lives; they did not regard those teachings.
Then that mantra-practitioner proceeded by stages until he reached the Bamboo Grove Monastery, where he saw a bhikṣu and said to him:
"Noble One! What skillful means are there by which one's desires may be fulfilled?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"You may go forth in the presence of the Blessed One.
The mantra-master responded:
"What may I do for you there? the bhikṣu replied, "You should practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) there for as long as you live;
engage in meditation and recitation, apply yourself diligently to study, and act in accordance with the teachings. In this very body, you will be able to extinguish all afflictions (*kleśa*)."
"If any remaining fetters have not been exhausted and the body passes away, whatever the mind seeks shall be accomplished in a future life.
The mantra-master replied:
"Noble One!"
"This matter is difficult to accomplish.
The bhikṣu said,
"If it cannot be accomplished, there is yet another expedient means."
"The World-Honored One and his foremost assembly of bhikṣus—you should invite them to provide them with food and drink.
The mantra-master replied, "This too is difficult to accomplish; I only pray that you will devise another expedient means for me."
The bhikṣu said:

"You should invite the four great śrāvakas and provide them with offerings of food and drink to the best of your ability; you shall then immediately make a vow, and whatever you seek will be attained."
"Why is this? The four great śrāvakas are like precious jars; if there are those who seek from them, they shall all obtain whatever they desire.
The mantra-master replied:
"This matter can be accomplished.
Thereupon, the mantra-master invited the four great śrāvakas and made offerings of food and drink to them.
Having completed the offerings, he immediately made this aspiration:

"By these roots of goodness, I vow that the Naga King Sunda will immediately vanish from his own palace and be reborn within that dragon palace, so that I may bring harm to the king, the city of Śrīparvata, the mantra-reciting practitioners, and the great multitude of its people."
The wife then asked her husband,
"What vow have you made, O virtuous one?
Her husband replied:
"I have made such and such a vow.
His wife said, "This vow is most excellent; may I be born as your wife."
The son of the mantra-practitioner then said to his father,
"I shall be the child.
The daughter spoke, saying:
"I shall become your wife.
His son's wife said, "I,
too, shall become your wife."
After the mantra-reciters had made their vows, they returned to their respective rooms and fell asleep.
At that time, clouds of five colors arose and a heavy rain poured down, soaking and destroying the walls.

At that moment, [the palace] collapsed all at once; the mantra-practitioner and his entire family were simultaneously extinguished. By the power of their vows, they were reborn in a dragon palace, where they expelled the long-residing Dragon King Sūndara and, surrounded by sixty thousand of their own kinsmen, took up residence within the palace.

That mantra-practitioner was thus named the Nāga King Sūndara; his wife was named Vajrāśani; his son was named Parvata; his daughter was named Vidyutprabhā; and his daughter-in-law was named Jayacakra.
It is the constant nature of the dragon dharma that upon birth, one immediately awakens to and understands three kinds of past events:
from what [karmic] retribution did one cast off to be born in this dragon palace?
It is entirely due to the power of one's vows.
For what reason did he make the vow to take birth here?
It was because he desired to destroy the people of Rājagṛha.
On account of this matter, he further reflected:
"One can only cause the destruction of worldly crops once they have grown and flourished.
Is it the growth of the crop that constitutes suffering?
Or is it the fact that it has not yet grown at all that constitutes suffering?"
"If this flourishing growth were to perish, it would surely be a great suffering.
Having thought this, he summoned his retinue and commanded them all to go quickly to the kingdom of Magadha to bring down a cool rain so that the crops might flourish.
These nāgas, relying on their command, sent down rain.

Once the various sprouts had flourished, the Nāga King Sunda, together with sixty thousand nāgas, arrived in the kingdom of Magadha. At once, they caused hailstones as large as *bīlva* fruits to fall, destroying the crops;
they poured down heavy rain, sweeping away roots and fruits until everything was utterly washed away.
At that time, the people of Magadha said to one another:
"Now this dragon has left not even a single stalk of rice behind.
Because of this, he was given the name and titled the Dragon King Śālirahaka (The One Without Rice Stalks).
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Volume Four;
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
Volume Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Command.
The internal summary verse says:
The Royal City, Nālandā, Pāṭaliputra, and Veṇuvana.
The Gaṅgā, the Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, the Echoing Sound, and Vaiśālī.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, by the Kalandaka Pond.
At that time, Prince Ajātaśatru, having been incited by Devadatta through various means and having accepted his words, proceeded to kill his father, the Dharma-king, and ascended the throne himself.

At that time, this king, wishing to commit various acts of harm against the Tathāgata, released a great elephant named Dhanapāla, as well as wicked horses and wicked dogs, intending to injure the Tathāgata.
At that time, the King’s mother, Vaidehī, having heard these matters, immediately said to her son:
"Do not act with contempt or disparagement toward the World-Honored One; the Tathāgata is always apprehensive that sentient beings might give rise to such acts of contempt."
"I fear that if the Blessed One departs from Rājagṛha, this land will lose its great benefit.
By the power of the Blessed One, all sentient beings in the kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha shall increase in welfare and happiness, and shall always dwell in joy."
Upon hearing these words, the king’s heart was filled with indignation, and he replied to his mother:
“There is no Tathāgata in other lands; could it be that those countries have perished and are devoid of sentient beings?”
His mother tried every possible means to dissuade him, yet he would not turn his mind [from his intent].
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"This Prince Ajātaśatru has committed immeasurable sins; I shall cause him to abide in rootless faith."
"It is not yet the right time; I shall go to Śrāvastī this very morning.

Having formed this thought, the World-Honored One, together with the assembly of śrāvakas, traveled by stages until he reached the city of Śrāvastī. Upon arriving at that city, he stayed at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the neighboring kings and others heard that Ajātaśatru intended to treat the World-Honored One with contempt; fearing this matter, the Tathāgata departed from Rājagṛha for Śrāvastī, and has now arrived there.
The kings of neighboring realms then thought to themselves:

"That minor king’s father was slain while remaining compliant with the True Dharma; yet out of insatiable greed, this man now even further insults and reviles the Tathāgata, who is honored by both gods and men alike."
"We shall all, from our various kingdoms, employ every possible means to seize his royal throne.

After these kings had sent envoys back and forth to inform one another, they assembled the fourfold army—namely, elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—and fully equipped with armor and weapons, they arrived at Rājagṛha. They completely destroyed the crops in the four directions and encamped their forces around the city.

At that time, the Nāga King Śālirāja again sent down great hail, causing further destruction; five hundred springs and ponds naturally dried up, and the heavens ceased to rain. Within the kingdom, famine prevailed and the people were ill at ease; furthermore, the flowing waters outside the city were all infused with poisonous drugs.

King Ajātaśatru was seized by intense and agonizing suffering; non-human spirits took advantage of his weakness, a great pestilence broke out, and deaths from disease became exceedingly frequent, such that funeral processions followed one another as they were sent out through the city gates.
At that time, Ajātaśatru was filled with immeasurable distress; a hundred kinds of sufferings afflicted his body and mind.
Because he harbored such grief, he rested his cheek in his hand and remained there sighing in lamentation.
At that time, Vaidehī, the mother of Ajātaśatru, seeing her son’s state of anxiety, asked:
"What are you thinking about?
He then replied to his mother:
"The hundred kinds of intense sufferings have all now manifested.
His mother said,
"I told you before:"

Truly, do not disparage or revile the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One. The Buddha is free from all fear; he only fears being slighted or insulted. Do not cause the World-Honored One to abandon the city of Rājagṛha.
If the Buddha were to leave this place, various evil omens would immediately appear within the kingdom.
"This is indeed that one," the King said.
"O Mother! [he continued].
"What should we do now?
The mother replied,
"You should go before the World-Honored One to offer an apology."
The King said, "O Mother!
I truly did not dare to face the World-Honored One in person; I only feel deep regret and resentment."
The mother said:
"Have you not heard that whether one uses sandalwood or a blade and axe, no different thought arises toward these two?
Furthermore, even if someone with pure faith were to smear sandalwood upon him, the Tathāgata would not give rise to a mind of joy."
"Furthermore, even if someone were to wound and cut [me] with a knife out of a mind of anger, the Tathāgata would not give rise to a mind of resentment toward them.
When King Ajātaśatru heard these words from his mother, he commanded a minister:
"Go at once to the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and prostrate yourself on his behalf, inquiring after the Tathāgata’s well-being."
"Is your venerable body light, agile, and at ease?
Furthermore, he spoke these words:
'Though your son has faults and afflictions, his father does not see them. I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion and pity, will travel to the city of Rājagṛha.'"
"If the Buddha does not come, the kingdom shall perish.
The minister said to the king, "It is so!"

"So be it! Following the king's command, the minister immediately went to the city of Śrāvastī and, upon reaching the Blessed One’s presence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying:
"King Ajātaśatru inquires after the Tathāgata’s well-being and has related everything as stated above."
The Buddha said,
"May the King and you yourself both enjoy peace and happiness.
The messenger addressed the Buddha:
King Ajātaśatru again addressed the World-Honored One:
"Even when a son commits transgressions, a father does not see his evil. I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion and pity, will journey to the city of Rājagṛha."
"If the Buddha does not come, the kingdom shall perish and be utterly destroyed.
The Buddha then accepted [the invitation] by remaining silent.
At that time, seeing that the Buddha was silent, the great minister withdrew and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One departed from the city of Śrāvastī and, traveling gradually with his bhikṣus, arrived at the border of the kingdom of Magadha. Through the Buddha’s majestic power, the various wind-kings raised a wondrous, harmonious breeze that blew away the poisonous waters until they were entirely dried up;
the water-kings all surged forth water of eight virtues, so that springs and ponds overflowed, while sweet rain poured down from the sky.
The benevolent deities who have faith in the Buddha all drove away the pestilence demons, and deaths from disease ceased.
When the military forces from the four directions heard that the Buddha had entered their territory, they each retreated. Within the kingdom, people gathered for trade and commerce;

hearing of this, those from foreign lands brought various goods to buy and sell with one another. The country became abundant and prosperous, and as people in the streets, alleys, and lanes marveled at the Tathāgata’s majestic virtue, all the other non-Buddhist practitioners remained silent and bowed low. Thus, the multitude of people were filled with great joy.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī, hearing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had arrived within the borders of Magadha, was filled with great joy. He commanded his ministers and officials, saying:
"You should prepare a thoroughfare two li and a half wide, clearing it of all tiles and stones, and sprinkle the road with sandalwood-scented perfumed water."
Furthermore, they used various kinds of exquisite silks and fabrics for marvelous and beautiful adornment.
Within the city of Rājagṛha, they burned fragrant incense of excellent reputation and scattered diverse flowers, awaiting the World-Honored One.
Having received the king’s command, these ministers and assistants extensively adorned the city of Rājagṛha and its various thoroughfares.
Then, by his own power, the King of Magadha, Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, set out with the fourfold army to welcome the World-Honored One.
Therefore, the World-Honored One, surrounded by those he had tamed, was followed by King Ajātaśatru and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas as they proceeded toward Rājagṛha.

As he was about to enter the city, when the World-Honored One had already lifted his right foot and was just crossing the threshold of the gate, at that moment the great earth shook in six ways, surging at the edges and subsiding in the center;
throughout this world, it was illuminated with radiance, such that even the most obscure and dark places were filled with great light;

in the sky above, the devas rained down various flowers upon the Buddha’s head—namely, blue lotuses (*utpala*), white lotuses (*kumuda*), and white water lilies (*puṇḍarīka*)—and further scattered powdered sandalwood and saffron, as well as *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, and various celestial robes.
When the Tathāgata entered the city, he manifested these various extraordinary and marvelous signs: all the narrow streets and alleys naturally became wide and spacious;
all the small groves immediately grew larger; those trees that were already tall lowered their branches of their own accord;
elephants, horses, oxen, and birds raised their voices with great joy according to their respective species; and so did all the household utensils.
Spontaneously, he let out a great roar: the blind gained sight, the deaf were able to hear, and the mute were able to speak;
those with incomplete faculties all became fully endowed. Those who were intoxicated were all awakened, and those who had consumed poison were likewise cured.
Hostile people simultaneously gave rise to hearts of loving-kindness, and as for those who were pregnant—
All were born immediately without any suffering or pain; those imprisoned and bound by shackles and fetters were naturally liberated, and the poor and destitute obtained various treasures.
A certain upāsaka, having witnessed such various benefits, spoke this verse:
"In whatever land the World-Honored One travels, In that land there are no fears;
Neither famine nor foreign armies prevail, And wind and rain are always harmonious."
"The multitude of people all cultivate merit; In peace and joy, they are entirely free from sorrow.
A hundred thousand rare and wondrous events— All are accomplished in this place.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the city of Rājagṛha and comforted the great assembly; there was no one who did not receive benefit. The World-Honored One then returned to the Bamboo Grove Monastery (Veṇuvana-vihāra).

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, from the kingdom of Magadha, went to where the Buddha was staying. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, after the World-Honored One had extensively instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him, he remained silent.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī of the kingdom of Magadha, having heard the various sublime teachings spoken by the Buddha, was filled with joy and exultation; he accepted them all with faith. He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms in reverence, and with a sincere heart, prostrated himself before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:

"I pray only that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will accept my invitation along with the assembly of bhikṣus to receive from me, for a period of three months, *cīvara* robes, as well as food and drink, together with bedding and seating."
"If there should be any illness, may you accept medicinal decoctions and all necessary provisions without any lack.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
When King Ajātaśatru realized that the World-Honored One had accepted his invitation through silence, he rose, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew with joy.

Returning to his own palace, he prepared offerings; for three months, he provided the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus with saṃghāṭī robes, various foods, drinks, medicinal decoctions, and bedding and seating requisites, without any deficiency.

At that time, the faithful devas within the city of Rājagṛha, seeing that the king was thus making such extensive offerings, all pursued the pestilence-demon spirits; they passed through the village of Nādikā and proceeded directly to the city of Vaiśālī, where they finally came to a halt.
The people of that city were all afflicted by an epidemic, and those who died were exceedingly numerous.
Along the streets, funeral carriages conveying corpses followed one after another without ceasing.
At that time, there was a brahmin in that city named Dumbara, who saw in a dream a protective deity of Vaiśālī addressing him, saying:
“The World-Honored One, the Tamer of Men, the most honored and supreme among gods and humans—
if he comes to this city, all calamities will surely be dispelled.
Having heard these words, the brahmin waited until the clear dawn and immediately informed the various householders, the Licchavis, and others within the city:
"I have seen such things in a dream.
When those people heard these words, they each said:

"What dharma should we perform, and whom should we dispatch to invite the World-Honored One to this city to dwell for three months, so that through solemn offerings and adornments, these calamities may be removed?"
The householders said to Dummukha, "You yourself should go to invite the World-Honored One; no one else is capable.
Then Dummukha thought to himself:
"I shall go to where the Buddha is, prostrate at his feet,
and say:
'World-Honored One!'"
I hope you are physically light and agile, with little illness or affliction, and dwelling in peace and happiness.
The lay devotees within the city of Vaiśālī have sent me to welcome you, requesting that the World-Honored One save these multitudes of people.
"If the World-Honored One does not go, the people of that city will all perish and be utterly destroyed before long.
Having had this thought, the brahmin Dummukha replied to the householder:
"The King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, of the kingdom of Magadha, has long delighted in killing; he is violent by nature and has committed many acts of malice and harm."
"If I go out to welcome the Buddha, it will surely bring about my own ruin.
Then that assembly of householders spoke in verse:
"When two nations are enemies, They do not detain their envoys."
"How much less could the messengers of the Tathāgata possibly cause him harm?
At that time, Drumā performed auspicious and virtuous rites and proceeded by stages until he reached the city of Rājagṛha.
Having rested from his fatigue, he went to where the Buddha was, greeted him with joy, and withdrew to sit at one side. He addressed the Buddha in full detail, saying:

"The assembly of lay devotees in the city of Vaiśālī prostrate themselves at the feet of the World-Honored One and offer their greetings to the Tathāgata, inquiring whether you have little illness and little affliction, whether your daily life is light and easy, and whether you dwell in peace and happiness."
The Blessed One asked,
"Are you and the people of Vaiśālī at peace? Drumala replied:

“I only pray that the World-Honored One will go to the city of Vaiśālī; if the World-Honored One abandons it and does not go, before long the people of that city will perish, and it will remain as nothing more than an empty name—whose dwelling will it be?”
The World-Honored One said:

"I and this assembly of śrāvakas have been invited by the king to remain for the three months of the rains retreat, and he has provided us with various requisites as offerings. You may go and report these matters in detail to the king."
"If Your Majesty grants permission, I shall immediately depart.
When Dhumrāyaṇa had heard the Buddha’s words, he dispatched a messenger back to his kingdom to report the Buddha’s message in full detail.

Those people all agreed with the Buddha’s words and sent a messenger again to Dhumrāyaṇa, instructing him to go to King Ajātaśatru in the kingdom of Magadha and convey our message, asking after his health:
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
He made this request, saying:

"I only pray that Your Majesty will grant the Tathāgata permission to go to the city of Vaiśālī. If Your Majesty does not permit the World-Honored One to go, the city of Vaiśālī will before long be destroyed; it will remain as nothing more than a hollow name, devoid of its people."
At that time, Drumala Bhṛguḍatta had this thought:
"Should I see the Great King first,
or should I see the Great Minister first?"
He further thought to himself:
"There is a traditional teaching that one should not first see the king; rather, one must seek out the great ministers.
Even if the king issues a decree, the ministers will be able to subvert it."
"Therefore, I shall first see the great minister.
Not long after he had entered for business, the minister asked:
"For what reason have you come?"
Dhūmra replied, "I have now come to invite the Tathāgata, but I must inform the King; I pray that you will assist me in informing the King.
The minister said:
"So be it. When the King asks, I shall certainly assist you.
Thereupon, the Malla went to Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, King of Magadha; having arrived, he praised the King with auspicious verses of eulogy and withdrew to stand to one side.
He addressed the Great King, saying:
"The people of Vaiśālī inquire after the Great King’s health:
Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy, and do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
The king replied to Dhaumrāyaṇa,
"Are those people all living in peace and happiness?
Then Dhaumrāyaṇa again addressed the king, saying:
“The people of Vaiśālī spoke thus in concert:

‘We pray that the Tathāgata will be permitted to go toward the city of Vaiśālī. Great King, if you do not permit the Tathāgata to go toward the city of Vaiśālī, this city will before long be destroyed and reduced to nothing more than a hollow name.’”
The Great King replied, "I have constantly harbored this thought:
'May the city of Vaiśālī be swiftly destroyed; this has been my long-cherished wish.'"
After the King had spoken these words, the Domba immediately withdrew.
At that time, a minister came forward and addressed the King, saying:
"How could the World-Honored One ever abandon a single sentient being to such suffering and distress?"
The king said:
"Virtuous one! No."
"If one does not speak thus, it would mean that Your Majesty lacks respect for the World-Honored One.
Whether Your Majesty grants permission or not, the World-Honored One will certainly go to the city of Vaiśālī for the sake of benefiting sentient beings."
The king said, "The Buddha’s intention is not something I know; if that is so, you should summon Dombila.
The minister, having received this command, immediately went to summon him.
The King said to Dummukha:
"Make a solemn vow: if you can provide offerings and pay respect to the World-Honored One just as I do, then I shall grant my consent."
When Drumala heard these words, he immediately dispatched messengers to the city of Vaiśālī to inform the people there, reporting the King’s message in full.
Upon hearing it, they replied to the messengers, saying:
"The King alone, by himself, is capable of making such offerings."
"How could we, this assembly of people, not be able to do so?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will come to the city of Vaiśālī; we shall offer the most excellent of offerings, and we hope that Your Majesty will rejoice in our merit."
Having received these words, the messenger returned and reported them to Drumala.
At that time, Drumala presented the matter in full to the King.
Then, King Ajātaśatru went in person to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the World-Honored One’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For as long as I live, I shall provide offerings to the World-Honored One and the assembly of śrāvakas.
Yet, because the World-Honored One constantly seeks to benefit all sentient beings, he does not accept my invitation.”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my humble invitation for one day.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Knowing that the World-Honored One had accepted through his silence, King Ajātaśatru rose from his seat and withdrew to his own palace.
At that time, during the night, King Ajātaśatru prepared a vast array of pure food and drink; when morning arrived, he sent a messenger to the Buddha’s dwelling to announce:
"The time has come."
The Buddha, having understood this, washed his hands, took up his bowl, and went to the king’s invitation for a meal.
The king himself held a golden pitcher before the World-Honored One and spoke these words:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will subdue all the evil nāgas and yakṣas.”
"Venerable Sir!

This dragon king, Apalāla, has caused me harm for a long time; though not an enemy, he acts as an enemy; though not a foe, he acts as a foe; though not an adversary, he acts as an adversary, destroying all crops, both those already grown and those yet to be sown."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will give rise to a heart of compassion and subdue the Dragon King Apalāla.
The World-Honored One silently accepted the request, bestowed blessings and recited incantations for King Ajātaśatru, and then returned to his dwelling place.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"I now wish to go to the town of Pāṭaliputra; you may follow me.
"So be it, World-Honored One; I am willing to follow," he replied.
At that time, the Blessed One was wandering among the people of Magadha and, proceeding by stages, arrived at the town of Pāṭaligrāma; having reached the site of a caitya, he stayed there.

At that time, the brahmins and householders of that village and town, hearing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling and had arrived at the Pāṭalīya Caitya, informed one another; they then gathered like clouds and went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha then addressed them, saying:
"You should know that for those who are heedless, there are five faults."
What are the five?

First, these brahmins and householders, due to negligence, engage in mutual strife; because of this cause and condition, they bring their disputes before the authorities, whereby all their wealth and property are completely lost—this is the first fault.
Second, there are also brahmins and householders who, due to negligence and quarreling, have their ill repute spread and pervade all directions; this is the second fault.

Third, there are further brahmins and householders who, due to negligence, give rise to arrogance in their minds; they go among the assemblies of kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and śramaṇas, yet in those gatherings they always harbor fear and hesitation, never acting as leaders but constantly bowing their bodies—this is the third fault.
Fourth, there are also Brahmins and householders who, due to negligence and quarreling, give rise to remorse in their minds at the time of death; this is the fourth fault.

Fifth, there are further brahmins and householders who harbor negligence in their hearts; because of this negligence and arrogance, they fall into evil destinies and are born within the hells—this is the fifth fault.
He further addressed the brahmins and householders, saying:
"For those who are heedful, there are five further benefits. What are these five?"
First, there are brahmins and householders who, by virtue of heedfulness, do not lose their wealth; this is the first benefit.
Second, there are further brahmins and householders who, through heedfulness and the absence of strife, have their good reputation spread throughout all directions; this is the second benefit.

Third, there are further brahmins and householders who, through heedfulness and without arrogance of mind, approach the assemblies of kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and śramaṇas; they always remain free from fear and wander about with joy—this is the third benefit.
Fourth, there are further brahmins and householders who, through heedfulness, experience no remorse at the time of death; this is the fourth benefit.
Fifth, there are further brahmins and householders who, through heedfulness, depart for the heavenly realms after the end of their lives; this is the fifth benefit of heedfulness.
"Therefore, you all should not be negligent.

At that time, the brahmins, householders, and others, having heard the Dharma, rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, joined their palms in reverence, prostrated themselves before the World-Honored One, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray only that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for us, will deign to stay at our lodgings this night."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Seeing that the Tathāgata had accepted their invitation through silence, those brahmins and householders all together prostrated at the World-Honored One’s feet, took their leave of the Buddha, and withdrew.

At that time, the brahmin Vassakāra was a high minister to the king of Magadha. He heard that the Blessed One, while wandering through the human world, had arrived at the village of Pāṭaligāma and was staying beside the Pāṭala Stūpa; he further heard that the people of Pāṭaligāma were all making offerings to him.

Having heard this, he immediately mounted a carriage drawn by pure white mules; attended by servants holding precious vases and golden staffs, and surrounded before and behind by five hundred *māṇavaka*s, he set out to behold and make offerings to the World-Honored One.

Having set out for the village of Pāṭaligāma and arrived there, he alighted from his carriage and approached the place where the World-Honored One was. Standing before the Buddha, he exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One; having completed his respectful salutations, he withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the sublime Dharma to him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him, and then remained silent.
Then the brahmin Varṣākāra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"I only pray that the Tathāgata and the assembly of bhikṣus will accept my offerings at home tomorrow.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
When the brahmin Varṣākāra knew that the World-Honored One had accepted his invitation, he immediately returned home.

At that time, the World-Honored One washed his feet, entered the room, sat cross-legged, straightened his body, and established right mindfulness; he then beheld the deity of great power in the village of Pāṭalī, who was measuring out the boundaries with a cord, intending to build a great city.
Having seen this, the Blessed One arose from his meditative absorption in the late afternoon and went outside, where he sat on the open ground together with the bhikṣus.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Have you not heard that they wish to build a great city at this village of Pāṭalī?"
Ānanda replied, “I know it,
World-Honored One!”
"The brahmin Vassakāra is consulting with the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens regarding the construction of a great city.
The World-Honored One replied:

"While I was in meditative concentration within my chamber, I beheld with my purified divine eye those deities of great power and the minor spirits in the village of Pāṭali, as well as the people of noble virtue, each dwelling according to their devotion to those spirits and all following the teachings and practices of the deities."

Because the various celestial deities dwell here, you should know that this city ought to be the most excellent; furthermore, it shall be free from the calamities of neighboring states and the destruction wrought by water or fire.
Then, at that very night, the brahmin Varṣākāra extensively prepared various offerings and foods. When morning arrived, he sent word to the Buddha and his assembly:
"We pray that you will know the time has come."
After he had finished eating and put away his bowl, the brahmin Varṣākāra took a golden pitcher filled with pure water, knelt before the Buddha, and made this great vow:
"By all the merit from my present offering to the Buddha and the noble assembly, I dedicate it to the devas dwelling in Pāṭaliputra, so that they may enjoy peace and happiness for a long night."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If there is a person of pure faith who makes offerings to the assembly of devas,
This relies upon the instruction of the Great Teacher, And is what the Buddha praises."
In whatever place a wise person makes their dwelling,
they provide food to those who uphold the precepts and offer them words of blessing.
They honor those worthy of honor and make offerings to those worthy of offerings.
"The various devas will protect him as their own child, and he shall constantly experience joy.

At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the brahmin; having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him, he rose from his seat and returned to his original dwelling.
Then that brahmin, having performed what was required of him according to his capacity, departed with a concentrated mind and right mindfulness, reflecting thus:
"The Blessed One has departed from the village of Pāṭaligāma; I now wish to build a city for the Blessed One’s use and erect a lofty gate, naming it the Gautama Gate."
“If you cross the Gaṅgā River, I shall also have a road constructed for you, called the ‘Gautama Road.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing what was in the mind of that brahmin, immediately departed from the center of the northern side of the village of Pāṭaligrāma and proceeded gradually toward the Gaṅgā River.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, thought to himself:
"I shall now personally make offerings to the World-Honored One, holding five hundred parasols with one hundred ribs each, providing a high canopy of shade over the Buddha."
Then the Licchavis of Vaiśālī all thought to themselves:
"Now that King Ajātaśatru personally holds the parasol to make offerings to the World-Honored One, we too should practice this same deed."
Having formed this thought, he immediately prepared five hundred parasols as an offering.
At that time, various dragon kings (nāgarāja) had this thought:
"Now the King and the Licchavis are performing such magnificent offerings; since my own body has fallen into an evil realm, how could I not offer to the World-Honored One?"
Having formed this thought, he took five hundred parasols and offered them to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the assembly of the Four Heavenly Kings also had this thought:
"Now these people, though they do not perceive the retribution of cause and effect, still offer worship of their own accord."
"How much more so for those of our kind, who perceive the fruit and thereby know its cause; how could we not make offerings?
Having formed this thought, they also prepared five hundred parasols to offer to the Buddha.
Furthermore, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven also thought to themselves:
"All the other devas and humans alike are making offerings; how could I now fail to practice such worship?"
Having formed this thought, he prepared five hundred parasols and came to make an offering to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"I shall now create a superior causal condition for all devas and humans, causing them to give rise to faith."
At that time, having formed this thought, the World-Honored One manifested his supernormal power, causing each member of the assembly to think:
"I alone am holding a parasol over the crown of the World-Honored One's head."

When the Blessed One had realized perfect enlightenment, two thousand five hundred devas and humans held parasols over the Blessed One’s head. All the bhikṣus, filled with doubt, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What virtuous karma did the Blessed One perform such that, upon realizing enlightenment, he obtained two thousand five hundred devas and humans holding parasols over his head?”
The Buddha said: "You should know!

In the past, I accumulated the provisions for enlightenment and performed various virtuous deeds, as described at length above; ultimately, one must personally experience the fruits of one's own actions."
"O bhikṣus, you should know that in the past there was a universal monarch named Mahāsudarśana, who possessed the fourfold army and was able to crush his enemies, achieving victory over them all."
He ruled the world according to the True Dharma as a Dharma King, fully endowed with the seven treasures; yet he lacked only one son to complete his retinue of a thousand.
All the sons born to the king were destined to follow him.
All the king’s consorts thought to themselves:
"Should we give birth to sons, they will inevitably be separated from us and divided among one another.
It is the nature of our king's law that once a son is born, he must necessarily follow [the king]."
"We shall now establish a mutual agreement that no woman who is pregnant shall inform the King.
Later, there was a lady who had become pregnant; the other ladies took her to a hidden place so that the King would not see her.

When the months were complete, she gave birth to a son whose physical form was upright and majestic; all people loved to behold him. His skin was golden in color and his head was shaped like a parasol. His arms hung down past his knees, his forehead was broad and even, his eyebrows met at the brow-center, and his nose was high and straight; all his limbs were perfectly complete.
When he had grown up, all the ladies-in-waiting cherished and loved him as if he were born from their own wombs.
Later, on another occasion, the Great King Suprabha was preceded by the seven treasures from the continent of Videha, surrounded by eighty thousand kings.
At that time, the sons surrounded him on all sides in a crescent formation, their majestic radiance so brilliant that it eclipsed the light of the sun and moon.
From atop a high tower, the princes whom the queens had previously hidden saw the royal father from afar and asked their mothers,
"Who is this person approaching?"
His mother and the others replied,
"This is your father, Great King Suprabha!
The son then asked his mother:
"After my father the King has passed away, shall I succeed him and inherit the royal throne?
His mother replied again, "The King now excludes you;
there is only one son missing from the full number of one thousand."
"Among those sons, after the king has passed away, the eldest shall succeed to the throne.
Since you are the youngest, it is not fitting for you to ascend to the succession.
The son asked again:
“After the King has passed away, as I am of low status, I shall not be able to inherit the succession;
I pray that my mothers will grant me permission to leave the home life.
With right faith, I wish to go forth from the household to the homeless state and cultivate the holy life with diligence.”
The mothers replied, "We feel the utmost affection for our son; do not harbor such a thought.
Then the son answered:
"I now resolve my mind and shall certainly leave the household life.
When those mothers saw his single-minded determination and that he would not turn back, they all said:
"If you are thus resolved, son, make a covenant with us, and we shall follow your heart's desire."
"When you later attain the supreme fruit, you must surely come to repay me.
The son immediately replied,
"I shall do as I am commanded."

The mother granted her consent to all of this, and the son’s wish was fulfilled. He went to a secluded place; without the instruction or guidance of an upādhyāya or ācārya, he spontaneously realized the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and attained the state of a pratyekabuddha through direct realization.
Having attained the fruit, he thought to himself:
"I previously promised my mother that once I had realized the noble fruit, I would certainly repay her.
I should now go and inform my mother and the others."

The Pratyekabuddha, the Noble One, manifested the Dharma through his physical body for the sake of benefiting others; he then went before his mother and extensively displayed miraculous transformations, emitting fire from the upper part of his body and water from the lower part, radiating great light, and manifesting various extraordinary signs.
When the ordinary people and others beheld this miraculous manifestation, they quickly gave rise to faith.
At that time, the mothers, seeing their sons’ miraculous power, fell prostrate like felled trees and immediately paid homage, all saying:
"Noble One!..."

"Now that you have been able to realize such a supernatural fruit of the noble path, Venerable One, we pray that you will accept food; seeking merit, we only wish that you would deign to remain in this grove and receive our offerings."
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha silently accepted the invitation.
Those mothers, in turn, sent food and made offerings to him every day.
Then the Pratyekabuddha thought to himself:
"Regarding this fragile, illusory body, I have accomplished what was to be done; I shall now enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

Just as a king of geese, fully endowed with wings, soars through the void and manifests manifold supernatural transformations—emitting fire from his upper body and water from his lower body, radiating great light—he, having displayed these miracles, enters *nirvāṇa*.

Then his mother and the others piled up fragrant firewood and set it ablaze; they sprinkled milk upon the flames and collected the remaining bones, placing them in a golden vase. Within the garden grove, they erected a stūpa, adorning the monument with various ornaments such as bracelets and rings, and hoisting banners, streamers, and parasols atop the stūpa.

Later, during the spring season, when the forest flowers in his park were exhaling their fragrance and many excellent birds were uttering beautiful songs, the King, accompanied by his queen and various court ladies surrounding him before and behind, went to the park to wander and observe.
Seeing a stūpa of a pratyekabuddha, he asked the park keeper, "What is this?
The keeper replied to the king:
"I do not know what has occurred within this palace.
He then questioned the palace attendants regarding the origins of the stūpa; the attendants, struck with fear, simultaneously prostrated themselves and stepped forward, saying:
"We only pray that Your Majesty will grant us freedom from fear."
The king said,
"I shall give her to you now.
At that time, the palace attendants fully explained the circumstances to the king in detail.
The king then spoke, saying:

"You have acted wrongly. Since that son sought after and delighted in the royal throne, why did you not inform me so that I might know it and install him as king, receiving the position of consecration?"
"He was one of great majesty; although he has entered nirvana, I shall place my crown, silken ribbons, and parasol atop his stupa.
At that time, out of love for his son, the Great King accordingly placed these items upon the stupa.
The Buddha told them:
"O bhikṣus! Do not harbor such thoughts; that King Bhadra was none other than myself."
In the past, I offered a parasol as an act of worship to a stūpa of a pratyekabuddha.
By virtue of this meritorious deed, I have already attained the rank of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) two thousand five hundred times.

Furthermore, by virtue of that karma, I have now realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and upon my head, all hold parasols with a hundred spokes, each made of two thousand five hundred celestial and human materials.

Had I not realized this supreme fruit, I would otherwise have been destined to attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) two thousand five hundred times; I dedicate all the maturation of my meritorious deeds entirely for the benefit of all the Śrāvakas.
If one sows a measure of pearls and exchanges them for a measure of non-glutinous rice, even among my disciples there would be no lack.
Bhikṣus, you should know:
by performing purely black karma, one experiences a black ripening result;
By performing purely white karma, one will experience a corresponding white ripened fruit, as explained at length above.
You, bhikṣus, should apply yourselves with diligence to this training.
When the Buddha had finished speaking, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*, Fascicle Five.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*.
Fascicle Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree during the Great Tang Dynasty.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, as well as the Licchavis of Vaiśālī and others, each constructed a bridge of boats.
At that time, the nāgas thought to themselves:
"We have now fallen into an evil realm; we ought to cultivate meritorious deeds.
Each raised its head, forming a continuous bridge over the Gaṅgā River, so that the World-Honored One and his company might step upon it and cross.
Having formed this thought, those nāgas each raised their heads one after another to form a bridge.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Regarding these three bridges, if you wish to cross over them, do so according to your own inclinations."
"I shall cross the waters of the Gaṅgā with Ānanda by means of that dragon-bridge.
Some of the disciples took the Unborn-Enemy Bridge (Ajātaśatru-saṃkrama), while others took the Vṛji Bridge; only the World-Honored One and the Venerable Ānanda crossed by way of the Dragon Bridge.
At that time, there was a layman who spoke these verses:
"The wise cross the great ocean by boarding a ship, not by building a bridge;
The foolish take the sea for their bridge, yet board great vessels upon rivers and streams."
The World-Honored One has already crossed the river; the brahmin stands upon the bank.
The śrāvaka departs by means of a raft, while the bhikṣu merely washes his body.
Since water flows level everywhere, why trouble yourself to seek a well elsewhere?
"Having severed the root of craving, what more is there to seek?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had crossed the Gaṅgā River, he saw a high plateau in the distance and said to Ānanda:
"Do you see that plateau?"
"I shall explain the causes and conditions for you to understand them.
Ānanda replied, "I only pray that you will reveal them to me."
The Buddha said, “This high plateau is the site where, in the past, King Mahāghoṣa erected a jeweled banner (*ratnadhvaja*).

That jeweled banner was one thousand *vyāma* in height and was adorned with pure gold and various precious gems. Having made extensive offerings of wealth and performed meritorious deeds beneath this banner, he then cast the jeweled banner into the Gaṅgā River.”
"Do you now wish to see this jeweled banner?
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"Now is precisely the right time; I and my bhikṣus all wish to behold it.
At that moment, the World-Honored One touched that high ground with his fearless hand, which was adorned with the thousand-spoked wheels and the mark of a hundred blessings.
At that time, there were certain nāgas who thought to themselves:
"For what reason does the World-Honored One touch the earth with his hand?
They immediately understood that the Tathāgata intended to display the precious banner for the assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, those nāgas emerged from within the earth, holding up a jeweled banner for all the bhikṣus to behold.
At that moment, there was a bhikṣu named Bhadrika, whose disposition was serene and tranquil; he was staying in a secluded spot, mending his rag-robe.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You must quickly observe the form and characteristics of this banner; before long, it will soon vanish and disappear."
Once the cessation had been seen, the bhikṣus said to the Blessed One:
"World-Honored One!
We all saw it, yet only the Venerable Bhadali—who by nature delights in solitude—did not look while mending his robes."
Is it for the sake of departing from craving and attachment?
Or is it because he has previously beheld [the Buddha] with his own eyes?
This is not the same as mere reverential worship.
"If one is free from desire, there is likewise one who is free from desire;
if you have previously observed this, in what place does it reside?
The Buddha then replied:
"You should know this!
Because this bhikṣu has already become free from craving and attachment, he was able to behold and pay homage [to the Buddha] once again.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"In the past, there was a king named Rāvaṇa who was a close friend of Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
King Rāvaṇa, having no offspring, harbored a longing in his heart and rested his cheek upon his hand, reflecting:
'I now possess many kinds of wealth and treasures; my kingdom, rank, ministers, and subjects are all fully provided for. Yet, as I have no son, after my death the lineage will surely perish.'"
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing King Krauñca, immediately asked:
"King, for what reason do you now sit with your cheek resting on your hand, lost in thought and dwelling in sorrow?
Then the king replied:
"I now possess many various treasuries; I am sorrowful because my lineage will be severed once I have passed away.
Śakra replied, "Do not be distressed.
When the signs of death appear among my sons, the devaputras, I shall urge them to become your son, O King."
It is the constant law of the devas that when one is about to die, the five signs of decay appear.

What are these five? First, their garments become soiled and greasy; second, the flowers upon their heads wither; third, a foul odor issues from their mouths; fourth, sweat flows from beneath their armpits; and fifth, they take no pleasure in their own seats.
Later, when the signs of decline appeared in a certain deva-son, Śakra urged him, saying:
"Virtuous one, you may take birth within the womb of the principal consort of King Raurava."
Then the deva replied to Śakra:
"All kings generally commit many transgressions.
If I were born there, I would likewise commit various wrongs; as one who violates the principles of the Dharma, I would surely fall into the Avīci Hell, and thus I do not wish to be born there."
Śakra replied: "O virtuous one!
I shall bestow my grace upon you so that you may attain awakening."
Then the deva replied:
"Lord of Devas, you should know!
The various devas are heedless and deeply attached to pleasure; how could they possibly remember me?"
Śakra replied: "O virtuous one!
Even though it is so, I shall ultimately cause you to remember, know, and become awakened."
When that deva-son heard these words, he went to the womb of the chief queen of King Krandana and took conception.
On the day of his conception, the king and all his people rejoiced and raised a great shout.
When the months were complete, she gave birth to a son whose countenance was upright and handsome, as described above in detail, even down to his high and straight nose.
At that time, King Rāvaṇa gathered his retinue and, wishing to establish a name for him, asked:
"What name shall we give him?"
The retinue replied:
"When this boy entered his mother’s womb, all the people cried out loudly; he should be named Mahāraṇa (Great Crying)."
The king followed his request and thus established that name for him.
At that time, the youth Mahāraṇa was entrusted to eight nurses to be cared for and nurtured:
two as wet-nurses, two to constantly wash him, two to always hold him in their arms, and two to provide him with play and amusement.

He was nurtured with various delicacies such as milk, curd, clarified butter, and fresh or processed ghee; like a lotus flower, he grew rapidly, becoming intelligent and awakened, and was able to master them skillfully. He attained complete proficiency in all eighteen kinds of arts, and his eloquence and wisdom were unimpeded in every respect.

Whenever a Kṣatriya king undergoes the consecration ceremony, he attains sovereignty over the human realm and possesses great power and influence, such that all kings, both near and far, submit to him.

To establish and govern his subjects, he must necessarily possess such skills as these: being well-able to train elephants, manage horses, and drive chariots; being adept at drawing the bow and nocking arrows; entering and exiting battle arrays with skill; being proficient with hooks and ropes, iron arrows, and iron lances; stamping the ground and clenching his fists; binding his hair in a topknot; and being skilled in the methods of archery.
Briefly, there are five kinds: first, shooting from afar and piercing through everything;

second, hearing the sound of the target and shooting immediately, being able to kill it every time; third, being able to shoot at any vital point; fourth, hitting the mark every time one shoots; and fifth, penetrating even the most solid and firm objects. He was thoroughly proficient in all these methods of archery.
It is the natural law for princes that while their father the king remains on the throne, their own names do not become prominent.
Later, at another time, when King Mahāraṭha had passed away, Prince Mahāraṭha was consecrated and ascended the throne.
When he first succeeded to the royal throne, he governed the people with the True Dharma; however, in later times, he reverted to practicing what is not the Dharma.
At that time, Śakra replied, saying:
"O Benevolent One!..."
"In the past, I exhorted you to become the son of King Rāvaṇa.
You should not now govern the kingdom through such unrighteousness; you shall surely fall into hell.
When King Mahāghoṣa heard these words, he governed his people according to the True Dharma, yet after a short time, he again practiced unrighteousness.
On the second occasion, Śakra spoke again:
"O worthy one!
Previously, I exhorted you to become the crown prince for King Rāvaṇa."
"You must not now practice such unrighteousness regarding the governance of your kingdom; you shall fall into hell.
Then King Mahāghoṣa replied to Śakra:
"We kings are often negligent and greedy for the pleasures of the five senses; having heard [your words], we immediately forget them."
“I only pray that out of compassion you will leave behind a sign of your presence.
Once I have seen it, I shall perform various meritorious deeds.
At that time, Śakra commanded the Deva of Skillful Artistry, known in Sanskrit as Viśvakarman:
