"You should now go to the majestic site of the Great Voice King’s palace and manifest a golden banner a thousand fathoms high, interspersed with various kinds of miscellaneous jewels."

At that time, having received the command, the Deva Viśvakarman immediately went to the majestic inner sanctuary of King Mahāghoṣa’s palace and manifested a golden banner, one thousand fathoms in height, adorned with various jewels.
When King Mahāghoṣa saw the golden pillar, he subsequently constructed a hall for offerings and cultivated various meritorious deeds.
The king appointed his maternal uncle, named Aśoka, to be solely in charge of overseeing the offerings.

At that time, all the people of the country delighted in seeing him; once they had beheld the banner, they would return to the hall of offerings with minds that could not let go, coming and going to make offerings until they eventually neglected their household affairs.
At that time, the kingdom’s tax revenue was insufficient, so the king’s ministers presented only a small amount.
When King Mahāśabda saw that the offerings were meager, he immediately asked,
"Why have you presented such a small amount of rent and labor taxes?"
The ministers replied: "Great King,
you should know that once the people of Jambudvīpa have finished eating at the hall of almsgiving, they immediately gaze upon the golden pillar and consequently neglect their livelihoods."
"Due to these causes and conditions, our tax revenue is insufficient.
The king then replied,
"The hall for almsgiving should be abolished."
The ministers, having received the command, immediately demolished it.

At that time, the people provided their own provisions and came to gaze upon and pay homage to the golden pillar; they did not depart, nor did they attend to their household affairs. Consequently, as before, the taxes and tributes could not be fully met.
The king asked again:
"Since you have already destroyed the hall for almsgiving at my command, why is the tax still insufficient now?
The ministers replied once more:

"Great King, you should know that those people have prepared their own provisions and, having eaten, gaze upon the golden pillar instead of attending to their household duties; for this reason, the taxes and corvée labor remain insufficient."
At that time, King Mahāghoṣa extensively practiced giving and performed various meritorious deeds; he then cast a golden banner into the Gaṅgā River.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor other thoughts!"
That maternal uncle of King Mahādeva named Aśoka is none other than the present bhikṣu Bhadrayaśas.
Because he protected and made offerings during his past causal stage, he did not come to behold and worship the golden pillar.
Then all the bhikṣus asked the World-Honored One,
"Where will this golden pillar perish?
The Buddha said:

"In the future, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, there will be a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Śaṅkha, who will govern the world according to the Dharma and transform people through the ten wholesome paths of action."
At that time, the king was fully endowed with the fourfold army, capable of subduing all and achieving victory over them all.

Constantly cultivating wholesome qualities, he was a great Dharma King, possessing the seven treasures: namely, the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder minister treasure, and the military commander treasure.

The king had a thousand sons, brave, heroic, and possessed of great strength; they were able to defeat his enemies, and throughout the four continents all were brought into submission, so that among all the people there was no longer any plundering or seizure.
Regarding those who commit crimes, he does not employ the sword or the staff, but instead issues proclamations according to the Dharma, whereby they are naturally subdued.
At that time, the king had a Brahmin named Sunetra, who was a high minister of the king; Sunetra had a wife named Viśuddhā, who constantly pervaded all beings with a heart of loving-kindness.
Later, when he gave birth to a son, he was named Maitreya.
At that time, the minister Sunetra was constantly teaching eighty thousand brahmin students (*maṇava*) the four Vedas.
He entrusted these students to Maitreya, charging him with their instruction and training in the four Vedas.
At that time, the Four Great Kings each brought forth hidden treasures and golden banners to present to Rāhula. These were as follows: the *Bheṅkela* treasure emerged from the kingdom of Kaliṅga;
the great *Pañcaka* treasury emerged from the kingdom of Mithilā;
and the *Elāpattra* treasury emerged from the kingdom of Gandhāra.
The great treasury of Śaṅkha arrived from the city of Vārāṇasī.

At that time, King Śaṅkha took this golden banner and gave it to Sunetra; Sunetra, having received it, gave it to Maitreya; Maitreya, having received it, gave it to eighty thousand *maṇava*s and others; and the *maṇava*s, having received it, divided it among themselves.
At that time, Maitreya, seeing this precious banner perish in an instant, realized that all phenomena are subject to total extinction; his heart was filled with sorrow and distress.

He immediately retired to a tranquil forest, gave rise to great compassion, and used the sword of wisdom to sever all afflictions, thereby attaining the wisdom of unsurpassed bodhi and being named Maitreya, the Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Once he had attained Buddhahood, on that very day, the seven treasures of King Śrīgupta vanished.
Upon seeing this, the king, surrounded by eighty thousand subordinate kings, also followed him into the homeless life.
At that time, the King’s daughter, a precious jewel named Viśākhā, also went forth into homelessness together with eighty thousand palace ladies and maidservants.
At that time, the minister Sunetra, along with eighty thousand young brahmins (maṇava), also followed him into homelessness.

At that time, Maitreya Buddha, surrounded by eighty million *koṭi* of bhikṣus, went to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to the place where the Bhikṣu Kāśyapa had left his skeletal body; as he pointed toward it, the mountain gate opened.

At that time, the World-Honored One Maitreya took the entire skeletal remains of Kāśyapa with his right hand, placed them in the palm of his left hand, and extensively expounded the sublime Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas, addressing the bhikṣus:
"You should know this!..."
In a past age, when the human lifespan was one hundred years, there was a Buddha named Śākyamuni who appeared in the world.
This Kāśyapa was a śrāvaka of that Buddha, possessing few desires and being content, and he was foremost among those who practice the dhūta austerities.
"After that Buddha has passed away, you will be able to compile and collect the teachings of Śākyamuni.
At that time, when Maitreya Buddha’s śrāvakas and others saw the relics of Kāśyapa’s preserved body, they felt sorrow and distress in their hearts, thinking:
"How could such a body as this have been able to realize all these various meritorious qualities?"
At that time, the disciples of the World-Honored One Maitreya, due to the arising of grief and distress, simultaneously realized the fruit of arhatship.
At that moment, there were ninety-six koṭis of arhats who, having been able to realize the dhūta practices, gave rise to weary detachment.
At that moment, the golden banner immediately vanished.
The bhikṣus then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions has King Śaṅkha appeared in the world at the same time as the World-Honored One?"
That Buddha replied,
"It is by the power of his vows.
The bhikṣu asked again:
"What is the power of aspiration?
At that time, Maitreya Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus:

"In the past, in the kingdom of Central India, there was a king named Masapa who governed the people according to the True Dharma. The realm was prosperous and joyful, free from disputes and litigation; it was filled with multitudes of people, always abounding in flowers and fruits. Rain fell in its proper season, and the five grains ripened."

At that time, in the kingdom of Northern India, there was a king named Bahudhana, who also ruled the world according to the True Dharma. The realm was prosperous and joyful, free from all disputes and litigation; it was filled with people, always abounding in flowers and fruits, with rains falling in due season and the five grains ripening in abundance.
Later, at another time, a high minister of the King of Central India gave birth to a son; at the moment of his birth, precious earrings spontaneously emerged from his ears, accompanying him.
Once the son was born, he immediately gathered his kinsmen to hold a celebratory feast and confer a name upon him.
Because the child had been born with jeweled earrings in his ears, they accordingly named him Ratnaprabha (Jewel Light).

At that time, this Jewel Light, at a later occasion, seeing old age, sickness, and death, felt deep distress in his heart; he immediately abandoned worldly ties and retired to the mountain forests, where on that very day he was able to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and was thereafter called the Tathāgata Jewel Light.
At another time, King Bahudhana of Northern India ascended a high tower, surrounded by his ministers in front and behind, and addressed his officials, saying:

"Is there any land like my own realm, where the people are prosperous and joyful, free from disputes and litigation, where rain falls in season, the five grains ripen, and one constantly experiences happiness?"
At that time, there was a merchant who had previously traveled to the kingdom of Central India;
he came forward and addressed the king, saying, "In that kingdom of Central India there is a king named Māṣapa, whose realm is prosperous and joyful, much like Your Majesty's."
When King Bahudhana heard these words, his heart was filled with great wrath, and he addressed his ministers, saying:
"You must immediately prepare the fourfold army; I shall now go in person to wage war against that King Māṣapa and destroy his kingdom."

Then King Bahudhana immediately led his military forces—namely, first the elephant corps, second the cavalry, third the chariot corps, and fourth the infantry—and having each arrayed their weapons, he proceeded toward Madhyadeśa; having crossed the Gaṅgā River, he took up position on its southern bank.
When King Māṣapa heard that King Bahudhana had led his fourfold army to the southern bank of the river, having heard this,
he likewise arrayed his fourfold forces, each bearing their weapons, and crossed to the northern bank of the Gaṅgā to take up position.

At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnaprabha, knowing that these two kings were ready to be tamed, came to the Ganges River and stayed there overnight; during that night, he gave rise to a worldly thought.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they give rise to a thought, Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protecting benevolent deities immediately know the Buddha’s thought.
Once those devas have known his thought, they come to where the Buddha is, prostrate at his feet, and withdraw to sit to one side.
The brilliant radiance of that deity illuminated the host of King Māṣapa’s army.
When King Bahudhana saw that light, his heart was filled with wonder and he asked his ministers,
"What light is this that shines upon those troops?"

The ministers replied, "In the kingdom of King Māṣava, a Buddha has appeared in the world named Ratnarcis Tathāgata; Śakra and all the devas have come to make offerings to him, for he possesses great majestic virtue and such radiance."
Then King Bahudhana said to his ministers:

"In the kingdom of that King Māṣava there has appeared this Jewel of a Buddha, a field of merit for bipeds, who has inspired the Brahmā kings and others to constantly come and make offerings. How could I now possibly harm that king’s person, his kingdom, his army, or his people?"
Then King Bahudhana immediately dispatched a messenger to inform that king, saying:
"Your Majesty may now come to meet with me. You possess great merit;
your kingdom has been graced by the appearance of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaprabha, a field of merit for bipeds, whom Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas have come to honor."
"However, I now wish to meet you, to clasp your hand and take my leave, so that we may both be free from fear and each attain peace.

When King Māṣapa heard these words, he felt doubt in his heart; he then went to the place where the Buddha Ratnaprabha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
King Bahudhana has sent a messenger to summon me, desiring to meet me and shake my hand in farewell.
I do not know now what I should do:
will the World-Honored One permit me to go?
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnaprabha replied:
"Great King!
You may go now to see him; you will surely find him in safety."
Then the king again asked the Buddha:
"When I arrive there and have met him, how should I perform the rites of greeting?
The Buddha told the king:
"He is a king of great power; you should pay him homage first.
Having heard these words of the Buddha, King Māṣava immediately went to King Bahudhana, intending to prostrate at his feet.
Then King Bahudhana rose immediately to receive him; they embraced and patted one another, offering mutual consolation.
Having taken their leave with joy, he returned to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Then Māṣa spoke, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Among all kings, who is the most honored and worthy of receiving salutations and respect?"
The Buddha replied to the king,
"A Wheel-Turning Sage King is worthy of receiving prostrations.
Upon hearing the Buddha's words, the king took them to heart and immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“May the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus accept our invitation to receive our offerings tomorrow.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
When the World-Honored One had finished eating, chewed his tooth-stick, and rinsed with pure water, King Māṣapa then made a sincere vow before the Buddha:
"I now take all the merit from making offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones, and by virtue of these roots of goodness, I vow that I shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
Having made this vow, he suddenly heard the sound of a conch being blown.
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnaprabha bestowed upon him this prophecy:
"In a future age, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, you shall appear in the world as a Wheel-Turning King, named Śaṅkha."
When the multitude heard this, they let out a tremendous cry.
Before King Bahudhana had yet gone far, he heard this clamor and asked his ministers:
"What cause or condition has arisen within the kingdom of King Māṣapa that such a great sound is being raised?"
The ministers investigated and questioned him, and soon reported to the king:
"The Tathāgata Ratnaprabha has bestowed a prophecy upon King Māṣava, that in a future age he shall become a Wheel-Turning Monarch."
When those people heard this prophecy, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; for this reason, they raised a great cry of exultation.

Upon hearing these words, King Bahudhana immediately turned his carriage around and went to the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaprabhāsa. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Who in all the world is worthy of receiving the prostrations of a Wheel-Turning King?
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Only the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is worthy of receiving the prostrations, offerings, and worship of a Wheel-Turning Holy King."
Then King Bahudhana rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will accept my humble offering tomorrow.”
When the meal was finished, and the bowl had been put away and the hands washed, King Bahudhana, giving rise to great compassion that pervaded the realm of sentient beings, made this vow:
"By the roots of goodness from this offering, may I quickly attain Buddhahood in the future and become a Teacher of Gods and Humans."
The Buddha then replied:
"Great King, you should know that in a future age,
when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, you shall become a Buddha named Maitreya, fully endowed with the ten titles."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"By the power of this very vow, both the Buddha and the Wheel-Turning King appear as two jewels simultaneously in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You may go with me to the village of Koṭigāma.

Thereupon, Ānanda accompanied the Blessed One on a journey through the Kṛṣi country, gradually reaching the village of Koṭigāma; not far to the north was the Veṇuvana forest, where the Buddha took up residence.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "You should know!
If these prohibitory precepts are broken, one's samādhi will also be lost accordingly."
If you are able to cultivate and maintain the precepts, this samādhi will remain ever-present.
By means of that wisdom, cultivate the body and mind, and attain right liberation from the three poisons.
Having practiced in this way and attained liberation, the noble one clearly understands:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
“You may accompany me to the village of Nadika.
Ānanda replied, “So be it,” and subsequently traveled with the Tathāgata through the country of the Kṛkis, gradually arriving at the Maṇḍalika Hall in the village of Nadika.
At that time, in the village of Nadika, there was a plague, and many people died.

During this period, numerous upāsakas—such as Culla Panthaka, Mahā Panthaka, Upavāna, Revata, Kṣemaka, Sobhita, Yaśas, and Uttara—all of whom were highly diligent, exceptionally noble, upright, preeminent among the multitude, and possessed of virtuous reputations, had already passed away.
At dawn, the bhikṣus took up their robes and bowls and entered the village of Nadika, going from door to door to beg for alms.
Those bhikṣus heard that many people had died in this village, including the upāsakas such as Cūḍapanthaka, Kolita, and Upāli, all of whom had passed away.

Having heard that people had died, the bhikṣus, after completing their almsround, returned to their original location, set aside their robes and bowls, approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We bhikṣus, having taken up our robes and bowls in the early morning, entered the village of Nadika to wander for alms, where we heard it said that many people in this village have died."
"Once those people have all passed away, through which realms do they each go to receive rebirth?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"That upāsaka Śuklodana, having severed the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni), immediately attained birth by transformation; he entered parinirvāṇa here and realized the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmiphala), attaining the state of non-retrogression within this very life."
"The other upāsakas and so forth were likewise. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "In that village of Nādikā, there were further two hundred and fifty-one upāsakas who all died;

they too had severed the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni) and attained rebirth by transformation (upapāduka), attaining parinirvāṇa here as non-returners (anāgāmin) and reaching the stage of non-retrogression in this world. Furthermore, in that village, there were three hundred upāsakas who also all died; because they had severed three of the fetters (trīṇi saṃyojanāni) and because their greed, hatred, and delusion remained only as slight obstructions, they attained the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin). After taking birth once more, they shall sever all afflictions and delusions."

In that village, furthermore, five hundred and one upāsakas passed away; because they had severed the three fetters, they realized the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna). They shall not fall into the evil destinies, but are certain to realize the fruit of enlightenment, taking birth seven times among gods and humans; once their transmigration has ceased, they will eradicate all afflictions.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know this!
Those who are about to die all come to question me; their vain lives have been a source of disturbance, yielding neither benefit nor peace."
Nevertheless, all who are born must return to death;
whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, birth and cessation are constant—what is there that is extraordinary?

Now, that which is the Dharma is the very realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Having realized and awakened to it through his own supernormal powers, the Tathāgata expounds, demonstrates, analyzes, establishes, reveals, and extensively teaches various sublime Dharmas, namely:

"Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair arise. Thus, this entire mass of pure suffering comes into being.
That is to say: because this does not exist, that does not arise; because that ceases, this shall cease. That is to say: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease;

with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. Thus, this entire mass of pure suffering ceases.
Nevertheless, I shall now speak to you, monks, the *Dharmādarśa-sūtra*.
Listen attentively and reflect upon it well!
What is meant by the *Dharmādarśa-sūtra*?

"You all should generate supreme faith and delight toward Perfect Awakening; this is called the *Dharmādarśa Sūtra*. Furthermore, you should generate supreme faith in the pure light of the noble precepts belonging to the Dharma and the Saṃgha; this is the *Dharmādarśa Sūtra*."
“Bhikṣus, you should know that what I have called the *Dharmādarśa-sūtra* is precisely this teaching.
At that time, the World-Honored One was wandering among the people of the Kṛṣṇa country and arrived at the village of Naḍika.
At that time, Lady Āmrapālī heard that the Buddha had arrived at the village of Nādikā.
Now, that lady had a parrot named Maṇicūḍa who was well-versed in human speech; she then dispatched this bird to Nādikā to pay homage to the World-Honored One, saying:
"Are you light and at ease in your daily life? Are you free from illness and affliction, and living in peace and happiness?"
“World-Honored One, if you intend to travel to Vaiśālī, I pray that out of compassion for me, you will first visit the Āmrapālī Grove.
At that time, having received these instructions, the parrot went to where the Buddha was; upon reaching Vaiśālī, he encountered the Licchavi youths and others leaving the city to play.
Seeing a parrot fly overhead, they cried out in unison, "The parrot of the Āmra slave-girl!
We shall now shoot it down with a volley of arrows!
Having spoken, they drew their bows and shot at the parrot; however, the arrow veered downward and struck the head of the boy.
Then that parrot spoke in verse:
"When two nations wage war, An envoy should not be killed;
How much more so I, the Buddha’s messenger— No one can harm me."
Then the youths also spoke in verse:
"Our arrows have no power; your words have proven true.
This is the majestic virtue of the Buddha; you should go without fear."

Then the parrot bird went immediately to where the Buddha was, prostrated with its head at the feet of the World-Honored One in respectful salutation, and fully recounted all the lady’s sincere faith. The Buddha said:
“Excellent!”
"May you be well and at ease.
He accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Thereupon, the parrot, knowing that the Buddha had accepted the invitation, paid his respects and departed; however, before he had reached the mango grove, he was seized and killed in mid-air by a wicked crow.
Having passed away, he was immediately reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Once born in that heaven, he thought to himself:
"By what cause have I come to be here?"
"What meritorious karma did I plant that I have been born here?
He then observed for himself and saw that it was because he had acted as a messenger for the Buddha that he had cast off his animal body and obtained this wholesome retribution.
He further thought to himself:
"I ought not to wait until tomorrow to repay the World-Honored One’s kindness.

Thereupon, taking his ornaments for adorning the body, as well as blue lotuses (*utpala*), kumuda flowers, puṇḍarīka flowers, māndārava flowers, and mahāmāndārava flowers, he went to the place where the World-Honored One was staying during the middle watch of the night. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, made offerings, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Due to the power of that celestial being’s bodily radiance, the village of Nādikā was exceptionally resplendent.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing their faculties and dispositions, preached the Dharma to the deva, namely the principle of the Four Noble Truths.
Having heard this Dharma, he used the vajra-pestle of wisdom to shatter the twenty-peaked mountain of the affliction of *satkāyadṛṣṭi*, and realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
When the devaputra had realized the principle of the Truths, he thrice exclaimed, "Excellent!

Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has brought me great benefit; this is something that neither my parents, nor my kinsmen, nor the Lord of Devas, nor śramaṇas, nor brahmins could have accomplished."

Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to uproot the sufferings of the hells, the animal realm, and the hungry ghosts; he establishes beings as devas and humans, transcends birth and death, dries up the oceans of blood and tears, leaves behind the mountains of flesh and bone, closes the gates to all evil destinies, and reveals the path to the pure heavens of Nirvana.

Since beginningless time, I have been accustomed to the mountains of false views; by means of vajra-like wisdom, may I be able to utterly destroy them and attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).

From this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, becoming an upāsaka. I shall never kill living beings and so forth; may the Buddha graciously accept me.

Filled with joy and exultation, he was like a merchant who has acquired great wealth, like a farmer whose crops have flourished, like a warrior who has vanquished a powerful enemy, or like a patient freed from all ailments. Having attained the supernormal powers, he prostrated before the Buddha and departed; by means of his supernatural power, he returned to his celestial palace.
At that time, the Blessed One said to Ānanda:
"I shall now go with you to the city of Vaiśālī. Ānanda replied:
“As you command.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with Ānanda, arrived at the Āmra Grove in Vaiśālī and stayed there. He addressed Ānanda, saying:
“You should go to the city of Vaiśālī, step upon the threshold of the gate, recite this dhāraṇī, and also recite these verses.”
The mantra says:
"Viśrātha viśrātha viśrātha viśrātha ruddhu ruddhu loka-anugupta-ajñāpanīya sarva-buddha-anu..."
Madhye sarvabuddhaparāvṛtānu-madhye sarvārhad-anumadhye sarvaśaikṣānumadhye sarvaśrāvakānumadhye sarvasatyavatinumadhye parājitānumadhye.
Rāmanumati-nāga-śivara-numati-indra-numati-devata-numati-asura-dhara-numati-asura-piśāca-numati-sarva-buddha-numati-viśara-viśa.
Rāviṣara viṣara vituduga nu gaṃgū kumānya ti vṛñcāta vṛñcāta.
It pacifies calamities, expels calamities, and drives out yakṣas.

“The Blessed One wishes to enter; Maheśvara, the Most Supreme Honored One, together with Śakra and Brahmā, wish to enter; the World-Lords, the Four Great Kings, together with their immeasurable retinues of devas, wish to enter; and the Asura King, along with his retinue and hundreds of thousands of immeasurable spirits and ghosts, having conceived great faith in the Buddha, the World-Honored One, also wish to come and enter for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.”
"You spirits and ghosts, do not conceive thoughts of harm; come forth quickly, come forth quickly! Depart quickly, depart quickly!
If you wish to give rise to evil intentions, you must depart at once;
if you possess a heart of compassion, you may remain as you please, for there shall be no fault."
Those who wish to provide protection may also be permitted to remain.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, the Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One has spoken thus:

The World-Honored One, out of compassion for the world,
desired to enter this city for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, and by means of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
This incantation accomplishes the gāthā; all devas and all sentient beings, by means of the most supreme wisdom and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), spoke this gāthā:
"Severing all fetters and habitual tendencies, One remains far removed from all craving and attachment."
One whose mind is always tranquil can bring you peace and happiness.
If there is anyone in the world who dwells well on the path to Nirvana and can expound all dharmas, they can bring you peace and happiness.
Amidst the cycle of birth and death, you act as a refuge for all;
benefiting the multitudes of sentient beings, may they bring peace and happiness to you.
With a heart of universal great compassion, you nurture and sustain all sentient beings.
With loving-kindness like that for an infant, he can bring you peace and happiness.
To all those who take refuge, even while within the cycle of birth and death;
by relying on him they obtain wholesome benefit—he can bring you peace and happiness.
Having realized all phenomena, Pure and free from defilement;
With body, speech, and mind in perfect stillness, May he bring you peace and happiness.
When he appears with courageous vigor, All wealth and resources shall increase.
Having accomplished all purposes and measures, may he bring you peace and happiness.
At the time of his ancient birth, the great earth shook;
all sentient beings rejoiced—may he bring you peace and happiness.
The great earth shook in six ways as he realized the path to enlightenment;
though the Māra King gave rise to a heart of affliction, he was able to bring you peace and joy.
He skillfully turned the wheel of the True Dharma, and his fame filled the ten directions.
He who proclaims the principles of the Noble Truths can bring you peace and happiness;
He who expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma, subduing all non-Buddhists,
And gathering in sentient beings can bring you peace and happiness.
May the Buddha, through his peace and happiness, Extend [his blessing] to Śakra-devānām-indra;
May all spirits and deities Constantly act as protectors.
By the power of the Buddha’s merit, May all the devas rejoice.
Whatever goals and aspirations one seeks shall all be accomplished without fail.
May all those with two feet and those with four feet be constantly protected;
may those who depart find safety, and may those who arrive likewise enjoy peace and happiness.
Finding peace and happiness at night, And likewise finding peace and happiness by day;
Encountering no evil matters, May all be peaceful and happy.
All the people of the world, As well as all the devas;
Those of other paths, ghosts, and animals— may all be free from affliction and distress.
May the spirits and deities who come here, whether moving upon the earth or through the air,
always maintain a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, performing virtuous deeds day and night.

Regarding the remaining portion of the *Avadāna* of Lady Āmrapālī: At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having received the dhāraṇī and the gāthās from the Buddha, immediately proceeded toward Vaiśālī; as he stepped upon the threshold of the gate, he performed all the rites according to the aforementioned method.

At that time, Lady Āmrapālī heard that the Buddha was traveling through Vaiśālī and had arrived at her Āmra grove. She adorned her attendants, who surrounded her in front and behind, and mounting a precious palanquin, she departed from the city to go to the place where the World-Honored One was, in order to pay homage and make offerings.
Upon arriving at the Āmra Grove, he descended from his carriage and, beholding the Honored One’s countenance from afar, prostrated himself in reverence.
At that time, the World-Honored One was seated, attended by an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, preaching the True Dharma for them.
Seeing Lady Āmrapālī from afar, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Each of you should dwell in right mindfulness according to your respective practice; Lady Āmrapālī is now approaching."
What is dwelling in right mindfulness?

One should abandon previously committed unwholesome karma; one should suppress and prevent the arising of unwholesome karma not yet arisen; one should not forget or lose previously cultivated wholesome karma, but diligently practice it so that it increases, becomes perfected, and leads to the realization of wisdom—one who acts in this way is said to possess diligence.
What is right mindfulness?

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one skillfully observes oneself; one arranges the *cīvara* robes, the water flask, the alms bowl, and so forth in accordance with the Dharma. Such observation is called right mindfulness.
What is right concentration?
One should observe the internal body for oneself, diligently cultivating right mindfulness and right intention, and relinquishing all unwholesome thoughts toward all sentient beings.

Furthermore, regarding the external body, the internal-external body; internal feelings, external feelings, and internal-external feelings; the internal mind, the external mind, and the internal-external mind; and internal phenomena, external phenomena, and internal-external phenomena—one perceives the phenomena in accordance with reality, diligently cultivates vigor, relinquishes all evils toward all sentient beings, and abides in right mindfulness.
"Now Lady Āmrapālī is about to arrive; she will instruct you, so you should practice well and rely upon my teaching.
At that time, Lady Āmrapālī went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of immeasurable skillful expedients, preached the sublime Dharma for her, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening her. Having done so, the World-Honored One remained silent.
Lady Āmrapālī rose from her seat, adjusted her robes, joined her palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, will deign to visit my home tomorrow morning to accept my offerings."
The World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted her invitation, Lady Āmrapālī paid her respects and departed.
At that time, the Licchavis heard that the Buddha had arrived at Vaiśālī and was staying in the Āmrapālī Grove; they each mounted their carriages and set out for the Buddha’s dwelling.
Their chariots, horses, and so forth were of various forms and types:
blue horses, blue harnesses, blue whips, blue carriages, blue parasols, blue turbans, blue swords, blue jewels, blue fans, blue garments, blue ointments, blue powdered incense, and blue attendants;
yellow, red, white, and other colors were likewise so.
Along the road they traveled, they drove them on with loud shouts, and no one dared to oppose them.
Having exited the city of Vaiśālī, they went straight to where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, seeing from afar that the Licchavis and their retinue were drawing near, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You have not yet seen when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven go out for recreation; you should now observe these Vaiśālī people.
Those hosts of devas, sporting in their groves by means of their sovereign supernormal powers, are no different from these people of Vaiśālī."
When the Vṛji people and others arrived outside the Āmra gate, they alighted from their carriage and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, then withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the Vṛjis and others, extensively expounded the essentials of the Dharma through immeasurable skillful means, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them.

At that time, there was a young brahmin named Viśuddha who arrived at the assembly together with them; he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"Sugata!..."
"I possess eloquence," he said.
Again he spoke: "O Sugata!"
"I possess eloquence and now wish to sing praises.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
Then the young brahmin spoke in verse:
“The Great King of Aṅga, clad in precious armor, Holds sovereign power over Magadha.
Within that king’s realm has appeared the World-Honored One, Whose fame pervades the ten directions like the Snowy Mountains.”
Together with kumuda and lotus flowers, their blossoms fully opened, exceedingly fragrant and pure;
the World-Transcender, sovereign in compassion, the Sugata whose fame reaches all directions.
When the sun rises, the red lotus blooms; when the moon rises, the kumuda flower flourishes.
When the multitude beholds the Buddha, they all rejoice, like seeing the bright moon in the sky.
All together we gaze upon the power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, like beholding a blazing fire in the night;
it can awaken the light of the eyes of sentient beings and dispel all doubts and delusions.
At that time, the Licchavis and others said to the young brahmin:
"Excellent words! Excellent words!
It is just as you have said."

At that time, because the young brahmin had praised them so well, the five hundred sons of the Licchavis each removed their upper garments and offered them to the young brahmin. Then they rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, joined their palms in homage to the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I pray that the Blessed One and the bhikṣus will deign to visit my home tomorrow at the proper time to accept my offerings.
The Blessed One replied,
"I have already accepted an invitation from Lady Āmrapālī."
When the Licchavis and others heard these words of the Buddha, they addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"We have now been brought to ruin by the Lady Āmrapālī, who possesses the most supreme wisdom."
"Now, because of that, we have not been able to go to the presence of the World-Honored One to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to him.
He further addressed the Buddha,
saying, "We shall, at a later time, make offerings to the Tathāgata and the assembly of bhikṣus."
The Buddha said, "Excellent!
Having heard that the Buddha had granted his permission, Vatsa and the other Licchavis departed with joy.
At that time, when the Licchavis had departed, the young brahmin rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to him:
"World-Honored One!
Those Licchavis, because I praised the World-Honored One so well, gave me five hundred superior robes."
"I now wish to offer these robes back to the World-Honored One; I pray that you will compassionately accept them.
At that time, out of compassion, the World-Honored One accepted the robes offered by the young brahmin.
Thereupon the Tathāgata addressed the māṇava, saying:
“When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, there are five marvelous qualities.
What are these five?

First, the appearance of a Teacher of Gods and Humans—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—who expounds the essential Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; whose phrasing and meaning are exquisite; which is pure and unadulterated; and which is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy life (brahmacarya). This is the first rarity.

Second, if there are those with faith who, regarding what the Tathāgata has spoken, listen and receive it with reverence, uphold the Dharma upon hearing it, and keep their minds from distraction—this is the second rare wonder.
Third, if there are those who hear the Buddha’s teaching and practice each point accordingly, this is the third rarity.

Fourth, those who hear the Dharma are able to realize it through direct knowledge, receiving it with joy and faith, giving rise to great roots of goodness, and becoming endowed with renunciation; this is the fourth rarity.
Fifth, if one hears profound verses of the Dharma and understands them through wisdom, this is the fifth rarity.
O Māṇava! Because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has appeared in the world, there are these five kinds of rarities.
At that time, the Tathāgata again addressed the young brahmin, saying:
"If even ordinary virtuous people do not forget a small kindness received, how much less so for a great kindness!"
"Therefore, you should diligently cultivate this matter.
At that time, the young brahmin, having heard what the Buddha had said, received it with faith and began to practice; he prostrated himself and departed.
At that time, during this night, Lady Āmrapālī prepared various kinds of food and drink, and finally sat upon a low seat for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
Then the World-Honored One, for the sake of Lady Āmrapālī, praised the merit of giving and spoke these verses:
"Those who give are loved by all and revered; Their fame is heard afar and their fragrance wafts everywhere."
Therefore, the wise constantly practice giving; seeking happiness and eliminating stinginess, they attain fearlessness.
Throughout the long night, they are born in the realm of Śakra, sporting together with the hosts of devas.
As the celestial palaces wait for them from afar, upon the cessation of this life, they are swiftly reborn in that heaven.
Carrying their own radiance, they roam the Joyful Garden, enjoying the five sensual pleasures with the celestial maidens;
when the disciples of the Buddha hear this Dharma, they will certainly be reborn in that heaven.
At that time, the Blessed One taught various dharmas to Lady Āmrapālī, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening her. Having done so, she paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
Then all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the Blessed One, saying:

"By what causes and conditions did those of the Licchavi clan—whether born in the heavens or born among humans—attain such great majesty and power as this, even sharing the same merit and reward as the Trāyastriṃśa gods?"
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know that those Licchavis of Vaiśālī, because they have accumulated the provisions of merit, [and so on, as extensively explained], even spoke this verse:
'Even if a hundred eons should pass, the karma one has created does not perish;'"
"When causes and conditions meet, the retribution of the fruit is received by oneself.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa appeared in the world, fully endowed with the ten titles."
That Buddha was dwelling in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana near the city of Vārāṇasī, surrounded by twenty thousand bhikṣus.
At that time, within that city, there were five hundred upāsakas who each prepared their goods and intended to go out to sea.

Together they constructed a ship and waited for a favorable wind; they then entered the great ocean and reached that island of jewels. They vied with one another to gather precious treasures, filling the ship to capacity. Suddenly, they encountered a malignant wind that drifted them onto a winding ravine, where they were unable to move despite their efforts.
Filled with fear and knowing no one on whom to rely, they gathered sand upon the riverbank for the Tathāgata Kāśyapa to form a stūpa, and they made offerings to it with various kinds of jewels.
While they were asleep, they encountered a great radiance, and a voice from within it said:
"You all must prepare your plans for departure; do not give way to negligence. On the seventh day, the tide of the ocean will surely come."
"By means of this ocean tide, you shall surely attain peace and happiness and reach your own country.
Then those merchants, at the break of dawn, spoke to one another:

"Let us deliberate on this matter: we have made various offerings to Kāśyapa, the World-Honored One, the unsurpassed field of merit; by this root of goodness, may we possess great majesty and power among gods and humans, no different from those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three."

"O bhikṣus! Those five hundred merchants were none other than these five hundred Licchavis of Vaiśālī today. In the past, they built sand stupas for the Tathāgata Kāśyapa and made offerings to them with precious jewels."
By reason of these causes and conditions, one attains great majesty and power among gods and humans, no different from those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Bhikṣus, you should know:
those who perform purely black deeds obtain purely black retribution;
Those who perform purely white deeds obtain purely white retribution;
those who perform mixed deeds obtain mixed retribution.
Therefore, you all should abandon purely black deeds as well as mixed deeds, cultivate various white deeds, apply yourselves with diligent effort, and do not be negligent.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, all the bhikṣus were greatly rejoiced; they accepted them with faith and practiced accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"You should follow me to the village of Veṇuvana."
He replied: “Indeed,
World-Honored One.”
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling among the people of Vṛji and arrived at the northern part of the village of Veṇugrāmaka, where he entered and stayed within a grove of śāla trees.
At that time, the country was suffering from a famine so severe that it reached a state of extreme distress; it was difficult to obtain almsfood through begging.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The world is currently afflicted by famine, and it is difficult to obtain almsfood. You, bhikṣus!"
As explained in detail in the *Durbhikṣa-sūtra*, as well as in the *Mārgavarga-āgama-sūtra*, the *Ṣaṭsūtra*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* regarding the practice of the Dharma.
At that time, the Blessed One said to Ānanda,
"Follow me as we go to the village of Avanti.
He replied:
"So be it. At that time, as the World-Honored One proceeded to a certain place, he suddenly smiled.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they smile, rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth—issue from the Tathāgata’s mouth and divide into two streams.
One ray ascends directly upward, while another descends directly downward.

That light which descends illuminates the hells of Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma.
Among them, those who were hot became cool upon encountering the light;
likewise, those who were cold became warm upon encountering the light.
All manner of most grievous sufferings were entirely stilled.
When those sentient beings in the hells had their suffering momentarily ceased, they all thought to themselves:
"Have we now perished from here and been reborn elsewhere?
To inspire deep faith in the minds of those beings, the Tathāgata manifested a transformed body and went there to teach and transform them.
Having seen the transformation buddha, they then thought:
"We have not perished here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere; furthermore, we have never before seen this sentient being."
"By the majestic power of the Buddha, we have all been liberated from our intense sufferings.

At that time, those sinful beings conceived supreme faith in the Tathāgata’s transformation body; once their karmic retributions were exhausted, they were reborn among gods and humans, where they attained reliance upon the true principles of the Noble Truths.

The light that ascended reached as far as the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and even the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Wherever the light reached, it issued forth sounds proclaiming impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and so forth, and further recited two verses of *gāthā*:
"You should seek liberation, And diligently practice the Buddha’s teaching;
Subdue the army of birth and death, As an elephant destroys a thatched hut."
"In this Dharma and Vinaya, by always practicing heedfulness, one can exhaust the ocean of afflictions and reach the ultimate end of suffering.
At that time, the light pervaded the trichiliocosm; having illuminated it everywhere, it followed behind the World-Honored One.
If he speaks of past events, the light vanishes from behind;
if he speaks of future events, the light vanishes from the front;
if he speaks of matters concerning the hells, the light vanishes from beneath his feet.
If he speaks of matters concerning animals, the light vanishes from his ankles;
if he speaks of matters concerning hungry ghosts, the light vanishes from the big toes of his feet;
if he speaks of matters concerning humans, the light vanishes from his knees.
If he speaks of the affairs of a Cakravartin King of Power, the light vanishes into his left hand;
if he speaks of the affairs of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), the light vanishes into his right hand;
if he speaks of the karma for rebirth in the heavens, the light vanishes from his navel.
If he speaks of the enlightenment of the śrāvakas, the light disappears into his mouth;
if he speaks of the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas, the light disappears into the tuft of hair between his eyebrows;
if he speaks of the matter of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the light disappears into the crown of his head.
At that time, the light circled the Buddha three times and vanished into the crown of his head.
Then the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked him in verse:
"Of a thousand variegated colors, Bound together, they issued from your mouth;
Its light illuminates the ten directions, like the full radiance of the sun.
Again, he spoke in verse:
"Pride, madness, and deceit are removed; it serves as the supreme cause for the world."
"With lotus-bud teeth and conch-white fangs, you do not smile without cause.
He further spoke in verse:
"At this time, because the Buddha has personally realized the Dharma, those who go there to hear it shall attain the most supreme state."
"The unsurpassed Bull among Men speaks these profound words, which can eliminate doubt through their purity.
The Buddha said: "Ānanda!"
It is so, it is so. Ānanda, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, does not smile without cause or condition. Ānanda!
"Do you see this place?
He replied, "I see it."
“Ānanda! This is the place where the three Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past sat.
Then the Venerable Ānanda immediately spread his seven-strip robe in four layers and invited the World-Honored One to sit, desiring that this spot become a place used by four World-Honored Ones.
The Blessed One took his seat and, after sitting for a short while, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"I now wish to go to the village of Mettī. Ānanda replied:
“Certainly! I wish to follow you.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm in the city of Vaiśālī and arrived at Mithilā, where he stayed in the Mahādeva Grove.
This is explained in detail as in the Mahādeva-sūtra and the Rājāvavādaka-parivarta.
Again, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"I wish to go once more to the place of the Anavatapta Well."
The details are as explained above.
Upon arriving at the side of the well, he saw a woman holding a water jar and rope, intending to draw water.
A man felt a sense of passionate attachment toward this woman, and she likewise felt deep affection for him; they walked together, conversing and laughing, until they reached the edge of the well.
The woman brought her young child along as she traveled.
As the mother watched the man and reached out to take his water, she mistakenly looped the cord around the child’s neck and threw him into the well; the child’s life ended instantly.

At that time, the woman had never heard a verse (*gāthā*) spoken since her birth; yet, due to the death of her child while she was bound [in grief], her eloquence manifested spontaneously, and she recited this single verse:
“I know the root cause of desire: it arises from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
If I do not engage in such discrimination, from where could desire ever arise?”
At that time, the Tathāgata followed the road and said to Ānanda:
"You should receive this verse; it was spoken by the Buddhas of the past. Because it has fallen into the mouths of foolish worldlings, this verse does not manifest its radiance."
As the Buddha has said:
"I have never seen any phenomenon that moves as swiftly as the mind.
At that time, a woman, having suffered extreme anguish over the death of her son, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One, knowing the woman’s inclinations and latent tendencies, preached the Dharma to her in accordance with her faculties.
Having heard the Dharma, the woman realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the true reality, he then spoke of himself, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Dharma I have realized was not created by my father or mother, nor was it created by kings or devas, nor by my kinsmen," as explained at length above.

This is the power of the World-Honored One, which can dry up the oceans of blood and tears, transcend the mountains of bones, close the gates to the evil realms, open the paths to heaven and liberation, establish the way to the celestial and human states, and cause beings to enter the stream of the fortunate realms.
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; from this day forward, I am an upāsikā.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"When I was a bodhisattva, there was once an ascetic here named Bhārgava who invited me to sit and made offerings of flowers and fruit."
"In other places as well, he likewise made such offerings.
He further addressed Ānanda:
"In the past, when I was a bodhisattva, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, took the form of a hunter and wore a garment of variegated colors."
At that time, for the sake of my renunciation, I removed my fine and soft upper garments and exchanged them for this one.
Faithful brahmins, householders, and others subsequently established the Kāṣāya-reception Stūpa at this spot; from then until today, all bhikṣus have paid it homage and made offerings.

Śakra, Lord of the Devas, took my kāṣāya robe and enshrined it in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, establishing the Kāṣāya Assembly Day; to this day, all in the Heaven of the Thirty-three continue to make offerings to it.
Proceeding further to another location, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"In the past, when I was a bodhisattva, I took a sword the color of a blue lotus and cut off my own topknot, casting it into the air. A faithful brahmin householder then erected the Śikhā-cchedana Stūpa at this very spot."
"O Bhikṣus!
You should now pay homage and make offerings to it.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, took my topknot and enshrined it in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, establishing the festival day of the Topknot, which continues even today without ceasing.
The Buddha again went to another place and said to Ānanda:
"In the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, it was here that Candaka led my horse-king Kaṇṭhaka back to the palace."
"Faithful Brahmins and householders have further established the Horse-Turning Stūpa at this site, where the Bhikṣus continue to offer worship to this day.
Continuing on, he gradually arrived at the village of Govindagrāma and said to Ānanda:
"The noble son Candaka was born here, and grew up until he reached maturity."
They arrived at that city once more.
When the kṣatriya Mallas and others within the city heard that the World-Honored One was about to arrive, the elders all said:
"Let the youths adorn the roads, while we ourselves adorn the interior of the city."

At that time, the youths vied with one another to decorate and prepare the road; seeing a large boulder in the middle of the path, they sought to remove it, but though they lifted it, they could not overcome its weight.
At that time, the Tathāgata went up to their side and asked,
"Vasiṣṭhas, what do you intend to do now?
They replied:
"I wish to prepare the road for the World-Honored One;
however, I cannot proceed unless I remove this rock.
The Buddha said:
"If this is the case, I shall remove it.
He said, "I pray that you will remove it for me."
At that time, the World-Honored One took up the stone with his hand and hurled it into the void; the stone rose so high and far that onlookers could no longer see it.
When those strongmen saw the immense force and sound of the hurled stone, they were all struck with terror.
The Buddha said,
"Do not be afraid. Then,
by means of his supernormal power, he caused that rock to be shattered into fine dust, which fell down from the sky.
When the Mallas had seen this, they addressed the Buddha, saying,
"From where have these motes of dust fallen?
The Buddha said:
"I have reduced that stone to these fine particles.
The Mallas and others replied,
"This is not well done."
The Buddha asked,
"Do you wish for these motes of dust to recombine and become the original stone? He replied:
"So be it. At that time, by the power of his liberation, the World-Honored One caused the rocks to close together again and placed them back in their original position.
The World-Honored One then sat upon the rock, and the five hundred strongmen likewise all sat together with him.
They said to him,
"By what power, World-Honored One, are you able to lift this stone?
The Buddha replied:
"It is by the strength born of my parents.
The Malla spoke again:
"By what power are you able to shatter this stone?"
The Buddha said,
"By the power of meditative concentration.
He asked again:
“By what power is it possible to join these stones together?
“By the power of liberation. He replied:
"How much strength is there in that which is produced by one's parents?
The Buddha said,
"Starting from the strength of ten men, it is equal to the strength of an ordinary ox."
Ten times the strength of an ordinary ox is equal to the strength of one blue ox.
Ten times the strength of a blue ox is equal to the strength of one small elephant.
Ten times the strength of a small elephant is equal to the strength of one large elephant.
The strength of ten great elephants is equal to the strength of one blue elephant;
the strength of ten blue elephants is equal to the strength of one red elephant;
the strength of ten red elephants is equal to the strength of one white-tusked elephant.
The strength of ten white-tusked elephants is equal to the strength of one *Bhinda* mountain elephant.
The strength of ten *Bhinda* mountain elephants is equal to the strength of one fragrant elephant (*gandhahastin*).
The strength of ten fragrant elephants is equal to the strength of one strongman (*mahānagna*).
The strength of ten *ṛṣabha* wrestlers is equal to the strength of one great wrestler.
The strength of ten great wrestlers is equal to the strength of one fierce elephant.
The strength of ten fierce elephants is equal to the strength of one *cāmaravara* yakṣa.
The power of a yakṣa dwelling in the tenth stage is equal to half the strength of a Nārāyaṇa;
the strength of half a Nārāyaṇa is equal to the strength of one full Nārāyaṇa.
"In every joint of the Tathāgata’s body, the strength of Nārāyaṇa is naturally present.
The summary verse says:
"The human and the ox, and the blue ox; the yellow, red, small, and great elephants."
The strength of the Malla yakṣas and others does not equal that of Nārāyaṇa.
This power of Nārāyaṇa is the innate, natural power of the Tathāgata’s parents.
The Mallas addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"Aside from this Nārāyaṇa and the power of liberation, are there any other powers?
The Buddha said:

“Because he possesses the power of merit and because that power of merit is perfected, the Tathāgata subdued thirty-six koṭis of various māras and demons at the Bodhi tree and realized unsurpassed awakening.”
He addressed the Buddha again, saying,
"Apart from the power of merit, is there any other power?
The Buddha said:
“Because of the power of wisdom and the perfection of wisdom, all afflictions accumulated since beginningless time have been completely cast away.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying,
“Aside from the power of wisdom, are there any other powers?”
The Buddha said, "I possess supernormal powers; because my supernormal powers are perfected, I am able to subdue the six heterodox teachers who are aged, ignorant, and arrogant."
He addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Aside from the power of supernormal faculties, are there any other powers?
The Buddha said:

"There is the power of impermanence; because the power of impermanence is all-encompassing, the Tathāgata’s power of parents, the power of meditative concentration, the power of liberation, the power of merit, the power of wisdom, and the power of supernormal faculties—all these powers of the Tathāgata have their radiance extinguished beneath the twin śāla trees."
The verse says:
Meditative concentration and liberation, The power of merit and wisdom—
Of all such powers as these, The power of impermanence is the greatest.
The Buddha told the Mallas:
"You should know that my body is like a peak of a golden mountain; by the power of impermanence, it will soon be worn away and destroyed.
Therefore, the wise person should seek that place which impermanence cannot assail."
The Buddha told the Mallas:
"You should know that in the present age,
the lifespan of people gradually shortens, and their physical strength and vitality become weak and inferior."
However, this stone was once a stone used by people of old for tossing and playing; look at the side of this stone, and you will still see traces of fingers holding it up and tossing it.
When the Mallas heard these words of the Buddha, they were greatly astonished; they conceived a sense of rare wonder and subdued their pride.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the dispositions, latent tendencies, and inclinations of the Mallas, taught them the Dharma of the realization and wisdom regarding the principles of the Four Noble Truths.
Having heard this, they shattered the mountain of self-view and view of a body—accumulated since beginningless time—with the vajra-wisdom, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"I shall now go with you to the city of Kuśinagara."
He replied, “Indeed.
Having proceeded gradually, there was the city of Vaṃsā along the way; without entering this city, he then went directly to the kingdom of Kuśinagara.
Having arrived in that country, the World-Honored One pointed to the twin śāla trees and said to Ānanda:
"I shall, before long, enter parinirvāṇa beneath those trees."
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling among the people of Kuru and arrived at the royal city of Kauśāmbī.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I know all outflows (āsrava); I declare that they are all extinguished."
"It is not that I do not know; it is not that I do not see. Bhikṣus!
How could it be that one who does not know and does not see has already attained the extinction of the outflows?"
That is to say: "This is form; this is the accumulation of form; this is the cessation of form.
It is likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to: "This is consciousness; this is the accumulation of consciousness; this is the total cessation of consciousness."
If there is a bhikṣu who constantly cultivates meditative concentration and gives rise to the thought of seeking liberation from the outflows (āsrava),
yet that bhikṣu does not attain liberation of mind by being free from those outflows.
Why is this? Because that bhikṣu does not practice cultivation.
One should answer in this way.
Question: "Why does he not cultivate it? Answer:

"It is because of not cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness; it is because of not cultivating the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the factors of the sevenfold awakening, and the noble eightfold path."
He answered thus:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that it is like a hen laying eggs— perhaps five, perhaps six, or twelve, and so forth."
At that time, the mother hen did not hatch her chicks at the proper season; she neither incubated them with warmth nor turned them over.
Nevertheless, she thought to herself:
"I have produced these offspring."
"Or one might use a beak or use claws to break its shell, hoping that the chick will emerge from the shell safely.
However, because that chicken egg was not prepared according to the proper method, it ultimately fails to achieve the goal of emerging from its shell."

Why is this? It is because that mother hen did not sit upon her eggs at the proper time; furthermore, she neither provided them with warmth nor turned them over, and for these reasons, they were not hatched.

The bhikṣu who practices concentration is also like this: that bhikṣu does not seek liberation from the mind through what is with outflows (sāsrava), nor does he attain liberation of the mind by means other than what is with outflows.
For what reason?
Because they have not practiced cultivation, they speak thus:
"How is it that one does not practice cultivation?"

This is because they have not cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the factors of the sevenfold awakening, and the noble eightfold path.
If there is a bhikṣu who exerts himself in the cultivation of concentration and gives rise to such a thought as seeking liberation from what is with outflows (sāsrava),
yet that bhikṣu does not attain liberation from what is with outflows.
Why is this? Because it is due to cultivation.
Thus he answered.
How is it cultivated?

It is cultivated by means of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and so forth.
By practicing in this way, he gave this answer:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
It is just as a hen lays eggs— whether five, six, or even twelve— and at that time,
the hen broods over her chicks, warming them according to the proper method without missing the right time.

"O Bhikṣus, you should know that the mother hen does not give rise to such a thought; rather, her chicks themselves use their beaks and claws to break through their shells, hoping thereby for their own safe growth."
That chick was thus able to achieve success; it was able to break its shell with its beak and claws and emerged safely from the shell.
Why was this? Because the hen-mother had nurtured it according to the proper method, providing warmth and turning her body at the right times, whereby it was able to achieve completion.
In the same way, that bhikṣu who practices and seeks meditative concentration does not give rise to such a thought:
"I have attained liberation of the mind from outflows."
That bhikṣu further does not attain liberation of mind from outflows. Why is this?
It is because he attains liberation through the practice of cultivation.
He answers in this manner. Why?
Because he practices the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eightfold noble path; it is because he practices these that he answers in this way.
"O Bhikṣus, you should know!
It is like a carpenter and his apprentice who constantly use an adze;
because of this constant use, finger-marks eventually appear upon it."
"O Bhikṣus, you should know!

That carpenter and his apprentice were unable to apply their own right knowledge and right view to the use of the axe handle; because they used it repeatedly, they did not realize it was wearing away."
Once the exhaustion [of the wood] has been seen, one first gives rise to the thought, "I know this handle is exhausted.

In the same way, it is with the bhikṣu who practices concentration; yet he is unable to proceed in accordance with right knowledge and right view, nor does he personally realize the extent to which his outflows have been severed. Only when he later reaches the exhaustion of outflows does he finally realize and know it for himself.
Why is this? Because of diligent cultivation.
How is it possible to realize it?
He answered in this way: "How is it cultivated?
It refers to the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eightfold noble path; it is because of such cultivation that this statement was made."
"Monks, you should know this:

it is just as a sea-going ship that has been in the water for six months, then brought out onto dry land during the hot summer months; when exposed to the wind and sun, it naturally falls apart upon encountering rain."
The bhikṣu who cultivates meditative concentration is likewise: all fetters associated with the mind, latent afflictions, and various obstacles naturally dissolve. Why is this?
Through cultivation, they are all able to attain liberation.
How does one cultivate so as to attain liberation?
It refers to the cultivation of equanimity and so forth, as explained in detail above.
"Through cultivation, one speaks thus.
At that time, when the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma,
sixty bhikṣus were freed from all outflows, and their minds attained liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm and arrived at the city of Devadṛśa, where he addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"In this city, Śākyamuni the Well-Awakened was born and raised."
Again, having arrived at the Lumbinī Grove, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"In this grove, immediately after my birth, I walked seven paces toward the south without the support of anyone else; observing the four directions, I then spoke these words:
'This is my final body; I shall not undergo further rebirth.'"
He then proceeded to the city of Kapilavastu and addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"King Śuddhodana was born in this city and there he long held the royal throne."
He then proceeded to the city of Viśvānara. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now, for your sake, analyze and explain the two retributions of good and evil."
Listen attentively, all of you, and reflect upon this well!
What is the "evil assembly"?
It refers to desire, hatred, delusion, fear, and confusion, which follow one another and bind through conceptualization; this is called the evil assembly.
What is the virtuous assembly?
It refers to those who do not follow after desire, hatred, delusion, fear, and so forth; this is called the virtuous assembly.
Thus have I now explained these two assemblies.
The Blessed One again arrived at the village of Kuṇa and addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"In this very village, the Tathāgata Kuṇālamuni was born; having attained perfect enlightenment, he entered parinirvāṇa on this very spot."
At that time, the World-Honored One again traveled to the village of Karṇa and addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:

"When I was a bodhisattva, while wandering through the villages of my father the king, I arrived at the foot of a jambu tree. There, reflecting and entering meditative concentration, I realized the first dhyāna free from outflows."
Again, going to another place, he said to Ānanda:
"This is where, in the past, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Konāgamana placed his saṃghāṭī robe upon the ground."
He then proceeded to the village of Snātika and addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"In the past, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kunāthamuni bathed here in this village; consequently, it was given the name 'Bathing Village' (Snātikagrāma)."
He then proceeded to the village of Skadhi. To the north of the village, he stayed in the Veṇuvana (Bamboo Grove) and addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a craftsman named Aṭṭhala who would always carry a bamboo pole upon his shoulder as he walked."
There was a disciple named Mṛḍaka who would frequently mount the bamboo staff held by his master and perform dances upon it.
At that time, the ācārya said to Mṛḍaka:
"You may climb onto my shoulders and mount the pole; you must always look downward."
Look at one another and do not allow any mistakes to occur.
As you climb the pole, take turns with each other so that neither is injured.
Once the dance is performed, descend the pole with steady caution.
"When the people see this, they will know that both you and I possess superior abilities.
Once they have conceived joy, we shall together acquire wealth.
Then Mileraka said to Aṭala:
"Do not speak such words.
Why? For now, you, Master, should simply guard yourself, and I shall likewise apply my own mind."
"Having performed the dance and music, they safely descended from the pole, neither of them suffering any loss.
When the people saw this, both parties obtained their wealth.
At that time, the Buddha said:
"As the disciple Mili has said, one should follow this principle. Why is that?
Because if one can protect oneself, one is thereby able to protect others."
If one wishes to protect others while being unable to protect oneself, how can one protect others by protecting oneself?
This is achieved through diligent exertion and repeated cultivation.
Because one guards oneself by following [the precepts], when sensory objects appear before one, one is thus able to protect others while protecting oneself.
How could it be that one protects others but cannot protect oneself?
Because they do not afflict others, nor harbor anger toward them, and do not cause them harm, but instead treat them with compassion and pity;
for this reason, they are able to protect others who cannot protect themselves.
Therefore, you bhikṣus, should train yourselves in this way:
if you wish to guard yourselves, you should practice the four foundations of mindfulness.
Whether you wish to guard others, or speak of guarding yourself and guarding others, you should likewise practice the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four foundations of mindfulness?
They are the foundations of mindfulness regarding the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
You, bhikṣus, should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the Blessed One arrived at the village of Cāpāla and stayed in a grove. He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I shall now remain in meditative seclusion in this grove for two months."
"Except for those who provide food and drink, none of the other bhikṣus shall come here.
When the day of the poṣadha arrives, they shall also send those who provide food and drink to come and receive the *chanda*."

At that time, the World-Honored One entered into meditative absorption; none of the bhikṣus went to him, except for the person who was providing the food and drink, who was able to reach the Buddha’s presence.
When two months had passed, the Blessed One arose from that meditative absorption, took his seat before the assembly of bhikṣus, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If any non-Buddhists should come and ask you:
'In what manner did the śramaṇa Gautama practice during these two months so as to enter into this state of meditative absorption?'"
You should reply:
"I have entered the samādhi of counting the breaths. Why is this?
For two months, I dwelt in seclusion practicing the meditation on counting the breaths.
While practicing this meditation, my attention was never distracted during inhalation; I understood it exactly as it was.
He is also without distraction regarding the exhalation, knowing it as it truly is.
He fully knows the long and short [breaths], their arising and ceasing, and all exhalations throughout the entire body.
He also fully knows all inhalations throughout the entire body.
He understands as it truly is: "I am breathing out while practicing pliancy"; he understands as it truly is: "I am breathing in while practicing pliancy.

He understands as it truly is: "I am experiencing [feeling]," "I am cognizing with the mind," and "I am experiencing pleasure. He understands as it truly is: "I am breathing in while practicing the mental formation of pliancy."
He breathes out while calming the mind, knowing it as it truly is.
He knows the mind; he gladdens the mind, concentrates the mind, and liberates the mind as he breathes in, knowing it as it truly is.
He breathes out with a liberated mind, knowing it as it truly is.
He breathes in while perceiving impermanence, perceiving relinquishment, perceiving disenchantment, and perceiving cessation, knowing it as it truly is.
"Up to and including the perception of the cessation of the exhalation, he understands it as it truly is.
Bhikṣus, you should know:

'I now mindfully recognize this to be a coarse activity; I now transcend this activity and proceed with a refined activity, a further, extremely subtle activity. This is because I have transcended that coarse activity and, through lightness, repeatedly cultivate subtle activity."
At that time, three devas came to where I was and sat down; one of them spoke thus:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has now passed away."
One said: "He has not yet ceased; he is now about to cease.
Another said:
"He has not yet ceased, nor does he wish to cease; he abides in meditative concentration. All those who are worthy of offerings abide in such concentration. O Bhikṣus!
