I shall now explain to you, in accordance with the Dharma, the practice of the noble ones, the practice of the devas, the practice of the Brahmās, the practice of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), the practice of those in training (śaikṣa), and the practice of the Tathāgatas.

All those who are still in training have that which they have not yet attained but ought to attain, that which they have not yet realized but ought to realize, and that which they have not yet seen before them but ought to see before them.
All those who are beyond training have already seen before them and shall cause that vision to increase.
"There is a learner who shall attain the vision of the Dharma and dwell in peace and happiness," as it is said in the *Mārgavarga-saṃgraha-sūtra*.
*The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*, Fascicle Seven.
*The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*.
Fascicle Eight.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Command.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm in Kośala and arrived at the village of Saṃkassa, where he stayed in the Saṃkassa Forest.
At that time, the brahmin Padmagarbha was the head of the village, having been bestowed [upon him] by King Jayasena.
He had a disciple named Āmrapālīputra, who was profoundly learned and widely erudite, with the peaks of his eloquence soaring loftily.
On that lotus stalk there were always five hundred disciples practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*), reciting the scriptures of the four *vidyās*.

They heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, having shaved off his hair and beard from the Śākya clan and donned the dharma robes, had left home with right faith and realized unsurpassed awakening. His fame pervades the ten directions; he is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān. For the sake of gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brahmins, he proclaims:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, there is no further existence, and what was to be done has been accomplished."

"Excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; its phrasing is skillful, pure and unadulterated, complete with the characteristics of the pure and holy life (brahmacarya). Wandering through the human realm, he arrived at Veṇuvana."
The Lotus-Stem thought to himself:
"As it is said in my own scriptures:
'If a person possesses the thirty-two marks, that person shall have two possible destinies:'"

First, if he remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) who rightly transforms the world, endowed with the seven treasures—namely, the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the woman-treasure, the minister-treasure of the military, the minister-treasure of the treasury, and the mani-jewel treasure. He will possess a thousand sons, majestic and courageous, of handsome and dignified appearance, who subdue enemy armies. Throughout the great earth, its mountains and rivers, there will be no thieves or robbers; without the use of blades or staffs, he shall govern the people through the True Dharma.
"Secondly, if one shaves off hair and beard, dons the robe of a field of merit, and goes forth from home with right faith, one shall attain perfect enlightenment.
Having heard this, he then said to the son of Amrapali:
"Do you know now?"

I have heard that Gautama of the Śākya clan shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and out of right faith went forth from home; he has even attained equal and perfect enlightenment, and his fame extends throughout the ten directions.
While traveling through the human world, I arrived at the Veṇuvana Grove.
In my sūtras, I have said:
"If a person possesses the thirty-two marks, that person shall have two possible destinies, up until the attainment of perfect enlightenment."
[He] related everything as previously stated.
He then addressed his disciples, saying:
"You may go to where Gautama is; having arrived, report back to me whether it was exactly as I said."
The disciple replied, "Yes, I shall do as you command.
Thereupon, that disciple went together with the elder brahmins to where the Buddha was; having arrived, they stood to one side.
When the elder brahmins had all exchanged greetings and inquiries after his health, they withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the sublime Dharma for the elder brahmins and others, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them.

At that time, Āmraputra, wearing a single leather garment, moved about restlessly with an air of arrogance; he did not listen to the Buddha’s teaching but repeatedly interrupted to inquire about its meaning.
Although the Tathāgata had answered him, Aṅgulimāla still did not intend to receive the Buddha’s words, yet he remained so disrespectful toward the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Aṅgulimāla:
"Those elder brāhmaṇas were all masters of the Three Vedas; how could you now presume to treat them with such contempt and challenge them with questions?"
Then Āmrapālī replied,
“Gautama, what question do I have?”
The World-Honored One said:
"I have been expounding the essentials of the Dharma for the leading brahmins and others.
Yet you, wearing a single piece of leather, move through the assembly and pose questions with such levity."
"I have already answered you, yet you still do not listen. Āmrapālī replied,
"If one belongs to the class of Brahmins, one may sit together with them to discuss the Dharma."
Since you are now a shramana with shaved hair, what fault is there in my coming and going to exchange greetings with you, who are not of the brahmin class?
You śramaṇas are mere worldlings; you travel upon evil paths and are largely defiled by unwholesome dharmas.
"Those such as you ought to be addressed with contempt; that is why I have acted thus.
Then the World-Honored One said to Āmrapālī, "You have come here seeking benefit."
"As I observe you now, it appears you have never served your teachers.
When Āmrapālī heard these words of the Buddha, she immediately gave rise to resentment; wishing to slander and disparage the World-Honored One, she spoke thus:
"The Kṣatriya Śākyas are truly great fools; they do not know how to show respect to superior persons who practice the holy life."
The Buddha asked Aṃmala,
“What fault have the Śākyas committed? Aṃmala replied:
"In the past, when I had business that led me into the city of Kapilavastu, the Śākyas who were on the high towers all pointed at me and said:
'This is a disciple of Padmaka.'"
"They treat me with contempt and do not show me respect.
The Buddha said,
"Do you see the śālika bird?"

"If he is already so free and at ease in uttering various speeches while remaining in his own nest, how much more so must the Śākyas be when they dwell in the city of Kapilavastu. The Āmra-putra said: "There are four kinds of people: 1. Those who are themselves bound but seek to bind others; 2. Those who are themselves bound but do not seek to bind others; 3.
Those who are themselves liberated but seek to liberate others; 4. Those who are themselves liberated and do not seek to liberate others."
First are the Brahmins, second the Kṣatriyas, third the Vaiśyas, and fourth the Śūdras.
These four classes of people all show reverence to the Brahmins.
"Only you, a foolish member of the Śākya clan, seeing one who is most venerable and superior, do not understand how to show respect.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"This son of Āmrapālī says, 'I am of the Śākya clan; from previous lives, my father was of the Śākya clan, but my mother was not.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One contemplated the parents of Ambaṣṭha in his past lives: what kind of lineage were they?
He knew that he was born from the clan of a Śākya slave-girl, and that the Śākyas were his former masters.
He then asked Āmrapālī, "What is your caste?
She replied:
“Gautama! I am of the Karṇa lineage.
The Blessed One replied:
"I have sought out your lineage; you are born of a Śākya slave-girl, and the Śākyas are your masters.
At that time, the elder Brahmins and others said to the Buddha: "Gautama!"
Now, you should not disparage him on account of his birth from a slave woman. Why is this?
This son of Āmrapālī is widely learned and possesses vast knowledge; his eloquence is unimpeded, and he is capable of engaging in debate and providing responses with the Gautama.
The Buddha addressed the brahmins:
"If you think that Āmraputra has gained the upper hand in debate with me, then all of you remain silent and observe as I respond to his questions."
"If they are unable to establish a thesis and engage me in debate, they shall remain silent.
You all! If you are able to establish a thesis and discourse with me, then you may proceed as you please."
The brahmins said, "That young brahmin Āmraputra is widely learned and thoroughly proficient; his speech is skillful and eloquent, and he is capable of being a debating opponent for Gautama."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Āmrapālī, saying: "Māṇava!
In the past, there was a king named Ikṣvāku."
The king had four sons:
the first was named Jvalanmukha (Flaming Face), the second Dīrghakarṇa (Long Ears), the third Gajaskandha (Elephant Shoulder), and the fourth Pādakaṭaka (Anklet-Foot).
At that time, because those four sons had committed transgressions, they were banished by the king.

At that time, having been banished by the king, the four sons each took their own biological sisters and went to the borders of another kingdom. Near the foot of the Snowy Mountains, on the banks of the Gaṅgā River, not far from the dwelling place of the seer Kapila, they each constructed grass huts. They married their respective sisters born of different fathers and settled there, whereupon sons and daughters were born to them.
Later, King Ikṣvāku remembered these four sons and asked his ministers,
"Where are my four sons now?
The ministers replied:

"The four sons of the King, having committed transgressions, were banished by the King; they now dwell beyond the borders at the foot of the Great Snow Mountains, on the banks of the Gaṅgā River, where they have fathered sons and daughters."
Then King Ikṣvāku said to his ministers,
"Can my four sons do such a thing?
They replied:
"Yes, he can.
At that time, King Ikṣvāku leisurely raised his right hand and proclaimed:
"My son can; he is most capable. Because a person of great majesty and virtue said he 'can,' he shall therefore be named Śākya, which in the language of Tang means 'capable.'"
The Buddha said to Ambaṣṭha,
"Have you heard of anyone else being reborn?
He replied:
“Gautama! I have heard that from of old, the Śākya clan has originated from this very place.
The Buddha said to Āmrapālī:
"Formerly, King Ikṣvāku had a maidservant named Tantuvāyā, who was of beautiful appearance and pleasing to all who saw her.
At that time, there was a seer of the Mātanga caste who lived constantly with this maidservant; consequently, they engaged in illicit relations and a son was born."
Once the boy was born, he was immediately able to speak, saying:
"Please rub, wipe, and wash my body; remove the impurities.

At that time, the spirits were called *kaṇabhājana*; because this child was born with the ability to speak immediately, they said that a *kaṇabhājana* spirit had been born, and thus the child was named *Kaṇabhājana*.
"From this point onward, there have been the Kāṇeyaputtas, Āmrapālī!
Have you ever heard that the Kāṇeyas were born from this?"
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, Amrapālī remained silent.
A second and a third time he asked her this same question, yet Amrapālī remained silent each time.

At that time, the Vajrapāṇi deity, holding a vajra in his hand, its brilliance blazing and its color like a fierce fire, saw that Āmrapālī remained silent and did not answer the World-Honored One. Grasping the vajra and aiming it at Āmrapālī’s head, he thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One has now asked Āmrapālī three times about her lineage in a previous life. If Āmrapālī does not answer the World-Honored One, I shall take this flaming vajra and crush Āmrapālī’s head into seven pieces."
At that time, due to the Buddha’s majestic power, Amrapālī saw him grasping the vajra; she was immediately struck with terror, her hair standing on end, and she said to the Buddha: “Gautama!
"I have heard that Kanibayana was born from him.
Then the elder brahmins and others addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We have not believed what the World-Honored One has said until now; we now know that the Ambaṣṭhas are born of a Śākya slave-girl, and his words are not false.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brāhmaṇas, saying:
"You should not revile Āmrapālī on account of her being born of a slave. Why is this?
In the past, there was a seer of great supernormal power and majesty; because King Ikṣvāku had once committed an offense against that seer, the seer rebuked him with a curse of an evil oath."

Having heard this, the king was filled with grief and terror, his hair standing on end; he then adorned his eldest daughter with various rare treasures, and taking her by the left hand and a golden pitcher in his right, he gave her to the seer to be his wife.
At that time, the seer did not accept the king’s daughter.

Then, seeing that the Blessed One had spoken of him as being of the womb-born caste (māṭṛjāta), Aṃpāra remained silent and haggard; with his face cast down and devoid of luster, he stood there lost in thought.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Because I have said that this son of Ambaṣṭha is of the lineage born of a slave woman, he remains silent and withered, his body devoid of majestic luster, dwelling in contemplation."
"I should now speak with him.
Having thought this, he said to Ambaṣṭha: "Māṇava!..."
Suppose, for example, a Kṣatriya youth were to marry a Brāhmaṇa girl and a son were born to them.
Would that boy be permitted among the assembly of Brāhmaṇas to sit and rise with them, to share in the ritual water-offerings, and to read the sacred scriptures?
Āmrapālī said, “I have, Gautama.”
The Buddha said,
"Māṇava! Did that man receive the consecration of a Kṣatriya?"
He replied, “I have, Gautama.”
"Why is this? Because he is the nephew of a brāhmaṇa, and because he is a son of the kṣatriya caste.
The Buddha spoke again to Āmrapālī:
“Suppose there is a Brahmin youth who takes a Kṣatriya girl as his wife, and later they have a son.
Would this son be permitted among the assembly of Brahmins to sit and rise with them, to share in the sacrificial water, and to read the scriptures?”
"Did you receive the consecration among the assembly of Kṣatriyas?
He replied, "I did, Gautama."
"Why is this? Because he is the son of a Brahmin and the nephew of a Kṣatriya.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Suppose a Kṣatriya youth, having committed an offense, is expelled by the Kṣatriyas.
Would he be permitted to sit together with the assembly of Brāhmaṇas?”
"May I receive the sacrificial water?
May I read the canonical scriptures?
He replied:
“I have received it, Gautama!
Did you receive the consecration among the assembly of Kṣatriyas?”
He replied: “I have, O Gautama!
For what reason? Because...”
"It is because of this intimacy," the Buddha said. "Māṇava!"

If there were a Brahmin youth who had been expelled by his fellow Brahmins, would he be permitted to sit and rise together with the assembly of Brahmins, share the sacrificial water, and read the sacred scriptures?
He replied, "I cannot, Gautama!"
“Can one receive the consecration within the assembly of kṣatriyas?
He replied, “One cannot.”
"Why is this? Because one who violates the fundamental precepts is designated as a 'Brahmin Caṇḍāla.
The Buddha said:
“Māṇava! You should know that among those born as kṣatriyas, their lineage and social standing are the most noble and honorable; the brahmins are not so.”
Therefore, Brahmā Sahampati, the Lord of the World, spoke this verse:
"The Kṣatriya who is the legitimate heir, The most honored among two-legged beings,
Perfectly endowed with wisdom and conduct, Shall stand above gods and humans."
"O Māṇava! I likewise spoke this verse again:
'The Kṣatriya who is the true heir, The most honored among those with two feet;'"
"With knowledge and conduct fully perfected, one attains a place above gods and humans.
"Māṇava, what do you think?"
"If a pure-practicing brāhmaṇa marries among the various brāhmaṇas, may he receive their sacrificial water and recite their scriptures therein?
He replied, "He may."
The Buddha said:
"It is because of marriage and social gatherings that one clings to lineage.
If anyone clings to their clan and says of themselves, 'I am a māṇava,' such a person cannot realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment."
"If one abandons the seeds of the conceit of 'I' and 'mine,' one is then able to practice and realize this unsurpassed perfection of knowledge and conduct.
At that time, Āmrapālī said to the Buddha:

"As for those like me who were intoxicated with madness and gave rise to contempt before the World-Honored One—in the past, present, and even the future—there shall be no such persons. I pray that you will preach such a sublime Dharma for my sake, whereby I may attain awakening to this perfection of knowledge and conduct."
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
Pay careful heed."

"O Māṇava! Buddhas appear in the world—Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpannas, Sugatas, Lokavidas, Anuttaras, Puruṣadamyasārathis, Śāstāras of devas and humans, Buddhas, Bhagavats. They teach the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its phrasing and meaning are exquisite, pure and unadulterated, fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy life (brahmacarya)."
If householders or the sons of householders hear this Dharma, they will be able to give rise to faith.

By virtue of that faith, they will practice with single-minded devotion, being able to understand that the life of a householder is a place where all manner of suffering and affliction accumulate, whereas those who have gone forth into homelessness seek the open wilderness.

If one is a householder, they are mostly bound by the hooks and shackles of sensory objects; thus, until the end of their life, they will be unable to cultivate the state of pure, unadulterated, and fully purified brahmacarya.
Nevertheless, having shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and with right faith gone forth from the home to the homeless life,
I have practiced with diligence; having attained decisive knowledge,
I have renounced and abandoned all— whether great wealth or little wealth, whether many followers or few followers— and have left the secular world to become a monastic.
Having shaved off his hair and beard, donned the *kāṣāya*, and given rise to right faith, he went forth from the home to the homeless life.
Abiding in pure precepts and wearing the robe of liberation, he was fully endowed with the practice of the Dharma;

even regarding minor transgressions, he felt deep trepidation in his heart, and having received all the categories of wholesome qualities, he trained in them and abandoned that which leads to slaughter.
Jīvaka laid aside his weapons and, toward all sentient beings, gave rise to loving-kindness and compassion;
he harbored no intent to harm even mosquitoes or ants, as is described at length in the *Śīlaskandha-varga* of the *Dīrgha Āgama* regarding the story of the Brahmin Ambaṣṭha.

At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at the village of Pāṭaligrāma and, having extensively expounded the *Caturbuddhasīna-sūtra* for the fourfold assembly, proceeded further to the village of Udayana.
There, he extensively expounded [the teaching] for two sisters, one named Bhadrikā and the other named Candraprabhā, as set forth in the sūtra.
The Blessed One again traveled through the human realm in Kośala and arrived at Śrāvastī.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The World-Honored One taught the essentials of the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; having done so, the World-Honored One sat in silence.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada rose from his seat, joined his palms in prostration, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus will come to my home tomorrow to accept my humble offering."
The World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, he took his leave and returned home. During that night, he prepared pure food and drink.
When morning arrived, he sent a messenger to invite the Buddha:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to visit my home.
When the World-Honored One had arrived and finished his meal, the elder took a small seat and sat down with single-minded devotion.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the essentials of the Dharma for the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him, he rose from his seat and departed.
The brahmins and householders then made offerings in succession to the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones.

At that time, when the bhikṣus were receiving food, they gave it first to poor children before even eating it themselves; consequently, the brahmins and householders all raised voices of derision and reproach.
At that time, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha of these circumstances. The Buddha said:
"You should first eat yourselves, and then give the remainder to poor children.
There were two beggars:
One was a young Brahmin boy and the other was a young Kṣatriya boy.
That Brahmin boy, being ignorant of the timing of events, came forward first to beg before the Saṃgha had yet eaten.
The bhikṣus had no one to give them food;
however, after the meal, the kṣatriya youth went begging and was given much by many.
The kṣatriya youth then asked that other youth:
"Did you obtain alms? He replied,
"I did not obtain any food."
Out of anger and resentment, he said:
"If I were in power, I would cut off the heads of all the disciples of Śākyamuni and cast them upon the ground.
The kṣatriya youth said:
"If I were sovereign, I would provide the Buddha and the bhikṣus with the six kinds of flavors as daily offerings.
After each of the two youths had spoken thus, they both fell asleep beneath a tree.
At that time, a horse in a carriage became startled and ran over a young Brahmin boy, who was consequently decapitated.
On account of this event, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The mind is always the forerunner; The undertaking of karma is supreme. When the heart harbors resentment..."
"Swiftly they receive their retribution; suffering comes to oppress their bodies, and the wheel severs their heads.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the meaning of this verse you have spoken?
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Do you see it now?"
Because that brahmin youth gave rise to unwholesome thoughts toward the Buddha and the bhikṣus and uttered harsh and evil words,
by reason of this cause, his head was crushed and severed by a wheel.
Ānanda replied, "I have now seen it.
The World-Honored One said:
"I saw this matter, and therefore I spoke these verses.
At that time, there was an elder in Śrāvastī who passed away without a son.
The brahmins and householders of the city deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Now this elder has passed away and leaves no offspring; whom shall we have to succeed him?
Seeing the Kṣatriya youth lying beneath the tree, at that time the sun was slanting toward the west, yet the shadow of the tree branch covered the youth and did not shift away.
When the people saw this, they brought him back to their home to succeed the elder as heir.
Once he had succeeded him, the youth thought to himself:
"This has come about through the power of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; I shall now invite the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus to provide them with various offerings."
Having formed this thought, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, took a small seat, and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the essential points of the Dharma for the youth, and the youth listened to the teaching.
Rising from his seat, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One, at the time of the morning meal tomorrow, will come to my home together with the assembly of bhikṣus to accept my humble offering."
The World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Then, at the time for the morning meal, the World-Honored One went to the youth’s house together with the bhikṣus.
After the meal was finished, he preached the Dharma to the youth according to his capacity.
At that time, the youth realized the fruit of stream-entry and attained the principle of the Four Noble Truths; he shattered his beginningless view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) with the vajra-pestle.
He declared:
"Now, with a faithful heart, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; as long as life shall endure, I shall never turn back.
The World-Honored One, for the sake of the elder’s son, had already expounded the essentials of the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him.
The son of the elder immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One returned to his original location and, before the assembly of bhikṣus, spoke these verses:
“The mind is always the forerunner; Volitional action is supreme. When the mind and its intentions are pure,”
"One will immediately receive a favorable retribution.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the meaning of this verse that has been spoken?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Do you see that Kṣatriya youth who conceived great faith toward the Buddha and the noble Saṅgha? By the power of this, the brahmins and householders of Śrāvastī have appointed him as the successor to the position of elder, and he now receives wealth and status."
Therefore, I have spoken this verse: "The mind is always the forerunner;
it is the mind that initiates action as the foremost. When the mind and its intentions are pure, one immediately experiences a favorable retribution."
At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at the village of Bālarāṣṭra, where he extensively preached the *Catubuddhasīsa Sūtra*.
He then proceeded to a village named Uttarakuru, where he again preached the *Catubuddhasīsa Sūtra*.
He then proceeded to the village of Siṃsapā, where he extensively preached the *Caturbuddhāsana Sūtra*.
He then proceeded to the village of Navagrāmaka, where he again extensively preached the *Caturbuddhāsana Sūtra*.
When the World-Honored One arrived at the city, he further preached the *Catubuddhasīsa Sūtra* within that city.
When the World-Honored One reached Rājagṛha, there were at that time two brahmins:
one named Āsana and the other named Prāsādika.
Those two brahmins resided by the side of a pond in Magadha; during the night, they would catch fish with hooks and eat them.
When morning came, they would sit upon a double-layered seat and constantly recite this verse:
"One who is able to practice the True Dharma is called a bhikṣu; having abandoned all worldly affairs..."
"This is the path of dhyāna.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the time had come to subdue that brahmin, went to his location and spoke these verses:
"The verses you have spoken should be realized in this way:"
Though you appear to be virtuous, your mind harbors impurity.
Be tranquil and self-subdued; do not harm sentient beings.
Abandon all evils—this is the path of meditation.
"If one does not commit any evil through body, speech, or mind,
and subdues oneself— this is the path of dhyāna.
When the two brahmins heard these verses spoken by the World-Honored One, they thought to themselves:
“Now Gautama truly knows my mind,” he thought,
and immediately paid him respectful homage.
The World-Honored One, observing his faculties and nature, preached the principle of the Four Noble Truths according to his capacity.
At that time, the brahmin destroyed the mountain of afflictions and various false views accumulated since beginningless time with the vajra-pestle of wisdom, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Later, when the bhikṣus saw that the brahmin had attained the fruit of stream-entry by repeatedly arranging his seat, they all imitated him.

There was one bhikṣu who sat upon a double-layered seat before the World-Honored One to listen to the Dharma; although he ought to have perceived the principle of the Truths (satyadharma), he instead failed to perceive them.
At that time, the World-Honored One observed that the bhikṣu was capable of perceiving the principle of the Truths; why then did he not see them?
He realized it was because the bhikṣu had been preoccupied with his seat and lacked respect for the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One then thought:
“Monks should not sit on double-layered seats, for there are many faults therein.
Thus he admonished the monks that they should not do so.
At that time, the World-Honored One departed from the city of Rājagṛha and went to the village of Bahulaka. Having put on his robes and taken up his bowl, he entered the village to beg for food.
In the city of Kapilavastu, there was a woman who lived as a wife in that village.

At that time, the woman saw the World-Honored One, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; a halo one fathom wide encircled his head, its brilliance as radiant and magnificent as a hundred thousand suns, like a mountain of jewels.
Having seen this, she thought to herself:
"Now this World-Honored One, the joy of all the Śākyas, has renounced his royal lineage, his women, his wealth, and his treasuries to leave the household life and pursue the path."
"Now I beg for alms to sustain my life; if you seek flour from me, I shall offer it to you.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing her thoughts, held out his bowl and approached her to beg, saying to the woman: "Sister!"
"You may set aside this bowl full of food and give it to me.
At that time, seeing that the World-Honored One knew her thoughts, the woman felt redoubled reverence and immediately offered the flour to the Buddha.
At that time, having accepted [the offering], the World-Honored One smiled.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that whenever they smile, they emit various rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—from their mouths; these rays of light may go upward or downward.

As for those below, they rescue beings from the sufferings of the hells, such as the Reviving, Black Rope, Crushing, Great Wailing, Small Heat, Intense Heat, and Avīci hells, as well as the eight cold hells:
Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Padma, Mahāpadma, and Utpala hells.

Those in the hot hells who encounter this light all attain coolness; those in the cold hells who encounter the Buddha’s radiance all become warm; and all the sufferings and afflictions of these sentient beings are thereby pacified and brought to rest.
Once their suffering had been relieved, they all thought to themselves:
"Have we died here and been reborn elsewhere?
Then, out of compassion for those sentient beings, the World-Honored One dispatched an emanation body to the hell realms. Upon seeing the Buddha’s emanation body, those sentient beings all thought:
"We have not perished from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere.
It is by the power of the Buddha that our various sufferings and afflictions have been stilled.
Thus they all gave rise to faith, and their karma of suffering was completely exhausted.
Passing away from the hells, they will take birth in the realms of humans and devas;
having been born among humans and devas, they shall later encounter a Buddha and realize the fruit of sainthood.

At that time, the light that ascended upward pervaded the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmā-purohita Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, and so on, up to the four heavens of the Formless Realm.
In all the celestial realms reached by the light, the devas all proclaimed: "Impermanent, suffering, and empty," and recited these two verses:
"You should seek liberation, And diligently practice the Buddha’s teaching;
Subdue the army of birth and death, As an elephant destroys a thatched hut."
"In this Dharma and Vinaya, always practice heedfulness;
you shall be able to dry up the ocean of afflictions and reach the ultimate end of suffering.
Having pervaded the trichiliocosm, the light gradually withdrew and followed behind the World-Honored One.
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, wishes to prophesy matters of the past, the light vanishes from the front;
if he wishes to prophesy matters of the future, the light vanishes from the back;
if he is to prophesy matters concerning the hells, the light vanishes from beneath his feet.
If he was to prophesy concerning the realm of animals, the light would vanish from his heels;
if he was to prophesy concerning the realm of hungry ghosts, the light would vanish from his ankles;
if he was to prophesy concerning human affairs, the light would vanish from his knees.
If he prophesies the matter of a Wheel-Turning King, the light vanishes into his left palm;
if he prophesies the matter of a Universal Monarch, the light vanishes into his right palm;
if he prophesies rebirth in the heavens, the light vanishes into his navel.
If he is to prophesy the matter of the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, the light disappears into his mouth;
if he is to prophesy the matter of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, the light disappears between his eyebrows;
if he is to prophesy the matter of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the light disappears into the crown of his head.
At that time, the Buddha’s light circled the World-Honored One three times and vanished into the space between his eyebrows.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, smiles with a joyful countenance; it is not without cause or condition.
He then spoke a verse to request [the Buddha's teaching], as the verses are otherwise [as in the standard formula].
At that time, the Blessed One said to Ānanda: "It is so, it is so!
Ānanda, it is not without cause or condition that a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha suddenly smiles."
“Ānanda, did you see that brahmin woman who, with faith,
gave me the parched grain? Ānanda replied, “I saw her.”
The Buddha said:
"By virtue of these roots of goodness, from this day forward, she shall not fall into the evil realms for thirteen kalpas.
Circulating through births among gods and humans, in her final body, she will realize the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha and be known by the name Shan-yuan (Good Vow), her fame spreading far and wide."

Because that Brahmin woman gave rise to faith and offered parched grain to the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One bestowed upon her the prediction that she would attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha in the future.

Her husband went into the forest to gather flowers, firewood, and other provisions, and there he heard that his wife had given parched grain to the śramaṇa Gautama and received the prediction that she would become a pratyekabuddha.
Having heard this, he became enraged and went immediately to the World-Honored One, saying:
"Did you come to my house?
The World-Honored One replied:
"It is indeed true that he has come," she said.
"When my wife gave him roasted flour, did you not grant him the prediction that he would become a Pratyekabuddha?"
The Buddha said,
“Brahmin, it is indeed so. [The Brahmin replied,] “You, Gautama!”

Having renounced the royal throne of a lineage of wheel-turning monarchs to go forth as a monk, you have uttered a great falsehood for the sake of begging for some grain; who would be willing to believe that you have obtained such a vast fruit from so few seeds?
The Buddha said:
“Brāhmaṇa! For this reason, I now ask you; you should answer as you please.”
"Brahmin! What do you think?
Do you see any extraordinary phenomenon?"
He replied, "Gautama!
Let us set aside other marvelous qualities for now."
"Gautama, listen for a moment as I describe a rare occurrence that I have witnessed here in the village of Bahulaka.
To the east of this village, there is a vast and luxuriant nyagrodha tree; beneath it, five hundred chariots may often be stationed without any obstruction."
"Because of this tree, the village has received its name.
The Buddha said, "Brāhmaṇa!"
How large are the seeds of that Bahuputraka tree?
Are they as large as a rice field, such that one cannot share them with a threshing floor, a millstone, a cart, an ox-cart, a winnowing basket, a bilva fruit, or a kapittha fruit?
He replied, “No.
It would be like one-fourth of a mustard seed.”
The Buddha said,
“Brāhmaṇa! Who would believe that this small seedling of yours could produce such a great tree?”
Then the brahmin replied to the Blessed One,
"Do you believe me or not?
I have seen it with my own eyes."
Nevertheless, that ground remains unharmed, fertile, moist, and sweet;
although the seed is not large, it is planted according to the Dharma, and when rain falls at the proper time, this tree grows and becomes great.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, spoke in verse:
"Just as the field and the seed, you have now seen with your own eyes;
Regarding karma and its retribution, the Tathāgata has personally realized them."
"Just as you have seen, a small seedling becomes a great tree;
so too do I see this: from a small cause, a great fruit arises.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue from his mouth until it reached the hairline, and addressed the brahmin, saying:
"What do you think?
If one were able to extend the tongue so that it completely covered the face, would such a person tell a deliberate lie for the sake of the position of a hundred thousand wheel-turning kings?"
The brahmin replied: “No, Gautama.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"I have never spoken a word of falsehood; The marks of my tongue have all increased through sincerity.
You should now speak in this manner: 'Fortunately, having encountered the Tathāgata, I have received awakening.'"
When the brahmin had heard this, he conceived a heart of faith and reverence.

The World-Honored One, knowing his inclinations and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), taught him the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths according to his capacity, as extensively explained before. He shattered the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) accumulated since beginningless time with the vajra of wisdom, and having realized the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*), he proclaimed:

"I have entered the stream. For the rest of my life, I take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; I accept the five precepts and become an upāsaka. May the World-Honored One bear witness to this."
When the brahmin had heard what the Buddha said, he rejoiced and accepted it with faith; he prostrated before the Buddha and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to the forest of the village of Cūḍābilvā and stayed there. This sutra is explained in detail as in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

The Blessed One arrived at a village on the edge of a region where there lived the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s maternal uncle, who had gone forth among the sages to practice the path; it was the venerable Maudgalyāyana who was able to discipline him.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Maudgalyāyana:
"You should take pity upon your maternal uncle.
Maudgalyāyana replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One.
Having heard the Buddha’s words, Maudgalyāyana knew that the time for conversion had arrived, and he immediately went to the place where the rishi resided.
At that time, a rishi said to Maudgalyāyana, "Stop and do not enter; this is a place where a brahmin practices the path.
He replied:
"I am also a brāhmaṇa. Then that seer spoke this verse:
"Though there be no sacred thread upon the body, And though one does not hold the sacrificial ladle;"
"A shaven head is not the practice of fire-worship; it is a false claim to be a Brahmin.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana also replied to the seer with a verse:
"Modesty is the sacred thread; right wisdom is the sacrificial ladle."
Constantly maintaining the water of pure precepts, one makes it pure as a ritual vessel;
taking truthful speech as the kindling fire, the inner mind remains eternally tranquil and settled;
constantly cultivating the practice of self-discipline—this is the true way of kindling the sacrificial fire.
Then that seer said to Maudgalyāyana,
"Even if it were so, I would not permit you, a shaven-headed śramaṇa, to enter my dwelling place. At that time,
the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately used his supernormal power to raise a great wind and rain, and went to the side of the pond to sit beneath a tree.
At that time, the attendants of the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda were dwelling in this pool and thought to themselves:
"The noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana is always held in high esteem by the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda."
"Nevertheless, I too should make offerings to him.

Then the nāga attendant emerged from his own palace, went to where Maudgalyāyana was, circumambulated the Venerable one seven times with his body, and finally stood there covering Maudgalyāyana’s head with his hood.

It is the constant law of the rishis that if they see the suffering of sentient beings pressing upon their bodies and do not give rise to the thought of rescue, they fall away from the path of the rishis.
At that time, the elder rishi thought to himself:
"If this renunciant should lose his life due to this heavy rain, I shall surely lose my own attainment of the rishi path."
Having formed this thought, he departed from the hermitage of the rishi and sought out a renunciant.
He saw Maudgalyāyana heavily encircled by the dragon seven times, with the dragon’s head covering Maudgalyāyana’s own head, and addressed him, saying:
"You may enter this hut."
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“Great Seer!
You have already lost your way as a seer.”
Having heard the sound of his voice and recognizing him as his nephew, the seer asked:
"Noble one! Are you Maudgalyāyana?"
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"People of that time called me Maudgalyāyana.
Maudgalyāyana reported this.
“O Seer! For what purpose have you come here?
The seer replied:
"I have come because I saw that you were being tormented by suffering and feared you might be harmed.
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana took the rishi with him and went to the place where the Buddha was; he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is my maternal uncle; he has gone forth in the path of the seers.”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and grant us protection.

Knowing the disposition, latent tendencies, and inclinations of those seers, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma according to their capacities. Upon hearing it, the seers immediately realized the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
At that time, the rishi rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated himself before the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:

“I pray only that the World-Honored One will accept me and grant me permission to go forth within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination, to become a bhikṣu, and to practice the holy life under the World-Honored One.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those rishis, saying:
"Welcome, bhikṣus!
As soon as these words were spoken, their hair and beards fell away naturally, saṃghāṭī robes appeared upon their bodies, and they were perfected in dignified deportment.
When the Naga youth saw Maudgalyāyana depart, he remained alone and felt uneasy; consequently, that village was soon struck by a severe drought.
That Naga youth then transformed himself into a rishi and sat in meditation at the dwelling place of that rishi.
At that time, the people of the village came to the place where the transformed dragon-ascetic was, prostrated themselves, and said:
"This village is now suffering from a severe drought; what plan should we devise?"
The seer replied,
"If you all come together to dwell here, you shall be able to eliminate this calamity.
Thereupon, all the people from the various villages came and settled there.
Because the nāga prince held a parasol over the crown of Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s head,
people thereafter collectively named it the City of Nāgadattacchattra.
Within this city, there was a faithful upāsaka who established a monastery at the site of Nāgadattacchattra, fully providing it with all necessary requisites.
At that time, the World-Honored One again arrived at the city of Mathurā and dwelt there in accordance with the occasion, explaining the matter in detail.
Then, while traveling through the human realm from the city of Kurukṣetra, the World-Honored One reached the village of Mahākoṣṭhaka, where he extensively expounded the *Rāṣṭrapāla Sūtra*.
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Volume Eight.
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
Volume Nine.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.

At that time, as the World-Honored One proceeded toward the city of Hastināpura, there was a brahmin who saw from afar that the World-Honored One’s body was adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics; his halo extended a fathom, its brilliance surpassing a thousand suns; and his gait and movements were like those of a precious mountain, his dignified bearing most virtuous and excellent.
Seeing the World-Honored One from afar, the brahmin approached the Buddha and praised him, saying:

"Your body is golden in color; your eyes are pure, long, and wide. You have perfected compassion and are endowed with all virtues. You are the God among gods, the Tamer of Men, who has crossed over the ocean of existence."
When the World-Honored One heard this praise, he immediately smiled.
It is the constant practice of all Buddhas that when they manifest a smile, they emit great radiance, which eventually returns and enters the crown of their heads.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, asking in verse:
“From the World-Honored One’s face, A thousand subtle and wondrous rays of light emerge;
Like the sun first appearing, They illuminate the ten directions.”
He further spoke in verse:
"Having abandoned arrogance and the inferior mind, The Buddhas are the supreme cause in the world;
Without a cause, they would not manifest a smile, For they have conquered the enemies that are the afflictions."
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Ānanda!"
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not manifest a smile without cause or condition. Ānanda,
did you see that brahmin praising the Buddha with verses?
Ānanda replied, “I have seen it.
The Buddha said:
"Because this brahmin praised the roots of goodness and merit of my [past] lives, for twenty kalpas he shall not fall into the evil realms and will always be reborn among gods and humans."
"From this point forward, in his final body, he shall realize the state of a Pratyekabuddha and be named 'Worthy of Praise' (Arhat).
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt; since only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can sever all doubts, they immediately questioned him.
The World-Honored One told them: "Listen attentively!
"Because this brahmin praised me with a single verse of gāthā, I have granted him the prophecy that he shall become a pratyekabuddha.

The Buddha said, "It is not only in the present time that one obtains merit by praising the Tathāgata; in a past life as well, when this brahmin praised me with a verse, I also bestowed upon that brahmin five large villages."
Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for you.

Long ago, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta who ruled the world with the True Dharma. The realm was peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, its population flourishing and free from all epidemics. That king took great delight in learning and scholarship.
At that time, there was a brahmin in the city of Vārāṇasī who possessed great learning and talent.
His wife said to him, "The season is approaching with cold; go to the king and offer him fine praises so that he may be pleased and grant you winter clothing."
The brahmin went to where the king was and saw the king riding an elephant as he emerged from the city.
Upon seeing the king, the brahmin thought to himself:
"Should I praise the king first?"
"Should I praise the elephant first?
Yet, since all these people love this elephant, I should praise the elephant first.
Then that brahmin praised it with a verse:
“His form is like that of Śakra’s elephant; his color possesses a wondrous and majestic countenance;
adorned with the marks of great power—such is the appearance of this king of elephants.”
Having heard the verse, the king was filled with great joy and likewise spoke in verse:
“My beloved elephant-king, whom all who see him rejoice in;
since you have praised him so skillfully and beautifully, I shall grant you five villages.”
“O bhikṣus, do not harbor other thoughts.
The elephant king of that time was none other than I myself.
The brahmin was this very same brahmin who praises the elephant.”
At that time, he praised me with a single verse and was granted five villages;
now, having praised me with a single verse, I likewise bestow upon him the prediction of pratyekabuddha enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to a great city. Within this city, he taught extensively as previously described, as has already been set forth in the *Catubuddhasīhanāda Sūtra*.

When the World-Honored One traveled to the city of Soreyya, there lived in that city a brahmin named Indaka. He was young and widely learned; considering himself clever and wise, he held no regard for his peers.
At that time, the World-Honored One was at a certain residence, preaching the essentials of the Dharma before a great assembly.
When a brahmin heard that the World-Honored One had arrived in the city, he thought to himself:
"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama is of handsome and upright appearance."
"Shall I now go to see if he is more handsome than I?

He immediately went to where the Buddha was and beheld the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics. His radiance blazed forth, pervading his entire body; its magnificent adornment surpassed that of a thousand suns, like a mountain of jewels, entirely virtuous and auspicious.
Having observed him thus, he further thought:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is more handsome than I, yet he is not taller than I.
He then looked at the crown of the Buddha's head, but was unable to see it.
He then climbed to a high place, yet still could not see it.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the brahmin:
"You have undergone great hardship; even if you were to ascend to the summit of Mount Sumeru, you still would not be able to see it."
However, as for the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, have you not heard that gods, asuras, and humans can never see it?
If you wish to know the dimensions of the Tathāgata’s body, beneath the ground at the site of the sacrificial fire within your home, there is a pillar of gośīrṣa sandalwood.
"You should lift it out and measure it, and you will then know the Tathāgata’s body born of his parents.
That brāhmaṇa further thought: "This is a rare occurrence;
I have never heard of such a thing before. I shall go and observe it."
He immediately returned home in haste, dug up the pillar at the site of the sacrifice, and found everything exactly as the Buddha had described.
At that time, the brahmin conceived faith and thought to himself:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"Since he has attained the certainty of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), I should now go to serve and make offerings to him.
Out of faith, he immediately went to where the Buddha was, and in the presence of the World-Honored One, he uttered various words of praise and joy, then withdrew to sit at one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his inclinations, latent tendencies, and faculties—as described in detail above—shattered the mountain of false views with the vajra-thunderbolt of wisdom, having destroyed the *satkāyadṛṣṭi* accumulated since beginningless time. Having realized the fruit of stream-entry, he proclaimed:
"World-Honored One!..."
I have renounced [the world]; I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. May you grant me the upāsaka precepts.
From this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge in the Triple Gem with pure faith.
At that time, the brahmin rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms in homage to the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the World-Honored One would grant me permission, I shall erect a pillar of ox-head sandalwood so that all may know and hear of it."
The Buddha said,
"Brahmin, do as you wish."
At that time, the brahmin took a sandalwood pillar and, in a secluded place, erected it with various ritual implements, and on that account further organized a religious assembly.

Furthermore, there were other brahmins and householders who, seeking merit and happiness, tied auspicious grass (kuśa) upon pillars; because the Brahmin Indraka established a ritual assembly there, it is called the Day of the Indra Assembly.

When the World-Honored One manifested great supernormal powers, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) retreated into formless states; gods and humans rejoiced, and virtuous people were filled with delight. The non-Buddhists dispersed and fled to the borderlands, or remained among the Brahmins and lay devotees.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm of Kosala and proceeded toward a brahmin village.
When the various followers of other paths heard that the śramaṇa Gautama was coming, they hurriedly went to the houses of the brahmins, householders, and nobles.
Having arrived, he spoke these words:
"May your merit increase, may your merit increase!
I take my leave."
Those people said, "Noble one,
for what reason are you leaving?"
They replied, “We saw that you were wealthy and prosperous; we did not wish to see you ruined and scattered, which is why we departed for a while.
The people asked:
“Noble One! What calamity has befallen us?

“You should know this: the śramaṇa Gautama is approaching with a retinue of twelve hundred men, raining down swords and hailstones; he has rendered countless and innumerable women who have sons childless.”
The people replied, "Noble One!
If it is truly so, you ought to remain here and assist us."
"How can it be right to abandon him?
This is unwholesome; we must certainly destroy him.
The non-Buddhists replied:
"You all must enter into a covenant with me; only then may you remain here. You must kill the śramaṇa Gautama.
The people replied, "We shall kill him."
They each took up swords, staves, bows, and arrows, donned their armor, and went out onto the main road.
At that time, there was an elderly man among the Śākyas who, seeing those people, immediately asked them:
"Where do you intend to go?"
He replied: "It is for the sake of harming the enemy.
He asked again:
"Who is your enemy?
He replied immediately,
"The śramaṇa Gautama is."
The old man replied,
"If the Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, is your enemy, who else could possibly be your friend?
You should turn back."
Those people were all unwilling to turn back.
At that time, the old man thought to himself:
"These types of people cannot be subdued by preaching the Dharma; one must employ various forms of power to force them into submission."
At that time, the old man immediately entered the village and set fires on all sides, burning the settlement.
All the people within the village cried out in unison.
When those who had harmed the Buddha heard the cries, they were all struck with panic and, speaking among themselves, said:
“The ascetic Gautama has gone far away; now there is a great loss occurring right here as the village is being burned.
You should turn back and first extinguish this fire.”
When they had turned back, unable to extinguish the fire, in a mere moment the Blessed One arrived and asked the people:
"Why are you so alarmed and frantic?"
The people replied,
"We are currently being burned by fire and cannot save it.
The Buddha then said in response:
"I shall now extinguish that fire for you.
The people replied,
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will extinguish the fire for us."
At that moment, as soon as the Tathāgata had finished speaking, by the Buddha’s majestic power, the fires were all extinguished.
Thereupon, all those people conceived faith and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"For what reason have you come now?
The Buddha replied,
"I have come here for the sake of benefiting you all."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the inclinations, latent tendencies, and natures of those people’s minds, preached the Dharma for them so that they might realize the Four Noble Truths. As previously described, he used the vajra-thunderbolt of wisdom to shatter the mountain of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—the afflictions accumulated since beginningless time—and caused all those people to fully realize the fruit of the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"Only the Tathāgata can sever our doubts.
The bhikṣus addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Observe this old Śākya, who, out of greed for his kin, has set fire to the village.
Because of this karma, he shall incur immeasurable retribution.”
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"It was not only in this present life that he burned down this village for the sake of craving.
In the past, throughout immeasurable and numerous lifetimes, he has already burned down villages for the sake of craving."
Listen attentively, all of you!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.
In the past, there was a village where five hundred monkeys resided; all the crops were completely destroyed by those monkeys.
The people of the village gathered for a council and deliberated, asking by what means this calamity might be brought to an end.
Among them, one person spoke forth, saying:
"It is necessary to kill everyone; only then will this calamity cease."
Furthermore, someone asked:
"How can one kill? He replied:
"Cut down all the trees on every side of the village, leaving only a single persimmon tree and surrounding it with thorns.
Once the persimmons have ripened, when the monkeys and others gather upon the tree desiring to eat the fruit, you should kill them."

At that time, the people then cut down all the trees until none remained, leaving only a single tree. They surrounded it on all four sides with thorns and stationed one man there to guard it constantly, instructing him to inform the crowd once all the monkeys had climbed the tree.
Among the monkeys, there was one monkey who said to the monkey king:
"There are persimmons that have now ripened; we should go together to gather and eat them."
At that time, the monkeys gathered together on the persimmon tree.
When the people learned of this, they all took up swords and staves and assembled beneath the tree, intending to cut it down.
Those monkeys, their hearts filled with fear, moved back and forth along the branches.
The monkey king was fundamentally free from anxiety or fear and ate the fruit with composure.
The other monkeys said to their king,
"Now that we have encountered this calamity, how can you eat the fruit without the slightest alarm or dread?"
Then the monkey king spoke in verse:
"For those who involve themselves in many affairs, obstacles arise naturally;
a tree that has grown large is difficult to fell suddenly—you must eat without fear."
“At that time, there was a young monkey among the troop who had previously been captured in the village; he sat with his cheek resting on his hand, filled with sorrow.
Seeing him thus distressed, another monkey went to comfort his companion, saying:
‘For what reason do you sit here in sorrow, resting your cheek upon your hand?’”
He replied: "Good friend, you should know, how could I not be distressed?
Since the people of this village wish to kill all our kinsmen, how could I not be distressed?"
Again he asked:
"Why do you not now exert yourself?
The young monkey replied:
"Now that we are bound and confined, how can we exert ourselves?
The assembly replied again,
"We shall now release you."
Then, once that bound monkey had been released, he set fire to the village, setting it ablaze on all sides.

The villagers raised a great clamor of distress; hearing the cries, the man who had felled the tree was struck with terror and said to his companions, "These monkeys are far away from us and cannot yet cause us harm."
"Since there is a fire, you should depart for now.
For the sake of extinguishing the fire, they all ran toward the village.
All those monkeys descended from their trees and fled to escape the danger.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor other thoughts; that little monkey of the past was none other than this Elder Śākyamuni."
Not only in this present life have they burned down villages out of affection for their kinsmen;
even in the past, they likewise burned down villages for the sake of their beloved relatives.
At that time, the World-Honored One traveled to the city of Kālā. Within the city of Kālā, he had previously given a detailed exposition on the "Account of the Four Buddhas' Seatings.

Thereafter, the World-Honored One proceeded to the city of Roruka and stayed within the palace of the yakṣa Hastibala. At that time, the yakṣa was conducting an inspection among the assembly of yakṣas.

At that time, the yakṣa Hastibala, hearing that the Blessed One had entered the city and was staying in his palace, immediately went to where the Buddha was. Upon arrival, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side.
When the Blessed One saw that the yakṣa was seated, he proclaimed for him the essentials of the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him, as described above.
At that time, the yakṣa Hastibala rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and with palms joined, addressed him, saying:
"I pray only that the Tathāgata will accept my humble invitation to dwell in my palace this night."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, the yakṣa Hastibala then constructed five hundred monasteries within his palace for the World-Honored One; in each monastery, he provided five hundred large beds and small beds, as well as various bedding, curtains, canopies, and awnings.
Once the construction was completed, he invited the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the assembly of bhikṣus to accept his offerings.

When the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus had accepted the invitation, there was a yakṣa friend of the yakṣa Gajabala named Kucika who resided in the kingdom of Kaśmīra. At that time, the yakṣa Gajabala sent a messenger to inform him:
"I have now invited the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus; you should send all the fruits from your northern region."

At that time, after the yakṣa Hastibala had dispatched his messengers, he immediately prepared food and drink during that very night; furthermore, within the five hundred monasteries, he swept and cleaned the grounds, arranged the seats, and set out pure water, instructing the attendants to know the proper sequence of events.

At that time, having received the command with faith, the yakṣa Kṛtikā filled baskets and boxes to the brim with grapes and other fruits, and ordered various yakṣas to carry them to the edge of the monastery grounds and pile them there for storage.
When the bhikṣus saw the fruit, none of them recognized it, so they questioned the World-Honored One:
"What kind of fruit is this?
How should it be consumed?"
The Buddha then replied, "The fruit from the north is called *drākṣā* (grape); once it has been purified by fire, it may be eaten.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the fruits and performed the purification for each one individually, which consequently caused a long delay.
The Buddha saw this and rebuked them:
"You should not perform the purification ritual for each individual fruit in this manner. You should take a single ember from the heap of fruit and purify it at three points."
At that time, the yakṣa Hastibala personally served various kinds of food and drink with his own hands to the Blessed One and the bhikṣus, as described in detail above.
When the great assembly had finished eating, the yakṣa Hastika took a small seat and sat down before the Tathāgata to listen to the Dharma.
The World-Honored One taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma to that yakṣa, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; thereupon, the yakṣa rose from his seat.
At that time, when the grapes had been eaten, there was still much left over.
The Buddha said, "You should press them to extract the grape juice.
When the juice did not cook properly, they then poured it out. The Buddha said:
"It should be boiled thoroughly and stored for the Saṃgha and others to drink as non-time (vikāla) gruel. At that time,
the World-Honored One, having washed his feet outside his dwelling, entered the room and sat in meditative absorption.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"I have now appeared in this world during a short lifespan; the time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived, yet there are many matters to be disciplined and accomplished."
"If I were to go to the northern regions and other such countries with the bhikṣu Ānanda for the sake of subduing [the beings there], it would be difficult to achieve success.
Now, I should instead go there with the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi to subdue them."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi with two verses:
"The mindful one is virtuous; The mindful one dwells in peace.
The mindful one sleeps in tranquility; Through reflection, they attain stillness."
"Those who possess mindfulness will have auspicious wishes; those who maintain mindfulness will be at peace.
Those who possess mindfulness sleep peacefully, having abandoned the mind of victory and defeat.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"You may go with me to Northern India to subdue the Nāga King Apalāla. "So be it,
World-Honored One," replied the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi,
and he traveled through the air together with the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One, seeing the green forest from afar, addressed the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Do you see this green forest?
He replied:
“Sugata, I have seen them.
He spoke again, saying:
"One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, you shall construct a saṃghārāma at this place called Andhavana; it shall be the foremost site for those practicing śamatha."
At that time, as the World-Honored One was traveling, he arrived at the village of Saṃkassa.
At that time, there was a yakṣa dwelling in that village named Balin who harbored a violent and evil mind.
The people of this village were constantly performing sacrifices; yet, despite their offerings, they were perpetually harmed.
When the villagers heard that the World-Honored One had arrived, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the people of the village, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, before remaining silent.
Then, the assembly of villagers rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"This yakṣa, Jālavat, has been our enemy throughout the long night, constantly causing us harm; we pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for us, will subdue this yakṣa."
At that time, the yakṣa Jñānabala was also seated in the assembly.
Then the Buddha addressed the yakṣa Jñānabala, asking him a second and a third time:
"Do you hear this now?"
Then the yakṣa Jñānabala replied,
“I have heard it.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"You should now quickly abandon this evil intent.
The yakṣa replied, "I now renounce my evil; I shall no longer cause harm."
At that time, the World-Honored One caused him to receive the precepts and take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Thereupon, the yakṣa immediately established a monastery at this very spot, naming it Saṃghāṭa; all those with faith provided offerings of requisites until they were fully supplied.
Once the temple was completed, the World-Honored One departed.
At that time, a yakṣa followed after the Buddha, and the World-Honored One said to him:
"You should return and protect this place."
I shall now assist you and protect this place.
After my parinirvāṇa, I will leave behind the bones of my shoulders here.
In the future, people will erect a stūpa at this site, which shall be known as the Stūpa of Accumulation (Caitika).
The World-Honored One again went to the village of Niduruka, where there was a yakṣa named Dharmavala whom the World-Honored One immediately subdued.
At that time, the yakṣa constructed a monastery as before, naming it the Niduruka Monastery.

The World-Honored One again went to the banks of the Indus River, where there was a boatman; at that time, the World-Honored One manifested various supernatural transformations to subdue him, leading him to realize the principle of the Truths (satyadharma), as well as subduing the yakṣa Mṛgalaṇḍika.
The Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers, empowered the yakṣa, who has now left behind these footprints.
Because of this, people of that time collectively established a name for it, calling it "The Footprints of the Yakṣa Mṛgadhvaja."
At that time, the World-Honored One again went to the abode of the seer; it was there that he tamed the seer Daṇḍapāṇi (Staff-Bearer).
Then the brahmins and householders together established a place for him to sit and lie down, and it was immediately named "The Seated and Lying Place of the Seer Daṇḍapāṇi."
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi:
"You may accompany me to the palace of the Nāga King Aśvatara.
"So be it, Blessed One," he replied.
At that time, the Tathāgata and the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi arrived at the palace of the nāga king.

When the nāga king Apalāla saw that the World-Honored One had entered the palace, he immediately became enraged; harboring thoughts of malice and giving rise to various afflictions, he ascended into the air and brought down a rain of hailstones along with clods of earth.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the dragon’s wrath, immediately focused his mind and entered the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta-samādhi*).

Having entered this state of concentration, the torrent of earth and hail that had been cast down transformed above the Tathāgata into clouds of powdered incense such as agallochum, sandalwood, and *tamāla*, which fell like rain.
When the dragon saw that he could not harm the World-Honored One, he immediately released the wheel and all his weapons;
these were instantly transformed into lotus flowers of four colors, which descended from the sky.
At that time, the Nāga King Vāsuki released clouds and smoke;
thereupon, the Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal power, also released clouds and smoke.
Then, the Nāga King’s arrogance and pride were thereby extinguished, whereupon he entered his palace and remained there in stillness.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"There are two causes by which one can subdue all evil nāgas:
either by instilling fear in them, or by inciting their wrath."
"However, this dragon king ought to be struck with fear.
Having thought this, he addressed the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"You should provoke and harass this evil dragon king."

At that time, the yakṣa, having received the Tathāgata’s instruction, struck the mountain peak with his vajra-pestle and shattered it; as the mountain collapsed, it pressed down upon half of the dragon pond.
Thereupon, the nāga king was filled with sorrow and fear, and immediately sought to flee.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the fire-element samādhi, causing all ten directions to become masses of fire.
At that moment, the dragon king had no way to escape, except for the spot where the World-Honored One’s feet stood, which remained tranquil and cool.
At that time, the Dragon King went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what reason have you troubled and disturbed me?"
The Buddha replied, "I am the Dharma King; how could I possibly trouble you?
Had I not attained such supreme compassion, I would have long since perished, leaving behind nothing but my empty name."

At that time, the World-Honored One stroked the crown of the Dragon King’s head with his hand—which was marked with a thousand-spoked wheel, a rim, and webbing, and was auspicious and fearless—and spoke these words:
“O Worthy One!
"You should know that because you made offerings of pure food and drink to the śrāvakas and gave a noble jar filled with pure water, you were reborn among the Thirty-three Gods;
yet, due to your improper aspiration, you have now received the body of an animal, sustaining yourself by harming other sentient beings, and after this body perishes, you shall fall into hell."
Then that Nāga King immediately addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will show me what I must do.
The Buddha told the Nāga King:
"You have taken refuge in the Three Jewels before me and received the pure precepts; therefore, you should grant fearlessness to all the people of Magadha.
At that time, the Dragon King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I now receive the pure precepts.
At that time, the dragon’s wife and children, along with all his kinsmen, joined their palms in prostration, bowed their heads to the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We, too, wish to take refuge in the Triple Gem and receive the pure precepts.
The Naga King Śālika further addressed the Buddha, saying,
"We nagas have many enemies and sources of harm."
Furthermore, there was a dragon king named Arrow who prayed, "I only wish that the World-Honored One would grant me the pure precepts and cause me to give rise to a heart of compassion.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the dragons and others, received the pure precepts and took refuge in the Triple Gem.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi saw that the Naga King Apalāla and all his retinue had been completely subdued; they took refuge in the Triple Gem, received the pure precepts, and leaped for joy.
At that time, having tamed the Naga King Viśvāmitra and his sixty thousand followers, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and departed.
Seeing a grove of green trees in the distance, the World-Honored One addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Do you see that grove?"
He replied,
"I have now seen it.
The Buddha said:
“Vajrapāṇi! Within this territory of Kaśmīra, during the hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there shall be a bhikṣu disciple.
After that bhikṣu has subdued the poisonous dragon Haruṭa, he shall request from the dragon a place for sitting cross-legged.”
By means of skillful expedients, he causes the True Dharma to circulate throughout this land.
Among all places for sitting and reclining, those who accord with vipaśyanā are the most supreme.
"Within the borders of that country, there shall be sixty thousand, six hundred, and sixty-three villages.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having arrived at the village of Pāṭaligrāma, tamed the ṛṣi and the Yakṣa Akarmaka, along with their retinues;
and in the village of Kāntika, he tamed the female Yakṣī and her retinue.
The World-Honored One again arrived at the city of Śāliśūka. There, within that city, he transformed King Jayasena’s mother, establishing her in the Four Noble Truths.

The World-Honored One then proceeded to the city of Nayardha. In this city there was a potter who, relying on his craft, was arrogant; regarding the vessels he produced, he would wait until they were dry upon the wheel before finally removing them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the time for their conversion had arrived, transformed himself into a potter and, together with that potter, spoke to one another:
"How is it that these vessels descend from the wheel?"
The potter replied,
"Once it is dry and finished, I will set it down.
The transformed person responded:
"I too shall descend once it has been baked dry, and you shall be my companion.
However, I possess a special technique by which I alone can bring it to maturity while on the wheel before descending.
The potter replied:
"Your skill surpasses mine," the transformed person replied.
"Not only can vessels for cooking mature food emerge from the wheel, but I can also produce various vessels made of the seven treasures."
Upon seeing this, the potter immediately believed and submitted.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One withdrew his transformative manifestation and resumed his original form, preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma so that he and his retinue were established in the Four Noble Truths.

At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded next to the city of Śyāmāka. Within that city, he preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the yakṣa Pūrṇaka and his retinue, causing them to take refuge in the Triple Gem and abide by the prohibitive precepts.
In the city of Rakṣita, he subdued the cowherd and the nāga king Sūcīla.
The World-Honored One next arrived at the city of Abhirati; there, he established King Devabhūti and his retinue in the realization of the Truths.
Furthermore, he subdued the seven sons of Caṇḍālikā, along with the yakṣa who guarded the pond and his entire retinue.
Beside that city was a great pond where Aśvaka and Punarvasu both assumed the bodies of nāgas within its waters.
After twelve years, they appeared once more, harboring anger and thinking to themselves:
"The World-Honored One did not preach the Dharma for us, yet he has caused us to fall into the evil realms and receive these dragon bodies; we must destroy his teaching."
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
