"These two venomous nāgas possess great power; after my parinirvāṇa, they will certainly be able to destroy my Dharma teaching and reduce it to ashes."
Having formed this thought, he went to the site of the pond and addressed the two nāgas, saying:
"I shall preach the *Pādaka-sūtra* for you, so that you may come to know it."
The two nāgas replied, "We are nāgas;
how could we possibly understand?
Having spoken these words, they immediately submerged into the water and further thought to themselves:
“The World-Honored One has preached the Dharma for me, yet I am unable to understand it.

At that time, the World-Honored One left his shadow at the site of the pond; when the dragon saw the Buddha’s shadow, he appeared again and again, constantly thinking that the World-Honored One was still dwelling there.
Furthermore, at that place, he subdued two yakṣī sisters:
the first named Nalikā and the second named Nataḍayā.

At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at the city of Kuṇḍina. In that city, there was a female yakṣa named Kuṇḍinī who resided there constantly; her heart was filled with violence and malice, and she was fearless, frequently devouring all the sons and daughters born to the people of the city.

Now, when the brahmins and householders within that city heard that the World-Honored One had arrived at the outskirts of the city of Mṛttikāvatī and was currently staying there, having heard this, they gathered together and all went out of the city at once to go to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the essential Dharma to the brahmins and householders, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them; thereafter, as described above, he remained in silence.
At that time, the brahmins, householders, and others rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, and with palms joined before the World-Honored One, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray that the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus will accept our humble offering at the time of the morning meal tomorrow."
When the meal was finished, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands, and then took a golden pitcher before the World-Honored One; seeking to make a request, he spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!"
Those various venomous nāgas and malevolent yakṣas have all been subdued.

However, this yakṣiṇī Mucilindā has, throughout the long night, treated us as enemies when we were not her enemies and as foes when we were not her foes; while I have always acted with kindness and righteousness toward her, she has constantly harbored malice and caused harm, and all the children born to me have been seized and taken away by her.
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and subdue the yakṣiṇī Cūḍā.
At that time, the yakṣiṇī was also present in the assembly, and the World-Honored One addressed her, saying:
"Do you now hear these words spoken by these people?"
The yakṣa replied:
"Sugata, I have already heard it."
He asked the female yakṣī again,
"Do you hear this now?
She replied:
“World-Honored One!
I have now heard it.
The Buddha said:
"You have come from afar to commit such unrighteous and sinful deeds.
He replied, "The people and I made a pact: if you can build a monastery for me, I shall forever cease [these actions]."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmins and householders:
"Did you hear these words of the yakṣiṇī?
They replied: [Yes.]
“World-Honored One!
I have now heard it.
The Buddha said:
"What do you think? The people replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"We shall certainly build a monastery for you.
At that time, having tamed this yakṣī and her retinue, the World-Honored One departed.
The World-Honored One then proceeded to the village of Kharjūrapālī; in this village, there was a young boy who was playing at building stūpas out of earth.
Having seen this, the Blessed One addressed Vajrapāṇi:
"Do you see this boy playing by making stūpas out of earth?
Vajrapāṇi replied to the Buddha:
“I have now seen it. The Buddha said,

“After my parinirvāṇa, King Kaniṣka— here translated as ‘Pure Gold’— will build a great stūpa at this site where the boy formerly played, naming it the Kaniṣka Stūpa, and will extensively perform Buddhist services there.”

From the village of Rājagṛha, as far as the palace where the Nāga King Aśvatīrtha dwells, the Blessed One, having tamed seventy-seven thousand sentient beings along the way, returned to the village of Rājagṛha and entered his dwelling to sit in meditative seclusion.
When the time of the afternoon meal arrived, he arose from his state of meditative stillness and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"We should go together to the village of the former kings.
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata previously said:
‘I shall go to Northern India to subdue the Dragon King Vāsuki; that land possesses five superior qualities.’”
"Now the World-Honored One has further said:
'Go with me to the village of the ancient king.
How is this to be understood?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"I have already gone together with Vajrapāṇi to North India to visit the Tāmrasa grove, and so forth, up to the earthen stūpa.
From Rohitaka to the palace of the dragon Anavatapta, throughout this interval, the Tathāgata has tamed seventy-seven thousand sentient beings."

However, in that country there are inferior conditions: the terrain is uneven, it abounds in thorns, and there are many shards and stones; the people are exceedingly wicked by nature, and the women engage in evil conduct.
At that time, as the Blessed One was traveling through the region of the Vijitāvins, he gradually arrived at the village of Pāṭaligrāma.
Then the Blessed One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"In the past, King Mahāsammata was the very first to receive the consecration here; because he was the foremost among kings, it is therefore called the village of Pāṭaligrāma."
Furthermore, the Blessed One arrived at the village of Bhadraśva. At that time, the Blessed One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"The assembly granted the king permission, and it was here that the horse-treasure appeared; therefore, this village is named the Village of Bhadraśva."
At that time, the Blessed One said to Ānanda:
"You may come with me to the village of Mathurā. "So be it;
I shall receive your instruction," he replied.
Then the World-Honored One proceeded gradually toward Mathurā; while on the road, seeing a green forest in the distance, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Do you see that green forest?"
He replied, "I have seen it. [The Buddha said:
"This is Mount Ulūka-munda. One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be two brothers, Māṭhara and the other, who—"
One is named Nātha and the other is named Bāṭha; having established monasteries there, they shall be called Nāthabāṭha.
For those who practice śamatha and vipaśyanā, these places for sitting and reclining are the very best.

In the village of Matula, there will be a youth who is an expert in identifying medicinal herbs named Guhya; he will have a son named Upaguhya, who, though lacking the marks and signs of a Great Man, will be equal to a Buddha.
"One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be one who leaves the household life within my Dharma to perform the work of a Buddha.
At that time, there will be a disciple of Ānanda named Madhyantika, who will ordain Upagupta as a bhikṣu; he shall be the last to transmit my Dharma."
Within the Nāṭapāṭa monastery, there was a cave eighteen cubits long, twelve cubits wide, and seven cubits high.

Whenever he converted someone through his preaching of the Dharma such that they attained arhatship, he would take a tally four finger-widths long and cast it into the cave; at that time, Upagupta entered parinirvāṇa.
Those disciples then took the counting-sticks (*śalākā*), gathered them in one place, and used them for the cremation (*jvālayati*).
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and asked the One who Severs All Doubts:
"The World-Honored One has prophesied that in the future there will be the venerable Upagupta."
"The Buddha now bestows this prophecy; out of compassion for the many sentient beings, he shall bring them benefit.
The Buddha said, "It is not only at this time that he brings such benefit; in past lives as well, he has brought great benefit."
"You should listen attentively and reflect upon it well.
The Buddha said:
"In the distant past, on this Mount Ulūka-mṛda, there were three dwellings."
In one place there were five hundred pratyekabuddhas, in another five hundred rishis, and in another five hundred monkeys.
At that time, the leader of this troop of animals was naturally of a wicked disposition; whenever any of the monkeys gave birth to offspring, they were all injured and killed by him.
The female monkeys, distressed by grief for their offspring, deliberated together, saying:
"Listen, all of you!
This leader of our troop constantly harms our children; we must devise a stratagem. None of us who are pregnant need inform him."
At a later time, one among them became pregnant; the monkeys then led her to a secluded place and concealed her in secret, where they gathered various fruits together and provided for her in private.
When the months were complete, he gave birth to a son. He concealed him in a secret place and ordered that he be nursed and raised until he grew large.
Once he had reached maturity, he drove the leader of the herd out from among the flock, causing him to leave his original group and roam separately in the mountains.
While wandering about, he heard the voice of a pratyekabuddha and immediately went to him, drawing near and staying by his side.
Without any fear in his heart, he gathered fruits, roots, and leaves, constantly bringing them as offerings.
The Pratyekabuddha took the leftovers of his meal and fed them to the monkey.
It is the constant custom of a Pratyekabuddha that, having finished eating, he sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
Upon seeing this, the monkey immediately imitated him and sat down.
Thereafter, those Pratyekabuddhas thought to themselves:
"This inferior body of mine has attained what was to be attained; that which was to be done has been accomplished.
Now I may enter into nirvana without remainder."

Having formed this thought, he immediately ascended into the air and manifested supernatural transformations: at times flames issued from his body, at times sweet rain fell from his body, and after emitting light from his body, he entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Then that monkey, harboring grief and distress in his heart, immediately began to search and reached the old cave, where he saw the abandoned body.
At that moment, he lifted the Pratyekabuddha’s robe with his hand.
At that time, a deva thought to himself:
"Now this monkey has taken the robe of a Pratyekabuddha; I fear he will damage the Relic Body.
Thereupon, that deva drove the monkey out and covered the cave with stones.
At that time, seeing the cave closed, the monkey wept with grief and distress; departing with lingering attachment, he returned to his original place and wandered about.
Since the monkey delighted in being near people, and because there were no people present, his heart found no peace or joy.

While he was constantly listening to the voices of men, he suddenly heard the sound of a seer’s speech coming from another place. Upon hearing it, the monkey ran toward the sound like one who has lost his way, whereupon he saw a seer practicing austerities—some with arms raised, some standing on one leg, and others scorching their bodies with the five fires.
The monkey took refuge with him, remaining in that one place for a long time without fear; he constantly provided the rishi with flowers, fruits, and tooth-sticks.
Whatever remained after the rishi had eaten, he would give back to the monkey.

At that time, the monkey disrupted the seer’s dignified demeanor and caused him to follow the practice of a pratyekabuddha; seeing the seer raise his hand, the monkey pulled it downward, then snapped its fingers and assumed the full lotus posture.
To the one standing on one leg, he pulled him downward, then immediately snapped his fingers and sat in the full lotus posture before the seer.
To the one performing the "five heats" asceticism, he extinguished the fire, then immediately snapped his fingers and sat in the full lotus posture before the seer.
At that time, the various seers said to their preceptor,
"There is now a monkey who obstructs us and causes us to abandon our ascetic practices.
The preceptor then asked, at which time the seers recounted the matter in detail as previously described.
The Master further told them:
"You should know that all these monkeys are capable of remembering events; they must certainly have seen such a seer practicing the path with such majestic deportment."
"You should follow my example and sit in the full lotus posture.
Having heard the words of their teacher, the sages sat cross-legged.
Because they possessed roots of goodness from the past, these qualities were about to manifest before them.

Although they do not receive instruction from an ācārya or an upādhyāya, they are able to personally give rise to and attain the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, thereby realizing pratyekabuddhahood in the present life.

At that time, the sages and others, having developed respectful faith toward the monkey and following the Dharma, would offer whatever new fruits and fine foods they obtained to the monkey before eating them themselves.

Eventually, at a later time, the monkey died; those pratyekabuddhas and others gathered various kinds of incense from various regions and countries, piled up firewood and grass, and cremated the monkey.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor other thoughts; the monkey who lived together with a pratyekabuddha in the past was none other than this Upagupta."
"In times past, he brought great benefit; now, once again here, I bestow upon him this prophecy, out of compassion for sentient beings and for their great benefit.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*, Fascicle Nine. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*.
Fascicle Ten.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
The Account of Nīlabhūti. At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm among the Śūrasenas and gradually arrived at the city of Mathurā.

Among them, the brahmins of pure conduct heard that the śramaṇa Gautama had arrived at the city of Mathurā and was extolling it highly, illuminating and awakening others, dwelling in analytical exposition, revealing and manifesting the fourfold dharma of purity for the various classes of people:
"If that śramaṇa Gautama enters this city, our gains and offerings will certainly be cut off."
"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama does not travel to places where he is not respected.
If there were someone who did not show respect toward that Gautama, he certainly would not enter the city of Mathurā."
"If we send inferior persons there, they may treat him with contempt; fearing the mind of Gautama, they might not consider this a matter of consequence.
However, if we send a preeminent and superior person who fails to show respect and instead treats Gautama with disdain and mockery, that would be most excellent."
"Among us, who shall be our leader?

At that time, in the city of Mathurā, there was a brahmin named Nīlabhūti, who was thoroughly versed in the four Vedas and the four Śruti treatises; he was able to elucidate his own school and refute the doctrines of others, and the words he uttered were always in accordance with reality.
At that time, a great assembly of Māṭhara brahmins and others gathered together and went to where Nīlabhūti was, addressing him thus:
"Upādhyāya!..."

We have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama has come to this city; he highly praises, illuminates, awakens, establishes through analysis, reveals, and manifests the fourfold dharma of purification for persons.
However, that Gautama has places where he does not feel respect and where his heart does not delight in going.
If there are people who do not show respect toward that Gautama, he will certainly not enter the city of Mathurā.
"If we cause lowly persons to go there and treat him with contempt, fearing that the mind of Gautama might take offense, he will likely not regard it as a matter of consequence;
however, if some eminent and superior person fails to show respect and instead treats Gautama with derision and mockery, that would be most excellent."
Aside from the Upādhyāya, is there indeed anyone else of such preeminent standing who could accomplish this task?
I only wish that you would show him no respect and revile him with harsh words.
Then Nīlabhūti replied to the people, saying:
"My tongue moves according to my will; if something is worthy of reviling, I shall revile it;
if something is worthy of praise, I shall praise it."
At that time, Nīlabhūti, together with the elder brahmins, surrounded him on all sides and approached the place where the Blessed One was staying.

From afar, the brahmin Nīlabhūti saw the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs; his halo extended a fathom, surpassing the brilliance of a thousand suns, like a mountain of jewels appearing magnificent on every side, sitting beneath a tree in perfect tranquility and composure.
Upon seeing the World-Honored One, Nīlabhūti’s heart leaped with joy, and he immediately praised him, saying:
“Nīla is filled with great delight, Praising the All-Knowing Sage;
Now he speaks of supreme virtues, Which all who hear shall love and rejoice.”
Well-tamed in all his faculties, He has purified body and mind according to the Dharma;
An ocean of vast merit— I now briefly praise him.
Foremost among those who debate, Tamed and free from fault;
Able to know the ultimate truth, he cannot be shaken by polemical debate.
His knowledge and conduct are perfected; he is well-versed in all the prohibitions and precepts.
His supreme concentration is like the king of mountains; his strength is equal to that of Nārāyaṇa.
With these words as the beginning, he praised the World-Honored One with five hundred verses.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the brahmin’s mind had conceived deep faith, preached the Dharma for him; thereupon, beneath that very seat, he realized the principle of the True Truth.
At that time, after Nīla had finished praising the World-Honored One, he took his leave and returned to his native city.
Then, the elders and brahmins of the city, having learned that Nīla-bhūti had praised the World-Honored One with various eloquent words, rebuked Nīla, saying:
"We previously requested our preceptor to go to the presence of the śramaṇa Gautama and speak disrespectful words; why, instead, have you offered such excellent praise to him?"
Then Nīlabhūti said to the brahmin:
"Did I not previously say these words:
'Indeed, my tongue moves according to its own will'?"
"If that person deserves reproach, I shall reproach him;
if he deserves praise, I shall praise him.
Seeing that the Śramaṇa Gautama possesses vast merit worthy of praise, I have therefore praised him.
"Therefore, you should not reproach me.

At that time, the World-Honored One and the great assembly, having dressed and taken up their alms bowls at dawn, entered the city of Mathurā to beg for food; within that city, they encountered a day of a festival for the worship of the lunar mansions.
Then the goddess Nakṣatrarājadhītā thought to herself:
"If the śramaṇa Gautama enters this city, my festival will surely be obstructed; I must devise a plan in advance to cause him to turn back."
Having had this thought, she stood before the World-Honored One in the nude.
The Buddha said to the goddess, "The female form, even when adorned with elegant garments and flowers, is not upright; how much less so when it is naked?"
When the goddess heard these words, she felt ashamed and shamefaced, and her form vanished from sight.
At that time, the World-Honored One moved to one side of the road, prepared a seat before the great assembly, and sat down. He addressed the bhikṣus:
"In this city of Mathurā, there are five kinds of faults."

First, the land is uneven; second, it abounds in thorns and brambles; third, it is filled with tiles and stones; fourth, the people eat alone; and fifth, there are many women; for these reasons, he did not enter this city.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and proceeded to the grove of the yakṣa Gardabha, where he sat beneath a tree surrounded by the great assembly, dwelling in profound stillness.

At that time, the brahmins and householders of the city of Mathurā heard that the śramaṇa Gautama intended to enter the city, but was obstructed by a goddess and unable to do so, currently residing beneath a tree within the park of the donkey yakṣa.

Having heard this, they each prepared various kinds of food and drink, loaded them onto their respective carts, and went to where the World-Honored One was; there they prostrated at his feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma for those faithful brahmins and lay devotees, as described in detail above, until he remained silent.
Then those brahmins rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"We have prepared various kinds of pure food and drink for the World-Honored One; each of us has brought it by wagon to offer to the World-Honored One. We only pray that, out of compassion, you will accept our offerings."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Let all the bhikṣus who reside within the palace of the Yakṣa Khañja be assembled; they shall eat together with us at this offering assembly."
Ānanda said: “So be it, World-Honored One!”
Then Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, summoned all the bhikṣus who were residing in the palace of the yakṣa Gardabha and caused them to assemble at that meeting place;
he then approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"All the bhikṣus, having gathered together in the assembly hall and sat down in order, pray that the Noble One will know the time.
The Blessed One went to the assembly hall; having arrived, he spread out his seat before the bhikṣus and sat down.

At that time, the faithful brahmins and householders of the city of Mathurā, knowing that the Buddha and the Saṅgha were comfortably seated and had finished eating, [acted] as extensively described above.
Having washed their hands and finished putting away the bowls, they stood before the Buddha and made this request, saying:
"Those venomous nāgas and malevolent yakṣas have all been subdued."

"This Yakṣa Domba has, throughout the long night, treated us as enemies when we were not his enemies, as foes when we were not his foes, and as adversaries when we were not his adversaries; all the children born to us have been seized and carried off by him."
“World-Honored One, would you not deign to show compassion for us and subdue the yakṣa Duṣṭāśva?
At that time, the yakṣa was already seated among the assembly, and the World-Honored One addressed him, saying:
“Did you hear these words?”
He replied,
"World-Honored One,
I have heard it."
He further addressed the yakṣa:
“Did you hear these words?
“I did, Sugata!”
"I have heard it.
He further addressed the yakṣa:
"This is an unrighteous matter; you should feel weary of it and renounce it."
The yakṣa said to the Buddha:
"If the multitude can construct a vihāra for the bhikṣus from the four directions, I shall depart and will certainly not cause them harm."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the faithful brahmins and householders of the village of Mathurā:
"Have you heard these words?
They replied:
“We have heard it,
World-Honored One!
We shall construct it.”

At that time, after the Blessed One had subdued the yakṣa Gardabha and his five hundred retinue, the brahmins and others constructed five hundred vihāras for that yakṣa and his five hundred followers.
Having thus gradually tamed the yakṣa Hrada, the yakṣa Vana, and the yakṣī Hāritī,
the World-Honored One then manifested great supernormal powers and entered the city of Mathurā, where he tamed the yakṣī Andhaka and her five hundred retinue;
the people of that city also constructed five hundred residences for the bhikṣus.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had tamed two thousand five hundred yakṣas both outside and inside this city, the faithful people within the city likewise constructed two thousand five hundred dwellings for them.
At that time, the Blessed One again traveled to the village of Uddala and stayed in the Uddala Grove.

There was a brahmin named Uddālaka who, hearing that the Blessed One was in that grove, mounted a carriage drawn by white horses. Holding a golden staff and a golden water-pot, and surrounded by his retinue, he departed from the city intending to go to where the Buddha was. Wherever the carriage road permitted, he proceeded by carriage;
wherever it did not, he proceeded on foot. Having reached the place where the Buddha was, he greeted the Blessed One with elegant words and withdrew to sit at one side.
The brahmin great householder Udraka addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I now have a few questions; I pray that the Buddha will grant me permission to ask."
The World-Honored One said:
"Brahmin, ask whatever you wish."
Then the brahmin said: "Gautama!
These five faculties have various objects; each perceives its own respective domain and does not perceive another's."
These are the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
Which are comprised within the elements (dhātu) and the bases (āyatana)? What is their locus?
The Buddha said:
"Brahmin! If these five faculties, belonging to various realms and locations, each grasp their own respective realm and do not grasp another."
That which is called the eye-element up to the body-element—these various faculties and so forth—are all apprehended by the mind.
Nevertheless, these five faculties have the mind as their basis.
The brahmin asked, “Upon what,
then, does the mind depend?
The Buddha said:
"Mindfulness is the support.
The brahmin asked:
"What is the support for mindfulness?"
The Buddha said,
"One relies upon the four foundations of mindfulness.
He asked again:
“What do the four foundations of mindfulness rely upon?
The Buddha said,
“They rely upon the seven factors of enlightenment.”
He asked again:
"Upon what do the seven factors of enlightenment depend?
The Buddha said:
“Knowledge and liberation are the support.
He asked again:
“What is the support for knowledge and liberation?”
The Buddha said:
"Nirvana is the basis.
He asked again:
“What does Nirvana rely upon?
The Buddha said, “Brahmin!”
"What you have now asked concerns a matter that is profound and far-reaching; you cannot reach its limit, which is Nirvana.
The holy life (brahmacarya) that I now practice is for the purpose of rightly severing suffering, so as to exhaust the very bounds of all suffering."
At that time, having heard the words of the Blessed One, the brahmin great householder Udayana felt joy arise in his heart; he rose from his seat, took leave of the Buddha, and departed.
Then that householder thought to himself,
"How might I cause harm to him? Previously,
the householder had heard that someone had offered food to the World-Honored One and his assembly of śrāvakas, and he had immediately made a vow:
"Whatever one seeks with the mind, all shall be obtained.
Having formed this thought, he returned to the Buddha's presence, adjusted his robes, joined his palms in prostration, and addressed him, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus will accept my offering of a meal at my home tomorrow morning."
The details are as extensively described above.
At that time, the householder, knowing that the World-Honored One had finished eating and had washed his hands and put away his bowl, took a small seat before the World-Honored One and sat down.
He then conceived an evil wish: "May these śramaṇas, Gautama and his disciples, who have eaten my food, become oxen for me."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in Udayana’s mind, immediately addressed him, saying:
“Brahmin! Your mind is contrary to the Dharma; you will ultimately not succeed.”
"These bhikṣus have already exhausted further existence; you may now formulate another aspiration.

At that time, having spoken these words of blessing for the gift, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and departed, returning to his original dwelling. He sat down on a seat prepared before the bhikṣus and addressed them:
"That Udayana conceived an evil mind because he sought a perverted aspiration."
"After you have finished eating, you should quickly recite the verses of the former Buddhas so that his evil wishes may not be fulfilled.
Then the bhikṣus recited the verses.

At that time, when the night had ended and it was the clear morning, the World-Honored One entered the village of Udayana to beg for alms, with the venerable Ānanda, his attendant, following at his left and right sides.
In that village there was an old woman named Kāṃcanā who, wishing to fetch water, was heading toward the well.
Seeing that the time for her conversion had arrived, the World-Honored One said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"You should now go to where that old woman is and say to her:"
"The World-Honored One requires water; you may bring it to him.
She replied, "Noble One!"
"I now offer you water.

Then that old woman, with a jar full of water, quickly went to where the Buddha was. There she beheld the Tathāgata, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiant brilliance surpassing a thousand suns, moving like a mountain of jewels.

At that time, having seen the World-Honored One, the old woman felt a sense of reverence as if toward her own beloved child; she immediately raised her hands, wishing to embrace the World-Honored One, and cried out:
"My son!"
"Son! the bhikṣus immediately stepped forward to stop him, saying,
"Do not embrace the World-Honored One."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You need not prevent this old woman. Why is that? Because—"
"This old woman has already been my mother for five hundred lifetimes.
If I do not allow her to embrace my body, she will vomit hot blood.

Seeing that she harbored the thought of him as her son and reflecting upon this bond of affection, the World-Honored One gave rise to a heart of compassion and pity; he then drew his neck forward, allowing the old woman to embrace him.
Having embraced him, his heart was filled with joy as he listened to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his faculties and disposition, expounded the teaching according to his capacity, enabling him to realize the principles of the Four Noble Truths.

Having heard the Dharma, the mother used the vajra-pestle of wisdom to shatter the twenty peaks of the mountain of afflictions consisting of the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi). She realized the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) and attained insight into the principle of the truths.
She then spoke these words: "This is my World-Honored One; such a supreme benefit as this could not have been achieved by my parents, brothers, or the various devas," as described at length above.
I have already shattered with the vajra-wisdom the mountain of twentyfold satkāyadṛṣṭi accumulated since beginningless time, and have attained the fruit of stream-entry.
He further spoke in verse:
"What a virtuous son ought to do Is to repay the kindness of his compassionate mother;
Now that I have received the Buddha’s light, I shall advance upon the path to nirvāṇa."
"How wonderful, how rare an occurrence! Having forever transcended the three evil realms, I shall now, with little effort, swiftly reach the state free from sorrow.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and departed.
At another time, having received her husband’s permission to go forth, she went to the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, and addressed him, saying:

“I pray only that the Blessed One will grant me permission to go forth and receive full ordination within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, so that I may become a bhikṣuṇī and practice the holy life under the Blessed One.”

At that time, the World-Honored One entrusted her to the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī. Then Mahāprajāpatī caused her to go forth from the household life and conferred upon her full ordination (*upasampadā*). She was instructed in the essentials of the Dharma; through diligent practice and study, she severed all afflictions and realized the fruit of Arhatship, as described in detail above, receiving the offerings of devas and humans.
At that time, after the Blessed One had briefly taught the essentials of the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs, he entered his room and sat in meditation.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Caṅkī took the essential points of the Dharma she had heard and explained them extensively to others.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my community of bhikṣuṇī śrāvakas, this Cchannā is the foremost in analyzing the sūtras and the Dharma."
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt. To sever their uncertainty, they questioned the World-Honored One:
"What karma did that bhikṣuṇī Caṇḍakāla commit in the past, such that she entered the religious life only when she was advanced in years?"
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions did you undergo such poverty and low status?
Why was it that in your final birth you were not conceived in the womb, yet further attained the state of a renunciant and realized the fruit of Arhatship?
Among all modes of preaching the Dharma, why is yours considered the most supreme?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Because this bhikṣuṇī Caṅkī previously performed white karma, she accumulated the necessary provisions, and thus she now experiences the fruit of that retribution herself."
"O bhikṣus, you should know!
In the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, she was once my mother.
Due to that karma, she has now gone forth as a renunciant in her old age."
In the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, my mother was an obstacle to me.
Because Yaśodharā did not perform wholesome deeds, while Queen Māyā constantly performed wholesome karma.
In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, Caṇḍakārikā, for the purpose of causing an abortion, reviled a śikṣamāṇā bhikṣuṇī, a bhikṣuṇī in training (śaikṣa), and a bhikṣuṇī beyond training (aśaikṣa), saying:
"You slave!"
"O slave!
Because of those karmic actions, you have now become a female slave.

However, because during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha you went forth as a renunciant, recited the scriptures, and heard the Buddha teach the Dharma—thereby gaining skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*), and skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*)—you have gone forth within my teaching, severed all afflictions (*kleśa*), and attained the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)."
The bhikṣuṇī Upādāyā went forth in the Dharma of that Kāśyapa Buddha, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; she was foremost among those who preach the Dharma, being able to analyze and explain it extensively.
At that time, when the bhikṣuṇī Caṅkī was approaching the end of her life, she made this vow, saying:
"Within the Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha, I have practiced the holy life and recited the scriptures, yet I have not attained the fruit."
Now, the Buddha Kāśyapa bestowed upon the young brahmin Uttara the prophecy of his unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment:
"In a future age, when the human lifespan is one hundred years, you shall attain equal and right awakening, and your name shall be Śākyamuni."
"By these roots of goodness, may I go forth in the Dharma of that Śākyamuni Tathāgata and become the foremost among those who preach the Dharma, just like my upādhyāya today."
"By virtue of that vow, this bhikṣuṇī is now foremost in preaching the Dharma within my teaching.
Monks, you should know:
from black-and-black karma, one shall obtain black-and-black retribution."
“...up to this point, you bhikṣus, should cultivate white karma; you should train yourselves thus.
At that time, the Blessed One said to Ānanda:
“Follow me as I go to the village of Verañjā.”
Ānanda replied, "So be it,
World-Honored One."
At that time, the World-Honored One departed with Ānanda and eventually arrived at a garden.
There was a brahmin there drawing water to sprinkle upon the garden; seeing the World-Honored One from afar, he thought to himself:
"If the śramaṇa Gautama enters this garden, he will defile the well water."
He then hid his water jar and rope and stood waiting.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered that garden by means of his supernormal powers.
Then the yakṣa general Pañcika tilted the well-water, so that it flowed and filled the garden.
At that time, the brahmin thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa Gautama possesses great supernatural power; he is able to cause the well-water to gush forth and flow in abundance."
Having had this thought, he immediately conceived faith and spoke these words:
"Gautama, come!
Here is a water jar and here is a rope for the jar; take water as you please."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Where there is water everywhere, what use is well-water?
When this craving and conceptualization are severed, what more remains to be sought?"
Then that brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will allow me to go forth within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya and receive full ordination, so that I may attain the status of a bhikṣu."
As extensively described above, [the Buddha said], "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
and he immediately became a renunciant. The verse says:
"The World-Honored One bid him 'Welcome'; His hair fell away and his robes and bowl were complete."
"All faculties are utterly tranquil, and whatever is brought to mind is fully accomplished.

Because that bhikṣu exerted himself with diligent cultivation, he severed all afflictions and realized arhatship; he became weary of and detached from the three periods of time, as described at length above, until even the gods of Śakra and Brahmā paid him homage.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm and arrived at the city of Vairaṇtī, where he stayed beneath a śiṃśapā tree.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Agnidatta who ruled as king in this city; the kingdom was abundant and prosperous, the people were peaceful and happy, and it was filled with inhabitants.
At that time, when the king heard that the Blessed One was traveling among the people of Yodheyya and had arrived there beneath a latthi tree, he thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama!..."
"Since various great kings respectfully provide offerings, honor, and praise [him], I too should provide for his support and offerings, lest neighboring countries mock and deride me, saying:
'King Agnidatta!'"
"The Tathāgata is within our territory and can also be honored here.
I should now invite the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus to provide them with offerings of every kind of requisite."

Having formed this thought, he immediately ordered his carriage to be prepared and departed the city, proceeding to where the Buddha was. He greeted the World-Honored One with various kind words of inquiry and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the king, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him, before remaining silent.
Then King Agnidatta rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus will accept my offerings of the four requisites for a three-month period of the rainy-season retreat."
“Food and drink, medicinal decoctions, clothing, and bedding.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted King Agnidatta’s invitation.

When King Agnidatta saw that the World-Honored One had silently accepted his request, his heart was filled with great joy; he rose from his seat, returned to his palace, and commanded his ministers, saying:
"You all should daily prepare eighteen kinds of rice and various delicious foods in abundance.
He further issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom:
"All of you people must not, during the three months of the summer retreat, provide offerings to the śramaṇa Gautama."
"If anyone should dare to request [this], their life shall be taken.
Having issued this command, the king fell asleep that night and dreamed that a white canopy surrounded the palace city.

Having awakened from the dream, he was struck with terror; his mind was filled with grief and distress, and the hairs on his body stood on end. He rose quickly from his bed, rested his cheek in his hand as he sat, and pondered: "What omen of calamity or auspiciousness is this dream?"
"Will I not lose my royal throne because of this omen, or will it even lead to my death?
When morning came, he informed the state preceptor and related his dream in detail:
"What does such a dream portend for me?"
At that time, the thought arose in the mind of the state preceptor:
"The dream the King has just had is a favorable omen.
If I can skillfully interpret it, I shall cause the King to increase his respect and offerings toward Gautama even further."
"I now interpret that king's dream as an evil omen.
Having formed this thought, he addressed the king, saying,
"This dream is not auspicious."
The king said to the teacher, "This dream is not auspicious; what retribution will there be?
The teacher replied to the king:
“Just as in the king’s dream, he will certainly lose his throne, or perhaps even meet his death.
At that time, the king reflected:
“Will I truly lose my kingdom?”
"Will this lead to death?
Having had this thought, he again addressed his teacher, saying:
"What skillful means are there by which one may avoid losing one's position and avoid dying?"
The teacher replied,
"For the three months of the summer retreat, stay in a secluded place so that no one sees you.
If you can do this, you will certainly not lose your position, nor will your life end."
When King Jotipāla heard these words, he said:
"This is very easy; I shall issue a command to the people within my realm that they must not see me."
Having spoken these words, he went everywhere to proclaim:
"By royal decree, during the three months of the summer retreat, none of the people shall see me again."
"If anyone should see him, his life shall be taken.
Having issued this command, he entered a place of concealment.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to the palace of King Jyotiṣka at early dawn; at the king's gate, he saw the gatekeepers sitting quietly and idly, doing nothing at all.
Having seen them, he asked:
"For what reason are you all sitting idly now, doing nothing?
They then replied:
“Venerable Ānanda, what should I do? Ānanda replied,
“O King Jyotiṣka!”
"Did you not invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to provide them with the four requisites for the three months of the summer retreat?
Why do you now sit idly, failing to prepare food and drink or to arrange seats and bedding, thereby causing the Buddha and the Saṃgha to fast for a single day?"
Then his disciple said: "Venerable One!
Although the King issued a command to prepare a meal for five hundred people in great abundance, he did not specify for whom it was intended."
Ānanda said to him, "You may speak. He then replied:
"Noble Ānanda! The King previously issued a proclamation throughout [the land]:
'During the three months of the summer retreat, let no one see me.'"
"If anyone sees [him] again, his life shall be taken.
Do we then possess a second head that we dare speak thus to the King?
When Ānanda had heard these words, he went to where the Buddha was and reported the matter in detail.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“You should now put on your saṃghāṭī, take a single attendant, and go into the great city—through the markets, lanes, alleys, and crossroads—and make this announcement:”
"Whoever possesses faith and is able to provide food, drink, and medicinal decoctions for the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus for three months—now is precisely the time."
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, the Noble One went and informed them, recounting everything as above.
The elders, brahmins, and others in the city spoke thus:
“Noble Ānanda!...”

"Each of us individually is capable of providing offerings; we shall provide food, drink, and the four requisites for the World-Honored One and the community of chief śrāvakas for three months without any deficiency."

However, because the King has issued a strict decree, for a period of three months, it is not permitted for the people within the realm to offer gifts at will to the World-Honored One, the foremost among them, and the Saṃgha of bhikṣus.
"If anyone violates this, the penalty shall be death.
Thus he proclaimed everywhere, yet in the end, no one was able to do so.
At that time, a merchant leader came from the north, bringing five hundred horses to this city, and he thought to himself:
"It is currently the rainy season; if I were to proceed now, I fear the mud would damage the horses, causing many to suffer from sore hooves.
Thus, for the three months [of the rains], he remained right there.
His own riding horse was fed two *śīrṣa* of barley daily, while the others received one.
The merchant leader also heard that the king had issued a strict decree. At that time, Ānanda went to the merchant leader and preached the Dharma to him; the latter then thought to himself:
"I shall not remain long within this king's realm."
Having reflected thus, he said:
"Venerable Ānanda!
My own riding horse receives two *droṇas* of barley daily as fodder; the others receive one *droṇa*."
"World-Honored One, if you would be so kind as to partake of this grain, I shall offer two *śronas* daily to the Buddha, and provide one *śrona* each to the other bhikṣus.
When Ānanda heard the merchant leader’s invitation, he went to the World-Honored One’s presence and reported the matter in full.
The Buddha had this thought:
"I myself have performed these actions; I myself shall experience their results.
As explained at length elsewhere, up to: "they are not experienced in the external world," and so forth, culminating in the verse:
"Even if a hundred eons were to pass, the karma one has created would not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, the retribution will surely be experienced by oneself.
Having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"You should now go among the assembly of bhikṣus and distribute voting sticks in order, announcing as follows:
'If you are able to dwell here together with the Buddha for three months and subsist on horse-grams, you may take this stick.'"
At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the Noble One went to distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*).
The World-Honored One, the Teacher, first took one stick himself, and four hundred and ninety-eight bhikṣus each took their own.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"I suffer from a wind disorder and shall be unable to eat barley for three months.
The Venerable Maudgalyāyana then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I shall also go along to attend upon the Venerable One.
The Buddha, together with four hundred and ninety-eight bhikṣus, entered the summer retreat there; the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana went to Mount Triśṛṅga and took up residence there.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came to invite the two venerable ones to accept his provisions for three months.
During this period, the merchant leader offered two *śronas* of horse-barley daily to the Buddha, and bestowed one *śrona* each upon the other bhikṣus.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"You may prepare these barley grains for me. Thereupon,
Ānanda took the barley and went to a village, arriving at the home of an elderly woman, where he said to her:
"Sister, you may prepare this barley for the Blessed One.
The old woman replied:
“Noble one! I am advanced in years and lack the strength to manage these affairs.
However, there is a young woman in this neighboring house who is capable of managing them.”
Then Ānanda went again to that place and said to her:
"Sister, would you be able to prepare these barley grains for the Buddha?"
The woman replied, "Noble One!
If you will allow me to ask questions and provide answers while you prepare this barley, I shall then prepare it."
Ānanda said, “So be it,” and he immediately made the necessary preparations.
At that time, the young girl asked Ānanda:
"Noble One! What is the meaning of the name 'Buddha'?"
At that time, Ānanda had this thought:
"The Buddha’s meaning is extremely profound, difficult to understand and difficult to fathom.
If I were to reveal it, they certainly would not comprehend it."
"For now, I shall proclaim the matters concerning the Wheel-Turning King.
He addressed her, saying: "Sister!"
If, in this world, a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears, seven treasures manifest accordingly.
What are these seven treasures?

They are the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the minister-treasurer treasure, and the military-commander treasure—namely, the wheel treasure and the others.
How does he appear in the world?
If it is a kṣatriya, an anointed universal monarch (cakravartin), who on the fifteenth day, having bathed and purified himself, ascends a high tower together with his ministers and attendants.
From the eastern direction, the precious wheel appeared, its thousand spokes, hub, and rim all perfectly complete, naturally formed of celestial gold.
Upon seeing it, the king thought to himself:

"I have heard it said that if a consecrated Great King of the Kṣatriya caste, having bathed and purified himself on the fifteenth day, ascends a high tower and a wheel appears, he will surely attain the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
"I shall now test it.

He immediately rose from his seat, knelt with his knees touching the ground, and took the wheel in his right hand, pressing it against his left palm; then he took it up again with his left hand, pressing it against his right palm.
The King then made this aspiration: "O sublime and wondrous Wheel-Treasure, may you manifest the deeds performed by the past Wheel-Turning Sage Kings."
The king, together with the wheel-treasure and the fourfold army, then ascended into the air.
Just as was the case for previous wheel-turning kings, wherever the wheel came to rest, the king likewise stayed.
At that time, eighty-four thousand minor kings from the eastern direction all went to the place where the Wheel-Turning King was and said to him:
"Welcome, Great Deva! This is your kingdom;
its people are flourishing, and it is peaceful, secure, and prosperous."
"We only pray that Your Majesty will remain established here, while we, your servants, attend upon you.
The Wheel-Turning King commanded them, saying, "Each of you should transform the world through the True Dharma; do not dwell together with those who act contrary to the Dharma."
"If it is thus, then attend upon me.
At that time, the wheel-treasure brought all regions under its dominion from the eastern direction as far as the edge of the ocean;
the same was true for the southern, western, and northern directions.
Following the manner of the wheel-treasure, it ascends into the air and travels everywhere, returning to the royal palace and coming to rest before the king’s hall.
Sisters! When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, such a wheel-treasure will necessarily manifest.
As for the elephant treasure, it is the color of a lotus flower; its seven limbs are perfectly formed, its physique is beautiful, and it is robust, powerful, and exceedingly delightful.
When the king saw this, his heart was filled with joy, and he spoke these words:
"The elephant-treasure is Excellent.
He then immediately ordered an attendant to summon a skilled elephant trainer and said to him:
"This precious elephant should be well-trained at once.
Once it has been well-trained and docile, send it to me.
He replied:
"As Your Majesty commands.
Within a single day, all those who were to be tamed were completely subdued.
This elephant-treasure was of such a noble and gentle nature that it could follow the methods of training like an elephant of a hundred years' age already skilled in the signs of discipline.
Having seen that the elephant was well-trained, he immediately presented it to the king and said:
"Great King! The precious elephant is thoroughly tamed; may Your Majesty know the proper time."
"O sisters! When the king wished to test the elephant, at sunrise he mounted it and traveled through the four quarters of the world, returning to his own palace by mealtime to eat."
When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, such a horse-treasure as this emerges in the world.
As for the horse-treasure, it is deep blue in color, with a glossy black head; its form is upright and handsome, and it is exceedingly delightful.
When the king saw it, he was filled with great joy, for this horse-treasure was endowed with the marks of a great noble being.
He summoned the groom and ordered him to break it in quickly.
Immediately following the king’s command, he instructed [the horse] in the methods of training for an entire day, just as previously described.
Having thoroughly trained it, he led it before the king and said:
"Great King!"
"The Horse-Treasure has been tamed; may Your Majesty know that the time has come.
When the king wished to test the horse, at the rising of the sun, he likewise mounted the Horse-Treasure and traveled through the four continents, as described in detail above.
Sisters! It is only when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world that this Horse-Jewel manifests.

As for the Jewel, it possesses such form and color: it is octagonal, complete in its proportions, the color of deep lapis lazuli, pure and brilliant, radiating a luminous splendor that dispels all darkness.
Sisters! Such are the merits of this jewel-treasure; it appears in the world only when a Wheel-Turning King has appeared.

As for the Woman-Jewel, her physical form is upright and graceful, and her countenance is peerless. She is neither too fair nor too dark, neither too yellow nor too red, neither too tall nor too short, and neither too stout nor too slender. From all the pores of her body issues the fragrance of *candana* sandalwood, and the breath from her mouth is as pure and fragrant as a blue lotus. When touched during the cold season, she is warm; when touched during the hot season, she is cool.

At that time, as the Venerable Ānanda was explaining the seven jewels of a wheel-turning monarch, he reached the jewel of the woman. At that moment, the woman had finished preparing the barley; she immediately prostrated at Ānanda’s feet, joined her palms, and made this aspiration:
“By this meritorious deed, may I become the jewel of the woman for a wheel-turning monarch.”
Then Ānanda carried it to where the Buddha was. There is nothing that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not clearly perceive; though they already know, they inquire for a specific purpose.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Who has prepared this barley?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
There is a certain brahmin girl."
The Buddha asked again,
"What conversation did you have with him?
He replied:
"Speak with her.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Relate to me everything that you have said to that woman."
Ānanda respectfully reported the matter as instructed.
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda, saying:
"For what reason did you not proclaim the virtues of the Buddha, but instead speak of a wheel-turning monarch?"
He addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
I had this thought:"
"The Buddha's virtues are exceedingly profound; I fear that woman will be unable to awaken to and understand them.
For this reason, he spoke of the Wheel-Turning King for her sake.
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! You have committed a fault.

Had you spoken of the Buddha’s virtues to that woman, she, upon hearing the Buddha’s merits, would certainly have resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and would never have regressed.”
"By the power of this vow, this woman shall certainly become the 'Woman-Jewel' (strī-ratna) of a Wheel-Turning King.

At that time, people from near and far all heard that the Brahmin girl had prepared the Buddha's barley and received the Buddha’s prediction that she would become the Woman-Jewel of a future Wheel-Turning Sage King.
At that time, five hundred women came to the bhikṣus’ dwelling place to prepare barley; they all made this vow:
"When that woman becomes the Woman-Jewel of a Universal Monarch, we all vow to serve and attend her."
At that time, the World-Honored One wished to eat horse barley, and the Venerable Ānanda wept with tears falling like rain, saying:
"Wherever the World-Honored One travels, kings and noble elites receive the dust from his feet upon their heads as a mark of veneration."
"Having cultivated all categories of wholesome qualities throughout three great eons, why do you eat such coarse barley in this city?
At that time, the Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda,
"For what reason are you weeping now, shedding tears like rain?"
He addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"Great Virtuous World-Honored One, you were born in a royal palace and were destined to receive the rank of a Wheel-Turning King to rule over the four quarters of the world;

yet you renounced national glory to leave the household life, and throughout three incalculable great eons, you extensively gave away your head, eyes, hands, and feet, perfected all-encompassing wisdom, and widely received the most excellent and wondrous offerings of devas and humans."
"Why do you now wish to eat horse barley?
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
"Can you now eat a single grain of barley from within the Tathāgata’s teeth?
He replied,
"I most desire to do so."
The Buddha took a single grain of barley from within his tusk and gave it to Ānanda, who immediately ate it.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Have you ever before obtained such sweet and delicious food?"
He replied,
“Venerable World-Honored One!
Although I was born into the lineage of a Wheel-Turning King, from the time I first began to eat on my own until now, I have never before obtained such exquisite flavor as this.”
The Buddha said:
"Ānanda! Whatever enters the mouth of the Tathāgata is always sweet and delicious, the most excellent among all hundred flavors."

At that time, the neighboring kings from distant and near lands all heard that King Agnidatta had invited the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the community of bhikṣus for a three-month *varṣā* retreat; they then entered their inner palaces and did not appear, nor did they offer any offerings, while the Buddha ate horse barley.
Having heard this, he dispatched a messenger to inform King Agnidatta. When the messenger arrived, he was not permitted to enter for an audience and remained waiting at the gate.

At that time, after the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had heard of these matters, he prepared five hundred wagons, each laden with exquisite non-glutinous rice, which were tightly sealed and covered, intending to send them to the Buddha’s location.
At that time, Māra the Evil One thought to himself:
"I have troubled the śramaṇa Gautama in many ways, yet I have found no opportunity; I must trouble him further, for now is precisely the right time."
Having formed this thought, he immediately transformed his body into the form of Ānanda and went to the place where the five hundred carts were, saying:
"O worthy ones, where do you wish to go?"
He replied, "Venerable Ānanda!
We have heard that King Agnidatta invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a three-month rains retreat, yet he failed to provide offerings, so that the Buddha and the Saṃgha ate horse fodder."
"This is why the householder Anāthapiṇḍika has sent this rice to be offered to the World-Honored One.
Māra said, "The devas, nāgas, and yakṣas revere the World-Honored One; they lift their bowls upward, and the exquisite, fragrant food of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is placed within them."
"For what reason has the World-Honored One eaten horse barley?
You should turn back at once.
Thus the people replied.
"I have already set out for the place where the World-Honored One resides; I do not wish to turn back.
Māra then thought again:
"These people will not accept my instructions; I must employ a skillful means."

He immediately ascended into the void and raised a great wind and rain, with the downpour as thick as chariot axles, causing all the rice carts to sink halfway into the mud; the drivers unyoked their oxen and departed as they pleased.

At that time, the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus were eating horse barley, while the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to Mount Triśṛṅga to receive the offerings of the devas.
When the three months had passed, the horse merchant came and requested of the World-Honored One:
"I pray that you will compassionately accept my humble offering, together with the community of bhikṣus."
The Buddha silently accepted the invitation.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, during that night he prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink, as described at length elsewhere.
When the meal was finished and the bowl had been put away, and after he had rinsed his mouth and washed clean, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and made this vow:
"By all my roots of goodness, may I become a Wheel-Turning King in a future life.
May the intelligent horse be my crown prince,
and may five hundred horses be my sons."
"The girl whom the Buddha has prophesied shall be my jewel of a woman;
the remaining five hundred girls shall be the ladies-in-waiting of my palace.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing her thoughts, addressed her, saying:
“O Caravan Leader!
Your aspiration shall surely be fulfilled in the future.
*Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (The Section on Medicines), Volume Ten of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
