At that time, King Jyotiṣka was within his inner palace, longing to see some auspicious occurrence.
Then Ānanda arrived at the gate of the king’s palace and addressed the gatekeeper:
“Good sir, please announce to the King on my behalf that the Venerable Ānanda is now at the gate and wishes to see the Great King.”
Then the gatekeeper addressed the king, saying:
"Your Majesty should know that the Venerable Ānanda is standing at the gate, hoping to see Your Majesty."

The King said, "I now hope to behold auspicious and fortunate matters; the bhikṣu Ānanda is a person of great nobility and distinguished lineage—he himself is the very embodiment of fortune and auspiciousness."

He possesses a good reputation, a fine countenance, and auspicious physical marks; his speech is always virtuous, and he cultivates all manner of wholesome qualities. He may be invited to enter the palace—dare anyone dare to obstruct him?
The gatekeeper, having received the king’s command, informed Ānanda, saying,
"The King requests that you enter the palace.
At that time, the envoys from the four directions also entered together with him.
Then Ānanda addressed the king,
saying, "May you be free from illness," and sitting to one side, he spoke to King Agnidatta:
“The World-Honored One sends his greetings to the Great King and informs him:
‘Having completed the summer retreat within your realm for the three-month period, we now wish to depart; please let the King know this.’”
The King said: "Ānanda!
I now prostrate myself before the majestic power of the World-Honored One; has he been dwelling in peace and comfort throughout this past summer retreat?"
"Are the food and drink abundant?
At that time, the envoys from all the various kingdoms addressed the king, saying:

"Your Majesty is most unrighteous; having invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha of Śrāvakas to provide offerings for three months, you have remained in your private palace and failed to come and pay your respects."
"The World-Honored One has been in this region, and for the duration of one summer retreat,
he has eaten coarse horse barley. The King said, "Venerable Ānanda!"
“World-Honored One, did the Saṃgha truly eat coarse barley for three months?
Ānanda replied, “It is exactly as you have said.”
The king then fainted and fell from his seat; only after cold water was sprinkled on his face did he regain consciousness. He summoned his ministers and officials and addressed them, saying:
"Did I not previously command that five hundred people be provided with daily meals—various exquisite, sweet, and fragrant delicacies, including soups, rice, and other foods?"
The ministers replied, "Your Majesty, you have merely ordered that fragrant food be prepared; you did not command us to whom it should be given.
We have received the imperial decree to provide daily meals, and we have prepared portions for five hundred people."
Then King Agnidatta went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit at one side.
The Blessed One taught him the subtle Dharma, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him; having done so, he remained silent.
The king rose from his seat, again prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
I have committed a grave transgression.”
"O Great Virtuous One, Sugata!
I have committed a grave transgression.

Because of my youth, folly, failure to distinguish between the noble and the wise, and lack of skillful means, I previously invited the World-Honored One and the assembly of śrāvakas for a three-month summer retreat, yet I remained within my inner palace and did not see the Buddha. I only pray that the World-Honored One will bear witness and hold me in his protective mindfulness; out of compassion for me, may you accept my repentance and grant forgiveness for my offense."
The Buddha said, “Great King! It is indeed as you have said.

That you personally invited the World-Honored One and the Saṃgha for a period of three months, yet they did not appear, was truly due to your youth and folly; you failed to distinguish between the worthy and the virtuous, and lacked all skillful means.”
However, Great King, you should know this:
if a person commits a transgression and gives rise to deep remorse, their offense will naturally be extinguished and their merit and virtue will increase.
For what reason?
“By seeing one’s transgressions, one is able to give rise to remorse.
The King spoke again to the Buddha:
“I pray only that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will accept from me clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for as long as my life lasts.”
The Buddha said, “Great King!
Life is short; yet since the Tathāgata appeared in the world, those who have not been tamed and transformed are immeasurable in number.”
"Nirvana is approaching; I shall not accept the King's lifelong offerings.
The King spoke again, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!"
"If you will not accept my offerings for as long as I live, I only pray that out of compassion you will accept them for seven years, or even for seven months and seven days.
The Buddha likewise did not accept.
The King spoke again to the Buddha:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, together with the community of bhikṣus, will accept my humble offering at the palace tomorrow.
The Buddha then had this thought:
"If he does not accept my invitation, the king will surely spit hot blood from his mouth and die as a result.
The Buddha then silently accepted the king's invitation.
Knowing that he had been accepted, the king prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and returned to the palace, where he commanded his ministers, saying:
"What clever stratagem do you have that will cause this great mass of food to be consumed entirely by the Buddha and the Saṃgha tomorrow?
The ministers replied, "It can be spread upon the ground;
we shall invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha to walk over it, which will be equivalent to eating."
The king said, "Excellent!
That very night, the king prepared various exquisite, pure, and fragrant delicacies, fully equipped with a hundred flavors.
Among the assembly was an elderly renunciant who harbored resentment and said:
"This unrighteous king has invited the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the community of bhikṣus for three months, yet has provided them with only coarse barley to eat."
"Now, displaying this food, he flaunts his clever skills.
He then kicked it with his foot, scattering the food and drink.
When the brahmins and elders saw this, they all mocked and reviled him.
"Noble one! This food is something to be eaten with the mouth; how can it be kicked away with the feet?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
“Because that bhikṣu nudged the food with his foot, such a fault arose.
From this day forward, one must not tread with the foot upon anything intended to be placed in the mouth.”
"If anyone violates this, they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, King Jyotiṣka, seeing that the assembly was seated, personally served the food until everyone was fully satisfied.
When the meal was nearly finished, he gathered the bowls and utensils; having rinsed and purified himself, he took a small, low seat and sat before the Buddha.
The Buddha again expounded the sublime Dharma extensively for the king and then departed from his seat.

At that time, when the bhikṣus had completed their summer retreat and finished washing their robes, each took up his robe and bowl and came together to the place where the Buddha was. Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, they stood to one side and addressed the Buddha in unison:
“Venerable World-Honored One!”
"We have completed our three-month summer retreat here; may we now demolish these grass huts?
This is explained in detail in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, Chapter Four.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
What karma did he previously perform?"
Having passed through three incalculable great eons, relinquishing his head, eyes, hands, and feet, and extensively practicing the giving of alms, he attained Perfect Enlightenment.
The Buddha, together with four hundred and ninety-eight bhikṣus, set aside all other affairs and went to the city of Vairambhya, where they ate coarse horse-barley;
meanwhile, the venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana received sublime offerings from the devas.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, I myself created this karma, and now I must experience its results myself.
This is explained at length as elsewhere stated.
As it is said in verse:
"Even if a hundred eons should pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, its retribution is received by oneself."
"You should know this!

In the distant past, when the human lifespan was eighty-four thousand years, a Buddha, a World-Honored One, appeared in the world, named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles."
Accompanied by a community of eighty-four thousand bhikṣus, he resided in the city of Sāketā, near the royal capital.
At that time, there was a brahmin in the city of Sāketā who instructed five hundred youths; the people of the kingdom honored and made offerings to him as if he were a true Arhat.
When Vipaśyin Tathāgata arrived at that city, the people of the kingdom neither showed him reverence nor paid him respect.
Consequently, this brahmin conceived feelings of jealousy toward the Buddha and his assembly of śrāvakas.

At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus, both those still in training and those beyond training, dressed in their robes and carrying their alms bowls in the early morning, entered the royal capital to beg for food. Having obtained various kinds of exquisite and fragrant offerings, they emerged with their bowls full.
When the brahmin saw this, he asked, "Come, bhikṣus;
let me see what alms-food you have received in your bowls.
Out of their sincere and straightforward nature, the bhikṣus each presented the food from their bowls.
Concealing jealousy, he gave rise to anger and told his students:
"This man is not a worthy recipient; he is incapable of receiving such sublime offerings. You should give him only the coarsest and most unrefined barley."
Then all the students replied together: "So it is! So it is!"
As the Upādhyāya said, "It is proper to eat coarse barley.
Among that assembly were two youths who harbored pure faith and possessed marks of noble virtue; they spoke as follows:
"Upādhyāya! Do not speak such words.
This one is truly an Arhat, endowed with great majesty and excellence, worthy of receiving celestial offerings; he is no fit recipient for human food."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think?
Was that brahmin of long ago someone else?"
I am that very person now.
As for those five hundred students, they are these four hundred and ninety-eight bhikṣus.
Those two youths who possessed faith and were virtuous are now Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.

"O bhikṣus! Because in the past, in the presence of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin and his disciples—both those in training and those beyond training—I harbored a mind of envy and gave rise to anger, using unwholesome words to speak harsh and evil speech, and because all those students followed my words;
by the power of that karma, I now undergo this retribution."
Therefore, the World-Honored One ate coarse horse-barley along with four hundred and ninety-eight bhikṣus;
as for Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, these two youths did not follow my words, and by the power of their wholesome karma, they now receive celestial offerings.
For this reason, I have always proclaimed:
black karma brings black retribution; white karma brings white retribution; and mixed karma brings mixed retribution.
You all should practice with diligence and train yourselves accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"You should now come with me to the city of Aparājita.

Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda immediately followed behind the Buddha as they traveled through the human realm until they reached the kingdom of Aparājita and stayed on the banks of the Gaṅgā River.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will briefly expound the sublime Dharma for me.
Having heard this supreme teaching, I shall receive it with single-minded devotion; through diligent effort and earnest application, I shall be able to attain thorough realization.

For this reason, I have renounced my noble lineage, shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and left behind worldly concerns to go forth into homelessness; until the end of my life, I aspire to seek the unsurpassed holy life, so that by means of my own wisdom, I may attain the Dharma and realize the Dharma for the benefit of both myself and others.
"My births are exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; I shall not undergo further existence.
When that bhikṣu had spoken these words, the Buddha turned his gaze toward the Gaṅgā River and saw a large, square timber floating down with the current.
Having seen this, he said to that bhikṣu:
"Do you now see these rafters in the middle of the river being carried along with the current?
He replied:
“I have seen it.

The Buddha said, “If there is a bhikṣu who, like that raft, does not stay on the far shore, does not stay on this shore, and does not stay in midstream, on the sandbanks, or on the islands; if he is not pulled out by men, nor carried off by non-humans, nor caught in a whirlpool, and neither decays nor rots—he will, before long, reach the great ocean and dwell therein.”
“Bhikṣu, it is thus: one does not dwell in this or that,” and so on at length, “until reaching nirvāṇa.
Then that bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Sir!”
"From this shore to the other shore, even to the point of being neither broken nor decayed—I do not yet understand this.
Excellent, World-Honored One!
I pray that you will briefly explain it for me, so that I may attain awakening and reach the state where there is no further existence."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The 'this shore' and the 'other shore' refer to the six sense bases.
The 'this shore' refers to the internal bases; the 'other shore' refers to the external bases."
"O Bhikṣus!
Although they know these six internal and external bases, those who dwell in the middle stream delight in craving and desire;
those who dwell on the sandy banks and islets, this is the state of *asmimāna* (the conceit 'I am')."
"Those captured by humans" refers to those bhikṣus who, with laypeople, engage in mutual visits and correspondence, sharing in their joys and sorrows.
"Those captured by non-humans" refers to those who, while practicing the holy life, have made this vow:
"By this root of goodness, may I be reborn among the devas, the hungry ghosts, and so forth."
"Those who enter the whirlpool are those who abandon the various rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).

'Rotten' refers to those who violate the pure precepts, commit various evil deeds, incite strife among the virtuous and good, become allies of Māra, and—while not being śramaṇas—claim to be śramaṇas; while not practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*)—claim to practice the holy life."
"Monks, you should understand it thus:
this is for the sake of both self and others, internally and externally," and so on at length, "until finally reaching nirvāṇa.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s excellent teaching, the bhikṣu rejoiced, accepted it with faith, paid homage, and departed.

Just as the Buddha had taught, this bhikṣu retained it single-mindedly and applied himself with diligent effort, until he realized: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence; I have realized the fruit of arhatship."
At that time, there was a cowherd named Nanda who stood leaning on his staff, listening from afar to the Buddha’s discourse not far away.
There was also a frog by the riverbank; the cowherd’s staff happened to rest upon its back, piercing its skin and flesh. Although it suffered this pain, the thought arose in its mind:
"If I make a sound, the cowherd Nanda will surely be distracted."
"To hear the Dharma is difficult.
Through this patient endurance, he conceived a profound and pure mind toward the World-Honored One; consequently, his life ended, and he was reborn in the palace of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Then the cowherd cast his staff aside, approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."

I do not now delight in dwelling on either bank; I do not follow the middle current, nor dwell on the sandbanks; I am not seized by humans, nor held by non-humans; I do not sink into whirlpools, nor am I decomposed.
I only pray, World-Honored One,

that you will grant me permission to go forth within the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination, to become a bhikṣu, and to purely cultivate the holy life in service to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha asked the cowherd,
"Should you not now return this herd of cattle to its original owner?
He replied:
"I will not give it.
"For what reason do you not hand it over?
He replied:
"Each of the cows has its own calf staying with its owner.
Because these mother cows are longing for their calves, they will return of their own accord when the time comes; that is why they have not been handed over."
I only pray, World-Honored One!

Grant me permission to go forth within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, and to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), so that I may become a bhikṣu and purely cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The Buddha said,
“Nandika! Wait but a moment.”
"Although this herd of cows knows its place of residence, you have already accepted clothing and food from another cow-herd; you ought not to act in this manner.
At that time, Nandika prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and departed, crying out in a loud voice:
"I am in great terror!"
"How truly terrifying!
he cried, and fled with great haste.
Seeing that the cowherd was filled with fear, about a hundred fellow cowherds asked him:
“Virtuous one, what do you fear in birth?
He replied, “I fear birth, I fear old age, I fear illness, and I fear death.”
When the cowherds heard these words, they also ran after him.
Other cowherds, shepherds, as well as grass-cutters and wood-gatherers who saw him on the road, all followed after him.
One who came from the opposite direction asked,
"What are you afraid of?
He replied:
"I am afraid of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Upon hearing this, all these people fled, desiring to reach the village where they resided.
When the people of the village saw the great multitude from afar, they became terrified; some fled, some gathered their belongings, and others donned armor and prepared their weapons.
Among them was a fierce man who emerged from the village, leading the vanguard to meet them, and asked:
"What is the matter? He then replied:
"There is fear! There is dread! he asked.
"What do you fear? He replied,
"I now dread birth, old age, sickness, and death."
At that time, the people of the village finally felt at ease.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra, who was seated in the assembly before the Buddha, saw that the cowherds had long since departed in joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Gopa the Cowherd was joyful and delighted by the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, and requested ordination.
For what reason, World-Honored One, did the Buddha first cause him to return home?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"It is impossible for the joyful cowherd to remain at home and enjoy the pleasures of the five senses;
once he has entrusted the cattle to you, he will immediately come here—you shall see this for yourself."

That noble son, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the kāṣāya robe, left the household life for homelessness out of pure faith; he practiced the unsurpassed Brahma-faring until the end and attained the vision of the principle of the Truths.
By means of his own wisdom, he has seen the Dharma and realized it for himself, and he causes others to realize it as well:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has now been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
On another occasion, after the cowherd Nandika had returned the cattle to their owners, he came to the Buddha accompanied by five hundred men and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!..."

"I have finished handing over the ox; I pray that you will grant me permission to go forth in this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination, to become a bhikṣu, and to purely cultivate the holy life in service to the World-Honored One."
Having seen them, the Buddha said: "Rejoice!

You and the five hundred who have come here with you are all permitted to go forth within this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya; you shall receive full ordination, attain the status of bhikṣus, and may practice the holy life."
Having gone forth, he diligently cultivated wholesome qualities until his mind attained liberation.
Such is the constant law: when one is reborn in heaven, three thoughts arise:
first, "From where did I die?"
"In what place was he born,
and by what karma?
Having been born in the heavens, the frog immediately surveyed his surroundings and cast off his frog body."
He was born in the palace of the Four Great Kings;
because he had conceived a pure mind toward the Buddha, by virtue of that karma, he was born here.
He then thought to himself:
"If I were to enjoy celestial pleasures first and fail to go see the Buddha, it would be a profound lack of gratitude and filial piety.
I shall now go beforehand to visit the World-Honored One.

At that time, the Devaputra Frog, adorning his body and head with celestial countenance and deportment, came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the middle watch of the night. The area by the side of the Gaṅgā River was brilliantly illuminated; he scattered exquisite celestial flowers over the Tathāgata, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down opposite him to listen to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, perceiving the faculties, latent tendencies, and inclinations of the Devaputra Maṇḍūka, taught him the Dharma in such a way that he brought him to realization regarding the Four Noble Truths.

Having heard the Dharma, he used the vajra-pestle of wisdom to shatter the twenty-fold mountain of the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), realizing the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) and transcending the mountains of bones while drying up the oceans of blood.

At that time, the Devaputra Maṇḍūka was filled with profound joy, like a merchant who has found a buyer for his goods, like a farmer who has obtained a timely rain, like an army that has achieved victory, or like a patient who has been cured. Rising from his seat, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and took his leave to return to his celestial abode.
These bhikṣus remained awake throughout the first and last watches of the night; seeing the light during the night, they became suspicious.
At dawn, they addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"During the night just past, did Brahmā, Śakra, the various devas, and the four world-protecting Heavenly Kings come to the Buddha’s dwelling?"
The Buddha said:
"He has not come.

However, while Gopāla was listening to my Dharma with joy, there was a frog that was pinned beneath his staff, its skin and flesh pierced through. Fearing that its cry might startle Gopāla as he listened to the Dharma, the frog conceived a pure mind toward me; enduring the pain until its life ended, it was reborn in the palace of the Four Great Heavenly Kings."
"He came to my presence, and I preached the Dharma for him.
Having heard the Dharma, he took his leave and returned to his own palace.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"What karma did Gopāla and his five hundred followers previously create,
such that they became cowherds, yet later went forth in the Buddha’s teaching, severed all afflictions, and realized the fruit of arhatship?"
"What karma did the Taduka King previously create that he was born as a frog and yet perceived the truth of the Dharma?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Because they themselves created these karmas, they now receive them themselves.
This is explained at length, culminating in the verse:
"Even if a hundred eons pass, the karma one has created does not perish;"
"When causes and conditions meet, one receives the retribution for oneself. "O Bhikṣus!

In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with the ten titles, who dwelt at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Seers near Vārāṇasī."

That cowherd, Nandika, went forth as a renunciant within that Buddha's teaching; he mastered the Tripitaka, became a great Dharma master, was well-versed in the rules of conduct, and was able to maintain and recite the scriptures.
He had five hundred disciples who received their training from him and followed his instructions.
When disputes arose among the assembly, this bhikṣu skillfully reconciled them and brought the strife to an end.
At that time, there were two bhikṣus who, harboring pride in their hearts, were unwilling to go to him to pay their respects and inquire after his well-being.
Later, on another occasion, when these two bhikṣus had engaged in a dispute with the assembly, they finally went to his location and prostrated at his feet.
He addressed him, saying:
"Venerable One!
There is this dispute; I pray that you will cause it to cease."
He then thought: "If I were to cause the dispute to be settled immediately, this bhikṣu would not come again;
it would be better to defer it to the Saṃgha, as this would not violate the Dharma."
Having reflected thus, he said:
"I do not know the cause of the Venerable One's dispute; let us go to the Saṃgha for now.
On account of that monastic business, he went out to a neighboring village.
The two bhikṣus went to the saṃgha, and the assembly brought about reconciliation between them.
Once the Tripiṭaka bhikṣu had finished his business in the village, he returned to his own place and asked his disciple:
"Have those two bhikṣus come again to seek me out?"
The disciple replied:
"Upādhyāya! The Saṃgha has already brought this dispute to an end."
He related all the matters and his intentions in detail.
Having heard this, he became enraged and uttered harsh words:
"This Saṃgha settles its affairs in such a manner that it is like the practice of cowherds."
"Furthermore, these bhikṣus were formerly cowherds before they went forth into homelessness.
Upon hearing this, the five hundred disciples also said, "O Upādhyāya!"
"It is exactly as you have said: the Sangha has been reconciled and the dispute settled, according to the method of the cowherd.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think?"
Was the Tripiṭaka Bhikṣu of former times anyone else?
He is none other than the cowherd Nanda today.
As for the five hundred disciples of former times, they are these five hundred cowherds today.
Because those individuals, in a former time, uttered coarse speech among the assembly of śrāvaka disciples of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, they were constantly cowherds for five hundred lifetimes.

Because they had cultivated the roots of goodness regarding the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the possible and impossible within that Buddhist teaching, those five hundred people went forth in my teaching, severed all afflictions, and realized the fruit of arhatship.
That Tadāga king had also gone forth in the teaching of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa and constantly practiced meditative concentration.
While traveling among the people, he arrived at a village and stayed in a monastery; during the first watch of the night, he sat upright, withdrawing his mind to enter samādhi.
However, the bhikṣus engaged in recitation were all chanting aloud, and their voices were able to obstruct his concentration.
Having heard those sounds, his mind could not be restrained, and he thought to himself:
"I should now enter meditative concentration during the middle watch of the night.
Again, during the middle watch, as he sought to collect his mind for concentration, the bhikṣus who were upholding the sūtras were all chanting them aloud.
Again he thought:
"It shall be during the latter part of the night.
During the latter part of the night, he once more sat upright, collecting his mind with the intent to attain concentration.
At that time, the bhikṣus were reciting aloud; because they had not yet abandoned desire, some harbored poisonous resentment and, giving rise to anger, spoke these words:
"These bhikṣus in the teaching of Kāśyapa have been making the sound of frogs from evening until late at night."
"O bhikṣus, what do you think?
Was the bhikṣu who practiced meditation in the past anyone else?
It was none other than the present Devaputra Śālūra."
Because he uttered such evil words toward the disciples of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, by virtue of that karma, he was born as a frog for five hundred lifetimes.

Having conceived a pure mind toward me, he cast off his body as a frog and was reborn in the palace of the Four Great Kings; because he had practiced the holy life within the teaching of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, he now perceives the Truth.
For this reason, I have always proclaimed:
black karma has black retribution, white karma has white retribution, and mixed karma has mixed retribution.
Therefore, you should abandon black and mixed karma, and cultivate white karma.

At that time, the World-Honored One wished to cross the Gaṅgā River; thereupon, five hundred flocks of geese, five hundred fish, and five hundred turtles circumambulated the World-Honored One to the right.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught him the sublime Dharma in three phrases, saying:
"O worthy one! All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all dharmas are without self; nirvana is quiescent extinction."
"You all should give rise to a pure mind and feel weary of this animal body.
When the geese, turtles, and fish heard these three phrases of the Dharma, they all thought:
"We have rarely heard the subtle flavor of the Tathāgata’s three-phrased Dharma; we should no longer think of other food."
He then ceased eating entirely.
Because the fire of hunger among those of the animal realm is extremely swift, he passed away and was reborn in the palace of the Four Great Kings.
It is the constant law for those newly born among the devas that, upon being reborn in heaven, three thoughts arise:
Where shall I die?
In what place shall I be born?
By what karma am I born?
He beheld himself having abandoned the realm of animals and been reborn in the palace of the Four Great Kings; there,
in the presence of the Blessed One, he heard the essential Dharma of three phrases, as described in detail elsewhere.
They all proceeded to where the Buddha was and scattered exquisite celestial flowers over him.

The World-Honored One, the Compassionate Father, observing their faculties, latent tendencies, and inclinations, preached the sublime Dharma for them, causing them to attain awakening to the Four Noble Truths.
Having heard the teaching of the Dharma, they realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*). They then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and took their leave together to return to the palace.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"We pray that the World-Honored One will explain what karma these geese, fish, and turtles previously committed that caused them to be born among the animals (*tiryagyoni*)."
"Furthermore, by performing what kind of karma does one attain birth in the heavens and perceive the principle of the True Dharma?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should know this!"
"The geese, turtles, and fish have themselves created these karmas and now must experience their results for themselves.
This was explained at length as above, culminating in this verse:
"Even if a hundred eons pass, The karma one has created does not perish;..."
"When causes and conditions meet, one receives the retribution for oneself.
"O bhikṣus, listen well now.

In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, fully endowed with the ten titles, residing at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages in Vārāṇasī."
Yet, because those geese, fish, and turtles had gone forth in that teaching and violated various other minor rules of training, they fell into the animal realm as a result of that karma.
Because they gave rise to a pure mind through their attachment to possessions, they were reborn in the heavens.
Having dwelled within the teaching of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa and cultivated the holy life, they have now been able to hear my Dharma and perceive the truth of the noble realities.
"For this reason, I have always proclaimed that you should train yourselves in this way.

At that time, after the Blessed One had crossed the Gaṅgā River, five hundred hungry ghosts appeared before him. Their skeletons were black and emaciated like charred pillars; their hair was disheveled and matted; their bellies were as large as Mount Sumeru, while their throats were like needles. Their entire bodies were ablaze, a mass of burning flames. Joining their palms in reverence, they addressed the Blessed One, saying: "O Virtuous One!"
"Because we committed various evil karmas in our previous lives, even in this present body we have not yet heard the names of water or drink, let alone obtained food."
"The Buddha is one of great compassion; let him give us water so that we may drink.
The World-Honored One gazed afar at the river and addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Now, drink your fill from this river for these hungry ghosts."
Maudgalyāyana, having received these instructions, was about to make them drink;
however, the throats of the hungry ghosts were as thin as needles, and Maudgalyāyana was unable to open them wide enough for them to drink.
By means of his supernatural power, the Buddha opened their throats, and Maudgalyāyana gave them the drink.

Because they were tormented by intense thirst, they drank excessively; their bellies then swelled and burst. Yet, having all conceived a pure mind toward the Buddha at that moment, they passed away and were reborn in the heavens, eventually realizing the fruits of the path, as described in detail above.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were again filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"What karma did these hungry ghosts previously create to be born here?"
"Furthermore, what karma did they perform to be reborn in the heavens and perceive the truth of the noble realities?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"They themselves performed those deeds, and now they themselves experience their results."
As explained at length elsewhere, up to the verse:
"Even if a hundred eons pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when causes and conditions meet, one must experience the retribution oneself."
"Listen well! In the distant past,
during this Bhadrakalpa when the lifespan of humans was twenty thousand years,
a Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, fully endowed with the ten titles, who resided at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages in Vārāṇasī."
The Buddha’s assembly of śrāvakas traveled about begging for alms to make offerings to the Triple Gem.
Later, as the Tathāgata Kāśyapa’s teachings gradually spread, those who went forth to beg became even more numerous.
Later, at another time, five hundred upāsakas were gathered together in one house for some business matter.
At that moment, a large number of mendicant bhikṣus went to their location and begged from them; the upāsakas then became filled with anger and uttered harsh words:
"These disciples of the śramaṇa Kāśyapa constantly practice begging, just like hungry ghosts."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think?
Were those five hundred upāsakas of long ago anyone else?"
These are the five hundred hungry ghosts.

Because they called out "hungry ghost" toward the assembly of Śrāvakas of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, by the power of that karma, they have undergone the retribution of hungry ghosts for five hundred lifetimes; thus, in this present body, they continue to experience the state of hungry ghosts.
Having conceived a pure mind toward me, they were reborn in the heavens;
because they had practiced the holy life within the teaching of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, they have perceived the truth of the noble realities.
For this reason, I have constantly proclaimed that the retribution for mixed karma—
black, white, and variegated— is as extensively explained above.
One should train oneself in this manner, up to and including the final point.
At that time, the World-Honored One crossed the Gaṅgā River and looked back and forth at the river.
Then the bhikṣus requested of the World-Honored One,
"For what reason do you look back and forth at the river?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Do you wish to hear the origin story (nidāna) of this Gaṅgā River?
They replied: [“We do.”]
“World-Honored One!
Now is precisely the right time. Sugata!”
"Now is the very time for this teaching.
We pray that you will speak it, for we long to hear it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"In the distant past, there was a king named Śāṇakavāsin who ruled the world according to the Dharma. The population was flourishing, the land was prosperous, joyful, and secure; sweet rains fell in their proper seasons, flowers and fruits grew lush and abundant, and there were no instances of fraud, theft, or pestilence, as he constantly governed by means of the Dharma."

In the spring months, the King went out with his court ladies to stroll in a fragrant garden, where he saw a man with white hair and wrinkled face, nearly decrepit in age, emaciated and haggard, his faculties dull and failing, walking while leaning on a staff.
When the king saw him, he asked, "Who is this man?
[The text continues] at length until: "...walking while leaning on a staff."
He replied: "Great King!
When youthful vigor has diminished and vanished, the suffering of old age appears."
The King said,
"Am I also like this, subject to the same law of old age?
He replied:
"Great King!
All things are thus.
Thereupon, the king became sorrowful.

Proceeding further, he again saw a person whose entire body was covered in festering sores, whose skin was cracked and withered, whose belly was swollen like a mountain, from which pus and blood flowed, and whose limbs were severed from one another.
With his body wrapped in cloth, he sighed deeply and gasped for breath; leaning on a staff and with a lame foot, he walked slowly.
Having seen him, the king said to his ministers, "What kind of man is this?"
As described in detail above, even to the point of walking with a lame foot.
The minister addressed the king, saying:
"This one is called a sick person."
The king asked,
"Am I also like this?
He replied:
"Great King! It is exactly so for all.
Due to having committed various evil deeds in previous lives, one receives these karmic retributions."
The king then thought to himself:
"If this is so, then no evil deeds whatsoever should be committed.

Having formed this thought, he proceeded forward and saw another bier. It was adorned with blue, yellow, red, and white silk streamers and covered with a canopy; conch shells were blown and drums beaten as many people—men and women, young and old—carried it together on four men. Furthermore, they carried firewood and walked ahead in opposition to the direction of travel, while a great multitude followed behind the bier, wailing and weeping aloud, crying out:
"Father, father! Brother, brother! Master, master!
he cried out in a loud voice.
When the king saw this, he addressed his ministers, saying:
"What is this? [The details] are as described above, up to the point where it makes a great sound.
The ministers replied:
"Great King!
This is called death.
The King said:
"Am I also subject to this law of death?
He replied, "Great King!"
"All things are thus; it is not merely this alone.

At that time, having witnessed these matters of old age, sickness, and death, the king was deeply filled with sorrow and distress. He turned his carriage back and entered the palace, dwelling in a secluded and quiet place.
Within the king’s realm there was a brahmin named Kāla, of great noble lineage, possessing abundant wealth and treasures, and whose learning surpassed that of the four Vedas.

Having heard that the king, upon witnessing old age, sickness, and death, had become deeply distressed and was dwelling in a secluded place surrounded by an immeasurable assembly of brahmins, he mounted a white chariot drawn by white horses, carrying a golden staff and a golden pitcher, and came to the presence of King Śālīya.
The ministers informed the king:
"A timely Brahmin has arrived at the palace gate.
The king then departed from the palace and ascended his royal throne.
Then the brahmin, having paid his respects to the king, took his seat and said:
"Great King,
for what reason do you dwell in such a secluded place?"
The King then explained to him in detail the conditions of old age, sickness, and death, as fully described above.
He then addressed him at that moment, saying: "Great King!
In this world, each person eats the fruits of their own karma; do not be distressed.
There are some sentient beings who perform various wholesome deeds, and there are some sentient beings who commit various unwholesome deeds.
"Since the beginning of sentient beings, they have created both wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Your Majesty is now a Wheel-Turning Sage King who constantly performs wholesome deeds; when your life comes to an end, you will certainly be reborn in heaven."
"Great King, you should know!

This Wheel-Turning Sage King surpasses all other men; having experienced various forms of peace and happiness, he attains rebirth in the heavens, where he experiences peace and happiness even more abundantly."
"Nevertheless, Great King, you ought now to convene a festival of giving.
The king addressed his ministers:
"You all should strike the drum and proclaim by edict: 'The Great King shall hold a great, unrestricted festival of giving.'"
"Let all those within the realm who have needs come to receive food and take the alms.
Having received these instructions, the ministers adorned the site of the distribution; they gave food to those who needed food and clothing to those who needed clothing.
The water used for rinsing rice formed a great moat that overflowed with surging currents; it was named the Anavatapta Lake (Pool Without Heat).
After twelve years had passed, the rice-washing water and rice-gruel juices pooled together and flowed out as a river; for this reason, the people of the world called it the River of Gruel Water.
At that time, as the World-Honored One was traveling and arrived at the city of Hastināpura, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"There was once a king born and raised in this city named Dīrghanakha; for this reason, the city is called Hastināpura."
Next, he arrived at the city of Aṅgadinna and stayed to one side.
The Buddha then smiled and spoke at length concerning the deeds and circumstances of the conversions of the four Buddhas.
Next, he arrived at the city of Ratnapradāna and addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"In the past, the Bodhisattva bestowed many precious jewels at this very spot; therefore, this city is named 'Bestower of Jewels' (Ratnadatta).
Next, they arrived at the Śālarāja tree, where [the Buddha] stood to one side. The Buddha then smiled and likewise extensively expounded upon the transformative traces of the four Buddhas.
Next, he arrived at the city of Suvarṇabhara and said to Ānanda:

"In this city, in the past, the Bodhisattva held a great assembly for almsgiving, offering gold measured by the *bhāra* (a load) to those who begged; for this reason, the world has named this city Suvarṇabhara."
Next, he arrived at the city of Sāketa and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"In this city of Sāketa there is a king named Dīrghanakha, who governs the world according to the Dharma; its inhabitants are numerous and flourishing, and it is prosperous, joyful, and secure."
At a later time, a fleshy tumor grew upon the crown of the king's head; it was as soft as cotton and caused him no discomfort or distress.
When the tumor ripened and burst, a son was born, whose form was upright and whose complexion was exquisite, deeply lovely to behold, as described at length elsewhere.
His faculties were fully developed; therefore, all people called him Mūrdhaja (Born from the Crown).
At that time, sixty thousand court ladies entered the palace after his birth; upon seeing him, milk flowed from all their breasts, and they all said, "I will nurse him!"
"I nourish [him]!
For this reason, he was called Nandika (Joy-Nourisher).
Now, there are some who call him Mūrdhaja (Head-Born), while others call him Nandika.

Māndhātṛ grew to maturity, but then he fell ill. Although various medicinal treatments were applied using roots, flowers, and leaves, his condition could not be cured; his illness became increasingly severe.
The king said to his ministers:
"You must quickly bring Māndhātṛ here and install him as my successor."
The ministers replied to the king,
"As Your Majesty commands," and immediately dispatched an imperial messenger to fetch Mūrdhaja.
King Dīrghāyu was afflicted by illness that enveloped his body; he issued a decree summoning [Māndhātṛ], instructing him to arrive with the utmost haste, for he wished to perform his consecration.
Before Māndhātṛ had arrived, the king passed away.
Again, another messenger was dispatched to inform Mūrdhaja, saying:
"The father-king has passed away; we pray that you will come quickly.
Mūrdhaja thought to himself:
"Since the King, my father, has already passed away, why should I go?
Having thought this, he turned back. The ministers sent another messenger, saying:
"The Prince must come to succeed his father upon the throne."
Mūrdhagata replied, "I possess my share of kingship; let it be right here.
The ministers then addressed him, saying:

"If one is to be consecrated as king, many preparations must be made, including a jeweled hall, a bathing pool, a lion throne, a parasol, and a crown; since the coronation should take place in the great capital city, you may come here."
He replied, "If I were to become a Dharma King, such things would come to me of their own accord, without being sought.

At that time, there was a yakṣa named Karoti who constantly followed Mūrdhaja; whatever he was commanded to do, he performed. He then took the jewel-pool, the lion-throne, the parasol, the crown, and the great city of the royal capital, and transported them there spontaneously.
"For this reason, this city is named 'Self-Arisen' (Svayambhū).
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*, Fascicle Eleven.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The Story of the Rice Porridge Well and the Golden Wheat; The Story of the Farmer and the Ox; The Story of the Leper Woman and the Rice Wash-water.
The Story of King Prasenajit, the Story of the Poor Woman’s Lamp, and the Story of King Mūrdhaja.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“You should now go with me to Śrāvastī.”
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, they immediately followed behind the Buddha as he traveled through the human world.
At that time, there was a brahmin who had not eaten during the night; while he was plowing his field on an empty stomach, his daughter brought him some rice gruel.

At that time, as the World-Honored One approached that place, the brahmin saw him from afar. The World-Honored One was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics; his halo blazed brilliantly, surpassing the light of a thousand suns. His gait was extraordinary, like a mountain of exquisite jewels, universally embellished by all manner of excellences.

Having seen the Buddha, a pure faith arose in his heart; he felt as refined, disciplined, and compliant as if he had been practicing for twelve years, as fresh, white, tranquil, and serene, as joyful and delighted as a childless man who finds a son, a poor man who finds treasure, or one seeking a king who finally finds a king.
Because that person possessed various roots of merit from previous lives, upon first seeing the Buddha, they were immediately able to give rise to this pure mind of reverence and honor.
At that time, the brahmin quickly took up the rice porridge he intended to eat and came to offer it to the World-Honored One, saying:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"Out of compassion for me, please accept this humble gruel.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a dry well for the sake of the brahmin, causing the gruel to enter the well; he then poured it in, and the well became filled to the brim.
Through the power of the Buddha and the power of the devas, the dried-up well overflowed with fragrant gruel.
The Buddha said to the brāhmaṇa,
"Virtuous one, distribute this gruel and give it universally to the Saṃgha."
He then went and gave [the water] to the entire Saṃgha, and they were all fully satisfied.
By the Buddha’s empowerment, the well remained full.
At that time, the brahmin conceived even greater pure faith toward the World-Honored One; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat down before him to listen to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing their faculties, latent tendencies, and inclinations, preached the sublime Dharma for them, causing them to realize the Four Noble Truths, as described in detail elsewhere.

Upon hearing the Dharma, he realized the fruit of stream-entry; his heart was filled with exultation, like a merchant leader obtaining a profit, like a warrior achieving victory in battle, or like one recovering from a severe illness.

Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, they received it with joy and faith, prostrated themselves, took their leave, and went to the place where the barley was being sown. Seeing that the barley sprouts were all golden in color, they laughed with delight and, struck by such a marvel, spoke this verse:
“The merit of the field of blessings is most supreme, Able to bring one free from all afflictions;
No sooner has the seed been sown Than its fruit is already summoned.”
At that time, the brahmin went quickly to the king’s presence, inquired after his welfare, and wished him freedom from illness and long life.
He then addressed the king, saying:
"Your Majesty, you should know this!"
"As soon as I sowed the barley, it grew and turned into gold; I only wish that Your Majesty would dispatch someone to take his share.
The king then dispatched men to take the barley portion.
At that time, the brahmin gathered and accumulated the harvest, and when he measured out the king's share, it subsequently changed back into barley.
The king said, "Gather them all in one place and measure them out again.
This was done seven times; though they were gathered and divided together, the king's portion likewise changed back into barley.
The king said, "That barley is the karmic reward of the brāhmaṇa; it is not something I can control. Let him measure out my portion according to his own will.
With an unimpeded mind, the brāhmaṇa measured out the king's portion, and it turned back into golden barley.

At that time, the World-Honored One departed from there and saw five hundred farmers engaged in plowing and sowing; their skin was cracked and withered, their hands were chapped and their feet split, and they wore coarse hempen garments. The oxen and calves used for plowing had wounds on their necks and broken skin, from which pus and blood flowed down as they heaved long sighs of exhaustion.
At that time, the farmers saw from afar the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks, as described in detail above.
Even those who had planted roots of goodness in previous lives were able to behold the World-Honored One.
The Buddha went to that place; desiring to subdue them, he approached one side and sat upon a seat within the assembly of bhikṣus.
When the farmers saw the Buddha seated from afar, they all approached him, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha observed their faculties, latent tendencies, and inclinations, as described in detail above.
Having heard the Dharma, they realized the fruit of stream-entry; all rose from their seats, joined their palms, and said to him:
"Venerable World-Honored One!..."

We only pray that you will grant us permission to go forth within this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination, to become bhikṣus, and to purely cultivate the holy life in service to the World-Honored One.
When the Buddha had seen them, he addressed them, saying:
"Welcome, O Bhikṣus! You may practice the holy life.
This is as described elsewhere, up until the verse which says:
“The World-Honored One commanded him to come; his hair fell away and his robes and bowl were complete.
All his faculties became tranquil and settled, and everything was accomplished according to his thought.
At that time, the World-Honored One instructed him according to his capacity; he then exerted himself, severed all afflictions, and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, the oxen pulling the plows snapped their ropes and all came to where the Buddha was, circling him and remaining there.

The Buddha taught the three-line Dharma to the oxen, as described in detail in the section on the geese and the tortoise, until they perceived the reality of the Truths and each returned to their celestial palaces.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"What karma did these farmers previously perform such that, in this life, they became farmers;
yet, having gone forth under the World-Honored One, they have severed all afflictions and realized the fruit of arhatship?"
"Furthermore, what karma did those oxen previously perform to be born among cattle, yet upon meeting the Buddha, were reborn in heaven and perceived the truth of the noble principles?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "One reaps what one has sown;
having performed the actions oneself in the past, one now experiences their results oneself."
As explained at length elsewhere, it concludes with the verse:
"Even if a hundred eons pass, The karma one has created does not perish;
When causes and conditions meet, One must experience the retribution oneself."
"Listen well! I shall now speak for you.

Long ago, in this Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of humans was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles, who resided at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī."

Those farmers all became renunciants within the Buddha’s teaching, yet they neither recited nor contemplated the teachings; they accepted food offered by the faithful, engaged in frivolous discourse, and were indolent and lazy rather than diligent and self-exerting.
"O bhikṣus, what do you think?
Were those five hundred bhikṣus anyone else?
They are none other than these five hundred farmers here now."
Those who were the donors of the monastery in the past are now these five hundred elders.
Because in the past they accepted the food offered by faith yet neither recited nor applied their minds to it, being indolent and lacking diligent exertion.
Due to this karma, for five hundred lifetimes he was a farmer who doubled his debts to his benefactors.

Because he went forth in the teaching of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa and realized the holy life (*brahmacarya*), he has now likewise gone forth under me, severed all afflictions (*kleśa*), and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
Furthermore, those oxen had also gone forth as monastics under that Buddha's teaching, where they violated various minor rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*).
Due to this karma, they were born into the realm of cattle.
Yet, having conceived a pure mind toward me, they have attained rebirth in the heavens.
By virtue of their former holy life, they have been able to perceive the Truths.
For this reason, I constantly proclaim:
"Regarding mixed karma of black and white, it is as explained extensively elsewhere.
You all should train yourselves in this manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Come, you may go to the city of Dvārakā.
Having heard these instructions, he followed the Buddha to that city.
There was a brahmin who was plowing the land; seeing from afar the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man—as described in detail elsewhere—he thought to himself:
"If I go to pay homage to the śramaṇa Gautama, this work will be neglected;
yet if I do not go to pay homage, I shall lose all merit and benefit.
Thus, so that his work would not be neglected and he might obtain merit and benefit, he held the whip and plow, speaking from afar:
"Salutations, salutations!
The Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"That brāhmaṇa has brought this error and fault upon himself."
In this very place, there are the entire bodily relics of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, remaining solemnly and undamaged.
If you come to me and pay respectful homage, you will thereby pay your respects to two Buddha-Bhagavāns.
At that time, Ānanda quickly adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and said:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will sit here; then this ground shall be enjoyed by two Buddhas."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Would you like to see the entire body-relics (śarīra) of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa?
They replied: [Yes.]
“World-Honored One!
Now is precisely the right time.
Thus he addressed the Buddha.
“Sugata! Now is precisely the right time.
If I am granted the sight of you, my mind will become doubly pure.”
At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to a worldly thought.
Such is the constant law: whenever a Buddha gives rise to a worldly thought, all sentient beings know the Buddha’s intention. The dragon then thought:
“World-Honored One!”
"Why has he given rise to a worldly thought?
[The Naga] then perceived that the World-Honored One desired to see the entire body-relics (śarīra) of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa.
The Naga then took up those Buddha-relics and held them in the midst of the sky.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should now carefully observe this sign; it is about to vanish.
At that time, King Prasenajit heard that the Buddha had manifested the entire body-relics (śarīra) of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, enabling the bhikṣus to behold their appearance.

Having heard this, his heart was filled with the desire to behold it; he immediately set out with his queens, palace attendants, court ladies, princes, and ministers, adorned in solemn regalia and observing proper etiquette, to go and witness it.

The deceased Crown Prince, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, the former friend Śuka, the son of the brick-maker, and Mṛgāramātṛ with her son Viśākha, each accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, all feeling it was a rare sight to behold, followed behind the procession to the site of the śarīra.
Because the roots of goodness from his past lives were activated, he was caused to go there.
At that moment, Śāriputra immediately vanished. When the multitude heard that Śāriputra had disappeared, they were filled with grief and distress, saying to one another:
"We have come in vain and have gained nothing."
At that time, there was an upāsaka who went to the place where the relics of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa were located; he circumambulated them with reverence and made this thought in his mind:
"By circumambulating and paying homage now, I shall surely obtain merit and benefit."
The World-Honored One, knowing that his mind was constantly seeking benefit and merit and possessed a pure heart, spoke these verses:
"Even if one were to gather hundreds of thousands of Jambū-river golds And offer them all as a gift to everyone,
It would not equal a person with a single pure mind Who exerts themselves to circumambulate a Buddha-stūpa to the right."
At that time, there was another upāsaka who took some clay and placed it upon the site where the relics were hidden. For his sake as well, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"Even if one were to take hundreds of thousands of Jambū-river gold coins And constantly offer them in charity to all beings;
It would not equal a person with a single pure mind Taking clay and placing it as an ornament upon a Buddha-stūpa."

At that time, there were hundreds of thousands of people who, having heard of the merit and benefit of offering this mud, all brought mud to place therein; some even took various exquisite flowers and perfumes and scattered them within it.
The Buddha also spoke in verse, saying:
"Even if one were to take hundreds of thousands of Jambū-river gold coins And constantly offer them as gifts to all beings;
It would not equal a person with a single pure mind Making offerings of incense and flowers at a Buddhist stupa."
At that time, there were people who, holding various flower garlands, lamps, banners, flags, and parasols, made offerings at this place, approaching with a pure mind to present these gifts.
The Buddha, knowing their minds, spoke a verse for each of them.
The World-Honored One further recited this gāthā:
"The field of merit I now describe, The Tathāgata’s virtues are boundless and immeasurable."
"The Perfectly Awakened One is like the ocean at the end of an eon; he, the unsurpassed leader, is most supreme.
At that time, the multitude of people all thought to themselves:
"The merit spoken of by the Buddha has already perished."
“If one makes offerings to a Buddha who is present in the world, what benefit and merit will there be?
Having known this thought, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“If there is one who can make offerings To a Buddha currently manifest or already perfected, [They shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood.]”
If one’s mind can be impartial, its merit and benefit will be without distinction.
The Buddha is inconceivable, and the sublime Dharma is likewise beyond thought;
the same is true for those who are pure—their karmic fruition is identical as one.
"The names and characteristics are likewise inconceivable; there is none who does not turn the wheel of Dharma.
Regarding the shore of the merits of perfect enlightenment, no one is able to reach its limit.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached this Dharma for the great assembly.

Having heard the Dharma, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings attained great benefit: some gave rise to the mind of a śrāvaka-bodhi, some gave rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha-bodhi, and some gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). Some attained the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata) or Peak (mūrdhan), some attained the first stage of Patience (kṣānti), and some realized the fruit of Stream-entry (srotāpanna). Some attained the fruits of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) or Non-returner (anāgāmin), and some severed all afflictions to realize the fruit of Arhatship.
Furthermore, many others took refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, placing faith and reverence in the Triple Gem, and planting various roots of goodness.
At that time, there were brahmins, elders, and householders of pure faith who established a great assembly for almsgiving at that very spot; they named this region "The Place of Water Donation."
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the kingdom of Kośala and arrived at the city of Śrāvastī, where he stayed in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that the Buddha had arrived, he went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha taught him the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him, and then remained silent.
At that time, the elder rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms in reverence, knelt with both knees upon the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Virtuous World-Honored One, together with the community of bhikṣus, please come to my home tomorrow to accept my humble offering."
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, [the householder] acted as described at length elsewhere, until the following day, when he sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is prepared; we pray that you will know the time."
The householder again commanded his gatekeeper, saying,
"Until the Buddha and the Saṃgha have finished their meal, do not allow any non-Buddhists to enter my residence.
At that time, the gatekeeper, having heard these instructions, respectfully complied.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the Saṃgha, donned his robes and took up his bowl, proceeding to the house of the elder, as described at length elsewhere.
Until finally, the entire assembly had been fully satiated; having finished rinsing their mouths, they took low seats and sat before the Buddha to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, with his beard and hair somewhat grown long and wearing a tattered robe of patched rags, approached the Jetavana Grove from a certain forest hermitage.
Seeing that there were no monks in the monastery, he asked the temple keeper:
"Where has the World-Honored One, the foremost one, and the community of bhikṣus gone now?
He then replied:
“Anāthapiṇḍada invites you to take a meal at his residence.
Mahākāśyapa then thought to himself:
“I should now go there to eat, so that I may pay my respects to the Buddha, who is the foremost, and to the community of bhikṣus.”
Having formed this thought, he went quickly to that place.
The gatekeeper addressed him, saying:
"Noble One!..."
"Do not enter therein. Mahākāśyapa asked,
"For what reason?"

The gatekeeper said, "By the instructions of the Elder, until the Buddha and the Saṃgha have finished their meal, do not allow any non-Buddhists to enter the house; afterwards, we shall also provide offerings to the other non-Buddhists."
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:

"I have now obtained these most excellent and sublime benefits; yet these brahmins, householders, and lay devotees of pure faith do not know that I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya. It is fitting for me now to go and compassionately rescue those who are poor, destitute, and solitary."
Having had this thought, he went out to stroll in the fragrant garden.
Again he thought:
"Whom may I now take pity upon so that they may obtain great benefit?"
At that time, there was a leper beggar whose joints were falling apart and from whose sores pus and blood flowed;
he lived by begging for alms. Mahākāśyapa went to his location and begged from him.

At that time, the leper woman had obtained some rice-water by begging. Seeing from afar Mahākāśyapa—his form preeminent, well-disciplined, and endowed with all dignified deportment—she thought to herself:
"It is because I have never given to one such as this that I have been born into this poverty and suffering, my body writhing with leprosy."
"If you see that the Noble One has compassion for me, I shall offer this rice-water to him.
At that time, Kāśyapa, perceiving her thought, immediately approached her, extended his bowl for her to see, and said: "Sister!"
"You may give me the rice rinsing water; you may place it in my bowl.
The woman then poured out the rinsing water, and a fly fell into the bowl. The woman wished to pick it out with her finger, but her finger fell into the bowl.
The woman thought to herself:
"Since this noble one has accepted my gruel out of consideration for my feelings, how could he possibly eat it himself?
When Kāśyapa perceived her thoughts, he sat down against the wall before her and ate the gruel.
He thought to himself:
"Now, because this noble one protects my feelings, although he has eaten my gruel, he must surely seek other, better food and drink.
At that time, Kāśyapa, perceiving her thoughts, said to the leper woman:
"Sister! You should now give rise to a heart of joy.
From this day until the time for tomorrow's meal, I shall sustain myself for one day and one night with your rice-water."
He was filled with great joy and thought to himself:
"Today I have obtained a most excellent benefit; Mahākāśyapa has accepted my humble offering."
At that time, this woman conceived a pure heart toward Kāśyapa; because of this, when her life ended, she was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saw that this woman had passed away after giving him rice-water with a pure mind, yet he did not know in which realm of existence she had been born.
One contemplates the hells but sees nothing there; one likewise sees nothing among the hungry ghosts, humans, the four world-protecting devas, or the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Even when looking down with the divine eye, one is still unable to perceive anything.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
joined his palms in reverence, and requested with a verse: “The great sage Kaśyapa, who wanders about begging for alms—
that virtuous man to whom the girl offered the rice-gruel wash— in what realm of rebirth has she now been born?”
The Buddha answered in verse:
“The heaven is named Tuṣita, where all desires appear at the mere thought of them;
the girl who gave the gift of rice-water has now been reborn therein.”
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought:
"Those people do not understand how to cultivate merit; they practice giving and perform various beneficial deeds [only out of necessity]."
Now that I know practicing merit brings reward, why should I not give alms and cultivate various meritorious deeds?
The Noble Kāśyapa takes compassion for those who are poor, destitute, sickly, and afflicted by suffering; I should now provide him with a single meal.
Having formed this thought, he immediately manifested a transformed body and went to a place of poverty, where he dwelt in a thatched hut as meager and solitary as a disordered bird's nest.
He transformed his own appearance into that of a hideous weaver, with disheveled hair and wearing coarse hempen clothes; with hands calloused and feet cracked, he performed his weaving work.
Lady Śākī became the weaver’s wife and spun the thread, while taking celestial, exquisite food and setting it aside beforehand.

At that time, Kāśyapa, wishing to have compassion for those in distress and poverty, was traveling about to beg for alms. Arriving there in due course, he saw them and felt profound pity for their wretched state; standing at the entrance of the gate, he held out his bowl and begged from them.
At that time, the emanated deva filled the bowl with exquisite celestial food.
However, Kāśyapa thought to himself, observing this mode of livelihood: "This is truly exhausting; from where could such exquisite celestial food have been obtained?"
"There must have been some other matter.
Having conceived this doubt, it is the constant rule that an Arhat,
if he has not previously observed it, does not know past events.
Even as he observed, he saw this Lord of Devas and said to him:
"Kauśika! For what reason do you now create obstacles for one who is in distress?"

Throughout the long night, the Blessed One has spoken of how you have pulled out the root of the arrow of doubt and other forms of frivolity, just like the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Awakened One.
Śakra addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa!
Why would I now create an obstacle for one who is suffering?"
Yet these people do not perceive their own merit, nor do they practice generosity or cultivate various virtuous blessings.
Now that I myself see it, why should I not practice generosity and extensively cultivate all manner of merit?
Did not the Blessed One indeed speak these words:
"Merit should always be cultivated; Without merit, one encounters suffering and calamity.
If there are those who cultivate merit, They shall enjoy peace and happiness both now and in the future."
From that time forth, Mahākāśyapa first surveyed the directions before begging for alms.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, took various celestial foods from mid-air and placed them into his bowl; Mahākāśyapa turned the bowl upside down, and the food fell to the ground.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Because of this incident, bhikṣus should carry bowl-covers.
At that time, the multitude of people all heard that the leper woman, having offered foul-smelling rice-water to Kāśyapa, was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven after her death.
King Prasenajit, having also heard of this matter, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha then extensively expounded the sublime Dharma for the king, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him, after which he remained silent.
The king rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One, together with the community of bhikṣus, will accept my humble offering for seven days on behalf of the noble Kāśyapa."
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, the king prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and departed.
During that night, he commanded the kitchen staff to prepare various kinds of exquisite and refined food and drink.
When the clear morning arrived, he prepared the seats, set out pure water, tooth-sticks, and tooth-powder, and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is ready; may the Buddha know that it is time."
The details are as explained elsewhere.
When they were all seated, the king personally served the food.
At that time, a beggar came among them and sat facing the senior elder; a pure faith arose within him, and he conceived deep reverence, thinking thus:
"Because the King cultivated various meritorious deeds in the past, he now dwells in a position of honor and is further able to practice generosity by making offerings to the Triple Gem.

The King then personally distributed food and drink throughout, ensuring that the Buddha and the Saṃgha were all fully satiated; he then provided pure water, tooth-sticks, and tooth-powder, and once they had finished rinsing and cleansing themselves, [he withdrew].
Because the king wished to hear the Dharma, he took a low seat and sat facing the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"Shall I recite a verse on giving for Your Majesty?"
"And who, then, shall obtain great merit?
The king thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One is now receiving my offerings; how can there be anyone else who obtains such abundant merit?"
Having reflected thus, he addressed the Buddha:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will speak words of blessing for the gift of one who has cultivated much meritorious karma.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke words of blessing for that beggar.

When the World-Honored One had thus spent five or six days reciting verses on the blessing of giving for beggars, the King became filled with anxiety; resting his cheek in his hand, he sat and thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has partaken of my offerings, yet he has uttered blessings for the giving of alms while addressing the names of beggars."
When the ministers saw the king sitting in sorrow with his cheek resting on his hand, they said to him:
"Great King!
For what reason do you thus dwell in such grief and anxiety?"
The king said:
"Why should I not be grieved?
The World-Honored One accepted my exquisite offerings, yet he addressed the beggar by name when pronouncing the prayer for the merit of giving."
At that time, an old minister came forward and addressed the king, saying:
"May Your Majesty remain at ease; tomorrow I shall invite the World-Honored One and, invoking Your Majesty’s name, recite the prayer for blessings."
At that time, the aged minister announced to the kitchen staff: "Tomorrow, you must prepare double the usual amount of various foods and drinks.
When the food was being served, one portion remained in the bowl while another portion fell to the ground.
The attendants, following his instructions, prepared the meal.
Once the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus had taken their seats, they served the food; however, a portion fell into their bowls while another portion fell upon the ground.
At that time, seeing the food on the ground, the beggar ran quickly to seize it.
The one distributing the food called out from afar to forbid him, but the beggar said:
"The King’s wealth is most abundant and his provisions inexhaustible; why does he not allow those who suffer like me to take some? Why let it rot upon the ground?"
At that time, the beggar’s mind became distracted, and he failed to show reverence or generate a pure intention.
When the Buddha and the Saṅgha had finished their meal, the king sat opposite the Buddha and thought to himself:
"Will the World-Honored One now teach me about giving, or will he speak for others?"
The Buddha then spoke these words of blessing for the king:
“With elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry fully prepared, And enjoying sovereign power over this kingdom and its cities—
O King, do you not see by what cause this was obtained?”
"It was due to the power of the gift of unsalted rice gruel.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Bhagavān, World-Honored One!"
"Although I have received the offerings of King Prasenajit on numerous occasions, I have never before heard such verses on giving.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Do you now wish to hear about the karmic conditions of King Prasenajit of Kośala’s past gift of dried rice gruel?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
now is precisely the right time.”
He addressed [the Buddha], saying: "Sugata!
Now is the very time for this teaching."
“Bhikṣus, having heard the Buddha speak of this causal connection of karmic actions regarding the past gift of medicinal oil by King Prasenajit, you will surely be able to receive and uphold it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“In the distant past, there was an elder in a certain village who, shortly after marrying his wife, became pregnant. When her months were complete, she gave birth to a son; the details are as described elsewhere.”
Once the son had grown up, the husband said to his wife, "O virtuous lady!
Our son is now an adult and capable of managing affairs; he has debts to repay others and requires food and clothing for his livelihood."
