"I am now taking my capital to travel to other regions to engage in trade.
His wife said,
"Noble son!"
"It ought to be done thus; this is a virtuous deed.
He then set out on his travels and passed away before reaching his destination; the small amount of property he had left at home was entirely exhausted.
After her husband had departed, the wife bore another son. An elderly neighbor said to the mother, "If you let my son work for me, I shall provide him with food and clothing."
The mother then gave it to him, and the householder had her provide him with his portion of food at the place where the crops were being sown.
Later, at another time, as a festival was approaching, the mother thought to herself:
"Now, tomorrow morning, this householder will provide for the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas and entertain his guests within the house; there will certainly be no one [to attend to me]."
"I should now go to him and beg for food to send to my son, so that he does not suffer from hunger.
Having thought this, she immediately went to the householder’s wife and related the matter in detail.
When the householder’s wife heard this, she became enraged and said,
"Before I have made offerings to śramaṇas, brahmins, and other noble guests, how can you, a servant, receive food first?"
"Stay for today; tomorrow morning I shall give you double.
The mother thought again:
"My son will surely suffer from hunger today. In the house there is a lump of unsalted, bland paste; I can take it and give it to my son."
He took it to his son’s place and recounted the aforementioned events.
He further said to his son:
"Fearing that you might suffer from hunger, I brought this saltless, bland paste from our home."
The son said,
"Mother! Set this aside and return home."

It is the constant law that when there is no Buddha in the world, there shall be a Pratyekabuddha who benefits and takes pity upon those in distress; he is the sole field of merit in the world, dwelling happily in secluded places.
At that time, a Pratyekabuddha arrived there; seeing him from afar—his mind and body tranquil and his deportment perfectly disciplined—he thought to himself:
"Because I failed to make offerings to such a field of merit in my past lives, I have suffered this hardship and distress in this present life."
"If you see me receiving this saltless, bland ointment, please feel free to offer it to me.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha, perceiving the poor man's thoughts, extended his alms-bowl forward and said,
"Noble sir!"
"Whoever wishes to give may place it in my bowl.
He then, with reverence and a sense of preciousness, placed the ointment within the bowl.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think?
Was that poor boy of the past anyone else?
He was none other than the present King Prasenajit."

Because in the past he offered unseasoned rice gruel to a pratyekabuddha, by the karmic retribution of that deed, he became the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven six times and served as an anointed king in this city of Śrāvastī six times.
Due to the remaining karmic retribution, he was also an anointed king in this very place.
Now that his retribution has been exhausted, I therefore speak these verses:
"Fully equipped with elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, He enjoyed sovereign power over the kingdom and its cities; Now that his merit is spent, he has fallen from that state."
“O King, do you not see that this exists because of a cause? It is due to the power of the gift of rice-paste without salt.
At that time, all the people of the kingdom heard of this matter.
Having heard the Buddha’s words, the king went to the World-Honored One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha then expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the king, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him.
Having heard the Dharma, the king rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, knelt with both knees upon the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Virtuous World-Honored One!
"Out of compassion for me, please accept from me, together with the community of bhikṣus, robes, food, medicine, and bedding for the duration of three months.
The Buddha then accepted the King's request by remaining silent.
Every day during that month, the king prepared a hundred kinds of exquisite, sweet, and fragrant delicacies;
for each bhikṣu, he provided robes worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Furthermore, he took one koṭi of jars filled with various fragrant oils, intending to hold a lamp-lighting assembly during the night.
Because of this distribution of food, it was treated with such great importance that a commotion arose throughout the kingdom.
At that time, there was a woman, impoverished and haggard, who lived by begging; hearing this clamor, she asked the people, "For what reason is there such a clamor?"
He replied to the poor woman:

"The Great King Śreṇika, for three months, has provided the Buddha—whom he honors as his head—and the community of bhikṣus with clothing, food, medicine, and bedding; to each individual bhikṣu, he has given garments worth hundreds of thousands."
"Tonight, we are holding a festival for the lighting of lamps to express our profound respect;
that is why there is this clamor. When the beggar girl heard these words, she thought to herself:
"This King Prasenajit cultivates merit without weariness; what can I possibly do?"
"It would be fitting to seek out a single lamp from somewhere to make an offering to the World-Honored One.

Having formed this thought, he took up his alms-bowl and begged for oil from various places. He lit the lamp and carried it to the place where the Buddha was walking to and fro; there, bowing low with palms joined, he made this vow:
"By all these roots of goodness, may I, like Śākyamuni Buddha, attain supreme enlightenment when I am one hundred years old."
Just as Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana stand in attendance at my left and right, perfectly harmonious and virtuous;

with the bhikṣu Ānanda serving as my attendant; with my father named Śuddhodana and my mother titled Māyā; with the city named Kapilavastu and my noble son Rāhula—such shall be my disciples, parents, kingdom, city, and offspring in the future.

Just as when the World-Honored One Śākyamuni entered parinirvāṇa, his physical body was divided and fragmented into śarīra relics, so too shall I enter parinirvāṇa like this World-Honored One, with my physical body divided into śarīra relics.
At that time, all the other lamps were completely extinguished, yet this woman’s lamp remained bright and clear, shining constantly in this manner.
The Buddha did not cease his stay, nor did the attendant stop his service; the Venerable Ānanda thought to himself:
"It is impossible for anyone to sleep or lie down amidst the light of the Buddha’s lamp."
"I should now extinguish this lamp's light.

He then tried to blow it out with his hand, but he could not; he tried again with his robe as a fan, yet he still could not extinguish it; even when he used a handheld fan to blow upon it, he was unable to put it out.
At that time, the Buddha asked the Venerable Ānanda,
"What are you doing? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
I recall that when the World-Honored One was within the lamp-light, he did not sleep or lie down, desiring to extinguish it.
He used his hand, his robe, and a fan to flick it out and blow upon it, yet in the end, he could not extinguish it.”
The Buddha said,
"Ānanda, do not weary yourself."
"Even if a great unobstructed wind were to blow upon this lamp, it could not extinguish it; how much less could you, with your hands, clothes, or fans, cause it to be blown out?
Furthermore, as for this lamp, that woman conceived a vast and noble resolve, and only with an infinite intention did she light it."

Ānanda! Yet that woman, in a future age of one hundred years, shall certainly attain perfect enlightenment, known by the name Tathāgata Śākyamuni, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. Her foremost disciples, both preceding and following her, shall likewise be named Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana; her attendant shall be named Ānanda; her father shall be named Śuddhodana; her mother shall be named Mahāmāyā; her city shall be named Kapilavastu; and her son shall be named Rāhula. After her parinirvāṇa, her relics shall be distributed.

At that time, people from near and far in the four directions all heard of this matter; having offered a single lamp as an offering to the World-Honored One, they received from the Buddha the prediction that they would attain Buddhahood in the future.
When the brahmins, elders, and householders heard this, they all said,
"This poor woman shall in the future be fully endowed with all virtues.
They all vied with one another to offer her clothing, wealth, food, and drink as acts of worship.

When King Prasenajit heard this, he conceived a sense of incomparable wonder; he immediately prepared one thousand large jars of fragrant oil and fashioned lamp bowls from the four kinds of precious gems, arranging them along the path where the Buddha would walk to light lamps.
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
For the sake of the noble Mahākāśyapa, I have invited the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus for seven days of offerings."

Having heard the Buddha explain the causal karmic conditions regarding my past offering of unseasoned rice gruel, I again invited the World-Honored One along with the Saṃgha for a period of three months to provide offerings.

I bestowed upon each bhikṣu robes worth one hundred thousand [pieces of gold], and I held a lamp assembly using ten million jars of oil; yet, I did not receive from the World-Honored One the prophecy that I would attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in the future.
"I pray that the World-Honored One will grant me the prediction of my future Buddhahood, so that in the future I may become a leader.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"

Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom; it is profoundly deep and difficult to illuminate; it is hard to understand and hard to realize, and one cannot easily approach it.
It is subtle and difficult to know, awakened to only by the wise; it is not something understood by the foolish, nor is it easily attained.
"It is attained through a single act of giving; it cannot be attained by a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand acts of giving.
Great King!

However, if you wish to seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, you must practice various forms of almsgiving, cultivate all manner of merit and virtue, draw near to spiritual friends, and maintain humility and reverence. Only then will there be the possibility of attaining the state of a leader."
At that time, having heard these words of the Buddha, the Great King wept with tears of grief; wiping his eyes with his robe, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Virtuous World-Honored One!
"When you were formerly seeking unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, what things did you give as gifts?
What meritorious deeds did you cultivate?
The Buddha told the Great King:

“Setting aside other kalpas for now, regarding the objects given and the various meritorious deeds performed within this Bhadrakalpa for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—I shall now briefly describe them; O King, listen attentively and apply your mind with great care.”
The Buddha told the Great King:
"In the distant past, when the lifespan of humans was immeasurable, there was a king named Dīrghaśuddha. A fleshy protuberance grew upon his crown, which was exceedingly soft, like cotton wool."

The blister ripened and burst of its own accord, giving birth to a son whose countenance was upright and handsome, exceedingly lovely to behold. He was neither white nor black, but like the color of pure gold; his head was shaped like a parasol, his arms were slender and long, his forehead was broad and even, his eyebrows met like a crescent moon, and his nose was high and straight. He was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.

After he was born, he entered the palace. Among the eighty-four thousand court ladies within the palace, they all saw the prince from afar, and milk flowed from their breasts; each of them made this vow:
"I shall nourish the prince."
He was thus named Rāma, meaning "Joy-Nourisher";
because he was born from the crown of the head, he was also called Mūrdhaja, "Born-from-the-Crown. This is explained in detail in the *Rājadharma-saṃyukta-varga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
While Prince Mūrdhaja was playing with his companions, six successive Śakras of the Heaven of the Thirty-three passed away at the exhaustion of their merit; subsequently, he became the crown prince.
After another six Śakras had passed away, he ascended to the throne as the reigning king.

Furthermore, after six more Śakras had passed away, he transformed the world through the Dharma in Jambudvīpa; within his inner palace, it rained down celestial garments, and outside, it rained down gold and jewels.
At that time, there were five rishis by the name of Vairūpya living near the city of Vaiśālī. At their dwelling place, various birds cried out in a chaotic clamor;
the rishis could not bear it and consequently cast a curse upon them, causing the wings and feathers of all those birds to fall off.
At that time, King Mandhātā heard of this and thought:
"This man has no compassion; how can he be allowed to remain here?
He immediately expelled him, ordering him to leave his realm.
The seer thought to himself:
"The king rules over the four continents; where shall I dwell?
He then proceeded to Mount Sumeru and took up residence on its lower terraces.
At that time, the king subsequently went to dwell in Aparagoyānī, where he remained for the duration of six reigns of the gods;
it was likewise so in Pūrvavideha and Uttarakuru.
While he governed and transformed his own realm upon these [mountains], on each of the seven tiers of golden mountains, more than six Indras of the devas passed away.
Then, ascending to the summit of Mount Sumeru, the king’s army, restrained by the seer’s incantations, was unable to move at all.
At that time, there was a yakṣa named Ākāśavāsin who always walked ahead. Seeing this, the rishi spoke these verses:
"O Pure Rishi, please cease your mind of anger; Nothing whatsoever can be accomplished [in this state].
This is King Mahāmandhātṛ; He is not like the various birds of Vaiśālī."
Then the king asked,
"Who is restraining the army?
They replied:
"This great seer has forbidden it.
The king asked again,
"What is this seer fond of?"
He replied,
"I love the person's topknot. Thereupon,
the king immediately spoke these incantations:
"May that rishi, with his hair tied in a topknot, become my attendant.
Having made this vow, the rishi’s topknot fell away of its own accord, and he ran ahead, holding a bow and staff in his hands.
The King’s Jewel-Woman spoke, saying:
“Great King! This is a seer;
do not cause him harm. I pray that Your Majesty release him.”
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately released the seer.
At that time, the seer felt great resentment in his heart; he then maintained his ascetic discipline and before long attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
At that time, the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda, seeing the great king and his host of troops, thought to themselves:
"These are asuras."
He immediately assembled the fourfold army and approached.
Upon seeing King Mandhātṛ, the entire host retreated and dispersed; the four great yakṣas, witnessing this, likewise fled and went together to the abode of the Four Heavenly Kings, where they said:
"Great King!..."
"Now a great army has arrived with four divisions, and we have all been beaten back.
He replied, "This is King Mandhātṛ, who possesses great merit and virtue; he intends to come to the abode of Śakra, and we cannot withstand him as an adversary."
"You all should accompany me and, taking various fragrant flowers and diverse offerings, go out before him to welcome him.
Having seen him, they exchanged greetings and immediately went together to the celestial palace of Śakra.
When Śakra saw them, he immediately vacated half of his seat and sat down sharing it with him.
At that time, the host of asuras, possessing the fourfold army, went together to the abode of Śakra; the yakṣa then came and informed Śakra:
"The asuras, leading the fourfold army, have emerged from the earth and already broken through five locations; you must make preparations."
"May the Lord of Devas take note of this and prepare accordingly.
Thereupon, Śakra desired to go forth to battle.
King Māndhātṛ then addressed Śakra, saying:
"Stay here for now!
I shall go to face the enemy.
He replied:
"So be it," the king replied. Thereupon, he led a host of one hundred and eighty thousand vigorous and powerful warriors, soaring into the air.
They spoke to one another, raising a great clamor: "We are mighty *mahā-vīrya* warriors!"
When the asuras saw those one hundred and eighty thousand mighty warriors making such sounds in the sky, they all covered their ears and fled in all directions.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja thought again:
"I should remain here; the people of Jambudvīpa are flourishing and prosperous, and all three continents now belong to me."
"Now I must take the position of Śakra and become the Lord of Men and Gods.
Having formed this thought, he immediately lost his supernormal powers, fell to Jambudvīpa, and was afflicted with a grave illness.
The King then spoke these verses:
"Those who possess billions of wealth are insatiable in their greed;
They have little joy and much suffering— The wise are able to distance themselves from this."
Even if one were to experience the pleasures of heaven, the mind’s delight would still not be sufficient;
to know where all such delight ends, look only to the Buddha and his assembly of śrāvakas.
They are like a mass of golden mountains, and also like the king of snow mountains.
One person alone is not enough; thus the wise understand.
Seeing that these roots of suffering arise from conditions, one realizes that all sensual desires are not to be relished.
Since human beings are pierced by the arrows of the aggregates (*skandha*), we should together train in the teachings of the Vinaya.
When the king had spoken these verses, he performed a great act of relinquishment.
He then spoke further in verse:
"I know this body is short-lived, And that it will surely bring suffering in the next world;
Now one must perform meritorious deeds to summon happiness in future lives.
If you delight in cultivating merit, give in charity according to your means;
for those who delight in performing meritorious acts, there is happiness in this life and in lives to come.
At that time, the Buddha said to the Great King:
"What do you think?
That King Mandhātṛ at that time was none other than myself."

At that time, even though I benefited sentient beings in such a manner, I was still unable to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; how much less could one attain unexcelled enlightenment through a minor gift? This is because there exists a causal retribution within saṃsāra based upon these conditions.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu, Fascicle 12.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu, Fascicle 13.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Regarding the circumstances of Viśvantara: The World-Honored One further addressed the Great King:
"You should listen attentively!"

In the distant past, when I was seeking unsurpassed perfect enlightenment for the benefit of sentient beings, there was a universal monarch named Mahāsumati, who possessed the seven treasures and attained the four supernormal powers; this has already been explained in detail within the sixty-third chapter of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

At that time, King Priyadarśana redoubled his delight in the True Dharma; he provided food and drink as offerings for five hundred pratyekabuddhas. Having presented them with food and drink, he gave each of them individually a high-quality cotton cloth (*karpāsa*) and spoke these verses:
“Having realized the vast mind, O benevolent ones, do not be heedless!
By giving to those who uphold the precepts, one’s giving will surely bring increase.”
"This donor is wise and discerning; through faith, he has attained liberation.
Having realized a mind free from fault, he shall obtain happiness upon rebirth.
At that time, the Buddha said to the Great King:
"Do not harbor other thoughts!
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King who possessed the seven treasures in their entirety and had attained the four supernormal powers was none other than myself.
Although I made such offerings at that time, I did not yet attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"By virtue of these causes and conditions, I have accumulated roots of goodness; therefore, I have now attained perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha further addressed the Great King:
"I performed meritorious acts of giving in my quest for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; you should listen attentively!"
In the past, there was a brahmin named Kāla who belonged to a great and noble lineage; he regularly practiced the giving of Dharma, bestowing it upon various brahmins.
He employed eight hundred and forty thousand great elephants, adorned with golden trappings, all covered with pure golden banners and draped with golden nets, entirely decorated with gold.
Regarding the gift of this elephant to the brahmins and others, it is explained in the *Vīramatī-sūtra* as it is in the *Madhyama Āgama*.
Having performed this meritorious deed, he spoke these verses:
"Having given, may they find happiness; through my gift, may they abide in fearlessness."
By offering gifts to the world, including the devas and all human beings,
one who seeks every happiness should practice giving and abide in fearlessness;
such a person shall attain liberation and become a sovereign of great wealth.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"The eminent Brahmin of noble lineage who, in times past, gave eighty-four thousand pieces of gold to adorn the elephant was none other than myself."
At that time, for the sake of practicing giving, I did not immediately realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
yet, through those causes and conditions, there was the condition of right faith, and therefore, with my merit now perfected, I have attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Great King, when I was seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I was able to practice relinquishment and bestow gifts for the sake of merit and benefit.
Listen attentively, Great King!

In the distant past, there was a universal monarch named Śaṅkha who ruled over the four continents, possessed the seven treasures, and had attained the three supernormal powers; yet he was without offspring.
Because he sought a son, he contemplated and devised a thousand expedients.
At that time, a man came and said to the king:
"There is a medicine called 'Many Sons' (*Bahuputrā*); if the palace women consume it, they shall immediately conceive sons."
Upon hearing that there was a medicinal drug for producing many children, the king immediately sought it out.
Later, the king obtained this medicine; he ground it finely and administered it to the women of the palace to drink, whereupon they all became pregnant.

The queen was unaware of this matter; when her months were complete, she gave birth to a son whose appearance was upright and majestic, with a face like that of a lion and possessing the supernatural power of Nārāyaṇa.
He gathered his kinsmen and held a birth festival, bestowing upon him a name, which was called "Mao Cao" (Thatch).
At that time, a wondrous conch and a wheel appeared spontaneously before the prince.
If the prince blows this conch shell, those of the enemy forces who hear it will all retreat and flee;
some who hear it will even go deaf on the spot.
As for those who hear the sound of its turning, people will all run to hide or throw themselves into houses and burrows.
Having subdued the external territories and brought all the kings into submission, he came to see his father, the king, and said:
"Great King! All the kings of the external territories have been conquered by me."
Upon hearing this, the father king was filled with great joy; he immediately had a consort selected for the crown prince from a neighboring kingdom.
Having determined an auspicious date through astrology and divination, he assembled his kinsmen and performed the wedding ceremony.
When the princess saw that the crown prince’s appearance was terrifying, she fled in fear.

At that moment, the crown prince took up a conch shell, a wheel, and a sword, and pursued her closely. Along the way, he saw all the elephants and horses belonging to the royal household being devoured by lions.
Then the keepers of the elephants and horses all came together and said to the Prince:
"The elephants and horses have now been devoured by a lion; we pray that you will save them."
"We ourselves possess our own private elephants, horses, and so forth; we shall give you one-sixth share of these for the Crown Prince.
At that time, the Crown Prince immediately blew his conch shell, and all the lions, tigers, and wolves fled in every direction.
At that time, the Prince said to the people:
"That portion which is rightfully mine—one-sixth—let it remain for me to take upon my return.
Having spoken, he pursued the king’s daughter; the Prince's kinsmen followed behind with their soldiers to pursue her as well, whereupon the Prince said:
"Turn back.
If you are determined to go, take your troops and proceed to the lady's house.
The Prince replied:
"I shall go now alone; I have no need for an army.
Having said this, the troops turned back and the Prince proceeded alone.
Later, he arrived at the kingdom of that queen's father. Upon seeing him, the queen's father addressed the Prince, saying:
"Take this girl away.
Having obtained the girl, he immediately turned back and went to the place where the elephants were being trained;
there he said to the elephant trainer, "Give me one-sixth [of the profit]."
The elephant trainer replied,
"The elephant was carried away by the wind.
Then the Prince spoke this verse:
“Even a young elephant in rut and intoxicated, when caught by the wind, is led away;
how much more so for cattle, sheep, and the like? One must know the mind for oneself.”

"At that time, the Prince bathed, anointed his body with fragrant ointments, and took up a mirror to look at himself. Upon observing his face, he saw that his countenance was terrifying, and he thought to himself:
'My face is like this; if people were to see me... "
"What use have I for this body now?
I must surely destroy it myself.
He then entered a thicket, intending to take his own life.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, perceived that the Prince was a Bodhisattva of this Bhadrakalpa; he thought, "If I were to harm him myself, I would surely undergo great suffering.
If I transform him into one who is handsome and upright, he will not take his own life."

At that time, the Lord of Devas gave a precious jewel from within the crown of the Prince’s spiral-tufted hair; having placed it upon his head, the Prince became like a celestial being, his appearance majestic and dignified, and he obtained the possession of the seven treasures.

Later, when his father passed away, the crown prince ascended the throne and ruled over the four continents in accordance with the Dharma. Possessing all seven treasures and endowed with great majesty, he became a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*).

In six hundred thousand cities, pavilions for the Dharma were established; the people followed the secular rites of sacrifice and devoted themselves exclusively to the practice of giving for many years.
After many hundreds of thousands of years had passed and all the brahmins had been provided for, he spoke these verses:
“If there be abundant enjoyments, Among both gods and humans;”
One may resolve to act but cannot give; one may possess great wealth yet fail to relinquish it.
When people are deluded and abide in stingy attachment, the Buddha teaches that one must give with urgency.
Wielding a staff is not true valor; a mind capable of giving is truly heroic.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"At that time, I was the universal monarch named Tṛṇa. I established six hundred thousand halls of righteousness and practiced the dharma of sacrificial giving, extensively cultivating merit."
"Great King!
Do not harbor other thoughts; that was my own body.
At that time, I was known as the universal monarch Tṛṇa."

"In this way, in all six hundred thousand cities, they established shrines for ancestral sacrifices according to worldly custom, bestowing gifts upon all and universally cultivating meritorious deeds.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"It was through the conditions of such relinquishment and giving that I attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Great King!

Do not harbor other thoughts. It was for this cause and condition, for the sake of the faculty of faith, that I cultivated these merits and accumulated roots of goodness so as to realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
Furthermore, Great King!
I also practiced giving and cultivated merit for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Great King, listen attentively!
In the distant past, there was a king named Trilomadevaka, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of attendants.
That king practiced compassion in his heart and mind, seeking the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.

When that country suffered from famine and scarcity, the king made a vow of truthful speech (*satyavacana*); immediately, the heavens sent down rain, and thus his kingdom was always abundant and prosperous.
Later, the king relinquished his throne and left the household life; following a seer (*ṛṣi*), he attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
At that time, there was a king in Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta who reigned over his domain; the population was flourishing, and the land was prosperous, joyful, and secure.
The physiognomist divined that for the next twelve years the heavens would not send down rain.
The king beat the drum to proclaim a decree to the people:
"Those who can provide provisions for twelve years may remain in this kingdom; otherwise, you must depart."
"If there is no one capable [of this], you may go wherever you please.
The people within the kingdom then discussed among themselves:
"Now that we face such famine and scarcity, what plan can be devised?"
"Where do you wish to go?
Among them, someone said:

"I have heard that in the kingdom of Matanga there is a rishi who speaks words of truth and oath; as soon as he speaks, the heavens send down rain, and it is always abundant and fertile, with food and grain in ample supply."
At that time, because of the scarcity of food, all those people fled to the kingdom of Maṇḍakya.
Having renounced the world for the sake of their father the king, the crown prince ascended to the throne.
For twelve years, all the people who came to take refuge in the kingdom were fully provided with sufficient food and provisions.
King Brahmadatta asked his ministers,
"Where are the people of my kingdom now?"
The minister replied,
"As described at length above, it is located in the kingdom of the seer Matanga.
The king then addressed his ministers once more:
"At this time, there is famine as if it were the age of the final kalpa.
By what means can we escape from this suffering?
The ministers replied:
“Mātanga, having now left the household life, has realized the path of the sages; it would be fitting to invite him.
King Brahmadatta immediately went to the hermitage of the sage Mātanga and addressed him, saying:
“In my kingdom there is a great famine, as if it were the final age of the kalpa.”
"I only pray that the Great Seer will deign to visit my kingdom and utter words of truth.
At that time, the Seer accepted the invitation and went to the kingdom of King Brahmadatta, where he uttered these words of truth:
"Though I was born among the Caṇḍālas, I have never harbored an evil heart or intent to harm."
All that has been spoken by the Three Conchs should be universally known; all gods and humans shall behold it.

Thus do I now speak these words of truth: having long practiced and cultivated a heart of loving-kindness for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, I pray that the dragons will send down rain to relieve the hungry.
From birth until now, whatever goodness I have cultivated, and because I have long practiced a mind of loving-kindness and compassion;
by these immeasurable words of truth, may the dragon send down rain to save all living beings.
"When the seer had made this vow, at that very moment, a great rain fell from the heavens upon Vārāṇasī; the famine having ceased, the land was transformed into one of abundance."
"All the people within the city who had previously been in the kingdom of Maṇḍakya have now returned and are all resuming their former occupations.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"The one who was King Trivalīmaṇḍaka at that time was none other than myself."
In the past, I practiced compassion in my heart and benefited sentient beings.
If I utter words of truth, the heavens will send down rain, which can eliminate famine and ensure constant abundance.
"Great King!

It was not solely through the practice of giving that I realized unsurpassed bodhi; rather, it was by further cultivating immeasurable causes and conditions of merit, accumulating roots of goodness, and giving rise to right faith that I attained realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The Buddha said to the Great King:
“For the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi, I have practiced giving and performed various meritorious deeds.
Great King, listen attentively!”
In the distant past, in the kingdom of Mithilā, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Mahādeva.
I have already explained this in detail in the *Madhyama Āgama*.
Seeing that he himself possessed great enjoyments, the king performed various sacrificial rites and spoke these verses:
"If one seeks great wealth, Both in the heavens and among humans,
One should practice giving according to one's means, Out of fear of poverty."
"The giver is honored by men, and later shall surely receive the offerings of the devas;
humans and non-humans alike take refuge in them, just as rain brings forth the ripening of fruit.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"Do not harbor other thoughts!

That Great Heavenly Wheel-Turning King at that time was destined for the good realms; constantly practicing the holy life, he attained the rank of a wheel-turning king throughout eighty-four thousand lifetimes."
"Great King!
Do not harbor other thoughts; the Universal Monarch of that time was none other than myself.
Furthermore, Great King!"
"How could I have realized unsurpassed awakening through this gift alone?

Rather, it is by cultivating immeasurable causes and conditions for meritorious deeds, by accumulating roots of goodness, and by giving rise to right faith that I have attained the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The Buddha told the Great King:
"In the past, for the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi, I practiced generosity and performed various meritorious deeds.
Great King, listen attentively!"
In the distant past, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Nimi in the city of Mithilā; I have also previously explained this extensively in the Āgama Sūtras.
Seeing that he himself possessed great resources, the king performed the rites of worldly sacrifice, giving alms to all, and spoke this verse:
"If one sees others performing wholesome deeds, One should follow them and likewise perform wholesome deeds;
He who is indolent and does not act Is a base and inferior man."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to King Nimi:
"You may come to my palace and enjoy the five celestial sensual pleasures; sport and play with delight, receiving happiness as you wish."
Then the King replied with a verse:
"Just as when one borrows another's utensils, they must be returned by the appointed time;
celestial music is likewise, like a temporary loan."
"I shall return to Mithilā and perform many meritorious deeds;
in the future, within that palace, I shall enjoy the fruits of my merit and be reborn in the heavens.
At that time, having returned to his native city, Mithilā practiced generosity and performed various meritorious acts, and spoke this verse:
“‘The virtuous and benevolent praise the practice of giving; they practice renunciation according to the occasion.
Whether Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, Caṇḍāla, or Śūdra—’”
When practicing renunciation during times of famine, the practitioner causes others to be fully satisfied;
such a person shall leave the miserable realms behind and will certainly be reborn in the heavens.
The wise who recognize this merit are able to practice giving.
"Through giving one attains liberation, and through wealth and nobility one is born in heaven.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Do not harbor such thoughts!"

In the past, when King Nimi, the Wheel-turning Monarch, went to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, Śakra invited him to share his seat and enjoy the pleasures of the five senses; yet even then, it was I who, at the sacrificial hall established at the gate of the city of Mithilā, performed sacrifices according to the Dharma and practiced giving to cultivate all manner of meritorious deeds.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"It was not solely by virtue of the meritorious deed of practicing this giving that I realized perfect enlightenment.
Great King!"
"Do not harbor any doubt; it is because he practiced giving, gave rise to right faith, and accumulated roots of goodness that he has now attained perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
"For the sake of seeking unsurpassed enlightenment, I practice giving and cultivate various meritorious deeds.
O King, listen attentively!
In the distant past, there was a king named Ānanda who had five sons; the youngest of them was called Ādarśamukha."

Later, when the Great King’s body was afflicted by illness, physicians prescribed various medicines consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, branches, and fruits; yet despite these treatments, his condition did not improve, and he only grew increasingly frail and gravely ill.
As his life was drawing to a close, he quickly summoned his ministers and said, "I am now approaching my end;
it is necessary that I appoint a successor king.
The ministers asked:
"Whom do you wish to establish?
He replied:
"For those with merit and those endowed with celestial fortune, place the precious sandals."
As for the palace attendants who receive the command:

one who perceives the six treasuries—perceiving the inner treasury, the outer treasury, the inner-and-outer treasury, and the treasuries within trees, mountains, and waters—may be established as king.
Having spoken thus, he passed away.
The ministers tested their sons to see which was capable of succeeding him;
only the youngest prince, Darpaṇamukha, was fit to inherit the royal throne and possessed divine endowments.
Once he had ascended the precious throne, they presented him with the precious sandals and led him into the palace.
When the palace attendants saw him, they all paid him their respects; they beheld the six treasuries exactly as previously described.
As for "even those hidden among the trees," it means that when the king dwells beneath a tree, there is a treasury below it;
the same applies to when he is among the mountains or in the royal gardens.
Regarding "hidden within the water": if the king were to sport in the waters of the earth, there would immediately be a hidden treasury.
When the ministers saw that Prince Mirror-Face possessed such karmic fruition, they honored him for his excellence and nobility, and immediately established him on the royal throne.
Having succeeded to the throne, he ruled the country according to the Dharma.

During a twelve-year period of famine and scarcity within the realm, he followed the customary rites of sacrifice, bestowing gifts upon all people and granting whatever was requested; knowing himself to be happy, he spoke this verse:
"Those who acquire wealth through the Dharma, The wise do not hoard it."
The giver is said to uphold the precepts when bestowing gifts upon those who receive them—
upon śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and upon the poor and destitute;
having cast off this body, they will surely be reborn in the heavens.
"Being thus wise and discerning, with right faith and mindfulness of liberation,
one should be courageous in practice and constantly give gifts without stinginess.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"Do not harbor other thoughts!
The king at that time was none other than myself.

At that time, I was named King Ādarśamukha; for twelve years, because of a famine, I practiced giving universally to all sentient beings, bestowing whatever they required for their use and even providing for all secular rites and sacrifices—it was I who did so."
"Great King, do not hold the view that one realizes unsurpassed bodhi merely through the meritorious act of practicing generosity.
It is because the Mirror-Face practiced generosity, gave rise to right faith, and accumulated roots of goodness that he has now attained bodhi."
"Furthermore, Great King!
For the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi, I practiced giving, performed meritorious deeds, and exerted the perfection of diligence."
"Great King, listen attentively!
In the distant past, in the kingdom of Pañcāla, there were two kings:
one ruled over the northern border and one over the southern border."

To its north was a king named Dhanu, whose capital city was named Nāgaka. That king governed the world through the Dharma; the population was flourishing, and the land was abundant, joyful, and secure. It was free from all forms of fraud, theft, and pestilence, and cattle, sheep, rice, and sugarcane were found everywhere in abundance.

That king ruled the country with the Dharma. Beside the city was a great pond, its surface completely covered with *utpala* flowers and the like, and it was further filled with various kinds of birds.

In the pond there was a dragon prince named Miaosheng (Wondrous Birth), who would occasionally go forth to raise clouds and send down sweet rain, causing the fields to be bountiful and the stores of grain to abound, so that all could practice giving.

The king of the southern border was by nature treacherous, evil, fierce, and coarse; he governed the country according to what is not the Dharma, constantly imprisoning and beating the common people with shackles and clubs.

Heaven did not send down rain, and the people were all struck with alarm and haste, abandoning their homes to flee to the city of Longge in the northern border in search of a means to save their lives.
The King of the southern border went out of the city on a hunting expedition, whereupon he saw that the village dwellings were deserted and the temples were in ruins.
He asked his ministers, "Where have all the people of this village gone now?"
The ministers replied:
"Recently, due to famine and scarcity, everyone was driven by hunger and desperation and fled to the King of the Northern Region.
Your Majesty, having granted us fearlessness, we have now fully explained the circumstances."
The King said, "Be at ease;
you have no cause for fear.
The ministers replied:

"In the northern region there is a king named Dhana who governs the nation by the Dharma and transforms the world by the Dharma. The people are numerous and prosperous, living in peace, security, and abundance. There is no fraud, theft, or pestilence. Cattle, sheep, rice, and sugarcane fill every place. He always delights in practicing generosity toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, providing them with abundant food, drink, and all necessary requisites for their use."

"The Great King’s nature and conduct are coarse and cruel; he imprisons and beats the common people with clubs, leaving them terrified. They have fled to the city of Longge in the northern borderlands.
The King asked, "What stratagem can be devised to cause them to return and dwell in our villages once more?"
The ministers replied:
"If Your Majesty, like that King of Wealth, practices compassion and benefits sentient beings, before long all people will flock to these cities and villages."
The minister spoke again to the king:

"That city possesses other excellent and marvelous things as well. Beside the city there is a pond, its surface entirely covered with lotus flowers, and it is home to many beautiful birds. Furthermore, there is a dragon prince named Wondrous Birth (Miaosheng) who sends down rain at the proper times, ensuring abundant harvests; for this reason, the people of that country live in happiness."
The king again addressed his ministers, saying:
"By what means can we cause that nāga prince to come and dwell here?
The ministers replied:
"If there is anyone who maintains mantras, they may come forth.

At that time, the king immediately commanded his ministers to beat the drums and proclaim an edict: "If there is anyone capable of maintaining vidyā-mantras, let the Naga prince Miaosheng from the city of Longge in the northern region come to my presence; he shall be rewarded with a chest of gold and provided with great abundance."
At that time, there was a mantra-practitioner named Snake-Charmer who came to the minister’s residence and said,
"If you will certainly give me this golden cage, I can summon the Naga prince Miaosheng here by means of my spells."
Then the ministers immediately presented him with a golden cage.
The incantation master said, "Wait until I have finished my incantations and brought the dragon here; only then shall you accept it.

At that time, the incantation master went to the city of Nāgapura, where he observed the interior of the pond from all four sides to discover the dragon's dwelling place. He then returned and informed the ministers:
"I shall come on the seventh day; you all should prepare the rites of sacrifice.

At that time, the dragon prince, knowing that the snake-charmer who recites incantations had arrived there and would reach his kingdom on the seventh day, thought: "What plan can I devise to avoid being separated from my parents, kinsmen, and relatives?"
"Where can I go to escape this situation?
Not far from the pond lived two hunters:
one named Varaka and the other named Paraka. They resided by the pond to earn their livelihood, catching fish and land animals with nets.
Before long, Phalaka died.
The dragon prince thought to himself:
"Since the hunter Phalaka is still alive, I must seek refuge with him."
At that time, the dragon prince transformed himself into human form, went to where the hunter was, and said to him:

"Do you know by whom this city has come to possess such a flourishing population, such abundance, joy, and security, free from all deceit, thieves, and pestilence, and filled everywhere with cattle, sheep, rice, and sugarcane?"
The hunter replied, "I know this matter;
it is entirely because Your Majesty practices compassion in your heart, benefits all beings, and sustains the common people."
The dragon prince replied,
"As you have said, it must indeed depend on the king, yet there is another matter involved.
He answered:
"Furthermore, there is a nāga prince in this pond who sends down rain at the proper time.
Because of this, the people are flourishing, living in joy and abundance, with food and drink in great plenty."
The dragon prince said:
"If that dragon prince were taken away by someone, separated from his parents and kinsmen,
what could you do upon seeing that person?"
He replied,
"I am able to harm him.
The dragon prince said to him:
"Do you recognize this Nāga son, O Wondrous Birth?
He replied,
"I have not recognized him until now."
He replied, "I am the Naga prince Miāoshēng.
Now, a master of the Pañcāla kingdom in the south named Zhòushé (Snake-Charmer) wishes to come and capture me to take me away; he is currently performing the rites of sacrifice and boundary-binding."

"When seven days have passed and you come here, you must drive stakes of khadira wood into the ground and encircle the four sides of the pond with threads of various colors; by performing this rite, you will surely take me away."

"You may hide yourself for a moment in one place; when you see from afar him stirring the water, you must immediately shoot an arrow at the vital spot of the sorcerer. Come quickly and compel him to withdraw the spell, otherwise cut off his head."
"You must first cast off the spell before you may kill me;
otherwise, I shall remain bound by this incantation until death and never be released.
Then the hunter said to the dragon prince:
"If I were to act solely for your benefit alone, I would still do so;
how much more so when it brings benefit to the entire populace of the royal city? Why should I not do this?
Do not have any anxiety."
At that time, the nāga prince led the hunter to observe his various hidden and secluded lairs.
On the seventh day, when the hunter reached each of those hiding places, the snake-charmer arrived and established an altar, performed sacrifices, and drew protective boundaries.
Following the ritual of mantras and mudrās exactly, he drove stakes into the four directions, encircled them with threads of various colors, and then shot arrows at him.
"Come quickly and advance to stir the waters of the pond!
Then the hunter drew his sword and declared, "Within my kingdom dwells the wondrously born Nāga prince; you wish to take him away."
"If you do not quickly release the spell, I shall strike off your head with a blade and cause it to fall to the ground.
At that time, the snake-charmer, suffering from this agony and fearing death, immediately released and withdrew the spell.
Having understood this, the hunter severed his life-force; the nāga prince was thus liberated. Emerging from the pond, he embraced the hunter and said:
"Virtuous one, you are my parents. You have come to rescue me, and I am now spared from the suffering of being separated from my parents and kin."
"Virtuous one, you may follow me into my palace.
They then followed one another into the Dragon King’s palace, where various kinds of exquisite food and drink were prepared, and he gave him a supreme jewel.
He further addressed his parents, saying:
"This is one who has entrusted himself to our kin; because of this person, we are now spared from the suffering of separation from those we love.
At that time, the dragon prince’s parents immediately ordered the hunter to make a request, and bestowed upon him immeasurable treasures.
Having caught it, the hunter immediately emerged from the pond.
Not far from the pond lived a rishi; the forest was lush with fruit, and various birds there sang harmonious and elegant melodies.
Now, this rishi delighted in practicing compassion and benefiting sentient beings.
This hunter went to the rishi’s dwelling three times every day.
On one occasion, he related the entire account of the nāga prince in detail.
Then the seer said:
"Why do you use precious jewels to seek such a minor boon?
Within that dragon palace, there is the Amoghapāśa; why do you not take it?"
"You may go there and seek to obtain this rope.
Having heard this, the hunter conceived a greedy desire; he immediately went to the dragon palace, where he saw the rope and thought to himself:
"That which I have sought is this very rope."
Entering the dragon palace, he saw the dragon prince Miaosheng (Wondrous Birth) walking together with various other dragons.
When the dragons saw the hunter, they were greatly delighted and bestowed upon him rare treasures.
The hunter replied, "I have sufficient treasures of my own; I require this snare."
The nāga said:
"This rope is of no use.
However, out of fear of the garuḍa, we must keep this rope to protect ourselves."
The hunter replied, "For you,
it is required only once every long period;
for my use, however, it is used daily."
"If you recognize this kindness and virtue, you should give me this cord.
The dragon prince then thought to himself:
"This person has bestowed much kindness and virtue upon me; I shall now consult my parents and may then give him the cord."
After the dragon prince had addressed his parents, he immediately gave him the rope.
Upon obtaining the rope, the hunter was filled with great joy, as if he had acquired the very substance of the earth.
Having emerged from the pond and returned home, the Great King of that city sported with his consort, yet she did not conceive for a long time.
Since he had neither son nor daughter, he rested his cheek in his hand and reflected deeply:
"I possess immeasurable wealth and treasuries, yet now that I have no child, my lineage shall come to an end."
"If everyone were to know that there is no heir, they would establish another king.
While he was reflecting thus, the king’s kinsmen, as well as the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, all marveled at the Great King’s arising of such sorrow and distress, and said to him:
"What is it that you are contemplating?"
The King related the matter in full detail.
He further addressed the King, saying:
"One must petition the celestial deities; then you shall immediately have a son."

In order to seek a son, the king then prayed to the forest deities, the park deities, the deities of the crossroads, the deities who receive offerings, the deities of birth, and the various benevolent celestial deities, vowing that he might have a son.
The Buddha said:
"If one could obtain them by seeking through such means, everyone would have a thousand sons.
It is only through the conjunction of three factors that a son comes to be."
What are these three?
First, a father; second, a mother; and third, the manifestation of craving—only when these are present will there be a son.
Because the king sought a son, a Bodhisattva of the Bhadrakalpa then entered the womb of the Great Queen of the kingdom.
A wise woman possesses five kinds of knowledge.
What are these five?
First, she knows when a man has a mind of desire, and so forth, as explained in detail above.
Having realized she was pregnant, she joyfully addressed the king:
"I am now carrying a child; since it is in my left armpit, I know for certain it will be a boy.
Upon hearing this, the Great King was filled with immense joy.
The lady thought to herself:
"When the ten months are complete, I shall give birth to a son.

He will be able to establish our lineage; after I have passed away, he will perform acts of giving according to his means for my sake, cultivate various meritorious deeds, and provide for those who beg."
"When she was born, she was able to follow behind me. When the consort was about to give birth, she was allowed to roam and wander freely;

she was provided with warm clothing when it was cold and cooling provisions when it was hot. Whatever garments she required were supplied, and she was consulted regarding medical prescriptions and food. Her diet consisted of the six flavors blended to perfection, and her body was adorned with various precious necklaces and ornaments so that she resembled a celestial maiden. Like the gods wandering through the Joyful Garden (Nandana), she was always conveyed by carriage, palanquin, or litter, and she heard the delightful sounds of music in fragrant and beautiful places.
When the Queen’s months were complete, she gave birth to a son whose appearance was upright and majestic, a sight that all people delighted to behold, and who was endowed with every auspicious mark.
At that time, the devas beat drums for celebration; when the King, his father, heard this, he was greatly astonished.
The palace attendants said to the king, "Because Your Majesty has a son, the heavens have struck the drums.

The king immediately issued an edict ordering that the cities and towns be cleansed and sprinkled with water, that various exquisite incenses be burned, and that precious banners and canopies be hung. He ordered alms to be bestowed upon all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the poor, the destitute, and the orphaned; furthermore, he proclaimed a general amnesty and arranged for various festivities.
Furthermore, for the Prince’s birthday festival, they began with the first seven days and continued through the third week to establish his name.
The ministers deliberated together, asking, "What name should we establish for him?"
The assembly deliberated and said:
"Since the king's name is Dhana, the prince may now be given the title Sudhana.
Eight nurses were provided for him, as described in detail above.
At that time, the Prince grew day by day, like a lotus in the water, before long reaching full maturity.

He was then sent to school to study various scripts, archery, royal law, arithmetic, the identification of precious gems, men, elephants, and horses, as well as the arts and crafts, various technical skills, and the sixty-four abilities; he became proficient in releasing bonds and reading, being intelligent and thoroughly accomplished.
The father-king established for him palaces for the three seasons—namely, those for spring, summer, and winter—and three types of gardens, each corresponding to one of the three periods.
Sudhana remained alone in the upper chambers of the palace, playing flutes and performing music as he enjoyed his pastimes.
At that time, the hunter Phalaka, while hunting birds and beasts, arrived at a mountain.
There he saw a rishi dwelling at the foot of the mountain, where flowers and fruits flourished and various beautiful birds abounded.
There was also a great pond, its surface covered with various exquisite lotus flowers, where those birds played and frolicked.
A hunter, while wandering about, arrived at the place where the seer resided.
He saw that seer with long hair and nails, his body clad in tree bark;
due to his ascetic practices, his body was withered and emaciated as he sat within a grass hut beneath a tree.
Having seen him, the hunter joined his palms, prostrated at his feet, and addressed him:
"Great Seer! How long has it been since you began these ascetic practices here?"
The seer said,
"I have been practicing asceticism here for forty years.
The hunter asked:
"During all this time, have you seen anything extraordinary?
At that moment, the rishi replied in a slow and gentle voice, "O noble one!"
"Do you see this pond?
He replied, "I see it."
The Great Master replied:

"This pond is named Brahma-stair (Brahmakrama); it is covered over by various wondrous lotus flowers, and various birds dwell within it. This pond is clear and cool; its water tastes like milk when mixed with the flowers."
On the fifteenth day of every month, there is a daughter of the Kinnara king named Manoharā, who, surrounded by a retinue of five hundred, comes to this pond with various fragrant flowers to bathe.
When I was bathing, various musical performances were played; hearing these exquisite sounds, all the birds in the pond ceased their cries.
When I heard them, my heart was filled with great joy, and for seven days my mind remained in a state of immense delight.
"O Worthy One!
I have witnessed only such rare and extraordinary things.
At that time, the hunter reflected to himself:
"I obtained this Amoghapāśa from the nāga prince.
By means of this noose, I shall capture Manoharā.
Having formed this thought, on the fifteenth day, he hid himself among the trees, holding the nāga-noose in his hand.
When the kinnarī came forth, wishing to enter the pond to bathe, the hunter immediately cast a rope and bound her, tying up the kinnarī.
When the girl saw that she was bound, she cried out in panic and fear, and her fellow girls fled hither and thither.
The maiden Manoharā attempted to escape by a ruse, but the hunter, seeing her exquisite beauty, seized her immediately by the hand.
The woman said, "Do not seize me;
I am unfit to be your wife, but I am fit to be the king's consort.
The hunter replied:
"If you do not grasp me firmly, I fear you will run away," the girl replied.
"I shall not run now; if you do not believe me, take the jewel from within my hair-knot."
"By means of this jewel, I can soar through the air at will.
The hunter asked,
"How can one know that it is the crest-jewel?"
He replied,
"If the treasure is with a person, I shall follow behind that person.
The hunter took the treasure in his hand, secured it with a rope, and proceeded forward.
At that time, the youth Sudhana was out hunting when a hunter encountered him; Sudhana’s countenance was upright and majestic, such that all who saw him were filled with joy.
"The girl is so beautiful that if the Crown Prince were to see her, he would surely carry her off.
Having had this thought, [the hunter reflected], "I shall rather offer her myself.
The hunter then went to the youth's location, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"This jewel of a woman is offered to the Crown Prince; we pray that you will accept her.
At that time, Sudhana beheld the young maiden, whose appearance was upright and majestic, a sight that all people delighted to behold, and he observed her physical marks.
There were eighteen kinds of female adornments, as fully described elsewhere.

Upon seeing them, Sudhana was overcome by the power of desire and his heart gave rise to attachment; like a moth rushing into a flame, the realm of form was like fire and like turbulent waves, impossible to still or stabilize;
it was also like a young bull’s tail or a garuḍa bird—swift and beyond restraint.
Like an object tossed by the wind, it cannot be turned back;
like a monkey that has found a tree, its confusion is difficult to restrain.

Because of the habitual tendencies of greed from beginningless time, because of the attachment to the flavor of pleasure in the objects of affliction, because the various objects of desire utterly defile the mind, and because of false conceptualizations—taking these as the bow and the objects of thought as the arrow, with the mind itself as the shaft—he spoke this verse:
“Sudhana beheld her face like the moon, Or like a flash of lightning amidst clouds and mist;
His heart was as agitated as an elephant struck by an arrow, And having received Manoharā, he quickly returned to the city.”
At that time, Prince Sudhana returned to the city of Nāgapura and bestowed extensive fields and houses upon the hunter.
He then took Mādrī with him and enjoyed himself together with her within the palace towers and pavilions.
That maiden was of exquisite beauty and possessed immeasurable grace; she protected Prince Sudhana, causing him to love her so that they were never parted.
Later, on another occasion, two brahmins came from the Jeta Grove to the city of Nāgapura.
One dwelt in dependence upon the king, requesting that the Brahmin be honored as his teacher and being granted many requisites;
the other dwelt in dependence upon Prince Sudhana, with whom the prince bestowed requisites upon him.
At that time, the brahmin said to Prince Sudhana:
"If the Great King appoints you as his successor and you attain the royal throne, what will you do for me?"
Then Sudhana said:
"Just as my father the king established you as his gate-teacher and the most honored among all the brahmins, so too do I establish you as my superior."
Upon hearing this, the royal preceptor became greatly incensed and thought to himself:
"I must now devise a plan so that the prince does not obtain the throne, let alone that brahmin becoming the royal preceptor."
Later, on another occasion, a separate kingdom rose in rebellion; he dispatched troops to invade it, but was instead struck down by the enemy.
This occurred seven times in succession, each time sending his generals with their armies to that place, only to be beaten back and forced to retreat.
The ministers said to the king, "The enemy forces have increased in strength and our country is suffering losses; we must assemble men of courage and skill.
At that time, the king’s state preceptor thought to himself:
"Now is precisely the time to send the Prince to campaign against foreign lands, so that he may die immediately.
He then addressed the King, saying, "The enemy army is powerful and flourishing; there is no one capable of opposing them."
The Great King replied,
"I shall go myself now.
The Brahmin said:
"The Prince is young and possesses great strength; let him be appointed as the Great General. If he goes there to face the enemy, he will surely achieve victory.
The King then commanded Sudhana, saying:
"You shall serve as the Great General and go to the kingdom of Kāśī to confront the enemy in battle."
Sudhana replied to his father, the king, saying,
"It is truly as you have said.
He then entered the palace and, upon seeing Lady Manoharā, forgot his father’s instructions.
The father king again commanded Sudhana:
"Go there at once and confront the enemy.
Having received the command, Sudhana returned to the palace; upon seeing Manoharā, he immediately forgot his father king's instructions.
Then the royal preceptor returned and addressed the king:
"Prince Sudhana is passionately attached to Manoharā; I pray that Your Majesty will assemble all the troops and command the prince to set forth before the king."
At that time, the king summoned Sudhana and commanded him to lead the fourfold army to go there and resist the enemy.
Sudhana addressed his father, the king, saying:
"I shall depart immediately upon seeing Manoharā."
The king said,
"Set out immediately.
Now is not the time to go and see Manoharā."
He spoke again to his father the king, saying:
"I take my leave of my mother and shall depart.
The king said:
"Take your leave.
Sudhana immediately went to Lady Manoharā and took the jewel from her hair-knot; he then went to his mother’s side, knelt down, and said to her:
"Please guard this hair-jewel well; do not give it to Manoharā."
"If there is great suffering and distress that oppresses me unto death, I shall immediately give it to him.
Once the mother had accepted [the vow], he circumambulated her three times, performed various musical offerings, and then set out for war.
Not far from the city, he stayed for a while beneath a tree.
At that time, the Deva King Vaiśravaṇa, leading his immeasurable retinue, happened to pass by that place and was unable to move it; he was greatly astonished and thought:
"I have traveled everywhere in the past, yet never before have I encountered such a thing."
He then saw from afar the youth Sudhana beneath the tree; he was a Bodhisattva of this Bhadrakalpa who, undergoing fatigue himself, had gone there to engage in battle.
"I must have an assistant who can go and subdue my enemies without causing them harm.
At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa immediately commanded the fifth yakṣa:
"You must go quickly to the city of Kāpila; once you have finished subduing those enemies for Sudhana, ensure that no harm is done."

At that time, having received the king’s command, the yakṣa immediately transformed the fourfold army so that the men were as tall as tāla trees, the elephants as high as great mountains, and the horses as large as elephants; they fashioned various weapons and manifested all manner of transformations, beating and blowing great drums to inspire terror.
Manifesting great power, he went to the place where the enemy was and displayed such a spectacle.
The walls on all four sides of the city collapsed simultaneously through the power of the yakṣa; the people were all struck with wonder and fear, and asked:
"From where have you come?"
The celestial soldiers replied:
"Open your gates at once; Sudhana will arrive immediately, and you may go out to welcome him.
If you delay any longer, you shall all die, with none remaining."
The city-dwellers replied, "We do not oppose the King, nor do we oppose Sudhana.

However, having been pressured by the King's messengers to close their gates, the people opened the city and, with various fragrant flowers and musical performances, went out to welcome Sudhana. He entered the city, where he took charge of pacifying it and established local officials.

When Sudhana returned to his country, that night the father-king dreamed that an owl took the king’s intestines and entrails and wound them around the four sides of the city, while the king’s body entered a jeweled chamber.
When the king awoke, his heart was filled with great terror and the hair on his body stood on end. Rising from his sleep, he rested his cheek in his hand and remained lost in anxious thought:
"I shall certainly be stripped of my royal throne; death is surely imminent."
The next morning, he immediately assembled the brahmins and others to explain the meaning of this dream. The king’s preceptor then thought to himself:
"Sudhana will certainly be victorious in battle and shall subdue the foreign kingdom."
"I must interpret this as an evil omen.
The brahmin then addressed the Great King:
"This is a nightmare; you will certainly lose your royal throne and will surely die."
"However, within the incantation methods of the Brahmins, there exists a ritual procedure that can exempt one from this calamity.
The King asked again:
"What method is it?"
He said: "Within the royal park, you shall construct a pond, adorned with great beauty and lined with white clay to make it exquisite."
Slay various evil beasts and collect their blood until it fills a pool.

Place this at the intersection of four roads; having entered from one side and exited toward another, command four eminent Brahmins versed in the four Vedas to lick the soles of the king’s feet with their tongues and burn incense made from the fat of *kiṃnaras*.
"If one performs such rites of expiation, the King shall long remain in his station, enjoying longevity and freedom from calamity.
At that time, the King said,
"All matters may be prepared."
"How can the fat of a kiṃnara be obtained?
The brāhmaṇa replied to the king,
"That which is easily obtained, you instead call difficult to obtain."
The king asked again,
"In what way is it easy to obtain?
The brāhmaṇa replied:
"The king's daughter-in-law, named Manoharā, is a kinnarī.
The king immediately replied, "Do not speak such words; my son’s life is bound up with hers."
He replied: "Great King!
Have you not yet heard the instruction of the scriptures:..."
“‘One should abandon one for the sake of kinsmen, Abandon kinsmen for the sake of a village;
Abandon the village to take a city, And abandon the whole earth for the sake of the self.’”
"The King must first protect himself and his youthful son;
only then will he be able to protect others. To do so, he must kill that Manoharā.
"Great King, for the sake of loving one's life, there is nothing one will not do."

At that time, having heard these words, the Great King immediately had a pond excavated according to the instructions, plastered it with white clay, slaughtered various fierce beasts, and filled the pond with their blood.
When the various palace ladies within Sudhana’s inner quarters heard of this matter, they all felt great joy and said to one another:
"We are all young, upright, and beautiful; if Sudhana arrives, we shall serve him."
At that time, Nandika, seeing their joy, asked the palace women in wonder:
"What cause for joy do you have?
He questioned them one by one, until a certain palace woman recounted everything as described above.
Having heard this, Manoharā was deeply distressed in heart; filled with grief and sorrow, she went to her mother, Sudhanā, and weeping, spoke as follows, recounting everything as above.
The mother said, "Wait a moment; I shall go and search for it myself, so that we may know whether it is real or false.
At that time, Manoharā came again and said:
"This matter is true.
Then the Prince’s mother said to him, "Now is precisely the time for you to depart; if I do not give you these treasures, it would be a betrayal of my heart."
He then gave Manoharā his crest-jewel, garments, and other items.
At that time, after the Great King had entered the pool to bathe, the brahmin licked his feet with his tongue up to the crown of his head, and the king commanded him to fetch the fat of a kiṃnara.
Then Manoharā, her body soaring into the air, spoke these verses:
"Because my body has been touched by passion, I dwell here in joyful laughter;
Like an elephant that has gained its release from bonds, Having already escaped, I soar away into the sky."
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*, Fascicle Thirteen.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*,
Fascicle Fourteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree:
"At that time, the Great King, seeing that woman depart like the wind, was struck with fear and anxiety. He addressed his preceptor, a Brahmin, saying:
'She for whom we should have acted has already fled.'"
The brahmin replied, "Great King, you have attained success; all calamities have been dispelled.
At that moment, Manoharā, remaining in the air, reflected once more:
"The various sufferings and afflictions I now endure here are all due to that rishi.
When I reach his dwelling, I must speak of this matter: 'For your sake, my body has encountered great hardship and calamity.'"
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to the place where the seer was, prostrated himself, and said to the seer:
"Because I spoke to people on behalf of the Great Seer, I have been bound; I have been so deluded by human desire that it will lead to my death."
He spoke again to the seer, saying:
"If Sudhana comes searching for me, take this finger-ring and give it to him,
reporting these words:"
"My dwelling place is on a path that is extremely perilous; I pray you will turn back and need not come further.
If you are unwilling to turn back, I wish for the Rishi to briefly inspect the road."
In this northern region there are three Black Mountains; beyond these mountains there are another three, and yet another three.
Having crossed these nine mountains, there is the King of Snowy Mountains (Himavat), and to the north of that mountain there is again a Black Mountain, from which water flows downward.
Furthermore, there are the various mountains such as Khadara, Ishadhara, Vajragarbha, Kāmarūpa, Ujugudaka, Irvataka, Abhivana, and Pimushana.
Having passed this mountain, he enters Mount Kharaṇāda; at the foot of the mountain there is a cave, and he enters this cave.
Having entered, there is a great stone pillar.
Once you have ascended the pillar, you shall clothe yourself in deerskin and remain there.
A king of birds will come and push you aside, allowing you to pass over the mountains.
Having emerged from this, there will be many variegated logs in the water, some shaped like humans, some like sheep, and some like rams.
He arrived again at a cave named Piṅgala, in which there was a flowing stream like fine flour. Within it dwelt a great python that came rushing forward with great speed.
"You must remain vigilant and cross over with extreme swiftness."
If an evil bird comes to the middle of a log bridge, you must shoot it through.
Furthermore, if there is a log bridge resembling two oxen fighting, you may strike its horns to break them; then you shall proceed on your way.
Alternatively, you may encounter a log bridge made of iron, with human figures holding iron swords, their forms terrifying; these too must be broken before you may proceed on your way.
Furthermore, there will be a log bridge shaped like a yakṣa, with an iron mouth; if you see it, drive iron nails into its forehead.
Furthermore, you will encounter a well named Fierce Rotation (*Tīvravartā*); you must pass over it while holding a staff in your hand.
If you encounter a yakṣa with a yellow head and eyes, you must strike it with a staff and sword as you pass by.

Furthermore, there are many rivers that must be crossed, within which are *jāla* dragons; these waters are known as the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Candrabhāgā, Rūpavatī, Asiknī, Viśvāsā, Vitastā, and other such rivers.
In the Kakutthā River there dwells a yakṣī named Kubjā;
in the Bahumatī River no one can dwell;
and in the Tāpinī River there are many crocodiles and dragons.
In the Citrā River dwell those of desire and form;
in the Ulūṣanī River reside the female servants of the kiṃnaras;
and in the Hāsani River dwell the wives of the kiṃnaras.
In the waters of the Aśiviśā River, there are snakes of various colors.
The waters of the Vitastā River are extremely turbid, foul, and impure.
When crossing the Gaṅgā River, one must maintain a mind of courage and vigor.
If crossing the Vaitaraṇī River, the mind must transcend it.
If crossing the Kālānadī River, one should cross with the mouth closed.
When crossing the Cindatārā River, one should sing various songs.
If crossing the Uluḍanā River, the mind must be fixed in right concentration.
When crossing the Hasana River, remain silent and do not speak.
When crossing the Aśvīsā River, one should recite a mantra for warding off poisonous snakes before crossing.
If you cross the Nādanadī River, you must hold a sharp sword in your hand and cut through the creepers to cross.

Once you have thus crossed these rivers, five hundred yakṣas will be guarding the gate that opens; you must exert yourself with diligence and by no means fear them, for this is the city of the Kinnara King.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated at the feet of the seer and departed through the air.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, having pacified the foreign enemies, returned to the city of Na-pu-lo.
At that time, as soon as Sudhana had finished his meditative concentration, he prostrated before his father, the king, and sat down facing him.
The father king then comforted Sudhana with words of affectionate concern.
Sudhana replied, "By the power of my father the King, I have returned in safety; I have subdued that hostile army and brought it entirely under control.
Furthermore, I have taken their precious sons and appointed them as tax collectors, making them pay tribute according to the law."
The father king replied, "My son has performed his duty; all that was to be done is finished.
Then the youth Sudhana took leave of the father king, saying:
"I wish to return to the palace.
His father, the King, told him:
"Stay for a while and eat with me."
He said to his father, the King:
"I have not seen Manoharā for a long time; I now wish to go and see her.
The King said:
"Stay for today!
Tomorrow I shall go to see him.
He then addressed his father, the King, once more:
"I must see Manoharā today.
The father king remained silent and did not respond.
At that time, the prince returned to his own palace and saw that it was devoid of splendor; not seeing Manoharā, he ran hither and thither searching for her, crying out as he went:
"Manoharā! Manoharā! Where are you now?"
The women of the palace gathered together, intending to distract Sudhana; however, his body and mind were as if pierced by arrows, and he focused solely on Manoharā, repeatedly asking again:
"Where is Manoharā?"
At that time, the palace attendants recounted everything as described above.
Upon hearing this, the youth Sudhana was filled with great sorrow and distress.
The attendants said to him, "There is yet another superior one within this palace; we pray you will dispel your grief."
