At that time, Sudhana, realizing that his father the king had acted ungratefully, went immediately to his mother’s side, prostrated at her feet, knelt down, and said:
"O Mother!..."
"I do not see Manoharā now.
Yet, Manoharā is of beautiful and dignified form, endowed with great merit.
Since I do not see her now, my mind is confounded and consumed by longing; I shall search for her in whichever direction she has gone."
"If Manoharā is not here, great suffering and distress will arise.
The mother said,
"I shall release her so that she may go, even if it means facing the hardship of a life-threatening danger for the sake of Manoharā's pleasure."
He asked, "What is this matter?
His mother recounted it in full detail.
Knowing that his father, the king, was ungrateful, Sudhana asked his mother again,
"In which direction did she go?
His mother replied:
"Manoharā is now heading toward this mountain, to the dwelling place of the Rishi Dharma-rāja.
At that moment, Sudhana, weeping out of the anguish of separation from Manoharā, cried out unconsciously: "Manoharā!"
The mother spoke again, saying:
"Within this palace, there are others even more excellent than that;
why are you so distressed? Sudhana replied:
“Mother! I have no affection for these palace women.
His mother comforted and enticed him with kind words, but his affliction increased all the more; he rose quickly to search, running hither and thither, and thought to himself:
"You may inquire further at the place where you obtained it.
He then went to the hunter's location and asked,
"At what place did you first obtain Manoharā?"
The hunter replied, "In those mountains there dwells a rishi.
There is a pond there, and Manoharā used to come to bathe in it; following the instructions of the rishi, I captured and brought her here."
At that time, Sudhana returned to the palace and thought to himself:
"I should now go to the place of the seer to obtain news of him.

Meanwhile, the father-king, having heard that the youth had departed from Manoharā, was overcome with great sorrow and distress; he wished to go into the mountains to the abode of the seer, whereupon the father-king said:
“Sudhana! Why have you become so bewildered as to reach this state?
I shall now provide you with even more excellent palace attendants.”
Having heard this, Sudhana said, "I have no pleasure; I cannot remain in the palace.

At that time, the Great King immediately issued a strict edict, ordering that at all crossroads, city gates, and major thoroughfares, everyone must be seized and detained so that the youth is not allowed to leave the city.
Sudhana was by nature one who reduced his sleep at night, thinking:

"I have heard that five kinds of people reduce their sleep during the night. What are these five? [They are: those who seek the Dharma, those who seek wealth, those who seek a wife, those who seek a son, and those who seek to escape from suffering."
First, a husband thinks of his wife, and a wife thinks of her husband;
second, a wife who has been scolded or rebuked by her husband;
third, a person who has committed robbery.
Fourth, a military general;
fifth, when a bhikṣu practices diligent asceticism.
Of these, I shall now become the first.
At that time, the youth thought to himself:
"If I go out through the gate, my parents will surely punish the gatekeeper.
Having had this thought, he immediately took the flower garland and placed it atop a banner, then departed from there by a place where no one was guarding the entrance.
Upon reaching outside the city at the time when the moon first rose, Sudhana wept toward the moon, longing for Manoharā, and spoke this verse to it:
“The full moon can illuminate the night, And is likewise the king among stars;
The constellation Rohiṇī is as dear as an eye, And is like a great guide.”
"Who has seen Manoharā, whose eyes are like blue lotuses?
Having spoken these words, he proceeded slowly, brooding upon the times of his former dalliances with Manoharā.
Upon encountering a deer or a roe deer, he said to it:
"You constantly feed on water and grass, wandering about without illness; you do not share my suffering.
He then asked:
"Did you see my Manoharā?

Having said this, he proceeded gradually until he reached a certain place where flowers and fruits were in full bloom. There, honeybees were feeding on the nectar atop the blossoms. Sudhana addressed him, saying:
"O one of stainless azure hue, possessing a golden radiance, with a wondrous body of two colors amidst the bamboo grove—have you seen Manoharā?"
Having spoken thus, he continued on his way.
He saw a python and said to it:
"You are a black snake; your tongue is like a tree leaf, and both your gaping mouth and eyes emit smoke and flames."
"I too have a fire of desire just like this, yet I harbor no poisonous heart.
Where do you see my beloved Manoharā?
Having said this, he proceeded to another grove where he saw a hundred-tongued bird (kalaviṅka) producing its beautiful song, and he addressed it:
"You, who are the most honored among all birds and roam amidst the forest trees—do you see her now?
There is a daughter of the Kinnara king named Manoharā, whose eyes and hair are like blue lotuses."
Having spoken thus, he proceeded next to the tree named Aśoka, whose branches were filled with exquisite flowers called Kalyāṇī; it was the king among trees. He addressed it, saying:
"When I remember Manoharā, my heart becomes bewildered and distressed."
"Your name is 'Free from Sorrow' (Aśoka); I now join my palms together, so that I may be free from sorrow.
Due to her mental confusion, she uttered various strange words.
Next, she went to the dwelling of a rishi and praised him, saying:
"Clad in garments of tree bark, always consuming the finest roots—I now prostrate before you, Great Seer Teacher;
I pray that you will quickly inform me of the place where Manoharā dwells.
At that time, the seer addressed Sudhana with words of reassurance:
"Please sit for a moment; first, let me describe what I have seen: his face is like the full moon, his eyes resemble blue lotuses, and his eyebrows are long and slender like the crescent moon.
His appearance is lovely, and all who see him rejoice."
"Furthermore, by eating roots and fruits, you shall later have no afflictions.
They are not difficult to find, so you need have no cause for anxiety.
Having spoken these words, he further addressed Sudhana:
"However, when Manoharā departed, she left this message as an entrustment, leaving behind this finger-ring:
'If Sudhana comes to search for me, you may give him this finger-ring.

Having spoken these words, she further described the perilous road, saying: 'You should inform the youth Sudhana that the path is extremely dangerous and difficult to traverse; he ought to turn back.'"
"If you do not turn back, you must look for the road.
At that time, the seer said to the youth,
"You should know that Manoharā gave this instruction:"
"In this northern region, there are three ranges of Black Mountains; beyond these, there are another three ranges, and yet another three ranges.
Having passed these nine mountains, there is the King of Snow Mountains."

On this mountain there is a medicinal herb; if one gathers it and boils it with clarified butter (sarpis) for consumption, one will be free from hunger and thirst, possess abundant physical strength, and have a nature such that mindfulness is stabilized.
Furthermore, one may capture a monkey and follow wherever it goes, maintaining control over it through the power of mantra.
Furthermore, take your bow and arrows, as well as the *vidyā-ratna* (luminous jewel) combined with *agada* fragrant medicines, which can cure snake venom.
Also carry three iron nails and a lute (*vīṇā*).

To the north of the King of Snow Mountains (*Himavat*) there is a green mountain; you shall go there and report to Sudhana that you possess great power, and you must transcend and destroy all those evil beings.
"Explain it in detail as previously stated, and perform it according to the sequence.

When Sudhana had heard the seer’s instructions, he followed them exactly as told, performing the rites in order, reciting the medicinal incantations, prostrating at the seer’s feet, and then withdrawing.
"All that was required has already been prepared; only the monkey remains missing.
He returned to the place of the seer, who immediately gave him the monkey. At that time, the seer again addressed Sudhana:
"You are all alone, without a companion; why do you need to labor so hard to seek out that Manoharā?"
"You shall certainly lose your life.
Sudhana replied, "I must find him by all means;
when the moon travels through the sky, who is its companion?"
It is also like the king of beasts, who, by the power of his fangs and claws, has no companion;
fire can burn him—whom could he have as a companion?
Even though I have no companion, what need is there for protection?
If one sees the great ocean, should one not enter it immediately?
If one is bitten by a venomous snake, should one not seek medical treatment?
Indeed, a person of great stature applies themselves with diligent effort to their tasks.
"If the task is not accomplished, no one shall be at fault.

At that time, Sudhana followed the instructions of Manoharā and, by means of various medicinal herbs and incantations, passed through all the treacherous mountains and rivers until he reached the city of the Kinnara King.

At that time, Sudhana saw from afar that city, which was exceptionally sublime and wondrous; all its gardens and groves were lush and beautiful, filled with various exquisite flowers, diverse birds, and flowing ponds and canals.
Furthermore, he saw immeasurable kinnarī maidens coming together to fetch water.
At that time, Sudhana asked the women,
"For what purpose do you fetch this water?"
He replied:
"The princess is named Manoharā; having recently been among humans, her body is stained with human odors, and she wishes to wash her body with water to remove that scent."
Sudhana asked the woman again:
"Is this water poured out for bathing all at once,
or is it given to you in succession, one after another?"
The woman replied,
"I pour them out in succession.
Sudhana then thought to himself:
"I have now found a favorable opportunity; I shall place this auspicious finger-ring inside a water jar to send a message to Manoharā.
Sudhana then silently cast the finger-ring into a water jar and said to the girl, "Use this water to first offer for the princess's bath."
At that time, the kinnarī thought to herself,
"There must surely be a reason for this," and immediately poured water before him.
The princess bathed her head, but a finger-ring fell onto her body.
At that moment, Manoharā called to the girl and asked:
"When you brought the water, who else was there?"
He replied,
"I saw a man," and described his appearance in full detail.
However, Rāmañjanī recognized that this was Sudhana; she had him quickly hide away, using skillful means to lead him inside so that no one would see him.
Following her instructions, he was brought there and concealed in a certain place.
Manoharā went to her father the king, knelt down for a long time, and said: "Father!
If you see Sudhana, what would you wish to do?"
The father king replied:
"Cut him into a hundred pieces and divide them into four heaps.
Since he is already a human being, what use could there be for him?"
Manoharā spoke again to the king,
saying, "If this were a human being, how could they have reached this place?
When the father-king heard this, his anger was finally appeased, and he said:
"If the youth comes here, you may give him all manner of ornaments, bestow upon him abundant wealth and treasures, as well as a thousand kinnarī maidens, and offer up even your own body."

At that time, having heard these words, Manoharā was filled with great joy; her delight pervaded her entire body, and she immediately ordered Sudhana to dress in fine garments and come to see the father king.

At that time, the Kinnara King saw Sudhana from afar; his human marks were fully perfected, his appearance was dignified and handsome, and he was pleasing to behold, which caused the King to feel wonder and astonishment.
Wishing to test his skills, they set up a great golden pillar seven *tāla* trees high;
they also placed seven drums and seven *xuan* (mystical) heights.
This youth Sudhana was, in fact, a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva is such that there is no skillful art or craft they do not understand, whatever they undertake, even the devas will assist them and create no obstacles.
Thereupon, before the king, they arranged a great offering:
they blew flutes, plucked kīṇaras, and played vīṇās, performing various kinds of music and artistic skills;
the devas in the sky also all joined in to assist.
At that time, the youth Sudhana held a great sword in his hand, its color like a blue lotus and its brilliance dazzling.

Before the king’s palace stood many *tāla* pillars; the king commanded Sudhana to cut these pillars with his sword, and he did so until they were as shattered as *khatvārī* leaves or crushed like sesame seeds. With his arrow, he pierced through a golden pillar, seven drums, and seven *emaga*, passing through them all.
His body remained as immovable and unshakable as Mount Sumeru, while the devas and kinnaras in the sky all let out great roars.

At that time, the Kinnara King, having seen and heard such a rare and extraordinary event, was greatly astonished. He immediately ordered one thousand kinnara maidens to be adorned so that their physical forms and facial features were exactly like those of Manoharā.
The King said to Sudhana, "Do you know who this Manoharā is?"
Then Sudhana immediately uttered words of truth and spoke this verse:
“Manoharā is a tree-nymph, whom I now hold most dear;
By the power of these words of truth, may she walk forward with slow steps.”
At that moment, Manoharā unconsciously took a single step forward. The assembly of kinnaras said to the Great King:

"This Sudhana possesses human power and transcendent diligence; he is endowed with a noble form and is a fitting match for Manoharā. Why must you press him so harshly and not give him Manoharā to take away?"
At that time, the assembly of kinnaras addressed the king in succession, saying, "Let her be given to Manoharā.
The king then issued a command; according to the custom of the kinnaras, he took the girl with his left hand and held a golden pitcher in his right hand, declaring:
"O youth! This beloved daughter, together with a thousand kinnarī maidens as her attendants and retinue, shall be given to you as a reward to be your wife.
The king said:
"A person should never be ungrateful; one must never abandon [a benefactor], nor should one ever take another wife.
Having heard the king's instruction, Sudhana immediately returned with Manoharā to their own palace, where they engaged in play, merriment, and music.
At a later time, Sudhana again thought of his family and the separation from his parents; filled with sorrow and distress, he discussed this matter with Manoharā.
"What do you wish to do?
Manoharā then informed her father,
the king, who said:
"Let it be as you wish; go together with Sudhana, but do not err in your conduct, for many people are deceitful and fraudulent.
Having thus issued his admonitions and instructions, the father king provided him with gold, silver, pearls, and various other miscellaneous treasures as provisions for his journey.
At that time, by the power of the kinnara, Sudhana returned swiftly to the city of Napura.
As he entered the city, various fragrances produced by the kinnaras filled the entire city.

When the King, his father, heard that Sudhana had arrived, he issued an edict to prepare various musical instruments, to sweep and sprinkle the city, and to remove all tiles, stones, gravel, and debris so that everything was made fresh and clean; he ordered the playing of music, the hanging of silken banners and canopies, the burning of various famous incenses, and the scattering of exquisite flowers.
Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of attendants, Sudhana entered the city of Napura. Having rested there, he took various precious jewels and went to his father, the king.
After prostrating at the king's feet, he sat before him and related in detail all that had transpired regarding the kinnaras, as previously described.
"At that time, the father-king, recognizing that his power was foremost and transcendent, immediately conferred upon him the consecration and established him on the throne.
Then Sudhana thought to himself:
'It is because I am husband to Manoharā that I have now succeeded to the consecrated royal throne; I know for myself that through past causes and conditions, I have obtained such a reward of merit.'"
"I must now practice giving even more extensively than in the past and perform various meritorious deeds.
Having formed this thought, within twelve years in the city of Hāstinapura, he established a hall for sacrifices according to the local customs.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Do not harbor any other thought regarding the one named the youth Sudhana at that time; it was my own body.
At that time, while practicing the bodhisattva path, I was known as King Sudhana."
For the sake of Manoharā, I exerted supreme diligence and power;
having finally seen her, I established a sacrificial hall for twelve years and performed offerings according to the Dharma.

"How could I realize unsurpassed bodhi through this merit of giving alone? Rather, it is by further cultivating other meritorious deeds, by accumulating roots of goodness, and through the causal conditions of right faith that one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete bodhi."
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, Great King,
for the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi, I practiced the giving of wisdom and performed various meritorious deeds."

"Great King, listen attentively! In the distant past, there was a king in the city of Vaiśālī named Vaiśravaṇa-mitra. He had duly ascended the throne and governed the world according to the Dharma. The people of that kingdom were prosperous, joyful, and at peace; it was free from all forms of deception, theft, and pestilence. Cattle, sheep, rice, and sugarcane abounded everywhere."
That king possessed true faith and was able to benefit both himself and others; he cherished his people and regarded them with a heart of loving-kindness.
Later, on another occasion, he sported with his queen, and before long, she became pregnant.
When ten months had passed, a son was born, whose appearance was dignified and handsome, endowed with all the auspicious marks, and pleasing to behold.
A birth feast was held, and as they deliberated on giving him a name, they said:
"This is Prince Viśvāmitra; he should be named Viśvantara."
He was entrusted to eight nurses, as described in detail elsewhere.

Like a lotus in water, he grew rapidly; he was then sent to school, where he mastered arithmetic, calculation, crafts and arts, the affairs of statecraft, horse-riding, and various marks and signs, all of which he accomplished, as described in detail elsewhere.

At that time, the prince was by nature virtuous and good, possessing a truly pure mind; he benefited both himself and others, his heart was always filled with compassion, and he cherished all people of the world, being able to practice every form of giving without exception.

Having heard that he constantly practiced giving, his mind was without interruption; regardless of distance, all those who were poor and destitute came to beg, and to every seeker he gave until their hearts were satisfied.
However, at a later time, the Bodhisattva desired to go out to observe and enjoy himself in the pleasure groves; his body was adorned with necklaces of the seven precious jewels.
Furthermore, he wore deerskin upon his person, mounted a palanquin, and proceeded swiftly while great drums and music were beaten, intending to enter the park.
At that time, there was a brahmin who praised the prince, saying:
"O kṣatriya youth, you possess great and supreme power.
He then spoke this verse:
"A vast multitude of people has gathered; you, O Benevolent One, possess great renown.
This palanquin should be given as a gift, bestowed upon one worthy of receiving such a gift."
At that time, the prince felt great joy in his heart; he quickly descended and gave this precious carriage to the brahmin, speaking these verses:
"I have originally renounced this carriage, Giving it away with a joyful heart;
May I likewise renounce the three realms And swiftly realize sublime Bodhi."
"Furthermore, at another time, the prince went out of the city to wander through the gardens and groves. He rode a white elephant adorned with jewels, which was like a white lotus;
it was also like a snow-mountain elephant, possessing various superior marks;
and it was like the elephant of Śakra, its physical form adorned by its own excellent characteristics, with its merits clearly manifest."
The elephant grew day by day, becoming the most excellent among all elephants;
the Prince, surrounded by his friends and kinsmen, was like the full moon encircled by the stars.

As the season of spring arrives, the hundred plants flourish and bloom; in the lush forests and clear ponds, flowers and birds reflect one another’s beauty. Peacocks, parrots, geese, wild ducks, and mandarin ducks—these various species warble their plaintive songs as they fly together in flocks, blending their voices in harmony.

At that time, there was a king of a bordering state who, knowing the prince was wandering in a fragrant garden with his court ladies, moving about from place to place, joyfully sporting and delighting in the practice of giving,
sent a brahmin to come quickly and beg for the elephant.
The brahmin went to where the prince was and, employing elegant and beautiful words, spoke this verse:
"O Deva-manava, your renown for excellent giving has spread beautifully in all directions;
now is the very time to give me the elephant upon which you ride."
At that time, having heard these words, the prince’s heart was immediately filled with joy; he quickly descended from the elephant and offered it as a gift.
He then made a vow in verse, saying:
“May I, by giving up this elephant And joyfully bestowing it upon a brahmin, [Attain the supreme enlightenment].”
"Thus renouncing the three realms, he swiftly realized sublime enlightenment.
At that time, the ministers came to report to the king:
"The enemy state of the outer borders has sent a brahmin to beg for the prince’s most excellent elephant; it has now been given to him."
Upon hearing this, the Great King was filled with extreme rage; he immediately summoned the prince and rebuked him in various ways, ordering him to leave the country.
Having heard his father’s reproach, the prince reflected thus and spoke these verses:
"I practice the conduct of a Bodhisattva, Gathering in suffering sentient beings with loving-kindness."
Having donned the firm armor, one should renounce this most excellent elephant;
all things within the home should be given as offerings according to one's ability;
one must resolutely practice in the forest of ascetic training with a focused mind.
"Having abandoned the home life to practice austerities, one should go to the forest of ascetic discipline;
if one does not speak such words, how could there be any giving to others?
After the Bodhisattva had spoken these words, he went to his consort's side and said to her:
"O Worthy One!
You must give away all your wealth and possessions.
You should enter the mountain forests and practice asceticism."
Everything was as previously described.
Upon hearing this, his wife, fearing the sorrow of separation from the prince, joined her palms and said:
"O virtuous son!
"May my body, whether male or female, likewise follow you to dwell in the mountain forests to practice the Way; I cannot bear to be separated from you for even a single thought-moment.
She replied to the Prince with these sublime verses:
"As the snow without the moon, As the great earth without its crops;"
"As a forest parched by drought is without water, so too is a wife without her husband.
The Bodhisattva replied, "We shall certainly be separated; in all the world, there must inevitably be parting."
How much more so for you, a woman, whose physical form is naturally delicate and soft, and who requires fine and exquisite food, drink, and bedding.
Yet here in the Forest of Suffering, there is only grass spread upon the ground; you must subsist on roots and fruits, and use the leaves of that very forest to clothe your body.
The wife said:
"Worthy son!
Though I hear of this suffering, my mind does not waver."
The Bodhisattva replied, "Regarding this vow,
you must constantly keep it in mind and never forget it.
At that time, the prince went to his father the King, prostrated himself with palms joined, and addressed him in verse:
"May my father forgive my transgression in giving this elephant to that brahmin;
because of this reproach, I shall depart for the forest, and may your treasuries always increase."

At that time, having heard these words, the Great King’s voice cracked and he choked with sobs; unable to bear the suffering of separation, he embraced the prince’s neck and spoke with words of affection:
“I pray you, my son, turn back and stay; do not practice such extensive giving anymore.”
The Bodhisattva replied in verse:
"Even if the great earth and its mountains were to turn back, and even if my own body,
wife, and servants were to be given away, this mind would never change."
When the prince had finished speaking these words, he knelt to take his leave of the King his father, surrounded by his wives, children, and retinue.
All the people within the city were deeply distressed and escorted the Crown Prince out of the city.
A hundred thousand attendants, all riding in carriages and litters, followed the Prince as he was escorted out of the city to the Forest of Austerities.
At that time, a certain man, hearing the multitude in the city wailing all at once, asked in wonder:
"What is this sound of weeping?"
The people replied,
"You should know that this prince of the city, Sudhana, has been banished from the realm.
However, it is the prince's very nature to delight in giving."
"The Great King has punished me and now wishes for me to enter the mountain forests;
because of this, the people within the city are weeping.
At that time, the Prince, bidding farewell according to the Dharma, addressed the people with these verses:
"Though all those one loves dwell together for a long time, When the time comes and life ends, they must part.
Like birds perching for a night beneath a tree before flying away, So it is with wives, children, and all kinsmen."
You should know that such is the nature of phenomena: In this world, there is always the sorrow of parting.
You must once again devote yourselves single-mindedly to your tasks, Abiding immovably like Mount Sumeru.
At that time, as the prince traveled gradually some thirty li or more from the city, a brahmin came and addressed him:
"Kṣatriya!..."
"Therefore, after leaving the city, I have traveled more than thirty li.
He then addressed the prince with these verses:
"I have come here because I heard your fame for generosity; On this road, I am utterly exhausted."
"Desiring to fulfill the original vow of giving, I pray that you may swiftly realize sublime Bodhi.
At that time, having heard these words, the prince’s consort uttered words she could not bear, replying in verse:
"You are an extremely wicked Brahmin; though you were cast out into the mountain forests, you still would not leave."
"Please show us at least a little compassion; it was because of this that the Prince lost his position.
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to the Queen:
"O Fair One!"
"Do not speak harsh and evil words to the brāhmaṇa.
A verse says:
"If there were no such seekers of wealth, where else would there be those who realize bodhi?"
"Among the six perfections, generosity is supreme; by practicing these six from this point on, one realizes enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva felt great joy in his heart and immediately gave the chariot to the brahmin, speaking in verse:
"I have broken the flow of my stinginess and anger; I give this chariot to the brahmin."
"Just as the Great Sage turned [the wheel], he attained the realization of the untainted Dharma.

At that time, having given away his carriage, the prince felt great joy in his heart; taking his sons and daughters in his arms, he proceeded gradually until he reached the distant forest of asceticism.
Having arrived at the forest, he practiced asceticism with a joyful body and mind.
Later, on another occasion, after his consort had gone into the mountain valleys to gather flowers and fruits, [he remained there].
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing the Bodhisattva in the forest of asceticism, transformed himself into a brahmin in order to test the Bodhisattva and addressed the prince, saying:
"O most eminent Kṣatriya youth, please listen to my words."
He then spoke this verse in praise:
"O handsome son of noble lineage, dwelling alone in the mountains and forests;
bring back quickly the son and daughter you love and offer them to me."
When the brahmin had finished speaking these words, the prince, out of love for his son, remained there reflecting for a moment.
The brahmin spoke to him again: “Kṣatriya!
I have heard your reputation that you are able to give all things and grant everything to those who seek it.
I pray that you will bestow your two children upon me.
Why delay? Do not hesitate.
And he spoke in verse:
"On earth and in the sky, All have heard that you delight in giving;
You should now quickly relinquish it, To fulfill the heart's desire of me who seeks it."
At that time, the Bodhisattva replied:
"Even if I were to sacrifice my own body, I would not begrudge it; how much less so in giving up my son and daughter?
As I reflect now, I have a further private thought."
He immediately took his children and gave them to the brahmin, speaking in verse:
"I now renounce these children so that I may dwell happily in the mountain forests;
I did not consult with my mother, which has given rise to resentment and the suffering of grief."
"Do not let people speak ill of me; the youth’s resolve is firm.
He would rather abandon his son than his own body, for he fears the censure of others. The Brahmin said:
"Kṣatriya youth! This is not so.
You were born into a royal lineage, renowned throughout the great earth; you have compassion for sentient beings and constantly practice benevolent giving."

Furthermore, he gave fragrant elephants as alms to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; toward all who were poor, destitute, or lowly, he was always able to provide for them, satisfying those who sought his aid so that none passed away empty-handed.
Since I have come from afar, let it not be in vain.
Swiftly tame the horse of your mind; do not retreat or give rise to divergent thoughts, so that my quest may not pass away empty-handed.
At that time, having heard the words of the brahmin, the Bodhisattva reflected again; his mind was bewildered by love for his son, and he spoke in verse:
"I now take my beloved son And give him as a gift to the brahmin;
That he has given rise to such suffering Is entirely due to separation from what is loved."
"If I do not give this away now, there will be no way for my ascetic practices to be perfected.
It would be better to undergo this separation; I must ensure that his quest is fulfilled.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, with single-minded resolve, determined to renounce it, and spoke these verses:
"In this great ocean of suffering among humans, all sentient beings are submerged;
since it is extremely difficult to cross over, I vow to become a boat and a raft."
When the Bodhisattva had finished speaking, his countenance was serene and joyful; with his right hand he took the boy and with his left hand he held the girl, bestowing them upon the brahmin.
At that moment, the eyes of the boy and girl were filled with tears as they wept and choked with grief.
After the Bodhisattva has given, he further makes this vow:
"By virtue of my giving away my son and daughter, may I proceed directly upon the path to Bodhi;
I vow to rescue all sentient beings and swiftly transcend the ocean of birth and death."
“At that time, after the Bodhisattva had given away his children and spoken these words, the great earth shook in six ways.
Because of this earthquake, all those practicing tranquility within the mountain forests were struck with alarm and said to one another:
‘What is the cause and condition for this shaking of the earth?’”
At that time, there was a seer of the Vasiṣṭha lineage who was skilled in divination and physiognomy. He addressed the other seers, saying:
“The young child in the forest ate fruit and drank water; Seeing him brought joy to the hearts of the multitude.
Seeking deliverance from the ocean of suffering, The Bodhisattva has abandoned his son, and the great earth trembles.”
At that time, when the two sons learned that their father had given them away to the brahmin, they wept with choked sobs and prostrated at their father’s feet. Joining their palms, they said:
"We have not seen our mother, And now she is being given away to him;
We pray for a brief leave-taking from our compassionate mother, To follow our father as he gives us to another."
At that time, out of deep affection, the Bodhisattva’s eyes filled with tears; he embraced his children around the neck and addressed them in verse:
“My heart feels great love for you, It is not that I lack a firm and compassionate mind;
For the sake of benefiting humans and devas, I joyfully renounce and give you away.”
For the sake of the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi, I seek to realize the state of nirvāṇa’s peace and bliss;
to uproot all sentient beings from the ocean of suffering, I vow to save them so they may be freed from the misery of saṃsāra.
At that time, the two sons, knowing their father was determined to give them away, made a sobbing sound and, with palms joined, said:
"Father, you are now determined to abandon us and give us to another."
When my mother arrives, please say on our behalf:
"In the presence of our parents, we beg for their forgiveness.
We were young, foolish, and ignorant."
"I have committed many transgressions; at times my speech was disrespectful and lacking in reverence. These are many faults, and I pray you will grant me your forgiveness.

Having spoken thus, he prostrated at his father's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and followed after him as they walked away gradually, reflecting on his father’s words while frequently looking back.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva, out of longing for his son, spoke words of compassionate love; he then returned to the grass hut and immediately made the great vow for unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, when the son departed, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and all the devas in the sky raised their voices and spoke these verses:
'The Great Being gives with resolute intent; He shall surely accomplish the unsurpassed task. "
"I shall give away my sons and renounce my daughters, remaining firm in heart without retreat.
When the devas had spoken these words, the mother, carrying roots and fruits intending to return home, again saw the earth tremble and increased her pace even more hurriedly.

At that time, a certain deva transformed himself into a lioness and guarded a vital pass, not allowing anyone to pass, fearing it would obstruct the Bodhisattva’s work of benefiting others as he practiced giving for the sake of all sentient beings.
The consort said to her mother, Siṃhī:
“You are the wife of the king of beasts; for what reason do you block the road?
If I am chaste toward my husband, I pray that you quickly clear the way.”
"You are the wife of the king of beasts, and I am the consort of the king of men;
according to the Dharma, we are sisters. Quickly make way for me!
At that moment, the lion resumed his original celestial form and immediately stepped aside to let her pass.
Seeing these evil omens, the consort reflected for a moment:
"Just as there are celestial deities and spirits, and as there are sounds from within the forest, there must be some calamity, anomaly, or inauspicious event occurring at my dwelling."
He then spoke in verse:
"My eyes now twitch, and the strange bird utters a strange cry;
there must surely be the suffering of parting, as to whether my son now lives or has perished."
"Furthermore, seeing the great earth tremble, my body and mind became even more unsettled;
I shall surely lose my two children, and my grief burns like fire.

Having experienced these various evil omens, he wished to go to his dwelling place; looking about everywhere, he did not see his two children, and his heart became bewildered as he searched for them in every direction.
Then he thought to himself:
"I should enjoy myself with the various insects and birds in another place, or perhaps I should sleep within the chamber.
He first went into the chamber and, seeing only the Prince, joined his palms and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Where are those young boys now?
The Bodhisattva replied,
"A certain brāhmaṇa came and begged from me."
"However, young man, please follow along with that person and rejoice.
At that time, having heard this, the compassionate mother fell to the ground in a faint, like a beast struck by a poisoned arrow;
she writhed in agony like a fish out of water.
It was also like a cow that had lost its calf, wailing with an unceasing sound of grief, as she spoke this verse:
"My child’s face was like a flower, And his hands were softer than lotus petals;
Never having experienced suffering before, Where has my beloved child gone now?"
You always played together with the young beasts, your nature as straightforward as that of a deer;
where is my son now?
Who has taken you to be their servant?
Choking with sobs, I followed you; weeping, my body endured suffering.
As you departed and I could no longer see you, who would have known the pain of parting from one born to us?
Within these mountain forests, you always fed upon flowers, fruits, and roots.
Having endured hunger and cold while serving others, you now encounter this bitter calamity.
Having abandoned your parents and severed ties with your kin, you are estranged from your circle of relatives;
all this is due to that wicked man, who has caused you, my son, to suffer such hardship.
Born into the kṣatriya caste, whom do you serve now?
Day and night you are driven about, constantly entangled and oppressed by manifold sufferings.
Due to the evil karma of the past, you have caused sentient beings to experience the pain of separation from those they love.
If I have always spoken words of truth, May all sentient beings give rise to equanimity.
By virtue of this vow of truth, May we never again be separated in life after life;
I pray only that my two sons may escape their lowly state And swiftly realize the fruit of nirvana’s peace and bliss.
At that time, the compassionate mother, seeing the trees her son had planted, was overcome with further grief and distress; she embraced the trees and wept, speaking again:
"These groves and medicinal herbs were all tended by my son’s own hands;
While the groves and flowers flourish alone, Only I and you are both withered and parched."
"Furthermore, as he proceeded gradually, he saw the cubs of various beasts. Moved by compassion, he spoke to them, saying:
'You used to play constantly with your cubs, your joy and affection never ceasing;
where have your cubs gone now?'"
“Seeking him out in distress.

Then the Prince’s wife, looking about in the direction where her son had gone, saw that the mountain cliffs were steep and precipitous and the path was impassable for human travel. She wept even more bitterly and addressed her in verse:
“Driven away by whips and staves, Along a path of steep and precipitous mountain cliffs;”
Driven forward by oppression, the brahmin lacks compassion;
choked with sobs, his throat is broken, and as he cries out, blood gushes from his chest.
Like a startled beast fleeing in terror, how can his feet, so weak, carry him along?
At that time, seeing them weeping incessantly in grief and distress, the Bodhisattva immediately employed various skillful means to exhort and console them, speaking in verse:
“I have no heart of anger, And thus I give away my two children;
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I relinquish what is difficult to relinquish.”
My son and my retinue, though difficult to relinquish, have now been forsaken;
they shall attain the fruit of a Great Being, the unsurpassed and sublime Bodhi.
I now vow to abandon my son for the sake of seeking liberation.
"The chariot, the carriage, along with my wife and children, I give to all people.
When his wife heard the Bodhisattva’s words, her mind became firm and steadfast; she joined her palms and said to the Bodhisattva:
"I have no obstructive intent; do not harbor any other thought."
If you wish to give me away as an offering, do so according to your will without harboring any doubt.
Severing my affection and abandoning my kinsmen, I seek Bodhi through this supreme vow;
may my aspirations be fulfilled, that I might deliver and rescue the masses who are lost in delusion.

At that time, Śakra, King of the Devas, felt a sense of wonder and marvel. Yet, because the Bodhisattva was diligently practicing austerities with the intent to bring about cessation and establish [the path], Śakra, during the night, surrounded by immeasurable devas before and behind him, arrived at the place where the Bodhisattva resided and remained suspended in the air. He illuminated the mountains and forests until they were brilliantly radiant and all-encompassing in their great light, and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"The people of the world are ignorant, deluded, and self-deranged."
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had finished speaking these words, he further thought to himself:
"However, the Bodhisattva has a consort who provides for him, serves him, and relies upon him; were she not there, it would be exceedingly arduous."
"I too must employ skillful means to seek her out.
Having formed this thought, he went to the Bodhisattva's side, transformed himself into a brahmin, and said to the Bodhisattva:
"Your wife is endowed with all auspicious marks, and her will is chaste toward her husband."
"Holding the hand of a maiden of noble lineage, you may bestow her upon a brāhmaṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s wife replied:
"A shameless man of great greed; such a brāhmaṇa is base and inferior."
"By habitually practicing what is contrary to the Dharma, you have destroyed my heart of purity.
At that time, the Bodhisattva gazed upon her with a compassionate mind, and his wife replied:
"I do not cherish this body, nor do I seek pleasure for myself;"
"If I follow him away, who will be able to serve you?
The Bodhisattva replied, "I cherish you deeply;
however, for the sake of seeking the inexhaustible Dharma, you should follow my wish and pursue this man."
"Even if you go away, my life shall surely end; nevertheless, I must make a vow to practice giving.
Having said this, he was filled with joy and reflected to himself:
"This is the final time I relinquish my wife; my mind is free from attachment and bondage."
He then took his wife by the hand and gave her to the brahmin, saying:
“You must provide for this venerable person with single-minded devotion; she is upright in heart and disciplined in conduct.
I love this wife most dearly and hold her in high esteem; O brahmin, I pray you, accept her with compassion.”
"At that time, as the prince was about to abandon his wife for the sake of seeking Bodhi, the earth shook in six ways; his wife, with a choked voice, followed after the brahmin."
Having lost both her son and daughter, and now being separated from her virtuous husband, suffering upon suffering arose and grief and poison缠繞 (bound) her heart. She spoke these verses:
"I previously committed such karma, Which has continued perpetually since beginningless time;
Like the pain of a cow losing its calf, My suffering exceeds even that!"
After the prince’s wife had spoken these words, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, restored himself to his original form and said to her:
"I am not a human, nor am I a brahmin."
"I am Śakra, Lord of the Devas, capable of subduing the asuras; it is for the sake of fulfilling the Bodhisattva’s great vow and unsurpassed bodhi, and out of compassion for sentient beings.
When the Bodhisattva’s wife heard these words from Śakra, Lord of the Devas, she leaped for joy with great delight, joined her palms, and said:
"O Lord of the Devas, may my son be freed from this state of servitude."
"To create a virtuous cause and condition, I shall send her to the presence of the King, her father.
Having spoken this verse, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, approached the Bodhisattva; holding his wife with his left hand, he said to him:
"I give this wife back to you; may she serve and attend to you as you wish."
"Please do not give this away to others, nor accept it as a trust to be used for other purposes.
At that time, Śakra, having deluded the two sons whom the brahmin was leading, caused them to head toward the kingdom of the Bodhisattva’s father-king.
However, the brahmins usually avoided that country; yet, because of Śakra, they unknowingly arrived in that city and began selling the king’s grandsons.
When the ministers within the city saw the king’s grandsons, they addressed the king, saying:
“We have seen the king’s grandsons—both the sons’ grandsons and the daughters’ grandsons.”
"Follow this Brahmin and sell him here in this city.
Upon hearing this, the king’s heart was stifled with distress and he fell into confusion; after a long while he regained his composure, and the king then commanded his attendants, saying:
"You all must go and bring him here immediately!"
"The ministers were about to arrive as commanded.
At that time, one minister came forward carrying the child and went directly to see the Great King.
Upon seeing his grandson’s body emaciated and weak, covered in extraordinary filth, and his clothes in tatters, the king fainted and fell to the ground."
The ministers assisted him in sitting up, and he spoke again to them, saying:
"Even while dwelling in the mountain forests, I have always delighted in practicing generosity;
you should quickly summon my son and his new bride."
At that time, Śakra, having paid homage to the Bodhisattva, withdrew and returned to his own palace.
All the people within the kingdom went to entreat the Bodhisattva to return to their own country and establish him as king in his native land.

At that time, that Bodhisattva was fully endowed with all forms of giving; to whatever śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the solitary, or friends and relatives came to beg, he gave everything to them, cultivating immeasurable meritorious deeds, and spoke these verses:
"For those seeking the state of a Bodhisattva, I am able to give extensively;
To kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, śūdras, and others."
Gold, silver, rare treasures, and various necklaces;
slaves and attendants—these he gave to those who uphold the precepts.
His wives and children, as well, he offered in service to the brahmins.
"This person shall receive their reward in this life and in future lives.
At that time, the Buddha said to the Great King:

"O Great King, he who at that time was known as King Viśvantara, who was able to bestow various kinds of gifts upon all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, beggars, friends, and kinsmen, and who cultivated immeasurable meritorious deeds—O Great King!"
Do not harbor any other thought; it was I myself who was that person.
At that time, I was able to practice giving, cultivate immeasurable meritorious deeds, and resolve upon the aspiration for unexcelled bodhi.
"Great King!
It is not by the power of this gift alone that one realizes bodhi;
rather, it is through my right faith, the accumulation of roots of goodness, the causal conditions of merit, and the further cultivation of immeasurable blessings that one realizes bodhi."
"Furthermore, Great King!
For the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi, I practice giving and cultivate various meritorious deeds.
Great King!"

In the distant past, in the great city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta who duly succeeded to the throne. He governed the world according to the Dharma; the population was flourishing and the land was prosperous and joyful. There were no deceits, thieves, or plagues, and cattle, sheep, rice, and sugarcane abounded everywhere.
At another time, the physiognomists and diviners predicted that for twelve years within this realm there would be a severe drought.
Thereupon, Brahmadatta beat the drum and proclaimed by edict:
"Let all people throughout the kingdom be universally informed and made aware."
The physiognomists have predicted that for twelve years there will be no rain and a severe drought.
If you all possess provisions sufficient for twelve years, you may remain;
if not, you should go to places where food and drink are abundant, and return to this territory when the harvests are plentiful again.

At that time, there was a householder in the city named Sthapati who was exceedingly wealthy and possessed vast riches; his enjoyments and various precious treasures, as well as his cattle, sheep, rice, and sugarcane, were so abundant and extensive that he was like King Vaiśravaṇa.
However, having heard the king’s command, the elder immediately ordered the person in charge of the treasury, saying: "Good man!
Do you know whether there are twelve years' worth of provisions within my storehouse?"
The keeper of the storehouse replied,
"There is. The elder, together with his kinsmen, then settled there with a peaceful mind.
As for the rest of the people who could not provide for their own sustenance, they all returned to the land of abundance.
If no Buddha were to appear in the world, there would instead be Pratyekabuddhas dwelling among humanity, out of compassion for those sentient beings who are impoverished.
At that time, a Pratyekabuddha was dwelling in a forest in the wilderness, where he was worthy of offerings from the people.
Later, on one occasion, there were five hundred Pratyekabuddhas residing in one part of Vārāṇasī, and in another part, there were another five hundred Pratyekabuddhas living.
At that time, five hundred pratyekabuddhas, at the hour of eating, took their alms bowls and went to the house of the householder Sthapati to beg for food.
These pratyekabuddhas addressed the householder, saying:
"Are you able, for twelve years, to provide meals as offerings for these five hundred renunciants?"
The householder replied, "Wait;
I must first consult the person in charge of the storehouse.
The householder then questioned the storekeeper, saying:
"O Noble Sir!
Is there sufficient food for my retinue and five hundred renunciants to suffice for twelve years?
He replied:
"Yes," he replied.
Thereupon, the elder invited the Pratyekabuddha and provided him with food and offerings for twelve years.
After the meal was finished and the Pratyekabuddha had departed, five hundred other Pratyekabuddhas came to the elder’s house and said:
"Would it be possible for you to provide food and cakes for five hundred of us who have gone forth for twelve years?
The householder replied,
"Noble ones!"
"We have already been invited once; why trouble yourself to come again?
The Pratyekabuddhas replied to the elder, "Those who came previously were others; we have only just arrived."
He replied:
"Venerable One!
Please wait while I ask the keeper of the storehouse."
The elder informed the steward, saying: "Good man!
Will the provisions we supply for all our kinsmen and the renunciants be sufficient for twelve years?"
He replied, "It is sufficient. Thereupon,
the elder invited five hundred pratyekabuddhas, together with the previous five hundred, and provided them with offerings of cakes and food for twelve years.
The householder asked again:
"Venerable One!
At what time each day do you eat?"
The Pratyekabuddhas replied,
"We always eat at the hour of midday. Thereupon,
the elder immediately constructed a dwelling place and, every day at the appointed time, invited a thousand Pratyekabuddhas to the monastery for a meal.
However, the householder asked the Pratyekabuddha:
"Noble One!
During this time of famine, when will it rain?"
He replied, "It may now rain.
The elder spoke again, saying:
"May I now plant my seeds?
He replied, "As you wish."
Once the householder had received this truthful account, everything he possessed was brought out and offered.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, observed these events and thought to himself:
"This man has made offerings to a thousand pratyekabuddhas; this is the most supreme among all gifts, and no gift surpasses it."
"I must assist the householder Saṃtarpaka in accomplishing his merit.
Having formed this thought, Śakra, King of the Devas, sent down a rain from the heavens at that very moment, whereby the sown seeds were transformed into gourds.
The farmers came and asked the Pratyekabuddha: "Noble One!
The seeds we sowed have grown into stalks that are all gourds; we do not understand how this can be."
He replied, "You need only irrigate.
The man then departed and irrigated according to the proper season; consequently, flowers and fruits grew, each flower and fruit being as large as a gourd or a large water jar.
The cultivator reported this matter once again, and the Noble One said:
"Do not damage it prematurely; when the time comes, it will open of its own accord.
Later, when it had ripened, the fruit split open spontaneously.
According to their respective kinds, the city became filled with inhabitants; famine was naturally dispelled and it transformed into a land of abundance.
People from all places came to take refuge in Vārāṇasī; even those who had fled far away to avoid the famine returned to this city.
At that time, the elder constantly provided fragrant and delicious food and drink as offerings to a thousand noble Pratyekabuddhas,
and spoke these verses: “Those whose minds are wise and awakened, Whose bodies and speech are likewise serene—
To such as these, the stainless ones worthy of offerings, I constantly give.”
Possessing supernormal powers and transformations, Stately and of renowned fame;
The food of those who are fearless, And the joy of body and retinue—
These are bestowed upon those worthy of offerings, Who are fully endowed with the observance of pure precepts.
"The karma of peace and happiness that has been sown, In this world as well as in the world to come.
*The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda* (Volume 14) *The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*
Fascicle Fifteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Command.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Great King:

"Great King, at that time, when the householder Saṭṭha provided sustenance for a thousand noble paccekabuddhas during twelve years of famine and drought, it was Śakra who assisted in this meritorious deed by sending down heavy rains."
Do not harbor any other thought; that householder Sthapati was none other than myself.
Great King!
In the past, I did not realize bodhi through this act of giving alone.

Do not harbor any other views; by virtue of my right faith and through the causes and conditions of the accumulated roots of goodness and the merit thereof, I further cultivated immeasurable meritorious deeds and realized unsurpassed bodhi.
The summary verse says:
The Horse-King and the Sage’s Witness; the Snake’s Life and the Bird-King’s Grace;
the Parrot and Mṛttikāvatī; the Tortoise and the Two Merchants with Ghee.
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, Great King!
For the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi, I bring benefit to and embrace all sentient beings."
Great King, listen attentively!
This was explained in detail in the *Madhyama Āgama*, in the *Sāṃkathyaviniścaya-yakṣa-sūtra*.
At that time, I became a horse-king named Bhalluka, and for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I manifested in that form.
"Furthermore, Great King!
Because I seek unsurpassed bodhi, I embrace the work of benefiting and bringing benefit to sentient beings.
Great King, listen attentively!"
In the distant past, not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, there lived a rishi whose mind was practiced in compassion and who felt pity for sentient beings.
Not far from his dwelling were two farmers who, while plowing and planting, fell into a dispute; they became angry with one another and proceeded to fight and strike each other.
They both went to the place where the seer was and together requested him to serve as witness. One of them immediately went to the king and reported the matter to him.
The king then said:
"In your mutual dispute, who has witnessed it?"
They addressed him, saying:
"Great King!
Between the two of us, who was the first to commit a transgression?"
The seer replied:
"If you act according to the dharma of a wheel-turning monarch, I shall bear witness;
if you practice another dharma, I will not bear witness."
The king said, "So be it. The seer replied:
"This person is angry with that person, and that person is angry with this one.
Since that person has struck this one, this one strikes that one in return.
The king said:
"If this is so, both shall be punished. The rishi said,
"I have already spoken these words:"
"If you settle legal cases according to the laws of a Wheel-Turning King, I shall serve as witness;
if you do not follow them, I will not serve as witness.
At that time, the king said:
"Great Seer!
How does one adjudicate legal cases according to the dharma of a Wheel-Turning King?
The seer replied:
“Great King!
According to the dharma of a Wheel-Turning King, one must eliminate what is unbeneficial and cause others to abide in what is beneficial.
The king then said to the two men:
"Go! Do not do this again.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"At that time, as for the seer who bore witness through the Dharma, do not conceive of him as anyone else; it was I myself.
Although I bore witness and saw it in the past, I did so by taking the Dharma as my witness, providing a testimony of truth."
By virtue of those causes and conditions, through the accumulation of roots of goodness and the cultivation of pure faith, he realized unsurpassed bodhi.
"Furthermore, Great King,
it was also for the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi that he gathered in sentient beings."
At that time, while the Bodhisattva was still in the stage of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*), he sacrificed his own life to benefit all sentient beings.
Great King!
Long ago, in a vast forest in a certain region, there dwelt a lion king.
Furthermore, there were five hundred merchants passing through a perilous road; because of their voices, a great python was startled awake, and the five hundred merchants were all surrounded by it.
At that time, the merchants were struck with great terror; they raised their voices in a cry for help, invoking the various heavenly deities.
Hearing this cry, the lion king arrived and saw that the merchants were surrounded by a great python.
Not far from there was a young elephant; at that time, the lion went to the elephant's side and said:
"These merchants are now surrounded by a great serpent and are about to be devoured; can you sacrifice your life to save them?"
The elephant replied,
"How do you wish for me to dispatch him? The lion said:
"I must mount upon your head; with my hind legs I shall seize your head and strike the snake's brain with my two front claws.
My two hind feet shall enter into your head, whereby you will surely die;
as I strike the snake's brain, the snake shall certainly die."
"The snake is exhaling venomous gas from its mouth; I too should die.
The elephant said, "Since this will bring benefit and deliverance to many people, how could I concern myself with my own body or life?"
Then the lion king mounted the head of the elephant and threw his body down to strike the python.
As the lion pressed down with his paws, the elephant passed away;
as he struck the python, the snake also died instantly.
Due to the venomous breath of the snake, the lion died;
all three perished simultaneously, and the merchants were thus preserved in their lives.
As the merchants were about to depart, the devas in the sky addressed them, saying:
"This Lion King is a Bodhisattva of the Bhadrakalpa; he has now sacrificed his own life for your sakes to rescue you all.
You should offer worship to this Bodhisattva before proceeding."
Then the merchants immediately made offerings of various kinds of requisites to the body of the lion king, circumambulated him, and departed.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"As for that lion king at that time, do not view him as anyone else; he was none other than myself."
At that time, while I was in the realm of animals, I was able to save five hundred merchants by sacrificing my own life to slay those venomous snakes.

Through the causal conditions of the merit from gathering roots of goodness and the power of right faith—arising from my compassionate mind’s embrace of sentient beings—I realized unsurpassed enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Great King!
In the distant past, in a certain region, there was a beautiful grove.
At that time, a Bodhisattva who was among the animals of the indeterminate realm took birth as a *saṃjīvaka* bird, having a single body with two heads:
One was named Dharma and the other was named Adharma.
At that time, Dharma ate fine, sweet fruits, while later Adharma ate poisonous fruits; both became dazed and confused, and they began to debate with one another.
First, they make an evil vow:
"May I always be born as an evil companion to you in every place where I am reborn, so that I may be able to cause you harm.
Second, they make a vow:
"May I, in every place where I am born, always practice a heart of loving-kindness and bring benefit to your person.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"What do you think?"
At that time, the one named Dharmā was none other than myself;
the one named Adharmā was Devadatta.
It was through my heart of compassion, by virtue of those causes and conditions, and by accumulating roots of goodness, that I realized unsurpassed enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Great King!
In the distant past, there was a beautiful flowing pond in a certain region.
At that time, the Bodhisattva took birth among the indeterminate class of beings as a bird, serving as the king of five hundred birds."

Among them was an old bird that could not seek food or drink from afar; it constantly ate small birds and the eggs of various birds. It moved slowly and feebly, and once it had eaten its fill, it would stand upon one leg.

At that time, the various small birds, who were constantly being devoured, were filled with great sorrow and distress; they went together to the king's side and, making the sounds of bird-voices, addressed him, saying:
"O King of Birds!
He recounted everything as before, filled with grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress.
The king of birds immediately set out to investigate this matter: who was devouring these fledglings?

Although the Bodhisattva was in an evil realm, his mind remained ever unchanged; thus he searched and observed until he saw an old bird, feigning weakness and walking slowly, standing on one leg by the edge of the pond.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, King of Birds, immediately perceived this harmer and spoke in verse:
“Devouring the eggs of various birds, As well as other small birds;
Standing with one foot raised, Like one who observes the precepts.”
"Gradually contracting his feet, speaking with a weak and feigned voice,
and curving his neck with such affectation— this must surely be full of deceit.
At that time, the old bird thought to himself:
"Now that the Bird King has already perceived me, I now take refuge in him.
The Bird King said,
"You must devise a plan so that the other birds do not learn of your grievance."
Upon hearing this, the old bird quickly fled.
At that time, the flock of birds was at peace and free from anxiety.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"At that time, do not entertain any other thought; it was I myself who was the king of birds.
While I was the king of birds, I was able to gather all sentient beings through loving-kindness."
By virtue of those causes and conditions, through the power of the roots of goodness and right view he had accumulated, he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Furthermore, Great King, in the distant past, in a certain place within a forest, the Bodhisattva was at that time among those of indeterminate destiny as a parrot, constantly able to speak human language."
At that time, however, there was a king in Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta, who had duly ascended the throne and governed the world according to the Dharma.
There was a bird that wished to harm a parrot; the parrot flew and threw itself into the hands of the Great King, saying:
"Great King!"
"Do not rule the world without the Dharma.

At that time, seeing the bird alight upon his hand, the king felt compassion in his heart; he immediately received the five precepts from the parrot and ruled the world according to the Dharma. He then commanded his ministers, saying:
"From this day forth, I grant the gift of fearlessness to all birds and beasts."
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Do not conceive a different view.
At that time, the parrot who understood human speech, because of its roots of goodness, realized unsurpassed bodhi."
"Furthermore, Great King!
In the distant past, there was a king named Brahmadatta who reigned righteously over Vārāṇasī.
Not far from there, the kingdom of Videha rose in rebellion; King Brahmadatta constantly desired to wage war against those insubordinates."

The army of King Brahmadatta was powerful and formidable; although the kingdom of Videha possessed superior troops and horses, its people always practiced compassion toward King Brahmadatta in their hearts and conduct.
King Brahmadatta, out of greed for his kingdom, mobilized the fourfold army and marched to attack the kingdom of Videha.

When the King of Videha heard that King Brahmadatta’s fourfold army was about to arrive, he immediately ordered the cities and towns to be swept clean of all debris and stones, hung silk banners and flowers, and prepared various foods and drinks.

Furthermore, he commanded his ministers to have the people within the city come out twenty-five *li* ahead of the procession to welcome him with incense and flowers, and to offer hundreds of words of praise extolling the King’s virtues.
When King Brahmadatta heard this news, his anger subsided, and he thought to himself:
"Since my kind words were met with opposition, yet I have not acted contrary to them, I may now turn back my army."
At that time, the ministers and officials of the kingdom of Vaideha praised King Brahmadatta, saying:
"We pray that Your Majesty will pass through our country; we shall prepare a grand assembly for all your troops."
King Vidūḍabha spoke in verse:
“May the Great King accept my confession; I shall personally serve and honor you.
I will attend to all matters according to your wishes; I pray that you will deign to be my friend.”
Then King Brahmadatta replied with a verse:
"Through patience one attains liberation; The mind of anger becomes stilled and does not arise.
Because it possesses all-capacity, It can overcome all people."
At that time, the two kings reached a reconciliation; King Brahmadatta returned to his own kingdom, and all the people of the kingdom of Videha were entirely free from fear.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Do not harbor any other thought regarding that King Videha at that time; he was none other than myself.
It was for the sake of subduing his mind, and by virtue of the roots of merit from his accumulated right faith, that I realized unsurpassed enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Great King!
Long ago in the distant past, when the Bodhisattva was still in the stage of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*), he was a king of tortoises in the great ocean.
Later on, five hundred merchants set out upon the sea in a ship, but their vessel was wrecked by a sea monster."
The tortoise took five hundred merchants and placed them upon its back, carrying them across the ocean.
At that time, all the merchants were safe and sound, their lives and bodies preserved intact.
The Buddha told the Great King:

"Regarding that Great Tortoise King at that time, do not entertain any other thought; it was none other than myself. Because I gathered sentient beings through compassion, and by virtue of those causes and conditions—the accumulation of roots of goodness through right faith—I realized unsurpassed enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Great King!
In the distant past, there were five hundred ministers in the kingdom of Videha.
Among them were two brothers who served as the chief ministers:
The elder brother was named Susena and the younger brother was named Sena.
As for the one named Sena, his mind was always inclined toward seeking out the faults of others and lacked any intention to benefit them.
As for Susena, he constantly practiced benefiting others at all times.

Because Susena constantly acted for the benefit of others, while Sina brought no benefit and instead harassed the people, the multitude in the city all came together to inform the king, recounting the harmful deeds he had committed.
The king immediately ordered him to be banished beyond the borders; he then went to the city of Vārāṇasī and served King Brahmadatta as a minister.
Later, at another time, Susena heard that his younger brother had been banished from the kingdom and was serving as a counselor to King Brahmadatta in Vārāṇasī. He then addressed King Videha, saying:
"I now wish to go to that Vārāṇasī to see my brother and perform acts of conciliation."
The multitude of people in the city were all struck with wonder and astonishment, saying:
"That younger brother constantly performed harmful deeds against his elder brother.

Yet, when that younger brother was banished by the king from the borders of the kingdom, this elder brother was still able to act for the benefit of his younger brother and reach a peaceful reconciliation with him."
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Do not harbor a different view; at that time, the one named the minister Susīna was none other than myself, constantly acting for the benefit of sentient beings."
By virtue of those causes and conditions, through the accumulation of roots of goodness based on right faith, he realized unsurpassed bodhi.
"Furthermore, Great King!
In the distant past, in a certain region, there was a great city."

Within that city dwelt two merchants who had loaded five hundred wagons with precious goods; as they traveled through a wilderness on a perilous road, the details are exactly as described in the *Madhyama Āgama*.
"One of the merchants had already been devoured by the yakṣa;
the second caravan leader emerged safely from the wilderness.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"You should not view that second merchant leader who safely emerged from the perilous wilderness as anyone other than myself.

It was through the gathering of roots of virtue born of right faith, and by means of those causes and conditions, that I attained unsurpassed enlightenment for the sake of gathering sentient beings with compassion."
"Furthermore, Great King!
In the distant past, in a certain region within a forest, there were many rivers and streams, and flowers and fruits grew in great abundance."
At that time, the Bodhisattva was in the stage of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*), having become a six-tusked elephant king dwelling within that forest.
The wife of this elephant king was named Bhadrā, who was the most noble among the female elephants.

At that time, the elephant king had left the herd and was in a secluded place; there was a certain female elephant, upright and pleasing to behold, who went to the elephant king’s location and engaged in secret dalliance with him.

Having become husband and wife, they treated one another with great affection; whether walking or staying, they followed each other, their minds never parting and their hearts bound together in attachment.
At that time, the female elephant Bhadrā became jealous and thought to herself:
"By what means can I kill this six-tusked elephant king along with his mate?"
As he dwelt thus in contemplation, his heart was filled with great jealousy; finding no other means to achieve his aim, he then made this vow:
"May I, in every place where I am born, be able to harm these two people."

Having made this vow, he threw himself down from the mountain peak and immediately passed away, being reborn in the womb of the chief consort of the Great King of the Videha kingdom. Thus did he dwell within the womb.

When the ten months were complete, she gave birth to a daughter endowed with all auspicious marks. As she gradually grew up, she was married to the Great King Brahmadatta of a neighboring kingdom as his chief consort.
Due to his past karma, he conceived great hatred toward the six-tusked elephant and others; however, the queen possessed the knowledge of past lives and addressed King Brahmadatta, saying:
"In that region, there is a great six-tusked elephant; I now require these tusks, so I pray the King will have them taken."
At that time, the king issued an edict to summon all the hunters from every city and commanded them to capture a six-tusked elephant.
Once the hunters had assembled, he told them,
"Go and fetch the elephant's tusks and bring them here."
When the king had thus commanded them, the hunters departed immediately according to his orders.
The chief of the hunters addressed the hunters, saying, "All of you disperse and return each to your own occupations; I alone shall go to fetch the elephant tusks."
At that time, the general immediately took the sacrificial offerings, along with his armor and poisoned arrows, and proceeded to that location.

There he saw the elephant king and the female elephant, both dwelling separately in a secluded place, each apart from the herd of elephants; having seen them, he approached from afar and gazed at them from a distance.
At that time, the hunter was clad in garments of patience, concealing his bow and arrows, and hiding all his armor within the grass, intending to kill them.
Then, seeing the hunter from afar, the female elephant immediately said to her mate:
"Let us quickly go elsewhere; someone has come now who wishes to kill us."
The Elephant King asked,
"What is that person’s appearance like?
He replied:
"Clad in the robe of patience, one manifests the appearance of compassion externally.
"If it is thus, one must be fearless;
within the *kāṣāya*, there shall be no unwholesome deeds."
Those who are covered by this banner-mark should abide in a mind of loving-kindness and compassion; they must be without fear and harbor no doubt.
Just as the moon is without heat, so too is this person.
At that time, the female elephant and the elephant king were free from all doubt and wandered about as they pleased.
Then, the hunter, having found his opportunity, released a poisoned arrow and struck the elephant king in a vital spot.
The female elephant asked:
"How can you say that those who wear the *kāṣāya* have no harmful intent?
At that time, the elephant king replied with a verse:
"The mind does not produce these faults, nor are they created by clothing;
these faults arise from the afflictions, born of the mind's lack of compassion."
Just as when copper is wrapped in gold leaf, the nature of the copper appears once it enters the fire;
though the afflicted person does not perceive this, the wise are well able to know it.
When a bow, its arrows, and the archer are all poisoned, they all become harmful because of that [poison].
"The *kāṣāya* is fundamentally quiescent; it is entirely produced by the mind.
At that time, the female elephant gave rise to anger in her heart and said to her husband:
"I do not contradict your words, just as you have now spoken."
"I wish to crush this man, breaking him limb from limb.
At that time, having heard these words, the Elephant King gave rise to this thought:
"What medical treatment can be applied to this affliction?"
"If it were the case that this bodhisattva’s wife gave rise to thoughts of enmity and harm, it would be improper.
He spoke in verse:
"Just as one whose mind is possessed by many spirits Sees a physician and immediately fails to offer him honor;
"The physician, seeing this, should feel no resentment, but rather give rise to such a heart of joy.
At that time, the mother elephant heard what the Bodhisattva elephant king had said and remained silent.
At that time, the herd of elephants went to the place where the elephant king was and thought to themselves:
"May this female elephant not harm the hunter.
Thus, even when a bodhisattva is among the animal realm, they constantly practice the conduct of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the elephant king went to the hunter and addressed him in human speech, saying:
"Do not be afraid or alarmed.
Fearing he might harm the hunter, the elephant king encircled him with his trunk, cradling him against his chest; he then had the female elephant go elsewhere before speaking again.
"O Noble Sir! The female elephant has already departed.
If you require anything from my person, take it as you please."
At that time, the hunter was struck with extreme wonder and alarm:
"This one is truly a human being, while I am no human at all.
I am but an elephant among men, whereas you are a man among elephants."
"While you were among the animals, you possessed such feeling and intelligence;
yet now that I dwell among humans, I am instead devoid of this wisdom.
Thus he wept and shed tears in sorrow.
The Bodhisattva asked,
"Why are you weeping?
The hunter replied:
"You have already harmed me.
When the elephant king heard this, he reflected:
"I manifested myself to save you; I have never caused you harm."
He further reflected:
"Could it be that a female elephant has come and caused this damage?
He then asked the hunter:
"Who has harmed you?
the hunter replied,
"O Elephant King!"
Your body possesses immeasurable merit; to inflict harm upon you who are innocent is to injure me.
Your body has been wounded by arrows, yet it can still be treated.
"My heart has been pierced; I am foolish and lacking wisdom, and thus difficult to heal.
He then spoke in verse:
"I now observe the gait of the Elephant King, Whose merit is as vast as the great ocean."
Even toward those who harbor malice, one should give rise to compassion; such a bodhisattva’s mind is difficult to find.
Though I may be called a human being by name, I lack such true wisdom and awakening;
possessing only this poisonous venom of anger and harm, my body is empty and devoid of even the slightest merit.
Though your adorned form resembles that of a human, it would be better to be born among the animals;
for you, while in the animal realm, possess human-like wisdom—you, O Elephant King, are the most honored among elephants.
One does not become a human being merely by physical form; nor is one a non-human simply because they are an animal.
If a person possesses the merit of compassion, then one should know that such a person is truly human.
At that time, the Elephant King said:
