"There is no need for you to labor over extensive speech, nor is there any use for you to recount many clever words.
Why have you now shot me with an arrow?"
"Tell me this matter quickly so that I may know it.
The hunter replied, "I have received the King's command that I must have your tusks; for this reason, I shot you."
The Elephant King said, "Whatever you require, please take it at once.
With the mind of a Bodhisattva, there is nothing I will not give away; feel free to pull out my tusks so that they may be used for your benefit."
He spoke in verse:
“May all sentient beings be benefited, And swiftly leave the drifting sea of birth and death;
May they realize the wisdom of unsurpassed bodhi, And only wish for them to enter early the city of nirvāṇa.”
At that time, the hunter felt ashamed and said to the elephant king,
"I need your tusks.
The elephant king replied:
"Pull it out at will," [the king] said. He replied,
"I cannot pull it out."
"If you command me to pull it out, I pray that you abide in compassion; only then shall I be able to extract it.
If you do not abide in a mind of compassion, my hand will surely fall off at the very moment of pulling."
The elephant king said,
"If you are unable to pull it out, I shall pull it out myself and give it to you.
Thus spoke the elephant king.
"It is because my tusk has entered deep into the flesh.
As it was being pulled out, white blood flowed forth.

Having pulled it out, he wished to give it to the hunter; the Elephant King’s body was as bright white as an *utpala* flower, and the blood flowing over his entire body was like snow covering a mountain, appearing like a patterned brocade.

"At that time, the Elephant King perceived his own physical form as it was within his own mind; fearing there might be a regression, he wished to strengthen his resolve so that it would not be disturbed.
Since this Bodhisattva has practiced such a nature for so long, how could there be any regression in his practice of giving?"
When reaching the path of death, one can only turn to the Buddha for refuge.
At that time, various extraordinary signs appeared; the devas in the sky, their hearts being fully satisfied, gave rise to joy and manifested rare wonders.
However, as the Elephant King performed this ascetic practice, a deva in the sky spoke these verses:
"We devas behold the Elephant King performing his ascetic practice;
at the very moment he was pulling out his tusks, he endured immeasurable suffering."
"With a heart still full of joy, he will certainly not retreat from awakening.
Then another deva asked that deva:
"If he suffers such pain from having his teeth pulled out, how can he set out for awakening?"
"Just as those suffering in hell can never give rise to thoughts of compassion.
At that time, the Elephant King, having extracted his tusks, remained silent.
The hunter thought to himself:
"Why has he pulled out his tusks and remains standing there?
Does he wish to repent?"
“Will you not give it to me?
At that time, the Elephant King, perceiving his intention, took up a white *udumbara* flower with his six tusks, extended his forefeet, and offered to give it to him with those six tusks, saying:
“Wait a moment!”
“Wait a short while!
I am now in extreme pain.
The elephant king then thought this again:
"The recipient is present before me; why must I linger long?
Why should I not give?
Originally, it was for the sake of these tusks that he wished to kill me; now that he has no tusks, what need is there to worry about anything else?"
He said to the hunter,
"You should listen well," and spoke this verse:
“O noble one, you should cast aside these evil things—the sharp swords, bows, and arrows you carry;
clad in this kashaya, the garment of a benevolent person, I now behold you with a joyful heart.”
There is giving that is pure and the recipient is also pure; there is giving that is pure but the recipient is impure.
Now I behold you as one who is pure and worthy of offerings; both the giver and the recipient are pure.
At that time, the Elephant King, seeing him clad in the robes of one free from desire, felt joy in his heart and immediately gave him his six tusks, saying:
"If you truly shot this poisoned arrow into my body, I did not give rise to even a slight thought of anger or resentment;
By this truth, I pray that you may quickly realize Bodhi And save those in saṃsāra to attain liberation."
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"What do you think?
Do not entertain any other thought regarding that Great Elephant King with six tusks at that time; he was none other than my own self."
Because I practiced compassion, asceticism, and generosity, I did not yet realize awakening.
By virtue of those causes and conditions, through the accumulation of roots of goodness based on right view, I have realized unsurpassed bodhi.
"Furthermore, Great King!
When I was once a hare and gave my own flesh as a gift to that rishi, you should understand the full account as it has been extensively told."
"Furthermore, Great King!
In the past, when both my parents were blind, I would constantly carry them upon my shoulders and back, leading them wherever they went to provide for their needs."
"Though an immeasurable period of time has passed, it remains unrealized; this should be understood as explained at length.
Furthermore, Great King, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings..."
"Great King, listen attentively!

There are those in the world with false views who, relying on worldly customs, cause their aging parents to starve, drown them in a river, or cast them into fire to burn their bodies, claiming that by doing so they will be reborn in heaven."
"I shall establish a method to prohibit and sever these unlawful acts; this should be understood as explained in detail.
Furthermore, Great King, there are immeasurable causes and conditions, all of which are explained in detail within the *Nāga-yakṣa-sūtra*."
“Great King!
When the Bodhisattva was in the stage of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*), he became a king of monkeys and was the most honored among five hundred monkeys.
At a time when Vārāṇasī was terrified by King Brahmadatta, I at that moment sacrificed my own life to save the five hundred monkeys; this should be understood as it has been explained in detail.”
"Furthermore, Great King!
When the Bodhisattva was in the stage of the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi), he was born with the body of a pheasant, as is explained in detail in the *Kapiñjala-jātaka*."
"Furthermore, Great King,
when the Bodhisattva was in the stage of the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi), he was born among elephants, as is explained in detail in the *Nāgapūrvajanma-sūtra*."

"Furthermore, Great King, when the Bodhisattva was in the stage of the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi), he was born into the realm of nāgas with the name Nanda, the Naga Prince; this is explained in detail in the *Nāgapūrvajanma-sūtra*."
"Furthermore, Great King,
when the Bodhisattva was in the stage of the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi), he took the form of a king of geese, as is explained in detail in the *Haṃsa-jātaka-sūtra*.
At that time, King Śreṇika Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
At what time did you first resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhi?"
The Buddha told the Great King:
"In the distant past, immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a king named Prabhāsa.

This King Prabhāsa possessed a precious elephant whose body was as bright white as an *utpala* flower; its seven limbs were perfectly formed, its appearance was dignified and majestic, and it was a sight that all people delighted to behold."
The king then issued an order to the elephant trainer:
"Train this elephant so that when it is fit for riding, you shall bring it before me.
Having received the king's command, the elephant trainer immediately began to train it.
Once it was completed, he returned to the king's presence.
The king immediately mounted the elephant, accompanied by the elephant trainer, with the king seated in the rear; they then went out of the city to hunt various kinds of birds and beasts.
However, the elephant king, having caught the scent of the female elephant, followed the fragrance and fled.
Seeing the elephant running as swiftly as the wind, the King said to the elephant trainer:
"I see the void spinning; The four quarters, above, and below all revolve."
The mountain ranges are like a potter’s wheel; the trees also seem to move through the air.
Though the elephant’s feet never shift, it appears as if it is leaping through the sky;
one perceives the mountains ahead rushing toward oneself, while those behind appear to be in constant motion.
“Bind the elephant firmly and keep it still; strike it severely until it is terrified.
Since this king of elephants has not yet been tamed, death or life lies right before us now.
At that time, the elephant trainer said to the king:
"I recite the spells taught by the Great Sage, and strike with an iron hook;
yet as I recite the spells and strike more urgently with the hook, all the methods employed prove utterly useless."
There is no rope or hook that can restrain it; O King, knowing there is nothing that can stop it, how could one do so?
When greed enters the mind, there is no one to tame it; when desire dwells within the heart, it is like a driven stake.
When this desire arises, it is exceedingly vast; there is no one who can bring it to rest.
At that time, the elephant trainer employed various methods, yet he was unable to stop the elephant or turn it back.
He then addressed the king, saying:
"The elephant is exhausted from running; I pray that Your Majesty will grasp a branch of a tree and release the elephant to go as it pleases."
They immediately encountered a tree, and the king and the elephant trainer climbed its branches to stay there, as if having been restored to life after death.
The king said to the elephant trainer:
"Since you have not yet tamed this elephant to perfection, bring it here at once for me to ride."
He said to the king:
"I have successfully tamed it; however, because that elephant smelled the scent of a female and became intoxicated with lust, he did not accept my instructions.
Although the elephant has departed, he still longs for his former place and will surely return on the seventh day."
"Why is this? Because after seeing a female elephant and engaging in sexual intercourse with her, he has been longing for the elephant stable.
On the seventh day, that elephant returned.
At that time, the elephant trainer hurried to the king and informed him.
The king said,
"You have not yet successfully trained this elephant."
The man said to the king,
"I have finished training the elephant.
The king rebuked him, saying:
"How is he disciplined?
[The king] replied,
"Please allow Your Majesty to test him, and you will immediately know whether it is true or false."
The elephant trainer then heated a large iron ball until it was red-hot like fire and ordered the elephant to take and eat it;
the elephant immediately went forward, intending to seize and swallow it.
The elephant trainer further addressed the king, saying:
"If the elephant eats this, it will certainly not survive.
Thereupon, the king said to the elephant trainer:
"Being tamed in such a manner would have confused me at that time.
He first addressed the king, saying:
"I have only been able to tame my body; I cannot tame my mind."
The king asked,
"Have you ever seen anyone who was able to tame their own mind?
The elephant trainer replied to the king:
"There is! Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to discipline both body and mind.
All sentient beings who wish to discipline their minds fail to do so and consequently retreat."
There are certain non-Buddhists who practice asceticism, yet the thicket of craving remains in their hearts and they are unable to uproot it;
there are also those who abandon sensory objects and leave behind the realm of desire and greed, yet fail to maintain this steadfastly and subsequently fall back into decline.

Asuras and others, as well as devas and humans, lions and various beasts, dragons, snakes, doves and pigeons, even flying geese and other diverse species—all sentient beings are bound by desire, revolving like a wheel from time immemorial.
From youth until old age, one must subdue the mind through various ascetic practices; for there are some rishis who subsist on wind and fruit, yet they do not subdue their minds.
Although the mind is signless, who among gods or humans can attain mastery over it?
As for those called "Great Kings," though they possess great power and are most preeminent in all battles, they likewise have not tamed their minds;
only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is free from desire and has attained mastery of the mind.

At that time, having heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possessed the power of diligence, practiced extensive acts of giving, and cultivated various meritorious deeds, the Great King immediately made the vow for unexcelled bodhi and spoke in verse:
"Cultivating immeasurable merit to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, May I become a Sugata, a Sovereign Honored One;
If there are those who have not yet crossed to the other shore, I vow to deliver them all and bring them to the shore."
Hearing that the Buddha has renounced desire and awakened the bodhicitta, And further practices generosity while transforming others through the True Dharma;
I vow that in the future I shall attain Buddhahood, Benefiting sentient beings so that their craving and desire are extinguished.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"What do you think?
Who else could that King named Prabhāsa have been at that time?"
"I am that very person.
At that time, I first conceived the aspiration for unsurpassed bodhi.
Then, King Prasenajit again addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Under whom did he first practice giving to attain the realization of unsurpassed bodhi?
The Buddha told the Great King:
"In the distant past, immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a city named Vikha-pṛthivī. In that city, there was a potter."
A Buddha appeared in the world named Śākyamuni, who had realized unexcelled, right, and true enlightenment, fully endowed with the ten titles.
He also had śrāvaka disciples named Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, as well as an attendant named Ānanda.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, the Truly and Perfectly Enlightened One, was traveling through the human world together with a vast assembly of bhikṣus and arrived at that city.
Then, that Buddha suddenly suffered from a wind ailment and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should go to the potter's house and beg for some ghee, oil, honey, and syrup."
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda went at once to the potter’s house and stood outside the gate, saying:
“Householder! ”
"The World-Honored One suffers from a severe wind-illness and now requires ghee, oil, honey, and syrup.

When the potter heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, he immediately took ghee, oil, honey, and other supplies; accompanied by the elder and his son, they went together to the Buddha's dwelling. They smeared the Buddha’s body all over with the ghee and honey, bathed him with warm water, and offered sugar-water to the World-Honored One. For the sake of curing the illness, he was immediately restored to health.
At that time, the potter knelt on his right knee and made this vow, speaking in verse:
“I have offered ghee and honey to the Tathāgata; May I obtain the benefit of vast merit and virtue.
May my lineage, name, and assembly of śrāvakas All be exactly like those of the Honored Śākya today.”
“Skillfully taming the multitudes of sentient beings, he has departed from all suffering to enter parinirvāṇa.
Then the potter’s son also spoke these words:
“May I, in a future life, be like the Buddha’s attendant.”
The Buddha told the Great King:
"At that time, by making my first offering to Śākyamuni Tathāgata, I attained the realization of unsurpassed bodhi.
That son was none other than Ānanda."
The King again asked the World-Honored One:
"From the beginning until the attainment of Buddhahood, how many Buddhas did you make offerings to before realizing unsurpassed bodhi?"
The Buddha told the Great King:

"From my first incalculable aeon (*asaṃkhyeya*) under Śākyamuni Tathāgata until the time of Lokeśvara Buddha, I made such offerings to seventy-five thousand Buddhas with a pure mind. Throughout that entire period, my offerings were never performed with a distracted mind; I sought only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
“Great King!
This is the second *saṃkhyeya*: from my first making offerings to Dīpaṃkara Buddha up until Ratnaśikhin Buddha, I made such offerings with a pure mind to seventy-six thousand Buddhas.”
Although I have passed through many lifetimes, my mind has remained unchanged; I have always made offerings to the Buddhas with pure faith.
Great King!
During the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, I first made offerings to the Buddha Ratnaśikhin, continuing thus until the Buddha Śānta.
In this manner, I made offerings to seventy-seven thousand Buddhas, and likewise continued until I reached Kāśyapa Buddha.
Although I made these offerings, my mind remained free from any dualistic thought; I always offered to all the Buddhas with pure faith.
While acting as a bodhisattva, I made such offerings, and all the Buddhas granted me the prediction that I would realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
They fulfilled my aspirations, for I sought perfect awakening with firm resolve and maintained it through compassion, gathering all sentient beings under my care.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, King Prasenajit was filled with great joy; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and departed.
Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One in verse, requesting:
“I pray only that the Honored One of the World will explain this for me in detail.”
Where did you first resolve your mind?
It was for the sake of seeking great enlightenment.
I further pray that the Unsurpassed One will explain the causes and conditions of your past lives.
"How many Buddhas have you previously made offerings to,
and for how long a time?
At that moment, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"The Unsurpassed Honored One among bipeds, who has compassion for sentient beings;
having resolved upon Bodhi toward him, I vow to ferry them across the ocean of the three realms of existence.
Hearing that the Buddha’s mind is free from desire, he extensively recounted the story of the intoxicated elephant."
Weary of and detached from the habituation to craving, he gave rise to the bodhicitta.
Firmly making his vow, he practiced giving as vast as the sands of the Ganges;
during the era of King Prabhāsa, he sought exclusively for perfect enlightenment.
When I first beheld Śākyamuni Buddha, I was a potter;
with ghee, oil, honey, and sweet juices, I made my very first offering.
I was also once a noble woman, possessing right faith in the Triple Gem.
I saw the Buddha Kauṇḍinya and offered him lamp oil as a gift.
During the time of the Buddha Anabhibhū, I served as a Tripitaka master;
competing with the great assembly, I reviled the Saṅgha with foul language, calling them "women."
Due to this evil karma of speech, my body was transformed into that of a woman;
once my mind turned back and became pure, it changed again into that of a man.
Long ago, in a past life, when I was a prince;
To the brothers Ratnaśikhin Buddhas, I offered lamps;
for three months I made offerings to the World-Honored One Ananta.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, I erected a stūpa for his relics.
In a former life, he was a wealthy elder who made offerings to the Buddha for three months;
after the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa, he erected a stūpa ninety cubits high.
Later, he encountered the Buddha Viśeṣagāmin, the most eminent among brahmins.
Raising my hands in reverent añjali, I made offerings to the Honored One among Men.
In former times, when I was a brahmin, I was fully proficient in the scriptures and treatises;
having encountered the Buddha Arthadarśin, I offered a seat to the Tathāgata.
In former times, when practicing austerities, I once dwelt in the way of the sages;
seeing the World-Honored One Kauṇḍinya, I grasped my body as I was about to fall from the mountain.
I once acted as a sage and encountered the Buddha Rāma.
The Buddhas came to his dwelling and he made offerings of roots and fruits.
In the past, when he was a rishi, he saw the World-Honored One Sunetra;
wearing garments of tree bark, he offered them to cover the Buddha’s body.
In the past, when he was once a king of men, he made offerings to Krakucchanda Buddha;
he immediately abandoned his fourfold army to seek unsurpassed bodhi.
From the time of the first Śākyamuni Buddha until the time of the Lokapāla Buddha;
Seventy-five thousand Buddhas, I have made offerings to them all.
This constitutes one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* of such practice of offering;
with a single mind free from distinction, I constantly resolve upon the vow for Bodhi.
Next I saw Dīpaṃkara Buddha, whose great learning was most lovely;
with seven blue lotuses, I made an offering as a brahmin.
I once served as a king and saw a Buddha named Lakṣaṇa.
At the place where the Buddha practiced, I made offerings to this Tathāgata.
Once I was a king, and there was a Buddha named Vihāra;
with exquisite forms, precious jewels, and melodic sounds, I made offerings to him.
I once was a king, when the Buddha was named Transcending Lions;
I offered jeweled banners and canopies to worship this Tathāgata.
I once was a king, when the Buddha was named Peaceful Sun;
The king possessed a thousand cities, all of which he commanded to perform offerings.
Once, when I was a king, there was a Buddha named Brahmin;
with scented water in a bathhouse, I bathed the Buddha according to the proper time.
In the past, when I was a king, I made offerings within the city to three thousand Brahmin Buddhas and one Śikhin Buddha.
I also once served as a householder in the city of Vardhana.
I made offerings to twenty-five Buddhas and practiced the holy life.
Once, when I was a householder in that great city,
I made offerings to Śikhin Buddha and established monasteries and stūpas.
In that monastery, offerings were made to the seven Buddhas, including the presentation of precious treasures,
as well as male and female servants, mansions, houses, gardens, and groves.
Having previously been a king who practiced faith and reverence, he [made these offerings] at the abode of Śikhin Buddha.
Furthermore, while in that city, he sought only the Perfect Enlightenment.
In the past, when he was once a brahmin, there was a Buddha named Nandana;
for the sake of seeking Bodhi, he first made an offering of fruit.
When I was once a householder, there was a Buddha named Sunetra;
with mani-jewels, I made offerings to this Tathāgata.
I was also once a caravan leader, and there was a Buddha named Sujāta;
Seated beneath the Bodhi tree, he first made an offering of cakes.
Among a thousand merchants, he once served as their leader;
seeing the Buddha seated at the Bodhi tree, he was named the Buddha Sumati.
He smeared fragrant mud upon the Buddha’s body and fanned him to bring coolness;
sitting beside the Buddha, he listened to the Dharma, and hearing it, his mind was opened to awakening.
In the past, when he was a leader of merchants, there was a Buddha named Śākyamuni.
With various precious flowers, I scattered them upon the Buddha.
In the past, when I was a merchant leader, there was a Buddha named High Peak (Gao Deng);
with banners, flowers, and music, I made offerings to such a Buddha.
I once was a king, and there was a Buddha named Most Supreme;
having transcended the ocean of all existences, he was offered many chariots by me.
I once was a king, and there was a Buddha named Most Honored;
Within a hundred li of where the Buddha traveled, the ground was strewn with various exquisite flowers.
In a past life, hearing that the Buddha was about to pass by,
I brought forth excellent banners and canopies from afar and surrounded him with the fourfold army.
When there was a Buddha wishing to cross a river, I served as his boatman;
seeing the Buddha, my heart rejoiced, and I ferried him to the other shore.
I once served as a merchant leader for a Buddha named Bhadra-ratha.
I built a bridge for the Buddha, enabling him to cross safely.
In a past life, I was a king; there was a Buddha named Mahābrahmā, and I constructed a monastery with ox-head sandalwood to make offerings to the Honored One.
I donned the saṃghāṭī robe to cover the Tathāgata;
in an age of scarcity, I bathed him with sandalwood, and as rain fell, people returned to the Buddha.
Once I was a king, and there was a Buddha named Viśuddhacandra.
When the land was plagued by many epidemics, the diseases were all eliminated through offerings to the Buddha.
In the past, when I was a king, there was a Buddha named Tiao-di (Dīpaṃkara);
I invited the Buddha to preach the wondrous Dharma for the sake of seeking the path to Bodhi.
In the past, when I was a king, there was a Buddha named Brahmottara;
I offered him a saṃghāṭī robe to cover the Tathāgata’s body.
At that time, there was a famine in the kingdom, so I used sandalwood water;
Bathing the body of the Tathāgata, people turn to the Buddha in abundance and joy.
In the past, when I was a king, there was a Buddha named Śakra;
when a calamity arose in his land, the King’s compassion brought it to rest.
In the past, when I was a king, I made offerings to the Buddha Tathāgata;
using millions of various jewels, I prepared food and presented it to the Tathāgata.
Formerly, as a faithful brahmin, I saw the Buddha named Siddhārtha.
With a hundred thousand verses of praise, he made offerings to the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
In the past, when he was a brahmin, the Buddha’s name was Śakradhvaja;
with palms joined and right faith, he made this vow: "May I become like the Buddha in the future."
Beginning from Dīpaṃkara Buddha, Up to Śakradhvaja;
To seventy-six thousand Buddhas, I have made offerings to them all.
For two full asaṃkhyeyas, I have made offerings to these Buddhas.
Never having had a different thought, he resolved his will upon the state of Bodhi.
During the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he likewise made offerings as a king;
the Buddha’s name was Anvaya-sūrya (Sun of Peace), and after his parinirvāṇa, a stupa was erected.
In the past, when I was a king, I made all manner of offerings to the Buddha;
fulfilling every wish, I erected a stupa named Dharmarāja.
Formerly, when I was a great merchant leader, I saw a Buddha named Sarvārthasiddha and made offerings to him.
With many golden flowers, I scattered them before the Buddha as an offering.
In the past, when I was a merchant, I saw a Buddha named Ratnaśikhin;
for the sake of that Buddha, I fashioned a golden net to cover over the Great Teacher.
Formerly, when he was a merchant, the Buddha was named Utpalottama;
he made offerings of silver flowers, scattering them over the Tathāgata.
Formerly, when he was a merchant, he saw the Buddha named Uttaraśrī;
With a most excellent chamber, I made offerings to the Tathāgata.
In the past, when I was a great king, the Buddha’s name was Viśeṣavādin;
on the day he attained perfect enlightenment, I protected him with the fourfold army.
In the past, when I was a merchant, I saw a Buddha named Vimala;
I built a stūpa and a bathhouse, as well as lighting lamps for illumination.
In the past, when I was a king, I saw a Buddha named Saṃbodhi;
Sitting upon a rock, he entered meditative absorption, while music was offered as an act of worship.
In a former life as a merchant, he saw the Buddha named Practice;
when that Buddha subdued his enemies and delivered the multitudes, he swept the ground for him to pass over.
Formerly, when I was a merchant, I heard the name of a Buddha called Viśuddhavāsa;
desiring to come and build a monastery, I established a park and a vihāra.
Formerly, when I was a great king, there was a Buddha named Lakṣaṇabhadra.
With mani-jewel offerings, I was then a bodhisattva.
In the past, I was a great king; there was a Buddha named Kṣema.
I constructed a stūpa for the Dharma King and made offerings of silk banners.
In the past, I was a great king; there was a Buddha named Śarabhaṅga.
I offered him a water jar and a staff, erected a stūpa, and held a religious assembly.
In the past, I was a merchant leader; there was a Buddha named Arthadarśin.
With gold, jewels, and pearls, and various kinds of incense, I made offerings.
As a great king, when the Buddha named Sarvasainyadharṣa traveled among the human world,
I welcomed and honored him with the fourfold army.
I was once a great king; the Buddha’s name was Tālajaṅgha.
Desiring to enter the city, I prepared music, incense, and flowers as offerings.
In the past, I was a leader of merchants; there was a Buddha named Tiṣya.
With various stalks of agarwood and powdered root-incense, he made offerings to the Buddha.
"In the past, I was once a great seer; seeing the Buddha Tiṣya in a jeweled niche, I praised the Buddha with but a single verse, thereby surpassing nine kalpas of ascetic practice."
In the past, he was a brahmin named Uttara;
seeing the Buddha named Vipaśyin, he held a torch in both hands and, with a joyful heart, scattered it over the Tathāgata as he resolved upon bodhicitta.
In the past, when the Bodhisattva was a merchant leader, he beheld the World-Honored Buddha named Śikhin, along with his assembly of śrāvaka disciples;
for three months, he provided them with clothing, food, and drink.
In the past, as a merchant of profound and correct faith, he provided clothing,
food, and bedding for three months to Vipaśyin Buddha and his assembly of śrāvaka disciples.
In the past, as a merchant of profound and upright faith, there was a Buddha named Kāruṇikadhvaja;
he invited the Buddha and gave away his entire household wealth in alms, then followed the Buddha forth from home to uphold the pure conduct.
In the past, as a merchant of profound and upright faith, he beheld the Buddha Kāśyapa;
having first constructed a monastery with deep reverence, he subsequently followed the Buddha into the homeless life.
In the past, when he was a brahmin named Jyotiṣka under the Two-Legged Honored One, Kāśyapa Buddha,
it was by hearing the words spoken by Nandīpāla that he was able to leave the household life and cultivate a pure mind.
When the Bodhisattva was formerly a king, he made offerings to the seer Maitreya;
entering meditative concentration, he saw that I would become a Buddha, whereupon the seer returned to make offerings to me.
From the Buddha Śānta to Kāśyapa, he made offerings to seventy-seven thousand Buddhas;
serving all these Tathāgatas, he was able to complete the count of three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
All served him with joy, their minds never for a moment wavering;
they all made the vow for supreme enlightenment, making offerings to the Buddha during his time as a bodhisattva.
Manifesting all manner of appearances, he bestows predictions, declaring to the assembly: "You shall all become Buddhas.
My former vows have all been fulfilled; I now reflect upon those original aspirations as they were.
May all these vows be fully fulfilled; may those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of great virtue, grant me the prediction of unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, when I was a benefactor to all, as well as in my life as the Great King Vimala—
Sacrificing body and treasures, they practice the perfection of giving;

upholding the precepts, they single-mindedly seek to reach the further shore. Able to harm their own bodies for the sake of the joy of the multitude, they cause all to cross over the ocean of suffering.
Constantly practicing the perfection of patience, even when his body and limbs were severed,
he did not retreat in mind because of that practice of patience, as told in the Jātaka of the Kinnara.
I once desired to exhaust the great ocean In order to fulfill the perfection of diligence;
all this was due to the truthful speech of my verbal karma.
When the ox and the brahmin debate the meaning together, One shall fulfill the perfection of wisdom.
The devas beat their drums to celebrate his joy.
Diligently cultivating the supreme dhyāna-pāramitā, a bird born on his head produced male and female chicks;
while remaining unmoved in meditative concentration, the bird was able to fly.
With a mind of loving-kindness, I am ever mindful; with a vast heart, I seek the aspiration for honor.
May all my vows and aspirations be fulfilled.
I shall make offerings to the Teacher of Gods and Humans, and to all sentient beings within the ocean of suffering of the three realms of existence.
All shall return to the path of Nirvāṇa; for this, I cultivate offerings as a Bodhisattva.
From the time after that King of Radiance until the World-Honored One, the Buddha Indradhvaja, he delivered one thousand koṭis of beings;
how much more so now that he has attained Buddhahood and delivers the boundless?
The World-Honored One, the Great Teacher, has already delivered the multitudes of humans and devas—both those already crossed and those yet to cross.
I have established bridges, boats, and rafts, firmly delivering all sentient beings.
After I have entered into parinirvāṇa, because I am able to deliver infinite beings,
all those who are capable of cultivating merit shall enter the city of nirvāṇa in the future.
If, after I have entered parinirvāṇa, one can cultivate and accumulate meritorious deeds for the Buddha’s sake,
making even a small offering to an image, they shall immediately attain immeasurable bliss in the heavens.
After I have entered parinirvāṇa, I shall leave behind the nectar-like flavor of the Dharma-treasure;
should any sentient beings hear this, they will all be able to practice it and attain liberation.
The above are the names of the Buddhas.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*, Fascicle Fifteen.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhaiṣajyavastu*.
Fascicle Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.

At that time, the World-Honored One was the unsurpassed field of merit; being revered and honored, he caused kings, various ministers and aides, brahmins, householders, merchants, and merchant leaders, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and even piśācas and pūtanas, to provide the World-Honored One and the saṃgha of bhikṣus with various robes, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all manner of medicinal supplies for treating illnesses.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Then, various non-Buddhist practitioners gathered together in their lecture hall and said to one another:
"Venerable sirs, do you know?"
"Recently, we have received here the respect, offerings, and provisions—such as clothing, bedding, and medicines—from various kings, ministers, householders, and brahmins."

"Now there is a śramaṇa Gautama who has appeared in the world; whatever respect, honor, offerings, and provisions—such as medicine, clothing, and bedding—we previously received, we shall all now bestow upon him, and we ourselves will be deprived of all gain and support."
"Now, how shall we proceed, and what plan shall we devise?
One among them spoke thus:
"Virtuous ones, you should know that if one who maintains the holy life (brahmacarya) were to engage in unchaste conduct."
At that time, the various non-Buddhists replied, “It is so.
Then another non-Buddhist asked, “How is this obtained?”
He said:
"In our community, there is a woman of upright appearance whom people delight to behold.
Teach her these words:"
“The ascetic Gautama is consorting with her for private matters.
The assembly all asked,
“Which of them is the handsome one?”
He replied, "She is the female ascetic of the Caṇḍāla sect.
The people then had her summoned; once she had arrived, they said to her:
"Little sister, you must know!
All the gains and offerings we previously received have been cut off.
Now, all our gains—robes, medicine, bedding, and so forth—are entirely offered with respect to the śramaṇa Gautama."
"Do you not assist me?
Are you abandoning us?
The woman asked.
"O virtuous one, what plan do you wish me to carry out?
She replied:
"You are the younger sister of my kinsman's family; can you not speak these words?"
“The śramaṇa Gautama has committed unchaste acts with me in private.
If you can do such a thing, you may be called a true adversary.
Then the people of the world will respect and make offerings to us, no different than before.
The woman replied, "I cannot slander the Śramaṇa Gautama;
he is the Teacher of Gods and Men, revered by kings and ministers, and his majestic virtue is immeasurable—who could possibly believe me?"
Then the non-Buddhists replied: "Sister!

If you cannot slander the śramaṇa Gautama and do not follow our words, we, this great assembly, will not speak with you, nor will you be allowed to enter our homes; we shall cast you out together, so that until your death you shall afterwards fall into hell."
The woman, being of little intellectual capacity by nature, then asked, "Venerable sir, instruct me; what should I do?
At that time, the non-Buddhist ascetics replied:
"You should go to the Jeta Grove from time to time.
Following these instructions, the girl went to the Jeta Grove every day.
Eventually, at a later time, the girl approached the Tathāgata with a bowl-cover placed over her abdomen.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded before and behind by an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people as he preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma. When this woman entered the assembly, the World-Honored One, seeing the female heretic approach, thought to himself:
"In the past, I once performed these very deeds; their accumulated causes and conditions are like a surging torrent, and now this female heretic, a māra-demoness, stands before me."
He spoke in verse:
“The sound of his voice is beloved by men; His words are beautiful and his speech refined.
It colored my womb and caused me to conceive; Now he speaks the Dharma once again.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse, saying:
"If a person utters false speech, they shall fall into hell.
The female non-Buddhist replied:
"If one says they did not do it when they have done so, they shall fall into hell.
The World-Honored One declared:
"Both fall into hell; whether one falls or does not fall is known by one's own mind."
"Those who slander the Dharma will suffer in their future lives; [this is] a brief verse, the original source of which has not yet been seen.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"That heretical woman has defiled the Great Sage and the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus."
Having formed this thought, he immediately employed his supernormal powers to cause the bowl to fall away.
At that moment, the māra-maiden was filled with great shame and quickly departed.
Then the leading bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why is it that when the Buddha preached the Dharma for King Prasenajit, he immediately bestowed upon him the prediction of his future attainment of Right, True, and Equal Enlightenment?
Furthermore, we now wish to go to the shore of Lake Anavatapta to each recount our own past deeds before the Tathāgata.”
The Buddha accepted his request by remaining silent.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that, having appeared in the world and not yet entered parinirvāṇa, they must perform ten deeds to teach and transform sentient beings.
What are these ten?
First, the consecration and prediction of those who have long planted roots of goodness, as crown princes of the Dharma King;
second, causing sentient beings who have not yet awakened the mind to give rise to the unsurpassed mind of bodhicitta.
Third, to establish the Three Jewels;
fourth, to demarcate the boundaries of the sacred precinct;
fifth, to renounce one-fifth of one's life span.
Sixth, he manifested great supernormal powers in Śrāvastī;
seventh, he manifested descending from the heavens at the village of Pāṭaligrāma;
eighth, he caused his parents to perceive the Truths.
Ninth, in the Anavatapta Lake, he spoke together with the bhikṣus on the causes and conditions of karmic retribution.
For this reason, the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, recounted the matters of his past karmic retributions in the Anavatapta Lake.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"You may go to the shores of Lake Anavatapta and each recount your own past karmic deeds.
When the bhikṣus heard the Buddha’s instruction, they all complied with his command.

The Buddha, together with a community of four hundred and ninety-nine bhikṣus, vanished from Śrāvastī and reappeared at the edge of Lake Anavatapta; they then proceeded to the haunt of the yakṣa Vyāḍa, a place where the flowers and fruits were exceedingly delightful.
Nevertheless, the waters of this lake flow into the four oceans:
first, the Gaṅgā River; second, the Sindhu River; third, the Vakṣu River; and fourth, the Sītā River.
That place was steep and perilous; none but those who had attained spiritual penetration could go there.
When the Buddha and the great assembly had arrived, the World-Honored One gave rise to a mundane thought.
At the moment he formed this thought, even the insects and ants knew the Buddha’s intention.
The nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, knowing the Tathāgata’s intention, wondered: "Why has the World-Honored One given rise to a worldly thought?
We see that the Buddha wishes to be in Lake Anavatapta with the bhikṣus, each recounting their past karmic causes."

Immediately within the pond, a great lotus flower manifested through transformation; it had a thousand petals like a chariot wheel, its color was like celestial gold, its stem and filaments were made of vajra, and it was surrounded on all sides by immeasurable thousands of flowers.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon this flower, and each of the bhikṣus sat upon a lotus flower.
Meanwhile, the Venerable Śāriputra was at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa near Rājagṛha, sewing a saṃghāṭī robe.
The Buddha told Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Go and summon your companion Śāriputra to come.
He replied:
"So be it. Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana vanished from Lake Anavatapta and appeared on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; approaching Śāriputra, he said to him:
"Venerable Śāriputra!"
At present, the World-Honored One is dwelling at Lake Anavatapta together with a community of nine hundred and ninety-nine bhikṣus.
Having received the Buddha’s command, I have come to invite you; you may now travel with me.
He replied:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
You may accompany me only after I have finished sewing this saṃghāṭī."
He said, "I will assist you with the sewing; do not act according to your own will.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana used his supernormal powers to turn his five fingers into needles to help with the sewing. Śāriputra then said to Maudgalyāyana:
"You should go on ahead; I shall follow immediately after.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana said, "If you do not go, I shall take you by force."
Then the Venerable Śāriputra reached out for the door-bolt and said to Maudgalyāyana, "Your supernatural powers are supreme;
take this door-bolt first, and then lead me away."
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately pulled the door-bolt; however, Śāriputra then thought to himself:
"He possesses such great majesty and power that if he pulls the door-bolt, he will take me away as well."
Thereupon, by means of his supernormal powers, he bound his body to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; the mountain immediately shook, and the land of Jambudvīpa shook simultaneously with it;
Nanda and Upananda, the Dragon Kings, as well as all the great virtuous ones within the Great Lake Anavatapta, were all moved together.
Then the bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"Was it the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda who caused the earth to tremble?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This is not the Naga kings Nanda and Upananda shaking this earth;
this is a Great Śrāvaka manifesting supernatural powers.
Then Śāriputra further thought to himself:
"If I were to bind myself to Mount Sumeru, it too would depart.
But now that I have bound my mind to the great lotus upon which the Tathāgata sits within Lake Anavatapta, I can no longer move."
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to Śāriputra,
"Venerable friend!
Having finished competing in supernormal powers, we may go to where the Blessed One is."
Śāriputra said, "You go on ahead; I shall follow later.

After Mahāmaudgalyāyana had departed, before he reached the Buddha's location, Śāriputra arrived first. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat upon a lotus flower, only then did Maudgalyāyana arrive.
The Venerable One asked, "Why have you been so very late?
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt; knowing only the Buddha could resolve it, they addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have recently observed that Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who was foremost in supernatural powers, is now surpassed.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
Not only now, but in the distant past, there was a painter in the kingdom of Madhyadeśa.
On account of some business, he traveled to another country; having arrived there, he stayed at the house of a painter."
However, the host fashioned a mechanical wooden woman, adorned with colorful paints, and commanded her to provide service and attend to him.
She stood facing the guest, who then called out, "Come; lie down here."
The wooden woman stood there in silence. The man thought to himself, "My master has sent this woman to attend to me.
He then reached out his hand to pull her, but the cord immediately snapped, and both his hands and body fell apart.
Feeling extreme shame, he thought to himself:
"Now that he has humiliated me in private, I must humiliate him before the public.
The man then drew a picture of himself on the wall above the doorway as if hanging himself; he then hid behind the door-panel and remained there.
The host, wondering why he had not risen even when the sun was high, went at once to look at him; upon opening the door, he saw that the man had hanged himself. He then thought to himself:
"For what reason did that man throttle his own throat?"
Furthermore, he saw a heap of wooden figures on the ground; because he had surpassed them, they had died as a result.
It was the law of that country that whenever someone died, it must first be reported to the king before the funeral rites could be performed.
The host hurriedly informed the king, saying:
"A painter from the kingdom of Central India came to live in my house; I provided him with a mechanical wooden woman."
"The rope by which he was being hauled up snapped; this man, overcome with shame, hanged himself and died.
I pray that Your Majesty will inspect the matter, for I wish to provide him with a funeral.
The King immediately ordered an official to go and look, and the messenger reported:
"Cut the rope first to see if it is cut through, and then examine whether he died by hanging himself or was strangled by the host.
At that moment, the host took an axe and began cutting, but he only struck the wall; the guest then said:
"Is this for life or for death?
Having thus addressed the king and his ministers, he felt profound shame.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What do you think?
The painter at that time was none other than Śāriputra.
The one who fashioned the wooden mechanical woman was none other than Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
"At that time, he was able to surpass him through his craftsmanship; now, by employing supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), he has once again gained the victory.
Furthermore, monks, listen attentively!"
In the distant past, in a certain village, there were two painters who vied with one another in their skills; each claimed, "I am superior, for I clearly understand the artistry."
They went together to the king's presence and said:
"I shall paint it tomorrow.
The second one also said: [the same].
"I can paint. Thereupon, the king immediately ordered that a face be painted on each of the walls, saying, "Once you have finished painting them, you shall know; I do not believe what you say."
One of the painters took six months to paint a single face.
The second painter merely polished and adorned the surface of the wall.
When the first painter had finished his work, he addressed the king, saying:
"I have finished painting the wall.
The king, together with his ministers, came to view the painted colors and said:
"Extremely handsome!
The second painter said to the king:
"Look at my painting; it is because the light and shadow from the previous wall-painting appear through this that it seems as though covered by a thin garment."
When the king saw this, he was greatly amazed and said,
"This is even more excellent than that.
After the man had prostrated at the king's feet, he addressed him, saying:
"This is not my painting; it is because of that mural that this reflection appears here.
Great King!
Is the painter more exquisite and beautiful?"
"Furthermore, is this place well-proportioned?
The king replied,
"If it were made by you, it would be exceedingly well-proportioned."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think?
The one who spent six months grinding pigments at that time was none other than Śāriputra."
The painter who lived at that time was none other than Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
At that time, he achieved victory through his craftsmanship; now, he has again achieved victory through his supernormal powers.
"Furthermore, bhikṣus, listen attentively!
It is not only now that my supernormal powers have been superior. Long ago, not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, there were two rishis:
one named Śaṅkha and the other named Likhita."
At a later time, when the heavens sent down heavy rain and the ground was covered in much mud,
the seer Śaṅkha tripped and fell, and his jar was struck and broken.
Due to the sage’s curse, it did not rain for twelve years.
King Brahmadatta and the people of Vārāṇasī all heard that the sage’s curse had caused the heavens not to send down rain for twelve years.
The king and the people of the country went together to the place where that seer was and said to him:
"Great Seer!
Do not act in this way."
The seer replied, "I cannot bear this;
I shall cause it so that no rain falls for twelve years.
King Brahmadatta and the others went separately to the seer Lekittha and informed him of the matter.
"Because this seer spoke words of truth, it was timely for the heavens to send down a great rain.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The seer named Kaśyapa at that time was none other than Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
"The ṛṣi Lekhita was none other than Śāriputra.
This is explained in detail as above.
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!"
Those two rishis had a minor cause for grievance, and the rishi Rikṣaka immediately sought forgiveness from Uśanas.
As he was prostrating at his feet, Uśanas stepped on the topknot of Rikṣaka’s head with his foot.
When he was trampled, he immediately made this oath:
"I pray that at the time of sunrise tomorrow, your head shall split apart.
Śaṅkha then likewise made an oath:
"May the sun not rise.
Since the sun did not rise, the world was plunged into darkness.
All the brahmins and the multitude of people in the city came and said to the seer Saṅkha:
"Do not do this. The seer replied,
"If I were to cause the sun to rise, my head would surely split asunder."
Ratitara said to Śakra, "You should fashion a clay head.
The seer immediately fashioned a clay head and placed it upon his own; as the sun rose, the clay head shattered.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not entertain any other view.
The rishi Śaṅkha at that time was none other than Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
"The ṛṣi Riktaka was the bhikṣu Śāriputra.
At that time he already surpassed him, and now he likewise surpasses him.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Listen further!
I shall now speak for you.
Long ago, in Central India, there was a skilled artisan who was well-versed in ivory work."
He then took an elephant tusk and carved it into one *dǒu* of polished rice to serve as provisions for his journey, and set out for the kingdom of Persia.
Upon arriving in that country, he went to the home of a skilled artisan and wished to stay there for a short while.
This man was not there, but only his wife was present.
Having seen his wife, he said to her:
"Take this peck of white non-glutinous rice and prepare a meal for me."
The artisan’s wife replied, “Leave this rice here; you should go now.
The man left the rice and departed immediately.
She then proceeded to cook it, but although both the firewood and the fuel were exhausted, the rice remained uncooked.
When her husband arrived home, he asked his wife:
"O virtuous one!..."
"What are you making now?
The wife then explained everything in detail.
The husband examined the rice and realized it was made of ivory; with a deceitful mind, he said:
"This water contains ash, so the rice cannot be cooked.
Use pure, sweet water to boil it, and the rice will cook immediately.
Later, when the person who had left the rice returned, his wife reported this to him.
"You should fetch some pure, sweet water.
The man took a clay jar to fetch water;
having arrived early, he quickly drew a pond, and within that pond, he drew a dead dog, its body bloated and putrid.
When the water-drawer reached the pond, he saw the dog; covering his nose with one hand and lowering the jar with the other, he looked at the dog and struck the jar until it broke.
Once the jar was broken, he felt ashamed.
The Buddha said,
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor other thoughts."
The skilled artisan who formerly fashioned the ivory rice was Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
The one who painted the lotus pond was the present Śāriputra. You bhikṣus!
The concentration attained by the Tathāgata is such that even the noble Pratyekabuddhas do not know its name.
The concentration attained by the Pratyekabuddhas is such that even Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana do not know its name.
The meditative concentrations attained by Śāriputra are such that even the other śrāvakas do not know their names.
The bhikṣu Śāriputra possesses great majestic power and surpasses Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Nevertheless, because he frequently manifested supernatural powers, it was said in secret:
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana is the foremost in supernatural powers.
Furthermore, Mahākāśyapa himself spoke of his own karma, reciting these verses:
Kāśyapa went before the assembly and fully recounted the Dharma practiced in his previous lives:
"By giving away even a small portion of merit, one obtains this immeasurable and supreme field of blessings."
Just as the lion king of the world Roams through the mountains and marshes without fear;
So now is Mahākāśyapa likewise, Expounding the ancient Dharma with a fearless mind.
In the past, I once offered a measure of chaff as alms to an untainted Pratyekabuddha;
while he dwelt in the most stainless samādhi, I now likewise receive it with faith.
Having made great vows within the Buddha's teaching, may I always hear such supreme Dharma;
by these causes and conditions, may I obtain the karmic fruit of being born a thousand times in Uttarakuru.
In that land, they were long-lived and free from the sense of "self" and "other";
gradually attaining noble status without deficiency, through the fruit of this single deed, they were born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven a thousand times.
That deva receives exquisite fragrant garlands, his physical form adorned with most excellent beauty;
when his karmic lifespan is exhausted and his life comes to an end, he returns once more to the heavens to obtain peace and joy.
Because he made a great vow through a single deed, he possessed abundant wealth and treasures yet felt no attachment to them;
seeking neither the five desires nor worldly pleasures, he immediately renounced his home to study the Buddha-way.
In the past, I did not encounter a great enlightened teacher, nor did I meet with the assembly of śrāvakas;
yet, upon seeing one clad in the dyed robes of the kaṣāya, I immediately prostrated myself and sought to leave the household life.
When I saw him thus going forth, sitting among the assembly before the Buddha, he rose from the crowd, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and declared: "The Buddha is my preceptor."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words:
"You are my disciples and I am your teacher;
if you seek liberation from all suffering and hardship, you should listen to and receive the pure and wondrous Dharma."
The World-Honored One preached the sublime Dharma for me, arousing great compassion toward me;
he caused me to cultivate and learn the four dhyānas, the ten powers, the six faculties, and the eightfold noble path.
I have now attained such a Dharma as this; with outflows exhausted, I shall not be born again.
This is my final reception of a body; I am a companion to all the noble sages.
The Tathāgata always speaks the Dharma of truth; may those who uphold the pure precepts have their wishes fulfilled.
May the vows I have made now be realized, so that this is my final existence and I shall not undergo further birth.
Birth and craving are now exhausted for me; the fetters of existence are severed and shall not bind me again.
I am the eldest son within the Dharma; by the power of the Dharma King, I am free from all suffering.
The Buddha has already declared me the foremost, the most excellent among those who practice *dhūta*;
having seen the true truths and realized the genuine Dharma, my delusions are now exhausted and I have attained immovability.

Before the Honored Sage, I recounted my past deeds; While dwelling within the great Anavatapta Lake, The Great Sage, the Compassionate Honored One, bestowed his grace upon me, And as I sat peacefully upon a lotus flower, I related these matters.
At that time, the elder śrāvakas and great bhikṣus asked the venerable Śāriputra:
"What karma did you perform in the past?
By virtue of that karma, you have attained great wisdom and unimpeded eloquence."
At that time, Śāriputra replied in verse:
“In the past, I saw a recluse in the mountain forests; he was a Pratyekabuddha, one who dwells in tranquility.
Relying on a secluded and empty place, he practiced pure conduct, his body clad in a tattered and soiled saffron robe.”
At that time, seeing him, my heart was filled with joy;
I immediately took his robe to wash and dye it, further mending and stitching it skillfully with needle and thread, and paid him reverent homage with sincere devotion.
He then felt compassion for me, leaping up with his entire body into the great void;
manifesting various supernatural transformations, he then soared away through the air.
At that time, having witnessed this divine transformation, I joined my palms with a sincere heart and made this great vow:
"May I always possess wisdom in every birth, Possess great power and abundant wealth and treasures;
Within those illustrious and noble clans, May I always be able to leave the home life and renounce the five desires."
By the power of this vow, he attained the going forth; for five hundred lifetimes, he remained free from the worldly net.
This is his final body, born among human beings;
there he personally served the Great Teacher, the Unsurpassed, Perfectly Enlightened One.
Now that I have gone forth under the teaching of the Lion of the Śākyas,
having attained the Dharma of peace and security, I have cast off heat and found coolness.
Within half a month, I have mastered the recitation and reached the further shore.
To my preceptor, before the assembly of monks,
he bestowed upon me this prophecy: "O Mahāmati, most eminent one,
you shall turn the wheel of Dharma in accordance with reality, causing all sentient beings to attain awakening and understanding."
"Śāriputra, O Great Wisdom, Amidst the great assembly of the Saṅgha,
Proclaimed his own past karmic retribution While preaching within the Anavatapta Lake.
At that time, the elder Śrāvakas and great Bhikṣus addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
“Śāriputra has already recounted his past karma; it is now your turn, Venerable One, to speak of the conditions for your own karmic retribution from former lives.
When these words were spoken, Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the elders with a verse, speaking this hymn:
“In the past I was a hermit, Dwelling amidst mountain thickets;”
At that time, a man came seeking to leave the household life under me.
I immediately shaved his hair and beard, bathed him, and dyed his robes;
I then gave them to him and had him put them on.
This person, in a secluded place, straightened his body and sat in the full lotus posture;
having realized the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, he rose and soared into the sky.
With palms joined in reverence, he made this great vow:
Now I have attained great supernormal powers:
"I vow to obtain such powers as these great seers possess.
By the power of these roots of goodness, wherever I am born, I shall always obtain blessings.
Having been born into the human realm, I have personally served the Great Teacher,
the Unequaled, Perfectly Awakened One.
I have attained the life of a renunciant and have already realized arhatship.
Heat was dispelled and I attained coolness;
the World-Honored One prophesied that I am foremost in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
By virtue of giving even a small portion [of an offering], I have now reaped this great fruit of retribution.
Listen well, O virtuous one, as I recount the cruel and evil karma of former times.
Having been born into a noble and wealthy clan, when I was first a young boy,
I went out from my courtyard to play.
Encountering my father and mother in union, I felt shame upon seeing them;
he then struck me with a staff.
Because of this, harboring resentment, I made a vow as I spoke: "When I grow up, I shall crush his body like a blade of grass."
When one makes such evil vows, one is born in the Black Rope Hell;
after having endured all manner of extreme suffering, one may be born among humans.
This is the final body, yet it remains due to residual karmic offenses.
Encountering this challenge from the non-Buddhist, my life-force was nearly extinguished.
Now that the retribution for my final transgression has been exhausted and nothing more remains,
I have given rise to pure faith toward my compassionate parents.
All living beings who fall into the evil realms,
Because their minds harbor evil deeds, Constantly experience suffering and find no joy.
Maudgalyāyana, addressing the venerable elders, Spoke thus of the retribution for past karma.
"In the great pool of Anavatapta, he sits serenely upon a flower pedestal.
At that time, the elder Śrāvakas and great Bhikṣus said to the venerable Bhikṣu Kalyāṇabhadrika:
"The venerable Maudgalyāyana has finished recounting his past karma; it is now your turn, O Venerable One, to speak of the causes and conditions of your own past karmic retribution."
Having spoken these words, at that time Sumukha spoke in verse, saying:
"In the past, when I entered a monastery, I saw that the ground was covered in dust and filth;
I immediately took up a broom And cleared away the refuse, sweeping and plastering it clean."
Because he gave rise to a pure and faithful mind, And swept and sprinkled [the ground] to make it clean;
By virtue of these roots of goodness, He was born with a handsome and upright body.
His parents bestowed upon him a name, Naming him "Wondrously Come."
Before his retinue and others, his timely, excellent,
and beautiful reputation was such that all people always delighted in seeing him;
those who saw him were filled with joy as he personally attended the Great Teacher, the Unsurpassed, Perfectly Awakened One.
I have attained arhatship; having left behind the feverish heat, I have gained cool serenity.
In the past I made this vow: "When my afflictions are exhausted, may I become one without outflows.
In Jambudvīpa and the other continents, I swept the ground with silken brocades.
If there is anyone who can sweep the place where those free from desire walk,
that person can sweep this earth and all other lands;
if there is anyone who can sweep the dwelling places of the Sangha of the four quarters.

If the ground of a stūpa is as level as the palm of a hand, even as large as the space where a bowl might rest, the merit of such a person will increase, and they shall also be able to attain self-awakening.
Therefore, you should know this: one shall become a Truly and Fully Enlightened One.
There is a great mass of merit; one should diligently make offerings at the stūpa.
To obtain such a great karmic fruit is entirely due to the time of the past;
it is only through the various wholesome deeds cultivated then that one now attains this peace and happiness.
Therefore, at a Buddha-stūpa, one should offer worship with a resolute mind;
To this unsurpassed field of merit, one should give with a pure heart.
Whether it be toward the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment, Or in the presence of the Buddha’s śrāvakas,
Giving little, one obtains great merit, because of the purity of one's observance of the precepts.
Before a vast and virtuous assembly, he recounted the retribution of his past karma;
dwelling peacefully in the Lake Anavatapta, he sat serenely upon a sublime lotus throne.
At that time, the elder śrāvakas and great bhikṣus said to the venerable Sumati:
"Suvrata has already described the retribution of his past karma; it is now your turn, Venerable One, to speak of your own past karma."
At that time, Subhūti spoke these verses:
"In the past, when I was a youth, Together with my companions,
Placing sumana flowers behind our ears, We went together to a grove of blossoming trees."
Seeing the Buddha Vipaśyin at the great stūpa,
the hosts of devas and humans all raised grand offerings;
with pure hearts, they held garlands upon their heads and ears.
Hanging them upon a lofty stupa, each made this vow:
"When I saw him offer flowers, I immediately stood before the great assembly,
took the flower from my ear, and hung it upon the Great Stupa of the Buddha."
By the power of these roots of goodness, one is born in the six heavens of the desire realm and constantly obtains great rewards.
For one hundred koṭis of years, one experiences sublime bliss among the gods.
Finally realizing non-arising,
the Perfectly Awakened One of great merit, who has diligently practiced supreme offerings—
the foremost Honored One in the world— one should revere his stūpa.
When the Great Master and his disciples, with a pure mind, give even a small portion,
they obtain boundless fruits of merit.
I call to mind a past life.
By performing such minor wholesome deeds, and through the power of this meritorious karma,
one constantly enjoys the pleasures of the devas;
having attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, one has already become an Arhat.
Heat departed, he attained coolness.
This is his final body; he shall not undergo further existence.
Named Sumana, he is liberated from the entire mass of suffering.
Having already crossed the ocean of existence,
the bhikṣu Sumanas, seated upon a lotus pedestal within the Great Lake Anavatapta, proclaimed before the assembly the karmic retributions of his past lives.

At that time, the senior śrāvakas said to the venerable Koṭīkarṇa Bhikṣu, "The venerable Sumanas Bhikṣu has already spoken of his own karma; it is now your turn to speak—what karma did you perform in the past?"
"By what karma did the Buddha declare you to be the foremost among those who are diligent?
At that time, the Venerable Koṭīviṃśa replied in verse:
"In the past, at the city of Sāketa, I constructed a vihāra."
Having completed the cultivation of a pure mind, he offered it to the Sangha of the four directions.
Within this monastery, he spread silken fabrics upon the ground;
with a joyful and harmonious heart, he made this great vow.
May I always aspire to serve the Buddha and attain the unsurpassed fruit;
may I realize the foremost nirvana and forever be free from all afflictions.
By virtue of this merit, throughout ninety kalpas,
Constantly receiving the bodies of humans and devas, they were always joyful and fearless.
Having remaining residual karma, he received this final body;
born into a noble family, he was my only son.
When the ten months were complete, I was born; my heart was filled with great joy.
At that time, my father bestowed upon me wealth numbering two million.
My feet were covered in golden hair, four inches in length both long and short.
Exquisite, peerless, and supple, like tūla-cotton;
having passed through ninety kalpas, his feet never trod upon the ground.
By the power of these meritorious causes and conditions, he personally attended the Great Teacher.
Through supreme, perfect enlightenment, one attains the bliss of gods and humans;
having realized arhatship, one leaves behind heat and gains coolness.
The World-Honored One has already declared me the foremost among those who are diligent.
All outflows are completely exhausted, and I have attained the stainless state.
I, Viśvabhū, amidst twenty koṭis of people before this assembly of elders,
declare my past karmic retribution within the Great Lake Anavatapta.
At that time, the senior śrāvakas and great bhikṣus said to the venerable Mañjughoṣa:
"The venerable ones consisting of twenty koṭis of bhikṣus have already spoken of their past karma; it is now your turn to speak."
At that time, the Venerable Ghosaka addressed him in verse:
"I previously planted roots of merit, Throughout ninety kalpas;
I did not fall into the three evil realms, But attained the bodies of gods and humans."
I did not yet recognize the Three Jewels; I saw only this stūpa of the Buddha.
The Buddha’s name was Vipaśyin, and I made a great offering to him.
Furthermore, with three gold coins, I purchased unguents and other offerings.
Placing it upon a Buddha stūpa with single-minded devotion and without turning back,
by the power of this merit, he enjoyed much happiness among gods and humans;
now having attained arhatship, he has cast off all heat and found coolness.
Before the Buddha’s stūpa, I made vast and subtle vows;
through this small offering, I have received immeasurable fruit.
The great assembly should now know that the Equally Awakened One possesses great merit.
By presenting a small offering before the stūpa, one obtains boundless karmic fruit.
The World-Honored One bestowed upon me this prediction:
"Among those of vast learning, you shall be the foremost, widely proclaiming wondrous eloquence within those gāthās."

"Before this great assembly, as well as before these elders, I have already recounted the matters of my past karma within the Great Lake Anavatapta. At that time, the elder Śrāvakas and great Bhikṣus addressed the Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, saying: [The text continues: "Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, you too should recount your own past karma before this great assembly, before these elders, and before the Blessed One. Then the Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja spoke thus to those elder Śrāvakas and great Bhikṣus: "Elders, listen to me as I recount the matters of my past karma. At that time, the Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja said to the elder Śrāvakas and great Bhikṣus: "Elders, formerly I was a master of the Vedas named Śroṇa. I had a son named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa. He was handsome, possessed of a pleasing appearance, and endowed with the marks of a great man. He was skilled in all the arts and crafts, and he was learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary branches. He was able to debate with the Brahmins of the four quarters, and he was capable of refuting them. He was also proficient in the five types of supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). "Elders, at that time King Bimbisāra of Magadha heard that there was a master of the Vedas named Śroṇa who had a son named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, who was handsome, possessed of a pleasing appearance, and endowed with the marks of a great man; who was skilled in all the arts and crafts, learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary branches, able to debate with the Brahmins of the four quarters, capable of refuting them, and proficient in the five types of supernormal powers. Hearing this, the king summoned him and appointed him as his personal attendant. "Elders, at that time the Blessed One, having set out on a journey through the country of Magadha, arrived at Rājagṛha. There the Blessed One dwelt at the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Elders, at that time King Bimbisāra heard that the Blessed One had arrived at Rājagṛha and was dwelling at the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Hearing this, the king went to the Blessed One, paid homage at his feet, and sat to one side. As he sat there, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened King Bimbisāra with a discourse on the Dharma. Having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dharma, King Bimbisāra rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and departed. "Elders, at that time King Bimbisāra, having returned to his palace, summoned the master of the Vedas named Śroṇa and said to him: 'Master Śroṇa, go to the Blessed One and pay homage at his feet in my name. Ask after his health, saying: "Is the Blessed One free from illness? Is he free from affliction? Is he dwelling in comfort? Is he vigorous? And say to him: "May the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus, accept tomorrow's meal from me at my residence. "Elders, the master of the Vedas named Śroṇa accepted the king's command and went to the Blessed One. Having approached the Blessed One, he paid homage at his feet and stood to one side. Standing there, he said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, King Bimbisāra pays homage at the Blessed One's feet and asks after your health, saying: "Is the Blessed One free from illness? Is he free from affliction? Is he dwelling in comfort? Is he vigorous? Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus, accept tomorrow's meal from King Bimbisāra at his residence. "Elders, the Blessed One consented by remaining silent. Then the master of the Vedas named Śroṇa, knowing the Blessed One had consented, paid homage at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. "Elders, the next day the master of the Vedas named Śroṇa returned to the king's palace and informed King Bimbisāra: 'Great King, I have informed the Blessed One of your request. The Blessed One has consented. "Elders, at that time King Bimbisāra, having prepared various kinds of excellent food and drink, had the time announced to the Blessed One: 'It is time, Venerable Sir; the meal is ready. Elders, the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, went to the king's palace together with the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus and sat upon the prepared seat. "Elders, at that time the master of the Vedas named Śroṇa saw that the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl. He took a low stool and sat down to one side. Sitting there, he said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, I wish to ask the Blessed One about a certain matter; may the Blessed One grant me the opportunity to speak. "Elders, the Blessed One replied: 'Śroṇa, ask whatever you wish; the Tathāgata will grant you the opportunity to speak. "Elders, the master of the Vedas named Śroṇa said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, how many kinds of recluses and Brahmins are there in the world? "Elders, the Blessed One said: 'Śroṇa, there are four kinds of recluses and Brahmins in the world. What are the four? They are: the recluse and Brahmin who is a seeker of gain; the recluse and Brahmin who is a seeker of honor; the recluse and Brahmin who is a seeker of fame; and the recluse and Brahmin who is a seeker of the Dharma. "What, Śroṇa, is the recluse and Brahmin who is a seeker of gain? Here, Śroṇa, some recluse or Brahmin, for the sake of gain, teaches the Dharma to others. This is called the recluse and Brahmin who is a seeker of gain. "What, Śroṇa, is the recluse and Brahmin who is a seeker of honor? Here, Śroṇa, some recluse or Brahmin, for the sake of honor, teaches the Dharma to others. This is called the recluse and Brahmin who is a seeker of honor. "What, Śroṇa, is the recluse and Brahmin who is a seeker of fame? Here, Śroṇa, some recluse or Brahmin, for the sake of fame, teaches the Dharma to others. This is called the recluse and Brahmin who is a seeker of fame. "What, Śroṇa, is the recluse and Brahmin who is a seeker of the Dharma? Here, Śroṇa, some recluse or Brahmin, seeking only the Dharma, teaches the Dharma to others. This is called the recluse and Brahmin who is a seeker of the Dharma. "Among these four, Śroṇa, which one do you consider to be the foremost? "Elders, the master of the Vedas named Śroṇa said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, among these four, I consider the recluse and Brahmin who is a seeker of the Dharma to be the foremost. "Elders, the Blessed One said: 'Śroṇa, you speak according to the Dharma. Among these four, the recluse and Brahmin who is a seeker of the Dharma is indeed the foremost. "Elders, at that time the master of the Vedas named Śroṇa, having heard the Blessed One's teaching, was filled with joy and delight. He rose from his seat, paid homage at the Blessed One's feet, and departed. "Elders, at that time the Blessed One, having finished his meal, gave thanks to King Bimbisāra and departed from the king's palace. Elders, the Blessed One then set out on a journey through the country of Magadha and arrived at Nādikā. There the Blessed One dwelt at Nādikā in the Brick House. Elders, at that time the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage at his feet, and sat to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, the master of the Vedas named Śro
“The Venerable Ghosila has already spoken of his past karma; it is now your turn to speak.
Thereupon, the Venerable Piṇḍola addressed them in verse:
“In the past, I was born into a noble family, Living with complete autonomy within my parents’ home.”
His father appointed him to oversee the storehouse, where he attended upon his parents.

who then distributed it to me in turn.
