we would cook more than a hundred ladles of rice to provide this food for those renunciants.
Having already provided him with food and drink, greed arose in him and he thought:
"Even my sisters, brothers, wives, sons, daughters, and kinsmen do not provide me with such food and drink;
yet this seer has sat here for three months—he must have many expenses."
How much more so regarding a number of five hundred!
I must cause that śramaṇa to meet his end;
if he should die, I would have no further need for him.
Once the sinful thought had arisen, he boiled the urine of a horse,
mixed it with food, and gave it to him to eat.
After he had consumed this meal, he immediately fell ill, and his intestines and stomach came out.
At that time, knowing he had died, that seer who had attained the Way [cried out].
Then the nāgas, devas, and others all spoke with a great voice:
"A great sin is this merchant's; he has wrongly killed the seer without fault."
I have attained mastery as a solitary buddha, one who is tranquil and free from outflows.
All my kinsmen are angry with me;
they should all examine this well, for it will give rise to much sinful karma because of my killing of that seer.
Having heard the words spoken by my kinsman, I immediately gave rise to sorrow and grief;
I invited the other seers and felt profound remorse for my transgression.
Having confessed before the Buddhas and repented with a heart mindful of my present faults, I am now purified.
He offered rice to five hundred sages, providing them with abundance and ensuring they were fully satisfied;
he confessed his own karmic offenses before those sages.
Having made this offering of food, he immediately made this vow:
"May it be so in the future: may I make offerings to this Great Virtuous One;
just as he has attained liberation, may I also be freed from bonds;
in birth after birth, may I leave behind impoverished families and never dwell in places of poverty."
Suddenly and constantly giving rise to stinginess and greed, he caused his mind to give vent to evil;
by harming that Pratyekabuddha, he committed an act that brought him sorrow and grief.
After death, he fell into hell, remaining there for a long time—ten thousand years.
They constantly undergo suffering and pain;
later, though they may obtain birth as a human being, they again receive the retribution of a short life.
They should possess abundant wealth and property to provide offerings to all people.
Constantly suffering from his intestines protruding, he passed away because of this.
He then attained the body of one who has gone forth; relying on the teachings, he established himself in practice and abandoned all greed.
"Upon the lotus seat of the Heatless One, he shall proclaim the causes and conditions of his past karma.
At that time, the Venerable Elder Bhikṣu addressed the Venerable Kṣudrakapāda, saying:
"The Venerable Satyaka has already spoken of his karmic retribution; it is now the turn of the Venerable to speak."
Then, Khandaka-Kāśyapa spoke these verses:
“I went to invite the assembly of bhikṣus for seven years without fail;
within that village, a time of famine occurred.”
That which I have obtained as my portion is a mind tamed and a tranquil spirit;
this is what the Pratyekabuddhas revere—free from affliction and profoundly cool.
Previously, I made a solemn vow: "I shall not give to those who beg."
"Even for one's own children or parents, nothing can be provided unless it is produced through labor.
Having formed such a thought, one consequently commits an evil deed;
since a bhikṣu does not engage in such work, why should food be given to him?"
He first sent this bhikṣu to walk upon the fields;
only when he had arrived at the house did he provide him with food and drink.
Due to the ripening of this evil karma, he subsequently fell into hell.
Living beings suffer amidst the scorching heat, enduring all manner of agonizing torments.
When the karmic retribution of hell is exhausted, one wanders through the various realms of rebirth;
there one is base and lowly, constantly beset by sorrow and suffering, and food and sustenance are exceedingly difficult to obtain.
This is my very last time that I have obtained a human body;
having placed unimpaired faith in the Tamer of Men, the Unsurpassed Honored One, the Perfectly Awakened One,
I have gone forth into homelessness.
Having eliminated all outflows and realized the six supernormal powers, I have attained the fruit of arhatship.
O virtuous ones, you should know that although I have realized great supernormal powers,
it was only after enduring the extreme hardship of walking meditation that I finally obtained food and drink.
Wandering to the farthest reaches, I eventually obtained a small amount;
as my life was about to be severed, I was able to find food at that time.
My clan is Kesi, and my name is Karṇa-mahātejas.
"Sitting upon a lotus in the Untroubled [Heaven], he spoke thus of the conditions of his past karma.
At that time, the elder bhikṣus said to the venerable Cūḍapanthaka, "The venerable Upagupta has already spoken of his karmic retribution; it is now the turn of the venerable one to speak."
Then Bandhaka spoke in verse:
"In a previous life, I was a pig-herder;
having tied the pigs' mouths, I was leading them across to the riverbank."
Having reached the center of the river, as I was about to reach the opposite shore,
the pigs' breath failed them, and because of this, they all passed away.
I was swept away by the current, drifting and submerged, bewildered and at a loss for what to do.
A seer dwelt by the riverbank, who out of compassion provided rescue and relief.
He drew me out from drowning in the suffering of grief and granted me the going forth;
through the samādhi of signlessness, he taught and transformed me until I was disciplined and compliant.
Having passed away from this state, he was reborn in the heavens;
having just relinquished his life in the heavens, he descended to be born among humans.
With devotion and reverence for the Samyaksaṃbuddha, he renounced worldly life to become a monastic.
Stubborn, foolish, and extremely dull-witted, he was unable to retain the instructions shown to him.
Within those three months, he could only recite a single verse;
yet once he had clarified the meaning of that one line, his afflictions and desires were entirely eliminated.
I recall with such mindfulness the karma I previously created;
having passed through immeasurable time, I have wandered in the ocean of birth and death.
Now, in the presence of the Father of the World, here at this Lake of No Heat;
"I, Cūḍapanthaka, have thus explained these black and white karmas.
At that time, the elder bhikṣus said to the venerable Āśīviṣa:
"The venerable Cūḍapanthaka has already spoken of his karmic retribution; it is now the turn of the venerable one to speak."
Then the snake-servant spoke in verse:
“After the Parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, I was his final disciple;
Though learned and possessing the Tripiṭaka, I was exceedingly stingy regarding the Dharma.”
I do not recite or explain [the teachings] for the sake of other bhikṣus,
fearing that other bhikṣus might surpass me.
When a bhikṣu comes to me wishing to inquire about even a small matter of meaning, I do not teach him.
Because I harbored ill-will toward those of ugly appearance, I rebuked them and refused to attend to their needs.
When the bhikṣus arrived, they came to admonish me for this view:
"Why do you not govern through the transformation of the Dharma, but instead act in such an improper and irrational manner?"
At the time of my death, my heart gave rise to extreme remorse;
that the sublime and wondrous Dharma I had mastered was not revealed to others.
My life now has but seven days remaining; the time passes and will not linger long.
I should assemble the ordained practitioners to repent for all my transgressions.
Having repented for my sins, I shall cease my stinginess regarding the Dharma;
thus, in the midst of the great assembly, I shall constantly preach the Dharma for seven days.
Having heard the well-spoken Dharma, they all listened and received it from me;
they explained it to one another and engaged in discussion together.
On account of my impending death, I preached the sublime Dharma for seven days.
He was reborn in the heavens, where all desires were fully provided.
When his karmic retribution in the heavens was exhausted, he descended to be born in the human realm;
he was born in Kapilavastu, within the royal clan of the Śākyas.
Possessing great wealth and noble status, his appearance was most pleasing;
all people revered and loved him, and his assets were never lacking.
The men and women of his clan renounced the secular life to enter the monastic order.
Bound by the fetters of desire, I felt no inclination for joy.
Yet the Peerless Great Man, out of compassion for me,
came repeatedly to my abode to exhort and encourage me to go forth.
I then prostrated before the Tamer of Men, the Unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One;
I pray that for seven years you will compassionately accept this offering of the ritual ground.
If you see that his offering is accepted, then the seven years will soon have passed.
One may only follow Mahāmati and truly go forth from the household life.
He told me that my life is precarious and fragile; it will not last even a moment, let alone seven years.
You should quickly practice giving, for the next breath is difficult to preserve.
The Buddha’s words are profound and revered; how could I dare to reject them?
He spoke, saying: "Within seven days, out of compassion, grant me the going forth.
Then, during those seven days, he provided for him with all his needs as he wished.
Within and without that city, all his kinsmen stood guard and surrounded him.
A supreme, great radiance shone everywhere across the city walls;
an inconceivable multitude of people emerged from outside the city.
Within the teachings of the Buddha-dharma, I left the home life out of pure faith;
yet for twenty-five years, my mind attained no true awakening.
Thereupon, a sinful thought arose, and I no longer wished to abide by this [teaching].
Unable to reach the nectar of immortality, it is better that you withdraw and return home.
Having given rise to such timidity and fear, I feel deep and great shame;
my relatives and family members will surely mock and deride me.
The thoughts that arise are not of a wholesome nature; I clearly recognize these as unwholesome matters.
It is fitting that I should harm myself with a blade; what use is this wretched life?
He then took up an extremely sharp blade and sat upright in the full lotus posture.
Placing a blade upon his head, his mind immediately attained liberation.
Once his mind was cleansed, he praised with every word:
"How marvelous are the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha! Such supreme and virtuous teachings exist!"
Formerly I harbored such thoughts that an ordinary person would have cast off their life;
disregarding my own life and limb, I realized unsurpassed tranquility.
In my former existence, I was indolent and extremely stingy regarding the Dharma.
Due to the retribution of this, it was with great difficulty that I attained liberation.
Furthermore, at the time of my death, you preached the pure and wondrous Dharma for me;
through the ripening of this karma, I have transcended and eliminated all desire for wealth.
“Dharmapāla, son of the Śākyas, and the serpent-servant Mahātejas;
at the Lake Anavatapta, they recounted this retribution for their past karma.
At that time, the elder bhikṣus again addressed the venerable Aniruddha, saying:
“The Venerable Āśīviṣadāsa has already spoken of his karmic retribution;
it is now the turn of the Venerable. Thereupon, Aniruddha spoke this verse:
“Formerly I had no means of support, Living in poverty by carrying grass for hire;”
Seeking refuge and announcing his name, he came to attend upon the Great Śramaṇa.
In this life, born of the Śākya clan, his name was Aniruddha;
he was skilled in song, dance, and performance, and capable of all exquisite melodies.
Rarely did we encounter the Great Teacher, the Fearless One of Perfect Enlightenment;
having seen him, our minds became pure, and we abandoned the secular life to go forth.
Having heard the teachings he proclaimed, we joyfully dwell in the presence of the Great Master.
With no moment of negligence in his conduct, he was always diligent, self-urging, and courageous.
Having fully attained the three types of clear knowledge, he fulfilled the Great Teacher’s instruction;
he perceived his past lives and all the deeds he had previously performed.
In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, he was reborn seven times;
Seven times he was born in the human realm, And likewise served as a sovereign of men.
A consecrated Kṣatriya, he alone transformed the world Throughout Jambudvīpa.
Seven there and seven here, he transmigrates fourteen times;
wherever he dwelt and enjoyed life, he knows every such place.
Regarding these various karmic fruits and retributions, there is nothing he does not fully know.
In whatever place I am born, my heart is filled with supreme joy.
Observing and knowing the realms of birth and death through which all sentient beings cycle,
and how this life transforms into another manifestation, I bind my mind in single-minded recollection.
The affairs of the saṃsāra of the five destinies, he perceives all clearly with his divine eye;
having attained the path of tranquility, his divine eye is exceedingly bright and pure.
The unsurpassed teacher of the world knows the thoughts within my mind.
The Buddha, through his supernormal powers of body and mind, has come to my presence;
whatever I have contemplated, he is able to explain with superior insight.
The Great Teacher is without fault, and what he teaches is likewise without error.
Having heard what was said by him, I dwelt in purity according to his instruction.
With a mind of supreme diligence, I constantly practiced without negligence;
having mastered the three types of higher knowledge, I have done what was to be done.
Having no joy in birth, nor any sorrow in death;
knowing only to await the arrival of the time, one dwells in right mindfulness and maintains dignified deportment.
At the village of Veṇugrāmaka in Vaiśālī, my life shall come to its end.
Beneath that bamboo grove, I desired to bring [the Buddha] back to conversion.
Because I previously offered him food, I have obtained this most excellent fruit;
I pay reverent homage to the Great Teacher, the peerless Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Having realized arhatship, the state of coolness and tranquility,
the Seers have declared me the foremost among those of great merit.
This Aniruddha, before the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus—
"In the Anavatapta Lake, he recounted this karmic retribution from his past.
Then the elder bhikṣus addressed the venerable bhikṣu Siṃhagalla:
"The venerable Aniruddha has already spoken of his karmic retribution; it is now the turn of the venerable one to speak."
At that time, Kāla spoke in verse:
"I was previously pressing sugarcane until I reached the sugar-boiling hall;
then a sick pratyekabuddha approached me, walking slowly."
Within those seven days, he constantly served him with sugar and oil;
after those seven days had passed, the Pratyekabuddha ascended into the sky and departed.
While I was away on business, my servant addressed me, saying:
"There exists such a supreme field of merit; compared to receiving offerings at home, [this is far superior].
Having heard these words, my heart gave rise to the utmost pure faith;
I quickly went to the place where he ascended into the air, regarding him with deep reverence and admiration."

Due to having previously aroused a pure mind, and further by the condition of giving oil and sugar, one proceeds through the realms of gods and humans; endowed with merit, the mind is luminous and clear.
This is my final birth, and I have also attained a human body.
With reverent devotion toward the Great Teacher, the Peerless, Truly and Fully Enlightened One,
I aspire to go forth under the instruction of the Great Śākyamuni;
may I realize arhatship, that state of coolness and tranquility.
I have now attained supreme peace; my gains and offerings are exceedingly abundant.
My clothing, food, bedding, and medicinal decoctions lack for nothing.
For a minor matter, I require four lumps of sugar.
Desiring to give clothing for sewing, I was about to prepare an offering of sugar.
The devas, knowing my thought, immediately informed King Bimbisāra:
"You should quickly bestow upon Kāla a refreshing syrup of refined sugar."
Because of this gift of the beverage, the King obtained great merit;
he should therefore send Jīvaka to carry mangoes and sugar.
He immediately dispatched four large elephants to transport the truly exquisite flavors.
The Great Fortunate King Prasenajit ordered that it be sent to my place;
once the king had dispatched the messenger, I received this sweet sugar.
It was provided for the sake of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
The Arhat Kāla, endowed with the six great supernormal powers,
spoke of this retribution for past karma within the Anavatapta Lake.
At that time, the elder bhikṣus again addressed the venerable Rāhula, saying:
“The Venerable Kāla has already spoken on the retribution of karma;
it is now the turn of the Venerable. Thereupon, Rāhula spoke these verses:
“I was once a former king, Residing in the capital of Vaiśālī;”
Setting forth to transform the world through the interdependence of the primary and secondary, I caused all beings to find peace and benefit.
At that time, a seer arrived, his majestic power most formidable;
he came before me and spoke these words:
"I am now a thief who drank water that was not given;
I pray the King apply the law for thieves and punish me according to the regulations.
I then replied to him:
"O Sage, if your dharma and virtue are complete, may the waters of springs, wells, rivers, and streams be permitted for you to drink as you please.
Yet, the doubts harbored within me cannot be entirely dispelled;
I pray that you witness my punishment for my transgression, so that I may immediately be free from such anxious thoughts."
He then addressed that seer, saying:
"You should enter the fragrant garden;
you must not eat for six days, after which you may go as you please."
"The karma I have committed was truly without malicious intent;
yet within the Black Rope and Intense Heat hells, I suffered for sixty years.
After that karmic retribution was exhausted, my body remained in the mother's womb for six years."
This was truly not created by the mind, nor were there any actions of body or speech.
Yet, due to these causes and conditions, one undergoes various bitter fruits;
as I speak before this assembly of elders, you should know that karma does not perish.
"This is Rāhula, who, in the presence of the Venerable Elders,
has here at the Anavatapta Lake confessed his former evil karma.
At that time, the elder bhikṣus again addressed the venerable Nanda, saying:
“Venerable Rāhula has already spoken on karmic retribution; it is now the turn of the Venerable One.
Thereupon, Nanda spoke in verse:
“In the teaching of Vipaśyin Buddha, I prepared fragrant bathing water at that time;”
Having bathed the community of bhikṣus, he then spoke these words:
"May I, in future lives, together with all such assemblies as these,
be pure and free from blemish or stain, with all afflictions and outflows eliminated."
"His appearance is upright and handsome, his complexion surpasses that of a lotus.
At that time, when his life had ended, he was reborn in the heavens;
the celestial realm is most transcendent, and the human realm is likewise exquisite.
Wherever the stream of rebirth arises, one will always abide in constant wealth and honor.
Later, assuming the body of a Pratyekabuddha, one shall erect a stupa, bright white and pure;
having adorned it with ointments and incense, it shall be covered over with yellow cloth.
Kneeling with palms joined, he said:
"May my faculties be complete;
may my physical form be like the color of gold, well-maintained and unchanging."
By virtue of these roots of goodness, he was born in Vārāṇasī as the second son of King Gādha.
Furthermore, seeing the stūpa of Kāśyapa, he gave rise to a pure mind through reverent devotion.
Within this very stūpa, a single parasol is suspended.
Because of his prior bathing of the Saṃgha, his smearing of the stūpa with yellow pigment,
and his offering of a parasol to the stūpa, he has obtained manifold peace and happiness.
By virtue of these remaining meritorious deeds, in my final existence,
I was born into the Śākya royal clan as the younger brother of the Tathāgata.
In this present body, I am fully endowed with the marks of a Great Man.
Possessing the thirty excellent marks, complete and without deficiency;
through the teaching of the Lion of the Śākyas, I have attained renunciation;
having realized the ultimate state of Arhatship, I have removed all feverish afflictions and attained cool serenity.
Having received the Buddha’s prediction for me, I am upright, dignified, and most delightful;
my births are all exhausted, and I have reached the unsurpassed state.
This virtuous one, Nanda, stands before the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus.
"At the Lake Anavatapta, he has thus explained this retribution for his past karma.
At that time, the elder bhikṣus said to the venerable Sthiramati:
"The venerable Nanda has already explained his karma and its retribution; it is now the turn of the venerable one."
Then, at that time, Ghaṭīkāra spoke these verses:
"In a previous life, I was a fisherman and a merchant;
Setting out on a trading journey, a seer came along as my companion."
He was a true and great Pratyekabuddha, whose outflows were exhausted and whose mind was unimpeded;
whenever I saw him passing by, I would always invite him to accept a meager offering.
Following him to wherever he stayed for the night, I would prepare various bedding for him.
Washing his feet and offering oil for them to rub, as well as lighting lamps for him;
always serving him with a devout heart while traveling together as companions,
they proceeded slowly until they reached the shore of the ocean.
Having reached the edge of the ocean, I immediately knelt before him and said:
"Virtuous One, for what reason have you come to this place?
We are all entangled in worldly bonds and do not shrink from any suffering."
"Entering into perilous places, into the boundless gathering of the great ocean.
He said, "I have removed my afflictions; may you always be at peace and happy.
In birth after birth, may you be endowed with great merit, possessing abundant wealth without lack."
I immediately took my upper robe, held it forth, and offered it as a gift;
prostrating with my head at his feet, I circumambulated him to the right with a devout heart.
Out of compassion for me, he accepted the robe I had offered.
The entire multitude gazed up with reverence as he ascended into the void.
Witnessing this supernatural power, I was immediately overcome with grief and distress;
bowing my body from afar with palms joined, I made this aspiration:
"May I always encounter such a Great Honored One of sublime virtue;
may I likewise realize and awaken to the wondrous Dharma he has attained.
May I meet a Buddha in the future and be able to leave the household life."
"By making offerings to the Saṃgha, one gives rise to great supernormal powers.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, one always enjoys bliss in the heavens;
likewise, when born in the human realm, one experiences much peace and security.
In every place where one is born, there will be abundant wealth and great nobility;
in both the heavens and the human realm, merit and virtue shall ever be radiant and clear.
From the first moment of receiving this retribution, this shall be the final body.
In the city of Kuśinagara, he was born as the son of a mighty warrior;
his appearance was exceedingly lovely and his countenance peerless.
All people revered and loved him, and he attained the pinnacle of great wealth.
Rarely do we encounter the Lion of the Śākyas, the Unsurpassed, Perfectly Awakened One;
having seen him, my mind became pure, and I abandoned the secular life to go forth.
I have relied upon the interior of the Bamboo Grove and dwelt amidst the mountain ranges.
The assembly of śrāvakas gathered together and troubled the community of bhikṣus;
because of the arrangement of bedding and seats, they spoke ill of the bhikṣus,
or else troubled them with derision and frequent mutual rebukes.
Seeing that he was endowed with these various holy practices, I immediately gave rise to a heart of compassion;
"At this time my birth shall be exhausted, and I shall serve as his attendant.
Thus, I constantly exhorted myself and perpetually cultivated the teachings.
Having realized arhatship and being endowed with the six supernormal powers,
he went to the Great Teacher’s presence; bowing with his head to the ground in prostration,
he joined his palms before him in reverence and made this request of the Unsurpassed One:
"May you grant me your permission, that I may provide for the community of bhikṣus;
free from attachment, aversion, and delusion, I shall treat all with an equal heart of loving-kindness.
The Great Teacher, knowing my intention, accepted my invitation by remaining silent.
He immediately had him reside within the monastery before the assembly of bhikṣus.
With his body he performed acts of compassion, and likewise with his speech and mind;
he provided for the community of bhikṣus, always honoring them with a humble heart.
To the bhikṣus who come and go, And to all those who practice the Way;
I see them with great joy, Comforting them and inquiring after their well-being.
From his five fingers he emits radiance, Like the kindling of a great, bright torch.
Having prepared various bedding and displayed great supernormal powers—
because the bhikṣu desired to see my miraculous transformations—
he came to me only when the time had grown very dark.
Next, they continue to arrive later, all treated with respect through a heart of loving-kindness;
for them he spreads out bedding, never giving rise to thoughts of anger.
"Whatever intentions I previously had, and whatever vows I possess,"
All that was to be purified has been fully accomplished; now it is all perfectly complete.
This noble son Sthiramati, with outflows exhausted and mind mastered, speaks of this prior karmic retribution at the Lake Anavatapta.
At that time, the elder bhikṣus said to the venerable Upāli:
"The venerable Sthavira has finished speaking on karmic retribution; it is now the turn of the venerable one to speak."
Then Upacara immediately spoke in verse:
"In a former time, I was a hunter roaming the wilderness;
seeking to kill deer and antelope, I carried a bow and poisoned arrows."
Seeking the mountains, he ascended steep and perilous heights, never weary by day or night.
When he encountered birds or beasts, a murderous intent would arise within him;
drawing his bow and loosing a venomous arrow, he severed their life-force.
At that time, carrying my bow and arrows,
I was wandering through the forests and thickets when I saw a great Pratyekabuddha dwelling beneath a tree;
upon seeing that śramaṇa, a great surge of anger arose within me.
He was free from transgression, disciplined and serene; yet I struck him with a poisoned arrow.
Having encountered the suffering of that poisoned arrow, he endured intense and manifold pains;
then, beneath that very tree, he relinquished existence and returned to nirvāṇa.
Due to these evil karmas, at the end of my life I fell into hell;
for immeasurable thousands of years, I underwent all manner of agonizing pains.
Once my life in hell had ended, I was reborn in the realm of animals.
Meeting with harm and dying in the mountains, they fall back again into hell.
In every birth they are constantly terrified; at every step they are filled with alarm.
Day and night they suffer from hunger and distress, becoming emaciated and exceedingly haggard.
Yet I constantly encountered a hunter, a fierce and powerful man harboring malice,
who immediately struck me with a sharp, poisoned arrow, and I fell down at once.
Seeing me fallen upon the ground, my life still within me, my body trembling;
Later, with sharp knives they were cut, their flesh sliced off and taken away.
Thus for five hundred lifetimes, they endured manifold sufferings.
Furthermore, in a certain place, for the sake of seeking food;
Then, at the foot of that mountain, I beheld a great multitude of mahāsiddhas,
fully engaged in various ascetic practices and endowed with great divine majesty and virtue;
having seen this assembly of sages, my heart immediately gave rise to thoughts of loving-kindness.
Gradually, his heart was filled with joy as he beheld the assembly of Great Sages;
through this, he gave rise to purity and attained rebirth in the human realm.
Thereupon, he saw a Great Pratyekabuddha coming to beg for food.
I immediately made a formal request, inviting him to my home to receive a modest offering.
Having made this offering to that virtuous one, I joined my palms and made this vow:
"May I, in future lives, always encounter such a venerable teacher."
"Seeing the Buddha, I gave rise to reverence and became a renunciant;
I attained fearlessness and severed all outflows.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, I was reborn in the heavens."
Furthermore, having been born in the human realm, Possessing great wealth and abundant riches,
He reverently served this Great Master, The Peerless, Truly and Fully Enlightened One;
Having seen the Great Muni, He renounced worldly life to enter the homeless state.
Having purified my mind and left the household life, I deeply delight in the Great Teacher’s instruction;
I have realized arhatship and possess the six great supernormal powers.
O Virtuous One, I have now severed all fetters and bonds.
As I am about to enter the mountain cave and prepare to meet my end,
a cruel and venomous snake shall fall upon my body;
at that moment, I shall return to stillness— this is what constitutes the realization of Nirvana.
"Virtuous ones, I have reflected upon the karma created in my previous lives;
having received immeasurable retributions, the deeds one has committed do not perish.
This Upacāra Bhikṣu, before the great assembly of the Saṃgha,"
"At Lake Anavatapta, he has thus explained this retribution for his past karma.
At that time, the elder bhikṣus said to the venerable Bhadrika:
"The venerable Upāli has already explained his karma and its retribution; it is now the turn of the venerable one to speak."
Then the Worthy Son spoke in verse:
"In times past, there was extreme famine; great terror and total darkness prevailed.
At that time, there were five hundred people who sought alms to sustain their lives."
I am the foremost among the assembly, acting as their guide;
when they have obtained food through alms, they all come to offer it to me.

He was reborn again in the human realm, named King Self-Power;
immensely wealthy and exceedingly diligent and courageous, all other kings served him.
By virtue of these virtuous deeds, he continued to be reborn throughout his transmigrations.
The roots of goodness are never severed, and further wondrous causes are continued.
Toward that supreme field of merit, one offers a parasol with a pure mind;
by virtue of this wholesome karma, one does not fall into the evil realms.
This is my final body, born within the human realm;
with reverent devotion toward the Tamer of Men, the Unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One,
I have been able to go forth under the teaching of Śākyasiṃha.
Having realized the state of Arhatship, he dwells in the place of tranquil extinction and coolness.
Mara transformed his body to be like a mountain, one yojana in height;
he assumed a form of great terror, like a dark cloud in the sky.
He declared:
"What thing is this that dares to cause such disturbance?
He perceived that it was Māra, who had come specifically to harass and afflict him.
He replied:
"Māra Pāpīyān, manifest yourself as you wish;
even if your head were as large as Mount Sumeru, you may come to my place."
Having realized arhatship, a śrāvaka endowed with the three knowledges dwells in peace and happiness according to the Dharma taught by the Buddha.
Having received a single portion of food from another, he remained in meditative concentration for seven days.
I have realized the intention of liberation; this is what I have cultivated.
Venerable sir, I reflect upon the wholesome karma I performed in past lives;
I have received its many fruits, which are delightful and most exquisite.
"This Bhikṣu Kṛttikā, before the great assembly of the Saṃgha,
at the Lake Anavatapta, has related this retribution for his past karma.
At that time, after each of the elder bhikṣus had individually related their own past karma, they addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“We have already spoken of the karmic retribution of our past lives; we only pray that the World-Honored One will further expound upon those prior deeds.
Great Virtuous World-Honored One!
What karma did we perform in the past?”
"After he had attained perfect enlightenment, mountain rocks collapsed and wounded his toes.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, when the Tathāgata was born among other species, he himself committed this karma, which he must necessarily experience for himself."

When they have increased and reached maturity, the conditions manifest before one; like a shadow following a form, the retribution must inevitably be experienced, and there is no one else who can receive it on one's behalf. You bhikṣus!

Whatever wholesome or unwholesome karma a person performs does not cause them to receive retribution within the external elements of earth, water, fire, or wind; rather, it brings about its maturation entirely within their own aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
He then spoke in verse:
"Even if a hundred eons should pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, the retribution is inevitably experienced by oneself."
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, there was an elder in a certain village who, shortly after marrying his wife, fathered a son. As the boy gradually grew up, his mother passed away."
The father, the elder, took a stepmother as his wife; before long she became pregnant and gave birth to another son.
Later, he provided the eldest son with a wife, and they had many sons and daughters.
Later, at another time, the stepmother died, and the younger brother went to live with his elder brother.
His wife asked her husband, "Whose son is this? He replied:
"It is my younger brother," his wife said,
"O Noble Son!"
"Should the family property be divided with his younger brother?
The husband replied,
"It should be divided equally."
The wife said, "Noble son!
He is but a single person, while we are many; how can he be divided?"
The husband said:
"O virtuous lady!
Such is the nature of worldly phenomena."
The wife said:
"Noble son! You should kill him."
The husband said:
"O virtuous lady!
How could it be permissible to kill one's own brother for the sake of wealth?"
The wife spoke repeatedly:
"One whose mind is stained by desire will commit no evil.
The husband went to a secluded spot and thought to himself:
"If you were to kill him in a village, the people would all know of it;
you should take him to a secluded place in the forest.
He then commanded his younger brother, saying:
"Take a vessel and come with me to the araṇya to gather flowers.
He replied, "As you command."
They then went together to a mountain slope, pushed his younger brother into a pit, and struck him dead with a stone.
"What do you think, bhikṣus?"
Was the elder’s son who killed his younger brother in the distant past anyone else?
It was none other than myself.
Because of wealth and profit in the past, I cast my own half-brother down a mountain ravine in the forest retreat and struck him with a stone until he died.

Due to this karmic retribution, for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years, they fall into hell and undergo various forms of torment and suffering.
"Due to the power of residual karma, even after attaining perfect enlightenment, mountain rocks collapsed and injured my toe.
Then the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!"
"What karma did he previously perform?
After [the Buddha] attained perfect enlightenment, a stake of purple *śiṃśapā* wood pierced the Buddha’s foot and wounded it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The Tathāgata himself performed these deeds in the past, and now he himself must experience their results.
This is explained at length, culminating in the verse:
“Even if a hundred eons should pass, The karma one has created does not perish;”
"When causes and conditions meet, the fruit of retribution is received by oneself.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, there was a great city. Within this city, there were two merchant leaders who were highly skilled in trade."
Having secured the ship, they set out toward the ocean's edge in search of treasures; driven by the force of a favorable wind, they reached the island of jewels.
One of them measured the gems as he loaded them, while the other, his greed insatiable, filled the ship without any calculation.
Later, while traveling within the sea, his ship was about to sink because he had failed to take proper precautions; he cried out to his fellow merchant-leader, saying:
"I pray that you, O virtuous one, will rescue me and allow me to board your vessel."
The man carefully measured out jewels according to his capacity and placed them within the ship, taking the drowning man by the hand and causing him to board.
The drowning man thought to himself:
"I have reached this island of jewels together with him; yet everything I gathered will be lost when the ship sinks. How can he possibly take the jewels home?"
"If I bore holes in the ship, the jewels will be scattered and lost.
Having had this thought, he secretly stood to one side and began boring holes in the ship with a staff.
The merchant leader saw him and said:
"O Benevolent One!
Do not do this; not only will our wealth and treasures be lost, but we shall all perish together.
Though he spoke thus, the other harbored malice within, his jealousy burning fiercely, and he ultimately refused the advice, intending to bore through as before.
His companion, the merchant leader, seeing that he would not follow his advice, immediately took a sharp spear and stabbed him to death.
O bhikṣus, what do you think?
Was the one who stabbed and killed the other in those ancient times anyone else? It was none other than this very person.
I am that very person now.
Because of this karma, for many years, hundreds of years, and thousands of years, I fell into hell and underwent all manner of agonizing torments.
"Due to the ripening of residual karma, even after attaining perfect enlightenment, a spear made of purple *śiṃśapā* wood pierced my foot and wounded me.
At that time, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!"
"What karma did he perform previously?
After attaining perfect enlightenment, he entered the village of Śālā to beg for food but obtained nothing, returning with his alms-bowl empty.
The Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus! The Tathāgata himself performed these deeds in the past; as explained at length above, up until the verse: 'The fruit of retribution is received by oneself.'"
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, within the great city of Vārāṇasī, there was a young brahmin (maṇava).
When no Buddha was in the world, there appeared a pratyekabuddha who, out of compassion for the poor and destitute, dwelt in a secluded place; he was the sole field of merit in the world."

At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha named Rataśānta who had appeared in the world; he was staying at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī, in the Abode of the Sages. In the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl, he entered the city to beg for food.
At that time, the young brahmin also went to beg at the house of a city elder, but he returned empty-handed with nothing obtained.
At that moment, a Pratyekabuddha who delights in solitude also came to beg at this same elder’s house.
The young brahmin thought to himself, "I shall observe him for a short while to see what the renunciant obtains."
He immediately followed behind her and stood discreetly to the side of the door.

At that time, the elder’s wife, seeing that the Pratyekabuddha’s body and mind were serene and tranquil, felt pure faith arise within her. She then took various kinds of exquisite food and drink, filled a bowl with them, and went to offer it as alms to the Pratyekabuddha.
Having received this food, as he was about to go out the door, the māṇava said:
"O renunciant, I wish to observe closely the food you have obtained."
However, it is the constant nature of Pratyekabuddhas that,
if they do not observe, they do not know the thoughts of others.
He therefore presented his alms-food so that the man might see it.
Out of jealousy, he gave rise to a mind of hatred and envy, striking the bowl with his hand.
The bowl then fell to the ground, spilling the food and drink; he then stepped upon it with his foot.
The Pratyekabuddha asked:
"O noble one! For what reason do you scatter and ruin this food?"
"If you require it, O Benevolent One, I shall offer it to you.
The māṇava then uttered various harsh and abusive words and stood to one side.
At that time, this Great Being, unable to obtain food, disciplined himself and went to the Deer Park.
"O bhikṣus, what do you think?
Was that young brahmin of long ago someone else?
It was none other than I myself."
Because I harbored a mind of jealousy and caused that Pratyekabuddha to be deprived of food and drink,

by the retribution of this karma, for many years, hundreds of years, thousands of years, and hundreds of thousands of years, I was constantly reborn in the hells, undergoing various torments and sufferings.
"Due to the power of the retribution for residual karma, although he has attained perfect enlightenment, he later entered the village of Śālā to beg for alms and returned with an empty bowl.
At that time, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!"
"What karma did she previously perform?
This courtesan of seductive appearance was instructed by a non-Buddhist brahmin to come and slander the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“O Bhikṣus! The Tathāgata himself performed these karmas in the past... [as extensively explained] ... until the verse says:
‘The fruit of retribution is received by oneself.’”
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, when the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
That Buddha had two younger brothers:
the first was named Vāsiṣṭha, and the second was named Bharadvāja.
Of these, Vāsiṣṭha, through diligent and unremitting cultivation of the Buddha’s instructions, realized the fruit of arhatship.
That Bharadvāja was a master of the Tripitaka; he had mastered its recitation and was a great Dharma teacher.
Later, at another time, there was an elder who conceived deep faith in the Dharma teacher and built a residence for him, fully providing all necessary requisites.
At that time, the Dharma Master requested the Arhat Vāsiṣṭha, wishing for him to come and dwell together with him.
Upon hearing this, the Arhat arrived immediately.

When the elder saw that his body and mind were tranquil and his appearance was exceptionally distinguished, his pure faith increased twofold; he prepared various kinds of fragrant and delicious food and drink as an offering, and presented exquisite garments as gifts.
The younger brother gave rise to jealousy and thought to himself:

"I have been the family preceptor for this elder for a long time; though we have come and gone together repeatedly, he has never bestowed such an upper garment upon me, yet upon merely seeing my elder brother, he has respectfully offered it to him."
Having formed this thought, he immediately sought to find fault with his elder brother.

The elder brother, perceiving that his younger brother’s mind was different, applied his attention and observed him; knowing that his brother was jealous, he took his upper garment and gave it to him.
Although he had obtained the robe, he continued to seek out faults and opportunities for conflict with his elder brother.
Later, on another occasion, when the elder’s daughter was performing needlework in the monastery, the Dharma Master said to her:
"Noble lady!..."
"Can you do this for me? The woman replied,
"Noble One!"
"What do you wish for me to send?
The Dharma Master replied,
"You may put on these robes and return home to attend to your work."
If the householder asks,
"From whom did you obtain this robe?
you should reply:
"Noble one!
Vāsīṣṭha. If he should ask again:
"For what reason did you give it?
He replied,
"It was because of a man's desire that I gave it to a woman."
The woman put on her clothes and returned home; when her family members questioned her, the exchange was exactly as before.
Upon hearing this, the elder conceived impure thoughts toward the Arhat.
"The manner of a great man is to deeply consider even slight disrespect;
therefore, he departed from there.
O bhikṣus, what do you think?"
Was the Dharma master of the past anyone else?
It was none other than myself.

Because I harbored hatred and jealousy and spoke words of slander, due to this karma, I have spent many years, hundreds of years, thousands of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years in the hells, undergoing all manner of agonizing suffering.
"Due to the power of residual karma, even after I have attained perfect enlightenment, the non-Buddhist brahmin will cause the courtesan Mṛgajā to slander me.
At that time, the bhikṣus again addressed him, saying:
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!"
"What karma did he previously perform?
After attaining perfect enlightenment, he was slandered by the young woman Cūḍāpanthaka.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The Tathāgata himself committed these deeds in the past,” as explained in detail above.
“In the distant past, in the great city of Vārāṇasī, there was a brahmin who had mastered the scriptures; five hundred young boys received instruction from him.”
The people living in the vicinity of Vārāṇasī all held him in high esteem, honoring and making offerings to him as if he were a true arhat.
At that time, there was a seer possessing the five supernatural powers who, while traveling through the human world, arrived at Vārāṇasī.
The people within the city, seeing that the rishi’s body and mind were tranquil and his countenance serene and harmonious, all conceived pure faith.
Engaging in meritorious deeds, they all went to the rishi’s dwelling to pay him respectful homage and offerings.
That brahmin was not revered by anyone and received meager offerings; harboring envy toward the rishi, he conceived evil thoughts and told the young students:
"This rishi is deeply possessed by greed."
Each of the young students also said, "It is exactly as our teacher says;
the seer truly harbors desire.
Then, wherever these boys went, they informed their relatives and other elders, brahmins, and so forth:
"Yet that seer harbors deep greed.
Upon hearing this, the people conceived doubts in their hearts;
thinking the noble seer was full of excessive concerns and contemptuous, they abandoned him and departed.
"O bhikṣus! As for that brahmin of long ago, was he anyone else?
It was I myself."
Those five hundred boys are these very five hundred bhikṣus.

Because I spoke words of lust out of envy toward the rishi, by the power of that karma, they fell into the hells for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, where they underwent various sufferings and afflictions.

"By the power of the retribution for residual karma, even after attaining perfect enlightenment, he will come with five hundred bhikṣus to slander me, appearing as a young girl with a beak-shaped face.
The Buddha further addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, in the great city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta who ruled according to the Dharma; the people were numerous, prosperous, joyful, and at peace."
Within this city there was a courtesan named Bhadrā, who supported herself by selling her beauty.
At that time, there was a man named Yaugandharāyaṇa, whose mind was possessed of an evil nature.
The man then sent clothing and necklaces to offer to that courtesan, seeking to enjoy her company.
As Bhadramukhā put on her clothes and was about to go to her lover’s place, she encountered another person at the gate who, holding five hundred gold coins, commanded her:
“Bhadramukhā! [Take this].”
"Come and enjoy yourself with me.
The woman thought to herself:
"If I go now, how can I obtain these five hundred coins?"
"Since we have come together for mutual support, you should not abandon me; it would be fitting for us to return home and enjoy a gathering.
Having thought this, she immediately commanded her handmaid to go and inform her partner:
"I pray that you wait a moment, while I attend to my grooming and adorn my person."
The maidservant went and reported this.
That man, who had many affairs to attend to, took his pleasure with her for a while and then departed.
The woman thought again:
"The time is fast passing; if I were to go there now, would it meet with their approval?
Having thought this, she again addressed her handmaid, saying:
"You may go once more to the place where they seek a mate and report to them:"
"Noble son!
Having finished your ablutions, from which fragrant garden have you come to sport with us?
After the woman had gone and reported this, he then asked:
"Is it being said that the preparations are not yet complete, or that they are already finished?
What kind of talk is this?
The maidservant, feeling resentment as she went back and forth, reported all the private matters in detail to her:
"Clad in robes of benevolence and adorned with garlands, you have dallied with another man, which is why I have uttered these words.
Upon hearing this, his lustful desire was instantly extinguished; instead, he gave rise to a murderous intent and a heart of wrath, replying:
"Come to such-and-such a fragrant garden."
When the maidservant had delivered the message, the courtesan arrived immediately. Her paramour said to her:
"Did you put on my clothes and ornaments to have sexual intercourse with another?"
The courtesan said, "Noble son!
This is my own fault; it is not your transgression."
"Women are prone to many faults and evils; I pray that you, O Benevolent One, will show me forbearance.
Because he harbored anger and a mind intent on harm, he drew his sword and struck off her head.
At that time, a maidservant who was following him saw this and cried out at the top of her voice:
"Alas! You have killed my master!
You have killed my master!"
Upon hearing the sound, the crowd all came running quickly.
At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha named Sukhāvatī who was dwelling in meditative concentration beneath a tree in this grove.
Terrified, the man hastily placed the blood-stained sword before the Pratyekabuddha and fled to one side, entering among the crowd.
A great crowd of people came to look and, seeing the blood-stained knife before the Pratyekabuddha, all said:
"The killer must certainly be this person.
They immediately surrounded him, and with hearts full of malice, each spoke these words:
"Alas! You who have gone forth, you who wear the dharma robes and bear the marks of the great seer’s banner, yet commit such evil deeds!
The Pratyekabuddha replied:
"What have I done? he asked.
The crowd replied, "You were enjoying yourself in union with the courtesan Śīlavatī, and then you killed her with a knife."
The Pratyekabuddha replied, "I harbor tranquility;
how could I permit myself to commit evil?
Although he spoke the truth, they all refused to believe him. They bound him with ropes from behind and sent him to the king's presence to report the matter as it had occurred.
The king did not investigate further, but immediately issued an edict, saying:
"Since this crime has been committed, he should be executed without delay; let a red garland be placed around his neck.
A butcher dressed in blue robes, holding a sharp blade in hand and surrounded by a formidable guard, made a proclamation throughout the city and at all crossroads:
"Furthermore, this renunciant has murdered a virtuous woman; by royal decree, the law must be strictly enforced.
Thus, they took the Pratyekabuddha to that fragrant garden, intending to put him to death.
Having seen this, he thought: "Alas for the life of renunciation!
To hold precepts and cultivate virtue, yet to suffer such innocent injustice—this is my own fault."
"To falsely cause another to go to his death is an act that ought not to be done.
Having thought this, he quickly went to the king's presence and addressed him, saying:
"Great King!..."

"Regarding this innocent person who has been unjustly subjected to these circumstances against an ordained monastic, acting in accordance with the imperial decree and the law—this is my own fault; I pray that Your Majesty will take this into consideration.
Having fully set forth the above matters, I hope for Your Majesty’s gracious clemency and forgiveness."
"O bhikṣus! What do you think?
Was he who was named Yugandhara in times long past someone other than this very person?"
I am that very person.
Because of this karma, for hundreds of thousands of years I have constantly dwelt in hell, undergoing various sufferings and afflictions.
Due to the remaining retribution of this karma, even after I had attained perfect enlightenment, others came to slander me.
Then the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
What karma did he previously perform?"
After attaining perfect enlightenment, he and four hundred and ninety-eight bhikṣus ate horse barley in a frontier city;
Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana received celestial offerings.
The Buddha said,
"O bhikṣus! The Tathāgata himself performed these actions in the past, and thus he himself must experience their results."
Listen attentively!

In the distant past, when the lifespan of human beings was eighty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. Surrounded by eighty thousand bhikṣus, he proceeded toward the royal capital of Bandhumatī.

At that time, there was a brahmin in the city who taught the brahmanical dharma to five hundred youths; he was held in high esteem by the people, who honored and made offerings to him as they would to an arhat, a Buddha, or the Saṃgha.
Upon arriving at the royal capital, that brahmin received no respect, offerings, or assistance from anyone; consequently, he conceived deep envy toward the Buddha and the Saṅgha.

At that time, many bhikṣus—both those still in training and those beyond training—donned their robes and took up their bowls in the morning to enter the city for alms. Having obtained various exquisite, superior, and fragrant foods, they returned with their bowls full.
A brāhmaṇa saw him and asked,
"Alas, bhikṣu! How have you obtained this food?"
"I wish to see it.
The bhikṣu, being straightforward, showed him the food.
He, increasing in jealousy, told his disciples:
"You all should know!
This shaven-headed śramaṇa does not deserve such superior delicacies; he ought to be given only coarse, whole barley.
When those disciples heard these words from their teacher, they each likewise said:
"It is exactly as the Teacher has said; we ought indeed to eat barley.
Within that assembly, there were two young brahmins who, harboring feelings of reverence and faith, spoke these words:
"Inform your preceptor not to say such a thing."
"These śramaṇas should be provided with celestial food, not merely human sustenance;
for what reason did you say, 'It is fitting that we eat barley'? "What do you think, bhikṣus?"
Was that brahmin of long ago anyone else?
It was none other than myself.

Because I harbored a mind of jealousy toward a śrāvaka disciple of that Buddha and uttered harsh and evil words, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, I have constantly subsisted on coarse barley.
Due to the ripening of remaining karma, even after attaining perfect enlightenment, he and these four hundred and ninety-eight bhikṣus still had to eat horse fodder.
As for those two young brahmins, they were none other than Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Then the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
What karma did you perform in the past that resulted in these six years of ascetic practice?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“In the past, the Tathāgata himself performed this karma; the full account is as previously explained.
... up to the verse which says:
"Even if a hundred kalpas were to pass, the karma one has created would not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, one must receive the retribution oneself.
Listen attentively!
In the distant past, in the village of Anupama, there was a potter named Nandipāla, as described at length in the *Rājadhamma-saṃyutta* of the *Madhyamāgama*.
"O bhikṣus! What do you think?
Was that unsurpassed māṇava of long ago someone other than this person?"
"I am that very person.
Because in the past, at the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I said:
'Austere practices have not yet resulted in the attainment of perfect wisdom.'"
"By the power of this karma, I was unable to realize unexcelled perfect enlightenment through six years of ascetic practice.

Had I not, at that time in the presence of that Buddha, felt regret and instead made a vow to seek future perfect enlightenment, I would still not have attained Buddhahood even after practicing all manner of wholesome qualities for three more incalculable great kalpas."
Then the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
What karma did he previously perform?"
"After attaining perfect enlightenment, my body manifested painful illness.
The Buddha said, "O bhikṣus!..."
The Tathāgata, in former times when he was born among other species of beings, performed these very actions himself, as described at length above. You bhikṣus!
In the distant past, there was a village, and within that village there lived a physician.
At that time, there was the son of a householder who, having fallen ill, invited a physician to treat him.
The physician provided a prescription and medicine, and the illness was immediately alleviated; the householder then presented the physician with a small amount of wealth.

Later, on another occasion, the householder fell ill three times; though the physician treated him each time and he recovered, the householder ultimately gave no special gift or reward for his services.
The physician harbored resentment and thought to himself:
"That man has suffered extreme pain on three occasions, yet despite my curing him, he cannot repay my kindness."
"Furthermore, should he fall ill again, you must give him such-and-such medicine so that the feelings within that foolish man are severed.
Later, at another time, the elder’s son was afflicted by a recurrence of his chronic illness, and as before, he invited a physician.
The physician, with malicious intent, administered unsuitable medicine, causing the patient's intestines to break into segments. O bhikṣus!
What do you think?
Was that skilled physician of long ago anyone else?
It was none other than myself.

Because of my evil intent in causing the elder’s son to consume that poisonous medicine, by the power of that karma, I fell into hell for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.
"Due to the remaining karmic retribution, after attaining perfect enlightenment, my body suffered from back pain.
Then the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!"
"What karma did he previously perform such that,
after [the Buddha] attained perfect enlightenment, when others slaughtered the Śākyas, the World-Honored One suffered a headache?
The Buddha said:
“O bhikṣus! The Tathāgata himself performed these actions in the past and must now experience their retribution, as explained at length elsewhere. You, bhikṣus!”
In the distant past, by the banks of the River Flowing Grace (Liuhui), there were five hundred men whose occupation was fishing.
At that time, two large fish suddenly entered the river from the great ocean; the men captured them and held a consultation, saying:
"If we kill these fish, their flesh will soon rot and stink, and no one will be able to carry it all at once. It would be best to bind them with ropes."
"If there are those who wish to buy, we shall continue to cut and weigh them for sale so that they remain fresh and high quality.
Having deliberated thus, they bound the meat with rope; whenever someone came to buy, they would cut off a portion and hand it over.
At the time of the slaughter, the fish suffered great agony; they writhed about as blood flowed, turning the river water crimson.
At that moment, there was a young boy who, seeing the color of the river water, felt joy and laughter in his heart, finding it a source of pleasure.
"O bhikṣus! What do you think?
Was that fisherman’s young son anyone else?"
I am that very person.
Because my mind was filled with delight at the time I was killing fish in the past,
due to that karma, I have suffered from headaches for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years.
"Due to the remaining karmic retribution, even after attaining perfect enlightenment, my head was in agony at the time I executed the Śākyas.
Then the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!"
"What karma did he previously perform that,
even after attaining perfect enlightenment, he still suffered from the wind-pain of back ailment?
The Buddha said:

“O Bhikṣus! Just as the Tathāgata, having been born in various states of existence in the past, performed these karmic actions and now experiences their results himself, as has been explained at length elsewhere.
You, O Bhikṣus!”
In the distant past, there was a young man who traveled through various kingdoms and arrived at a royal capital.
That king also possessed a great champion whose strength was without rival.
The two men, knowing one another, wished to wager their garments and so immediately began to wrestle.
According to the usual custom of such athletes, they grasped each other's hands, whereby they could immediately discern who was stronger and who was weaker.
Once the outsider had grasped the hand of the king’s champion, he realized that the local wrestler could not prevail.
The king’s champion then addressed the outsider:
"You should know this: my lineage resides here, having lived long in the royal capital and been renowned for generations."
"You know that I am capable and virtuous; do not strike me down, lest my clan reproach you.
I have a beautiful daughter whom I shall give to you as a wife.
Hearing these words, he remained silent and yielded his strength. This occurred three times, yet he still did not give him his daughter, and a feeling of unbearable resentment arose within him.
Upon the fourth attempt, while wrestling, he used a ruse to lift him high and, with the force of his wrath, threw him to the ground; the king’s wrestler’s spine was broken, and he died.
"O bhikṣus! What do you think?
Was that outsider wrestler of long ago, who broke the spine of the king’s wrestler and caused him to die, anyone else?"
I am that very person.
Due to this evil karma, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, I fell into hell and underwent various bitter retributions.
Because of the remaining karmic retribution, even after attaining perfect enlightenment, I still suffered from back pain.
For this reason, I have always proclaimed:
black karma brings black retribution; white karma brings white retribution; and mixed karma brings mixed retribution.
You should abandon black and mixed karma, and constantly cultivate white karma; thus you should train yourselves.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished recounting his past karmic retributions at Lake Anavatapta together with five hundred arhats, he immediately vanished and appeared at his dwelling place in the East of Śrāvastī, in the Mṛgāramātṛparka.
Upon hearing that the Buddha had arrived, he quickly went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet;
the Buddha then preached the sublime Dharma to him, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him, after which he remained silent.
Then Mṛgāramātṛ rose from her seat, bared her right shoulder, joined her palms toward the Buddha,
and said: "World-Honored One,
I pray that out of your compassion you will accept my humble offering tomorrow at my home, together with the assembly of five hundred noble ones."
The Buddha remained silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted [the invitation], he took his leave and returned home. He prepared various kinds of exquisite and superior fragrant foods and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha. [The messenger] delivered the message at length until it was known that the assembly was satiated; then, having withdrawn the bowl and finished washing it, he took a low seat for the sake of hearing the Dharma and sat down facing the Buddha.
The Buddha taught her the subtle and wondrous Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening her. She then rose from her seat and went to her residence.
Having taken her seat, she addressed the bhikṣus:
"The Mother of Migāra forgot to request the Buddha and the Saṃgha to accept an offering at her home; she did not request the World-Honored One to recite the verses on giving."
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll 18.
